14 fall ill after dining at Eaton HK hotel restaurant
Preliminary investigations revealed that all five clusters are epidemiologically linked, Centre for Health Protection says
Hong Kong health authorities have detected seven additional suspected food poisoning cases linked to a hotel restaurant in Yau Ma Tei, raising the total number of affected diners to 14.
The Centre for Health Protection said on Saturday it had identified three additional food poisoning clusters involving The Astor restaurant at Eaton HK, after initially announcing two clusters on September 3.
“The centre’s preliminary investigations revealed that all five clusters are epidemiologically linked,” it said, adding that 14 people had been affected.
It said that officers from the centre and the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department jointly conducted an on-site investigation and required management to implement control measures.
“All affected people had patronised the buffet there before the operation,” it said.
The latest clusters involve one man and five women who consumed buffet meals at the restaurant between August 29 and 31. Between 16 and 40 hours later, all six developed symptoms including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and fever.

Third worker rescued from Nepal tunnel, woman found alive in rubble 10 days after devastating floods
Two people were rescued in separate operations in Nepal, 10 days after the devastating floods hit the country, officials said Saturday.
A man was rescued from a hydropower tunnel, according to a social media post by the country's prime minister's office, bringing the total to three workers pulled alive from the Trishuli hydropower project. Two Nepalese workers were rescued from a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant on Friday.
Nepal's army said a joint rescue team of Nepalese military personnel and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from 738-foot tunnel and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Images showed him being evacuated by helicopter, with an army medic checking on him during the flight.
A photo released by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed two rescuers carrying the man out of the tunnel.
Rescue efforts have increasingly focused on 12 hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said. Specialized rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects, hoping to find survivors.
In flood-hit Nuwakot town, a woman was rescued alive from a house, Nepal's army spokesperson said Saturday. Officials said she was being airlifted to Kathmandu.
Images released by Nepal's army showed rescuers finding the woman covered in mud. They gave her bottled water before pulling her to safety, wrapped in a gray blanket.
At least 1,300 people were killed in the Aug. 26 floods, which were likely caused by a glacier collapse, and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal's disaster management agency.

Line warns Taiwan users to add phone numbers to avoid account deletion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:20:29 UTC
18:20:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Some Line users risk losing access to their accounts, purchases, stickers, coins, and chat histories at the end of the year unless they add a phone number.
The rule applies to accounts linked only to Facebook that do not have a phone number set, with deletion scheduled after 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 31, per TVBS.
Users can check their status in the Line app by opening “Home,” tapping “Settings,” selecting “My Account,” and looking at the “Phone Number” field. A blank field means no number has been linked, and the setup can be completed entirely inside the app without using a webpage, per Line’s notice.
The company warned that phone numbers cannot be shared across Line accounts, while moving a number to another account can cause the original account to stop working.
Similar restrictions apply to email addresses and Apple and Google accounts. Reusing those credentials on a new Line account will remove their links from the original account and may render that account invalid, according to the notice.
Accounts should have an email address and password set, while at least one Apple or Google account should be connected. Both Apple and Google accounts can be added.
The phone-number requirement is intended to reduce dummy accounts and fraud risks and make the service safer. Users are also encouraged to help older relatives or friends who are less familiar with smartphone settings check their accounts.

Taiwan prepares testing facility for car imports from US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:19:53 UTC
18:19:53 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ministry of Transportation is budgeting NT$400 million (US$12.63 million) for next year to prepare for the liberalization of car imports from the US, reports said Friday.
As a result of the Taiwan-US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed in February, Taiwan will have to remove its import limits on cars from the US. With safety test standards differing from country to country, Taiwan has to set up a new post-market surveillance system including a safety test lab, per CNA.
The import quotas will be removed for cars conforming to the US Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and to US emission regulations, the report said.
To improve its testing capacity, the ministry is proposing the NT$400 million budget, which includes the constructions of a test lab and other buildings, equipment, and machinery. The center will also require an environmental impact review, an evaluation of its power needs, and fire safety permits.
The ministry said it had discussed the required measures and legal amendments with associations representing Taiwan’s car industry, CNA reported. The changes will be designed to guarantee the safety of consumers, the ministry said, adding its proposals still required approval by the Cabinet.

Hualien Physical Education High School eyes third dragon boat world title
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:19:52 UTC
18:19:52 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Hualien Physical Education High School captured its second gold medal at the 15th International Dragon Boat Federation Club Crew World Championships on Friday, winning the Premier Open 10-person small boat 200-meter final in 46.56 seconds at Liyu Lake in Hualien County.
The crew, which had topped the preliminary round in 46.54, held off Germany by 0.84 seconds in a rain-affected session that tested both technique and nerve on the choppy waters, Liberty Times reported. Team captain Lin Sheng-ju (林聖儒), a 2018 Asian Games dragon boat gold medalist, reportedly said the squad now hopes to challenge for a third title in the 2,000-meter race before the championships end Sunday.
The team’s first gold came on Wednesday in the Premier Open 10-person small boat 500 m. It finished in 2 minutes, 5.03 seconds to give the nation its first medal of the meet.
The Aug. 29–Sept. 6 event marks the first time the International Dragon Boat Federation’s (IDBF) flagship club world championship has been held in Taiwan, drawing teams from 21 countries to Hualien County.
Races feature 20-person standard boats and 10-person small boats over 200-m, 500-m and 2,000-m formats. There are open, women’s, mixed, and age-group divisions, plus inclusive categories such as Paralympic and cancer survivor crews.
Dragon boat racing is a team paddling sport in which crews of 10 to 20 athletes propel long, narrow boats decorated with dragon heads and tails. A drummer at the bow sets the pace with a drumbeat while a steersperson at the stern controls direction.
The sport traces its roots to Chinese rituals honoring the poet Qu Yuan, who is said to have drowned himself in Hunan Province’s Miluo River more than 2,000 years ago. According to legend, villagers raced out in boats to save him or retrieve his body, beating drums and splashing paddles to scare away fish.
This tradition evolved into the modern-day Dragon Boat Festival held on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month in Taiwan, which falls in May or June.
Modern competitive dragon boating emerged in the late 20th century as Hong Kong and other Asian cities standardized boat specifications and race formats, leading to the formation of the IDBF in 1991.

US ambassador visits Palestinian town amid rise in West Bank settler violence

US ambassador visits Palestinian town amid rise in West Bank settler violence
TURMUS AYYA, Ramallah, Sept 5 - U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee met on Saturday with Palestinians, including the families of U.S. citizens killed by Israeli settlers, in a Palestinian town in the occupied West Bank that has been the target of repeated settler attacks.
Settler violence in the West Bank has risen sharply since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition government, the most right-wing in Israel's history, took office in late 2022.
Several settlements have been established around Turmus Ayya, the Palestinian town near Ramallah that Huckabee was visiting on Saturday. Its residents say that harassment by militant Israeli settlers is common and that they are unable to stop them from entering the town and damaging their homes.
"We have many issues that we will address," Nawwaf Zaghoul, the town's mayor, told reporters ahead of the meeting, describing what he said were constant attacks by settlers.
He said that the town's residents would be asking the ambassador to help secure their safety and security. About 80% of the town's roughly 3,000 residents were Palestinian Americans, he said.
Huckabee, a Baptist minister and longtime supporter of Israeli settlements, has called for violent settlers to be prosecuted, while saying he believes their actions represent a minority of the wider settler community, which numbers around 750,000. Israeli settlers accused of carrying out attacks in the West Bank targeting Palestinians are rarely prosecuted.
"We are hoping that (the ambassador) will do something for us regarding these lawless settlers," Turmus Ayya resident Sameer Hazama said ahead of the meeting with the ambassador.
Huckabee visited Taybeh, one of the only Christian villages remaining in the West Bank, in June 2025 after a church there was vandalised. Huckabee said at the time that the desecration of a place of worship was an act of terror and a crime.
Netanyahu's government has also overseen an expansion of settlements across the West Bank, further entrenching Israeli control over territory that Palestinians seek for a future state.
Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law, with the United Nations and most countries deeming the territory to be occupied. Israel's government says that the land is disputed, not occupied.
Huckabee refers to the West Bank by its biblical name, Judea and Samaria, a term used by the Israeli government but not adopted by the U.S. government. He has visited Shiloh, a settlement near Turmus Ayya, at least twice since 2025. REUTERS

Sweden confirms 458 Britons deported or forcibly removed since Brexit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:16:01 UTC
18:16:01 KST

Sweden has confirmed 458 British citizens have been deported or forcibly removed by police since Brexit.
It is the first time the scale of the deportations of citizens who failed to secure residency in Sweden post-Brexit has been made public and comes amid mounting criticism of a cruel and hardline approach to Britons who had chosen to make the country their home before Brexit.
Some have been told to go after more than 25 years in the country and even vulnerable elderly people with dementia have been affected. One man was deported even though he had lived in the country since he was 10 years old.
Susanna Fonsell, a unit manager and legal expert at the Swedish Migration Agency, told Sverige Radio: “A rejected application does not necessarily result in deportation… and according to the agency statistics, the agency’s rejections of an application for resident status has been accomplished by a deportation decision in only approximately 400 cases,” she told Sweden Radio.
The Migrationsverket, the Swedish government agency responsible for migration, confirmed to the Guardian that 458 British citizens had been deported since Brexit. “According to the agency’s statistics, the Swedish Migration Agency’s rejection of an application for residence status has been accompanied by a deportation decision in only 458 cases,” a spokesperson said.
David Milstead, who heads up the 9,000-strong activist group Brits in Sweden, said it was important for Sweden to release full and transparent figures in relation to removals and deportations and their circumstances.
“We need to understand exactly what the 458 represents. Does it capture people who gave up and left when they realised their withdrawal agreement application was unlikely to succeed? Does it include people who were refused withdrawal agreement status, subsequently obtained a permit under national law and were only later ordered to leave?
“It certainly does not capture people who are currently managing to remain in Sweden on temporary permits, with little certainty about their long-term future.”
He said the figures illustrated a “broader problem” in that the data was issued piecemeal and sometimes in an opaque manner. “We still do not have basic published figures showing how many people submitted a missed-deadline application and the fraction of these which succeeded,” he said.
The last available data shows that there were 14,233 applications for post Brexit residency, which included family members joining British citizens after the deadline by 2024. Of those, just under 4,000 were rejected, a refusal rate three times higher than any other member state and considerably higher than the EU average of between 3% and 4%, according to Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) analysis.
Deportations are still happening. This week, the Swedish wife of a former business director from Cambridge told how her husband was detained in Stockholm on Tuesday ahead of a forced removal.
She said they had been fighting to overturn the decision by the migration authorities for five years and felt that they had been “hunted”.
Earlier this week, the Guardian revealed a 34-year-old British man, John Sellers, who had lived in Sweden since he was 10, had been deported, separating him from his wife, Caroline, in Gothenburg, who said people needed to know how Brexit had “crushed families”.
Another woman, 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomas, has been told to remove herself from the country before next Wednesday. Friends are trying to get an injunction and have appealed to the European Commission for help.
If she fails to comply, not only will she face a forced deportation, but the court of appeal has told her she could face a “re-entry ban” and be “registered on a watchlist” preventing potential entry into a Schengen country, which includes Sweden “as long as the re-entry ban remains in effect”.
The Swedish Migration Agency told the Guardian it had “no indication that Sweden has in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other member states. The Swedish Migration Agency has applied applicable law, and there has been an opportunity to appeal rejection decisions.”
Late applications for post-Brexit residency are allowed under the Brexit withdrawal agreement, both in the EU and the UK, but applicants have to show “reasonable grounds” for missing the deadline.
The FCDO has said that “in practice” late applicants in Sweden “are not likely to have their reasonable grounds accepted”.
Earlier this week, Sweden’s migration minister, Johan Forssell, said his government had followed the rules but that it was willing to look into the matter. “The relationship with the UK is very important to Sweden and the government will continue to safeguard the correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. As part of this, the government is investigating whether further measures can be taken to facilitate the process in the future,” he said.
A spokesperson for the FCDO said: “We continue to raise this with the Swedish authorities and welcome their statement that they will look at this issue. We are ready to support them in doing so.”
Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for Sweden’s opposition Centre party, said the government needed to go much further. He pledged to bring in new laws if his party won power at the next general election to allow British to reapply for post-Brexit residence, saying “a touch of humanity” was needed.

UK Halts Large Military Exercises as Funding Shortfalls Hit British Armed Forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:11:10 UTC
18:11:10 KST

- Category
- World
UK Halts Large Military Exercises as Funding Shortfalls Hit British Armed Forces
The British Armed Forces have suspended military exercises involving 90 or more personnel due to budget constraints at the Ministry of Defense, according to a report by The Sun.
Units were instructed to stop collective training with immediate effect unless they are getting ready for deployment on active operations, leaving many troops with little to do.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the new directives, service members will continue to train in small squads to maintain basic skills, including vehicle operation, physical fitness, weapons handling, and drone usage.
However, company-level exercises, which usually involve 90 to 120 soldiers, as well as battle group training involving several hundred troops, have been significantly reduced.
The cutbacks affect major events, including a six-week exercise with tanks and attack helicopters scheduled to begin next week in Wales. Regular preparation will only continue for personnel preparing to deploy abroad or take up operational duty within the UK.
The Royal Navy and Royal Air Force have also been instructed to scale back training activities to save funds, though the impact on their operations is expected to be less severe.
According to The Sun, the cuts stem from a shortage of funds for current operating expenses this year. Although the Defense Investment Plan allocates an extra 2 billion pounds for training, those funds will not become available until 2027.
The Ministry of Defense acknowledged that the military must “determine priorities,” while noting that command staff exercises will continue so top leadership can practice managing large-scale operations.
The Chief of the Defense Staff, Rich Knighton, previously warned in late June 2026 that the UK Armed Forces were facing a financial deficit that could force military leaders to scale back training and operational activities.
“If you look back 20 years, the ratio between expenditure on current needs and capital expenditure was roughly 80/20. Today, it stands at roughly 60/40 — 60% for current activities and resources, and 40% for capital expenditure. Under current forecasts, by 2030 this ratio will be 50/50,” Knighton stated at the time.
One of the main reasons for this funding imbalance is the UK's large and costly rearmament programs.
These initiatives include building Dreadnought-class nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines, developing a sixth-generation fighter jet under the GCAP program, constructing Type 26 frigates, and managing the troubled Ajax armored vehicle program.
Previously, the British Ministry of Defense shaped its new strategy around Ukraine's playbook of low-cost systems defeating high-value targets, with innovation cycles measured in weeks rather than years.
The plan redirected resources away from up to eight traditional warships, including Type 83 guided missile destroyers and Type 32 frigates, and instead committed approximately $6.7 billion to a broad drone transformation. Britain allocated funds to establish Europe's largest drone testing center alongside a dedicated task force, aiming to continuously scale up production and adapt to changing battlefield technologies.

Following meetings in the Russian capital, he concluded that his warnings were delivered, but they failed to break the stalemate. The visit was interpreted as "an attempt to convince Putin to stop the war, and Putin read this as weakness."
The primary goal of the visit was to communicate to the Kremlin that if it expects a complete handover of the Donbas region by Ukraine, "this simply won't happen," while also stressing that continuing Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine is not in Moscow's interests.
According to sources cited by The Washington Post, the Trump administration specifically chose FSB Director Alexander Bortnikov, an influential member of Putin's inner circle who previously participated in prisoner exchanges, as the main contact for these talks.
However, Ratcliffe's perspective differed sharply from Putin's view of the situation. Following the CIA director's visit, Russia intensified strikes on Kyiv, killing at least 9 people over 4 days and damaging the main building of the Security Service of Ukraine for the first time.
A source close to the Russian diplomatic corps stated that the strikes were intended as a signal to Washington that "Russia is continuing its offensive operation and sees no reason to shift its stance to a more flexible one."
Despite growing domestic economic problems—including a budget deficit reaching 6.5 trillion rubles ($78.5 billion) over 7 months and the loss of a third of its gasoline production due to strikes on oil refineries—the Kremlin maintains its strategy. It believes that continuing the action for several more months poses an acceptable burden for Russia, but a severe issue for Ukraine.
A business executive source explained that "Putin hopes time is on his side because, despite problems with fuel and growth, the population of Russia is not as ready to protest as the Ukrainian population."
US President Donald Trump’s special representatives, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, will travel to Moscow first for discussions before arriving in Kyiv on Sunday, September 6.
The US envoys will make their first trip to the Ukrainian capital to address Russia’s full-scale invasion. Their arrival in Kyiv will follow scheduled talks with Russian officials in Moscow on Saturday, September 5.

Presidential office director laid off 13 staff over two years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:10:00 UTC
18:10:00 KST

Presidential office director laid off 13 staff over two years
Office of the President Director Krista Zibo has laid off 13 staff members over the past two years, with two protocol advisers departing this Friday — barely a month before the new president takes office. Zibo herself recently secured a permanent contract.
Nearly two years ago, at President Alar Karis' proposal, Krista Zibo — formerly with the Government Office — became director of the Office of the President.
"Her previous professional path has given her balance and strong experience in leading different teams, as well as a clear understanding of topics important to Estonia, which I saw confirmed when we worked together at the National Audit Office," Karis said at the time.
Two employees — advisers in the office's protocol field, Pille Heinsoo and Sigrid Herodes — had their last working day this Friday. This is only about a month before the new president, Ülle Madise, takes office.
Layoffs justified by a structural change
"A structural change was what they told us," Herodes said sadly, adding that she herself would also like to know what the exact reason for the layoff is. She said that tasks were redistributed in the office, meaning the work done by Herodes and Heinsoo will not remain undone.
Herodes noted that it remained unclear to her what will happen to her position. "In my opinion, it is disappearing now," she said. When asked whether 13 layoffs in two years is a lot, Herodes answered yes.
Zibo said in an emailed comment that the office is changing its work organization according to the president's needs.
"In recent years, changes have been made both in support functions and in the circle of advisers to the head of state — tasks have been redistributed, work roles changed and responsibilities consolidated," Zibo noted. She added that the personnel changes made are part of this process and stem from changes in work tasks and the need to use the office's limited resources more efficiently.
Layoff patterns also exist from earlier
One of the best‑known people Zibo had laid off from the presidential office was then‑presidential adviser Toomas Sildam. This happened in February 2025, only about five months after Zibo became director. "The domestic policy adviser's duties will be taken over by the domestic policy department," the office announced at the time.
Layoff issues also followed Zibo at the Government Office, where she worked before becoming director of the Presidential Office. In 2019, ERR wrote that the Government Office laid off protocol chief Ülle‑Marika Põldma, who had worked in that position for more than ten years. At the time, Zibo, who worked as head of support services at the Government Office, also commented that Põldma was laid off due to work reorganization.
Allegedly, the reason for the layoff was poor cooperation, but the Government Office did not officially confirm this. Similar to the current situation in the Office of the President, the Government Office did not hire a new person as protocol chief at that time.
The director received a €10,500 bonus
The staff is not the only thing changing in the office before the new president's term begins. For nearly two years, Zibo held the director's position under a fixed‑term contract (a fixed‑term transfer from the Government Office). As of 1 July this year, Zibo is permanently on staff.
In a letter forwarded by presidential office's spokesperson, it was explained that the task of the office director is to ensure the continuity of the institution's work, including during a presidential transition. If the new president wishes to see someone else as director of the office, a new person can be hired in place of Zibo.
When asked why the contract was changed only now — a few months before Karis's term ends — the office replied that Zibo must ensure stable leadership and daily work of the office until the end of Karis's term and during the presidential transition. Whether this could not have been done with a fixed‑term transfer contract was not clarified in the response.
"President Alar Karis and his team will carry out their duties fully until the end of the term," the letter stated. It added that the incoming president will in turn have the opportunity to shape their team of advisers.
President Karis appears clearly satisfied with the director's work. On 29 January this year, Alar Karis issued an order setting Krista Zibo's new base salary at €6,010 per month starting 1 January 2026. Previously her salary was €5,500. When she took office on 2 September 2024, it was €5,000.
On 24 November 2025, Alar Karis decided to pay Zibo a €10,500 bonus for good service‑related achievements.

Ukraine war: how escalating attacks are upending lives in Kyiv
Russia is now using more jet-powered drones, which are faster and harder for Ukraine to intercept than propeller-powered models
Commuters stranded; children rushed underground in the middle of the school day; festivals cancelled; walks punctuated by booming air defences. Near-constant drone attacks are the stark new reality in Kyiv, and daily life is likely to get harder.
Kyiv has survived many traumas since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Despite the initial shock of war and the advent of attack drones and ballistic missiles, residents adapted and managed to impose a semblance of normality.
But as a fifth full winter of war approaches, that is becoming harder to maintain.
Over the summer, Moscow began sending swarms of high-speed, jet-propelled drones that are more destructive and harder to shoot down than older propeller-powered models.
For the last 10 days, air attacks have been around-the-clock rather than mainly at night, puncturing Ukrainians’ sense that their country’s own long-range drone campaign against Russia was swinging the war back in their favour.

UN nuclear agency members draft resolution reporting Iran

Under those obligations, part of the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, Iran is legally bound to declare all nuclear material and activities and allow inspectors from the Vienna-based International Atomic Energy Agency to verify that none of it is being diverted from peaceful uses.
The diplomatic move has been under consideration since June 2025, when the IAEA board found Iran officially in noncompliance with its nonproliferation obligations for the first time in 20 years — one day before the US and Israel launched attacks against Iran’s nuclear sites.
A possible referral of Iran to the UN Security Council shifts responsibility to a higher authority that can enact further legally binding measures, including sanctions or asset freezes.

‘What would it take for US to hold Israel accountable?’: Two years since Aysenur Ezgi Eygi’s murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:05:39 UTC
18:05:39 KST

September 6 marks two years since Aysenur Ezgi Eygi, a 26-year-old Turkish-American activist, was shot in the head by an Israeli sniper while observing a peaceful protest against illegal settlement expansion in Beita in the occupied West Bank.
Since then, her family has buried her in Aydin, Türkiye, found ways to keep her memory alive, and spoken to dozens of lawmakers in an effort to hold those responsible to account.
They are still calling for the same thing: an independent investigation into her killing, the identification of the soldier who shot her, and accountability for what happened.
The Israeli military has acknowledged that one of its soldiers fired in the area where Eygi was standing. But its preliminary investigation concluded that she was "highly likely" hit "indirectly and unintentionally" while troops were responding to a "violent riot."
No soldier has been charged.
For Eygi's family, that explanation has never amounted to accountability. Two years later, her husband Hamid Ali says the frustration has only deepened.
“We still don't have any results of any investigation, either from the Israeli government or otherwise,” Ali tells TRT World.
“The US government has not been open to investigating, and hasn't communicated with us about any updates on her case or any willingness to investigate it or hold Israel accountable for killing one of its own citizens,” he explains.
Yet Ali says the past year has brought something else too: a sense that Eygi has not been forgotten.
“We've seen so much support from our community in Seattle and across the US, and it's really meaningful to see that, still, even after two years,” he says.
Washington has yet to investigate
Washington's position has remained largely unchanged across administrations.
Then-US President Joe Biden described Eygi's death as a "tragic error".
In December 2024, then-Secretary of State Antony Blinken told the family that Washington was waiting for Israel to complete its investigation.
That position hasn’t changed under the Trump administration, either.
Brad Parker of the Centre for Constitutional Rights, part of the family's legal team, says no US federal agency, including the Department of Justice or the FBI, has opened an investigation into Eygi's killing, despite their jurisdiction to investigate the killing of an American citizen abroad.
In the weeks after her death, more than 100 members of Congress signed letters calling for a US investigation. The family and its supporters have continued to press lawmakers for action, but Washington has yet to open the investigation they have sought.
With no federal investigation forthcoming, the family has also turned to lawmakers in Eygi's home state.
“We were pushing for a piece of legislation, a joint memorial, that outlined how Aysenur was killed and the need for accountability and investigation,” Ali says.
The measure would formally ask the federal government and President Trump to investigate Eygi’s killing, but the family says they have yet to receive a response or see any progress on that front.
“We've seen the genocide of children, men, and women in Gaza. We've seen brutal killings by settlers in the occupied West Bank, with the aid of the military. We've seen my wife shot in the head, unprovoked and unjustified,” Ali says.
“It's hard to understand what exactly it would take for this government to wake up and hold the Israeli government accountable, not only for killing innocent men, women, and children, but for killing its own citizens, without any pushback or change in the relationship,” he adds.
Türkiye pushes the case forward
While Washington has declined to open its own investigation, Türkiye has pursued the case through its own legal channels.
Ankara's chief prosecutor opened a criminal investigation within days of Eygi's killing, while then-Justice Minister Yilmaz Tunc said Türkiye had enough evidence, including video footage, to pursue international arrest warrants and an Interpol Red Notice for the Israeli personnel involved.
The case has since become part of Türkiye's broader legal efforts against Israeli officials.
Most recently, Ankara sought a Red Notice for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as part of the domestic case before Istanbul's 11th Heavy Penal Court linked to the interception of the Global Sumud Flotilla.
Türkiye has also sought to bring Eygi's killing into the ICC's Gaza-related proceedings and joined South Africa's genocide case against Israel at the ICJ.
Those efforts have given the family another avenue for accountability, even though they have yet to result in criminal charges against the soldier who shot Eygi.
A case that reaches beyond Eygi
The family has also continued to push for action closer to home, in Washington State.
State lawmakers introduced companion joint memorials, Senate Joint Memorial 8014 and House Joint Memorial 4010, calling on the federal government to investigate her killing independently. The measures received hearings in the state's Law and Justice Committee earlier this year.
The family has worked with the For Aysenur campaign, CAIR-WA and the Rachel Corrie Foundation, drawing a connection between Eygi and Rachel Corrie, another activist from Washington killed by the Israeli military in Gaza in 2003.
Corrie's family spent years seeking accountability but did not see criminal charges brought against the Israeli personnel involved.
“On one hand, it's beautiful that this tragedy connected our two families. I consider the Corries close friends of ours. That's a beautiful thing,” Ali says.
“But at the same time, I wish we'd never had a reason to meet them this way. It's really sad that all of their advocacy over the last two decades hasn't changed anything.”
According to Ali, Aysenur felt the same way Rachel Corrie did.
“She was killed the same way Rachel was killed. And there's been no justice for either of them, still,” Ali says.
“As for my grief, the Corries actually helped us understand this early on. They told us it never gets easier, even after twenty years. You just get stronger and better at carrying the pain,” he adds.
Two years after Eygi was killed, Ali will mark the anniversary by travelling to Aydin’s Didim to visit her grave.
Ali says the family’s demand remains the same: justice.
“Justice means holding the soldier responsible for killing Aysenur, the person who pulled the trigger, the person who gave the order, the person who wrote the policy… all the way up the chain, to the high-ranking officials who support this kind of action or fail to take responsibility for it,” Ali says.
And for Ali, accountability for Eygi is only one part of what justice means.
“True justice includes accountability for every single Palestinian who's been killed the same way, or worse. There are thousands of stories in Palestine we'll never know, too many in the occupied West Bank and in Gaza for us to ever know them all.”
Ultimately, there can be no true justice until Palestine is liberated, he adds.

amsterdam fashion week 2026 turns the city into a stage for design and performance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:01:58 UTC
18:01:58 KST

Amsterdam Fashion Week returned from September 1 to 5, 2026, spreading more than 40 shows, presentations, exhibitions, talks and workshops across the Dutch capital. Rather than concentrating the programme around a single venue, this year’s edition continued to treat Amsterdam itself as part of the fashion week, moving between museums, historic buildings, shops and unexpected everyday settings. The programme brought emerging designers together with established names while entering the second phase of AFW’s partnership with Copenhagen Fashion Week, which introduces its Sustainability Requirements framework into the selection process ahead of a full rollout in September 2027.
The week began by bringing fashion into dialogue with material and spatial design. Amsterdam Fashion Week’s opening dinner gathered 130 guests inside a monumental canal house on Kloveniersburgwal, where designer Sabine Marcelis collaborated with natural-stone company SolidNature on the setting. Marcelis designed bespoke stone candleholders that ran along communal tables, framed by translucent curtains and soft lighting, turning the dinner itself into a carefully composed installation. The event introduced an edition in which the boundaries between fashion, objects, interiors and experience remained deliberately porous.
ULKUHANBATUHAN | image by Olivia Witmond
FASHION, MEMORY AND EVERYDAY LIFE
That looseness also appeared in designers looking directly at Dutch identity. At the monumental Molen van West, Ruben Jurriën presented Maak Nederland weer Gezellig!, mixing embroidery, comic drawings, oversized denim, reinterpretations of the Dutch clog and the recurring figure of Toetie, a childhood plush toy turned superhero. The collection approached national symbols through affection and humour rather than nostalgia, while asking what ideas such as kindness, familiarity and gezelligheid might mean today. Elsewhere, The New Originals transformed Nxt Museum into something closer to a gathering than a runway for Home Is Where the Heart Is. Created with filmmaker Ebeneza Blanche, the presentation combined streetwear, live music, performance and film while connecting the Amsterdam platform’s community with stories of migration, family and belonging.
Other presentations used clothing to explore less tangible states of presence. Under his label Jinchoe, Youngjin Choe returned to the Rijksmuseum passage after winning Lichting in 2025, presenting Shadow Stepping as an investigation into destruction and reconstruction. Dense black outerwear, exaggerated layers, displaced panels and obstructed faces gradually shifted towards earthy colours and white, giving physical form to the idea of carrying darkness rather than erasing it. DEFIJTER&VANBRUGGEN, meanwhile, looked back to the nineteenth-century flâneur and flâneuse for De Belofte van Buiten. Exaggerated tailoring and sculptural silhouettes inhabited a set filled with furniture, street lamps and domestic objects, where models eventually sat, read and watched the audience, turning physical presence itself into part of the performance.
Ruben Jurriën | image by Resa Steenvoorden
WHEN THE SUPERMARKET BECOMES A RUNWAY
Perhaps the clearest example of AFW26’s interest in collapsing fashion into ordinary life came from Camiel Fortgens, who staged his SS27 show inside an Albert Heijn supermarket at Stadionplein after opening hours. Models pushed shopping trolleys and carried baskets through aisles of cheese, frozen food and soft drinks while employees continued stacking shelves. Against this deliberately mundane backdrop, Fortgens’ familiar vocabulary of cotton shirts, denim, bombers and layered outerwear revealed exposed seams, raw hems, reversed construction and apparently accidental combinations. The intervention was almost invisible: rather than transforming the supermarket into a fantasy, the clothes absorbed the gestures, repetitions and small imperfections of everyday use.
The runway became more overtly symbolic for ULKUHANBATUHAN, whose Mens, erger je niet transformed the familiar Dutch board game into a system of uneven rules. Designers Ülkühan Akgül and Batuhan Demir treated models as pieces moving across an imaginary board, using distorted proportions, sculptural hats, upcycled escalator brushes, wooden structures and garments covered with bells to address patience, conformity and unequal starting positions. Across AFW26, such experiments suggested that the most interesting runway might no longer look like a runway at all. From a supermarket aisle to a windmill, museum or domestic interior, Amsterdam Fashion Week used the city as a testing ground for how fashion can communicate through space, performance, material and collective experience, as much as through clothes themselves.

The New Originals | image by Lois van der Wildt

‘Sinn Féin traitors!’: how far-right rhetoric derailed party’s path to power in Ireland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:00:32 UTC
18:00:32 KST

For Siobhán Fenton, the dream of Sinn Féin winning power and leading a progressive leftwing government evaporated the day she was canvassing in Dublin and felt a cold, sharp sting on her neck.
She was in the passageway of a block of flats in the inner city, knocking on doors, and looked around for the source. Fenton, a media adviser to the party leader, Mary Lou McDonald, felt another sting on her shoulder, then another on her forearm.
They were coins, thrown from a balcony above, where a man’s voice was shouting. “Sinn Féin traitors!” he roared. “Mary Lou Mohammad! Ireland is full!”
It was May 2024, and instead of steaming towards victory in local and European elections – widely deemed a foregone conclusion, to be followed by a historic triumph in a general election – the party was experiencing a backlash fuelled by anti-immigrant sentiment in what was usually a bastion of working-class support.
The coins left Fenton with gashes and bruises that augured an electoral hammering.
“By the time the party realised how bad things had gotten it was almost too late,” she said. “The far right had infiltrated lots of Sinn Féin strongholds and we hadn’t picked up on it.”
In a rupture to the party’s reputation for secrecy and discipline, Fenton has written a rare insider’s account, titled Ourselves Alone: Sinn Féin Behind Closed Doors.
It lifts the lid on a debacle that ambushed the party on the path to power. Instead of winning a general election and turbo-charging the campaign for Irish unification by ratcheting up pressure for a referendum, the party stumbled and today remains in opposition.
It is a cautionary tale for progressive movements across Europe and elsewhere that struggle to reconcile tolerance for immigrants and refugees with clamours for crackdowns on new arrivals.
A surge in xenophobia among grassroots supporters had blind-sided and, for a time, paralysed party leaders, Fenton said in an interview. “There was a moment of genuine sheer panic and just not knowing what to do. We were struggling to adapt because it was a sense that things had started to spiral out of control.”
The book, published this week, depicts a largely well-intentioned but hapless party, and is also an account from a member of an organisation that many perceive as secretive and still in thrall to former IRA leaders on both sides of the Irish border, a perception Fenton disputes.
Fenton, 34, was an atypical “Shinner”, the informal name for party adherents. She came from a middle-class Belfast family that abhorred the violence of the Troubles and favoured constitutional nationalism, not flinty republicanism.
Fenton briefly worked for the Social Democratic and Labour party (SDLP) before studying English literature at Oxford, researching gender-based violence at Cambridge and becoming a London-based journalist for the Independent before returning to Northern Ireland in 2016, where she freelanced for the BBC and other outlets, including the Guardian, and wrote a book on the Good Friday agreement.
In early 2020, Sinn Féin offered Fenton a job in Dublin. The party was on a high. It had just won 24.5% of first preference votes in the Irish general election, overtaking Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael, two centrist parties that had alternated in power for a century.
As successor to Gerry Adams, McDonald, a Dubliner universally known as Mary Lou, offered a fresh alternative, especially to young voters who blamed the political establishment for a housing crisis.
Sinn Féin had run too few candidates to capitalise on the breakthrough, so Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael mustered enough seats to form a coalition, leaving Sinn Féin in opposition. Analysts expected it to win power after the next election.
After Sinn Féin became the biggest party in Northern Ireland in 2022, which paved the way for Michelle O’Neill to become first minister at Stormont, the onus was on the party’s southern branch to ensure McDonald became taoiseach at Leinster House. “Don’t fuck it up,” a Belfast colleague half-jokingly told Fenton.
For three years, Fenton, having relocated to Dublin, experienced the giddy nervousness of a party soaring in the polls while the ruling coalition slumped. The republican mantra – “tiocfaidh ár lá”, our day will come – seemed apt.
A section titled “the long fall” chronicles the unravelling amid missteps and a volatile public mood.
McDonald appeared to blame police for a riot that rocked Dublin in November 2023, and alarmed middle-class property owners by suggesting average Dublin house prices should fall to €300,000. More damagingly, the party failed to navigate growing xenophobia, the result of a housing shortage, a cost of living crisis, an influx of migrants and refugees, and far-right activism on social media and the streets.
“It was a blind spot,” said Fenton. Covid-19 restrictions and a focus on the parliamentary party withered grassroots networking, leaving leaders unaware of the extent to which conspiracy theories and hostility to Muslims had taken hold, she said.
The party should have tried to combat racist narratives by peeling people away from smartphones and having “really difficult conversations”, said Fenton. “Go door to door, talk about community concerns but be very, very clear that scapegoating immigrants and refugees is the wrong response.”
Instead of gains in the May 2024 local and European elections, the cascade of coins on to Fenton foretold haemorrhaging support, especially in working-class strongholds that branded McDonald a “traitor” for not seeking greater curbs on migration. Months later the party limped into a general election that kept Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael in power.
Fenton’s contract was not renewed and she returned to her native Belfast, where she now works as a writer and analyst. She is no longer a member of Sinn Féin.
Immigration remains a fraught issue for a party squeezed between those wanting a harder line and those who favour solidarity, said Fenton. Leaders may be tempted to sidestep the issue until the next election, then take a stance, she said. “It will be dependent on what the political environment looks like then.”

====================================================================================================

The pressure on Burnham to appease the right is huge. But now is the time to step out of Reform’s shadow | Andy Beckett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:00:32 UTC
18:00:32 KST

Despite the bright start to Andy Burnham’s premiership, and Reform UK’s sudden disarray, a shadow still hangs over British centre-left politics. Labour has a small poll lead, a cautious air of confidence and a leader who seems energised rather than overwhelmed by trying to solve the country’s problems. Meanwhile, Reform is having a terrible 2026: mired in deepening funding scandals, losing winnable byelections and, thanks to the drama and novelty of Burnham’s leadership coup and new government, no longer the freshest story around.
Yet Reform UK’s support has either held up or fallen only slightly in most polls since Burnham entered Downing Street. Even in the Makerfield byelection, where he beat it more decisively than expected, Reform’s vote share and total support actually rose. Nigel Farage may have spent the year uncharacteristically avoiding journalists, or in his prickly rather than jolly public mode, but the overwhelming majority of Reform supporters, almost a quarter of the electorate, remain faithful. “Power is within our grasp!” insisted Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesman, at its party conference in Birmingham on Friday, and they applauded with determined gusto.
Meanwhile, their preoccupations continue to shape politics and how the media processes it. Immigration, crime, the benefits system, “wokeness”, net zero policies: all are constantly presented as out of control and contributing to national decline. From our overcrowded prisons to our almost exhausted North Sea oil- and gasfields, what are widely considered to be the most politically realistic options for the government are generally what most Reform voters would like to happen. The likelihood that permanent crime crackdowns and further large-scale fossil-fuel drilling – which the government looks increasingly likely to approve – will be disastrous for a country with an ever more obvious climate crisis and unprecedentedly large prison population, by historical and European standards, does not disturb this deep-rooted rightwing consensus. The pressure on Burnham to go along with it as prime minister will be never-ending.
Yet the risks of governing under Reform’s shadow, while less discussed, are much larger. So far, Labour’s fragile poll recovery has mainly been built by taking support back from the Greens and Lib Dems, as the dip in their poll ratings since a Burnham premiership became likely has demonstrated. This change would almost certainly be undone if Burnham decided to follow a Reform-defined agenda. Keir Starmer’s abrupt announcement that he will leave parliament is the ultimate result of him making exactly that mistake in Downing Street – and has given the Greens’ leader, Zack Polanski, a chance to reverse the momentum shift from his party to Labour by standing as a byelection candidate.
Meanwhile, with Reform, Restore and the Tories all competing to be the most rightwing, and this country’s many reactionary media outlets doing the same, many right-leaning voters are even more convinced than usual that no Labour government is acceptable. So the appeasement of conservative Britain, designed by Morgan McSweeney and carried out by Starmer, not always with conviction, was never likely to win many converts for long. In a deeply divided country, the days of Labour premiers attracting and holding on to large numbers of rightwing voters, as Tony Blair, Harold Wilson and Clement Attlee once did, are gone, at least for now.
As a politician unusually keen by modern standards on cross-party collaboration and broad coalitions, Burnham could waste much of what may not be a long premiership trying to build bridges with the right. But there are some early signs he may pursue a more streetwise strategy. His debut contributions as prime minister in parliament this week mixed consensual catchphrases such as “problem-solving over point-scoring”, which made the Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, sound rigidly confrontational in response, with sweeping attacks on areas where the right is vulnerable. Austerity, Brexit, privatisation and the centralisation of power in London have dwindling electoral support and even less credibility, however loudly the Tories and Reform defend some or all of them, because for decades these old-fashioned rightwing remedies have clearly failed to revive the country.
“Far from ‘taking back control’, the combination of those policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain,” said Burnham, deftly turning a key promise of populism back against the rightwing populists. He knows that while Margaret Thatcher is still revered by Farage and Badenoch, the sometimes brutal economic changes that she and her Conservative successors drove through are not popular with all Tory and Reform voters. They may never switch to supporting Labour, but could support parts of Burnham’s programme, such as stronger public control over “the essentials of life” currently provided at excessive cost by toxic Thatcherite creations such as Thames Water.
The approval, tacit or otherwise, of usually hostile voters on a specific issue can provide useful political cover for a government – especially an unpopular one, which Burnham’s is likely to be, however he performs, given the number of parties arrayed against him in our fragmented political landscape. He may well need that cover if his government is going to restructure the economy even half as ambitiously as he promises. The shareholders, financiers, lawyers and corporate executives who have done extremely well out of privatisation are not going to give up their gains and privileges without a fight.
A temporary coalition of leftwing and rightwing voters may be the only way to overcome them. The economy is not democratic – much to the disappointment of generations of radical leftists – but in a democracy, powerful interests can be curbed or even defeated if they are challenged by a premier acting with broad public consent, as Attlee and Franklin D Roosevelt once did against some of the 20th century’s most entrenched economic elites.
Yet if Burnham is to govern with anything like those legendary reformers’ effectiveness, then in other policy areas his government is going to have to stand up to Reform supporters. New research about them by King’s College London and UK in a Changing Europe shows that, despite this summer being the UK’s hottest ever, almost two-thirds “want to scrap the 2050 net zero target”. Meanwhile, a new Ipsos poll shows that immigration remains the number one public issue, particularly for Reform and Tory voters, despite the fact that immigration is rapidly falling.
Sooner or later, Burnham is going to have to use his celebrated communications skills to tell Britons some home truths, whether rightwing voters want to hear them or not. Otherwise, Reform’s shadow will chill his government for good.
- 
  Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

The Swiss Catholics who don’t recognise the pope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The Swiss Catholics who don’t recognise the pope
Switzerland loves being different. Its four national languages, referendums and the militia army are among the best examples. But there is another, much more low-key one: a Catholic church that doesn’t recognise papal authority.
Sometimes encountered while leafing through a document or a set of statistics, its name often intrigues; its very existence even more so. The Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland is, however, very real, even though many Swiss people have never heard of it. Although officially recognised in several cantons, it remains almost invisible within the Swiss religious landscape.
With some 12,000 to 13,000 members, it accounts for between 0.1% and 0.2% of the population. Such a modest proportion that it disappears even from official statistics: the Federal Statistical Office classifies it under the generic category of “other Christian communities”, alongside the Orthodox and the numerous Evangelical churches.
A rarity on a global scale
Globally, Christian Catholics constitute a tiny minority. They belong to the family of so-called Old Catholic Churches, which emerged in the 19th century following disagreements with Rome and are now grouped together within the Union of Utrecht.
The movement is present in only a few countries, mainly the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland and Austria. Yet, within this small religious community, Switzerland plays a far more significant role than its membership figures would suggest.
One might think of it as a little-known curiosity. Yet the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland has around 30 parishes, more than half of which are located in the cantons of Bern, Aargau, Solothurn and Basel. It also has its own bishop and ranks among the world’s leading Old Catholic communities.
The paradox is therefore very real: while most Swiss are unaware of its very existence, this small Church possesses structures that many larger organisations might envy.
A split dating back to the 19th century
To understand its origins, we must look back to a Europe in the midst of transformation. In both Germany and Switzerland, the young modern states were seeking to assert their authority against Rome.
In 1870, the First Vatican Council proclaimed, among other things, the dogma of papal infallibility and strengthened the pope’s authority over the entire Catholic Church. For many Catholics, this development posed no problem. Others, however, saw it as an excessive centralisation of religious power.
In Switzerland, the controversy quickly took on a political dimension. Against the backdrop of the Kulturkampf, which pitted liberal authorities against the Roman Catholic Church, priests and the faithful rejected Rome’s new direction and decided to go their own way.
The split was finally consummated. In 1871, the Christian Catholic Church was founded. At the time, there was no indication that this movement would endure for decades. Yet, more than 150 years later, it has survived disputes that most Europeans have long since forgotten.
A Catholic church with liberal leanings
Anyone attending a Christian Catholic service for the first time is likely to be surprised by what does not surprise them. The liturgy does indeed bear a strong resemblance to that of a Roman Catholic Mass. The prayers, the sacraments and a large part of the rites are familiar. At first glance, there is little or nothing to distinguish the two Churches.
The differences become apparent above all when one looks behind the altar. The bishop, for example, is not appointed by Rome. He is elected by the National Synod, where laypeople play an important role alongside the clergy. Christian Catholics also trace their lineage to the tradition of the Church of the first millennium and therefore do not recognise certain dogmas adopted later by Rome, notably that of papal infallibility.
But it is, above all, some of their reforms that have attracted attention. From the very beginning, the Church adopted national languages for the liturgy and permitted priests to marry. Divorced people may enter into a new religious marriage. Since 1999, women have been admitted to the priesthood. Since 2022, same-sex couples have also been able to enter into a religious marriage.
Not exactly what one would expect to find in a Church founded in 1871. Though small in numbers, the Christian Catholic Church has often proved more daring than institutions a hundred times its size.
Between Rome and the Reformation
Ultimately, the Christian Catholic Church’s originality lies in its unique position. It retains the liturgy, sacraments and episcopal structure inherited from the Catholic tradition, while placing great emphasis on the participation of the faithful and on reforms generally associated with the Protestant world.
This middle ground is reflected even in the training of its clergy. Future Christian Catholic priests study at the University of Bern, within the Institute of Christian-Catholic Theology, which forms part of a faculty historically shaped by the Protestant tradition. This situation sums up the identity of this Church rather well.
This openness is also evident in its relations with other Christian denominations. As a member of the Utrecht Union of Old Catholic Churches, it is in “full ecclesial communion” with the Anglican Churches. In layman’s terms, this means that ministries and sacraments are mutually recognised, a closeness that few churches can claim.
More than 150 years after its founding, the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland thus continues to occupy a unique place in the European religious landscape. Neither quite Roman nor truly Protestant, it has forged its own identity over time. In short, a Church too Catholic to be Protestant, but too independent to be Roman.

NANCHANG, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- One person has been confirmed dead and 11 others are missing after a mudslide struck a village in Suichuan County, Ji'an City, east China's Jiangxi Province at around 4 a.m. on Saturday, local authorities said.

Three people have been rescued, two of whom are in stable condition while one has been confirmed dead. All-out search and rescue operations are underway, while efforts are also being made to relocate affected residents and prevent secondary disasters.

China's Ministry of Natural Resources raised its geological disaster response for Jiangxi from Level IV to III at 11 a.m. Saturday and dispatched a work team to the site to guide rescue efforts.
The China National Commission for Disaster Reduction and the Ministry of Emergency Management activated a Level-IV national emergency response for natural disaster relief, and sent a work team and an emergency survey team with equipment including slope radar to assist with rescue operations.
Local fire and rescue authorities have dispatched 41 vehicles and 224 personnel to the site, while communications and reconnaissance drones in nearby areas have been deployed for rescue.
China has a four-tier emergency response system, with Level I being the most severe. ■

China Focus: China moves to create phone-free classrooms, help minors navigate digital age
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:59:48 CST
17:59:48 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- For Ye Hui, the past summer break has been a digital tug-of-war.
Every time she confiscated the tablet, her 10-year-old son found a way to crack the password. So when the new semester began, she finally felt relief -- not just because he was back in class, but because the law was now on her side.
"Teachers will be more persuasive, given that the ban on smart devices is no longer just a school policy," said Ye, who lives in southwest China's Chongqing municipality.
The ban Ye spoke of is stipulated in a local law on minor crime prevention, which took effect on Sept. 1. It prohibited Ye's son and his counterparts from bringing phones, tablets and other smart devices into school.
Official statistics showed that China has close to 200 million underage internet users, with over 97 percent of minors having online access.
Minors' attention being eroded by the algorithm is a problem faced by countries across the world in the digital age, said Wang Peng, a deputy research fellow at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences.
Putting a mobile device school ban into law is necessary, as it provides legal support for schools to enforce the ban to keep students from such erosion, Wang said.
Chongqing is the latest to elevate a phone ban from a school policy to legislation, as the entire country is working to build a safe and healthy internet environment for children's wholesome growth.
A similar legal ban has already been put in place in Guangzhou in Guangdong Province, Zhengzhou in Henan Province and places across Fujian Province.
The aim is better prevention of internet addiction among underage students, according to Chongqing municipal legislature, noting the provision cited a 2021 guidance document on the protection of minors' rights and interests in school by the Ministry of Education.
In mulling over the local law on minor crime prevention, Chongqing's legislative body found that exposure to bad information as a result of smartphone usage caused some school-age children to develop unhealthy ideas and values, and even commit crimes.
Ye was one of the worrying parents struggling to keep their children away from smartphones' bad influence. Her son spent nearly eight hours every day on screen and even paid for virtual skins and props for online games during the past summer vacation. "He could always find a way to unlock the tablet."
Strict restrictions on smart device use could help nip internet addiction in the bud, Ye hoped.
Xiao Junyi, a student from the 29th Middle School in Chongqing, welcomed the phone ban in school, admitting phones had proven detrimental to students' level of concentration and undermined their learning.
"We would secretly take out the phone and surf online when class was on," Xiao said.
Teachers believe when the phone ban becomes a law provision, it will be more convincing to students and easier for them to enforce.
"It will save a lot of unnecessary lecturing," said Hu Ranrui'an, a deputy head teacher at the Science City Middle School Affiliated to Chongqing Normal University.
But in reality, some children, particularly middle school students who have no parent to take them from and to school, do need cell phones for emergency contact.
"It's not a one-size-fits-all ban," said Jiang Yongsong, a supervisor from the 29th Middle School. There is a provision in the law that allows parents to file a written application if students need phones in school, he said.
Countries around the world have also been introducing bans, with smartphones increasingly seen as a source of classroom distraction and a potential threat to students' well-being.
UNESCO's latest Global Education Monitoring Report showed that 114 education systems now have a national ban on mobile phones in schools, representing 58 percent of countries worldwide.
However, experts cautioned that restriction is not enough to address the problem, calling for joint efforts from society, school and family.
After physically isolating minors from the digital world, there will be room for efforts to foster their concentration and capabilities for in-depth and critical thinking, said Wang Peng.
Ye Hui has already mapped out the reclaimed hours from the screen -- board games on Mondays, jogging on Wednesdays and weekend hikes to replace the virtual battles. "It's about proving the real world can win the battle for his attention," she said. ■

====================================================================================================

Across China: Exhibition bridges gap between centuries-old Chinese encyclopedia, public
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:59:27 CST
17:59:27 KST

LANZHOU, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- An art gallery in Lanzhou, capital of northwest China's Gansu Province, has turned a colossal ancient encyclopedia into something anyone can enjoy.
Instead of displaying dense classical Chinese that only scholars can master, it exhibits 122 images from this seldom-presented 18th-century compendium, such as a sketch of an ancient Indian unicorn, a star map nearly a millennium old, and the private scribbles of a stern, diligent emperor.
These images form part of a years-long project to digitize a copy of the Siku Quanshu, which translates as the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, one of the most comprehensive collections of Chinese classical works in Chinese history.
Compiled during the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911), the book runs to nearly 800 million characters across thousands of volumes, covering everything from Confucian philosophy to farming techniques. Seven copies were originally produced, but only three and a half survive today, preserved in Beijing, Taipei and Lanzhou, respectively.
For decades, this massive treasured book was locked away. To better preserve its copy, Lanzhou built a dedicated library in an underground repository with constant temperature and humidity. In 2021, a project was launched to digitize it.
By the end of May 2022, the scanning work of the text was finished, and the project moved into data processing. A team of young editors then spent more than two years checking the data page by page, and along the way, they discovered something unexpected: the playful side of the massive and complex text.
"Most people think such a book would be too difficult to read," said Zhang Yang, deputy director of the digital publishing center at Duzhe Publishing & Media, the project's lead. "But as we went page by page, we found plenty of vivid images that could spark modern readers' curiosity."
What started as a routine check soon turned into a curatorial mission. The team selected 122 of the most striking images and organized them into twelve sections, covering tea culture, astronomy, architecture, medicine, costume, and even weapon-making. The editors gave the sections funny titles such as "Ancient Gardening Know-How" and "Ancient Stargazing Guide," bridging the gap between centuries-old social life and the modern day.
One section is called "World Mystery Box," featuring images from geographical works by Western missionaries during the Qing Dynasty. These images depict the Colosseum in Rome, the Colossus of Rhodes, and exotic and mythical creatures, such as lions and mermaids.
"We had long heard of the Siku Quanshu by name, but this is our first time seeing it up close," said Liang Tao, a visitor from Xi'an. "It's both fun and awe-inspiring."
That reaction echoes the goal of the exhibition. Song Xuejuan, who heads the digitization project, said the exhibition "transforms 'static preservation' into 'dynamic sharing', and turns an academic treasure into a public experience."
For a long time, there was a disconnect between traditional culture and younger generations. In recent years, however, new technologies, fresh perspectives, and innovative storytelling have helped connect ancient heritage with contemporary trends.
The Mogao Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage Site dating back to the 4th century, also in Gansu, are an example. In the 1980s, local researchers began exploring digital documentation. Today, they have completed high-precision digital capture of 323 caves. The images rendered on screen are now even clearer than what the naked eye can see on site, revealing details that once required climbing ladders to inspect.
Another example is the immersive interactive digital exhibition of oracle bone inscriptions, held in Tianjin in April. Using artificial intelligence and mixed reality technologies, it allowed visitors to experience the ancient ritual of oracle bone divination.
The Lanzhou gallery said it had previously received only a few hundred visitors per day on average. But since this new image exhibition launched, it has seen attendance surge to over 3,000 on peak days. Among the crowds were many children accompanied by parents.
For Song's team, they were no longer editors merely checking for data errors, but rather communicators sharing the treasures with the public.
"I used to think the Siku Quanshu was unreachable," said Song Jia'ni, a 34-year-old editor on the team. "But once you get into it, you will realize you don't have to begin with big history. One picture, or one detail, is enough to hook you." ■

South Africa rolls out baboon-proof bins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
08:55:47 UTC
17:55:47 KST

South Africa rolls out baboon-proof bins
The first 2,200 of 6,000 lockable baboon-proof bins are due to reach priority areas of South Africa’s Cape Peninsula from mid-September 2026, while a northern fence project awaits final environmental and administrative approvals.
The Cape Peninsula Baboon Management Joint Task Team (CPBMJTT), made up of SANParks, CapeNature and the City of Cape Town, said the rollout will initially focus on areas where baboon activity and conflict with residents have been reported most frequently.
The first areas to receive the new bins are Plateau Road, Castle Rock, Heron Park, Murdoch Valley South, De Oude Weg, Da Gama, Capri, Welcome Glen, Scarborough, Tokai East and Fir Grove. Simon’s Town is not included in the initial rollout because the Seaforth and Waterfall troops are earmarked for relocation to the planned Urban Wildlife Centre. Preparations are also under way for a northern boundary fence running from Zwaanswyk south to Constantia Nek.
According to the CPBMJTT, the process is expected to begin later in September once environmental checklists and administrative approvals have been completed. The task team said the fence is intended to prevent baboons from entering urban areas and farmland in the northern part of the peninsula, while securing habitat for an estimated 250 baboons.
A memorandum of understanding has been signed between seven wine-farm landowners bordering Table Mountain National Park in the Constantia Valley, the Cape Baboon Partnership and the City. The agreement sets out shared responsibilities for construction, maintenance and the long-term operation of the fence. The landowners and Cape Baboon Partnership will share the construction and upgrade costs, while the City has committed a once-off R10 million contribution.
The CPBMJTT said construction is expected to take about six months if all goes according to plan. Once the fence is in place, rangers will encourage the CT1 and CT2 troops towards the mountainside and will continue monitoring the troops and patrolling the fence.
The fence forms part of the approved Cape Peninsula Baboon Strategic Management Plan and is intended to create a clearer boundary between Table Mountain National Park and neighbouring agricultural and residential properties.
The Cape Baboon Partnership has appointed an experienced sanctuary manager, while stakeholders, environmental groups, community representatives and residents have visited the site over the past two months.
A Swansea University research project involving the Da Gama troop ended on August 21. The study tested non-invasive approaches using olfactory, auditory and visual cues to examine how baboons respond to simulated risks. The collars used during the research were designed to self-release and have now been collected. Data analysis is underway, with the findings expected to be made public once the study has been completed.

Ulrich Siegmund could for the first time lead the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt into government. At a campaign family festival, around 10,000 people hail the 35-year-old as a beacon of hope for his promised political shake-up.
Supporters queue in lines stretching dozens of metres for a photo with him: AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. The 35-year-old is standing for the party in Sunday's state election in Saxony-Anhalt.
The state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution — a department of the Germany's interior ministry — has classified the Saxony-Anhalt AfD as a confirmed far-right extremist organisation. Siegmund is the young rising star of the AfD in eastern Germany.
"I finally want to make policy for our own country again," Siegmund tells Euronews. He wants to overhaul migration policy, freeing up money he says is "currently being handed out around the world, for people who are here illegally, who commit crimes here." Policy, he says, should serve "our own interest, for our own country."
Within his first 100 days in office, Siegmund plans to introduce a "work obligation for asylum seekers", he says. Fire service driving licences and the display of flags at schools are also right at the top of his list. "Of course this is not turning the really big wheel, but these are the first concrete steps where you can see the first progress in all areas of this society." What has been destroyed will take a few years to rebuild, the AfD politician goes on to say.
Here at the "family festival", as the AfD calls it, near the Magdeburg city centre, thousands cheer and celebrate their "Ulli". His likeness is emblazoned on countless T-shirts and placards. Time and again chants of "We are the people" cut through the crowd. Some AfD supporters also chant "We are the Wende". In between, musicians take to the stage or techno beats blare from the speakers.
The party has rolled out the heavy artillery – its best-known politicians fire up the crowd, including Thuringian AfD politician Stephan Brandner and co-chair Tino Chrupalla. Whenever the speakers mention the CDU, SPD or other parties, the crowd boos and whistles. Some shout "Shame".

She does not want to give her real name, like many at the event. The fear of possible consequences is too great.
Even a heavy downpour does not stop his fans from waiting for Siegmund’s appearance. For them, everything is at stake: for the first time, the AfD could govern at state level – as part of a coalition or possibly even on its own.
CDU politician: working with the AfD would spell the end of the Union
Current polls put the AfD at around 41 percent, according to Forschungsgruppe Wahlen on behalf of ZDF. The CDU trails far behind in second place with 23 percent, the Left party is third with 11.5 percent. In the last election in 2021, the AfD won 20.8 percent. Back then the CDU won by a clear margin (37.1%).
This time the AfD hopes to be able to win the election outright. But that might still not be enough for the state government. The party may get too few votes to govern alone. It rejects any coalition with the CDU. The CDU also rejects a coalition. It has adopted an incompatibility resolution.
Dennis Radtke, the head of the CDU’s workers’ wing (CDA), warns that his party would be doomed if it formed a coalition with the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt. "The moment we start working with this party, bringing it into positions of responsibility, the CDU is finished," Radtke said on ZDF’s "Maybrit Illner" programme.
Only the BSW can imagine tolerating an AfD-led government, meaning supporting an AfD single-party government with its votes. But the BSW is currently on four percent in the polls and could thus fail to clear the five-percent threshold. The SPD and the Greens, too, have in recent weeks been shaky contenders hovering just below the threshold. They have now climbed to 8.5 percent and six percent respectively.
Lead Left party candidate optimistic
Given the current polling figures, Saxony-Anhalt may face a complicated coalition-building puzzle after the vote. A coalition of AfD and CDU appears to be ruled out. A CDU–Left party alliance as the basis for a majority government with the SPD and Greens also looks unrealistic for now, because the Union’s incompatibility resolution also applies to the Left party.

She has been a member of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament since 2002. "The climate is very hostile to women. Hate and incitement are what define a parliamentary sitting." This has now also arrived in society and on social media.
Despite the current forecast, she is looking "optimistically" towards election day, the Left politician says. She is "firmly convinced" that the AfD will not manage to form a single-party AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt. "People have understood. They want to fight for diversity in Saxony-Anhalt."

The death toll from flash floods and mudslides along the Nepal-China border rose to 1,375 on Saturday, while 5,531 people remained missing 10 days after the disaster struck, according to official data.
