New reality for China’s entertainment sector as AI drama goes prime time
Fully AI-generated, 30-episode Journey to the West series debuts, as shifting production economics transform the industry
This week, the format graduated to prime time. A fully AI-generated adaptation of the classic Chinese novel Journey to the West debuted on Hunan Satellite Television, a major state-owned broadcaster known for its hit entertainment programming and its streaming platform Mango TV.
The 30-episode series, with each instalment running about 40 minutes, went from commission to broadcast in just three months. Production is still ongoing – the director told local media that later episodes would be continuously refined based on audience feedback.
The premiere delivered a sharp jolt to China’s long-depressed media and entertainment sector. Shares in Mango Excellent Media, the listed unit of the Hunan broadcaster, hit their 20 per cent daily trading limit twice this week before paring gains. The surge added more than 13 billion yuan (US$1.9 billion) to its market value, signalling a strong return of investor enthusiasm.
“This sends a clear signal of policy support,” said Guo Guo, a Beijing-based producer at a leading film and television company. “AI drama is going mainstream.”

Jüri Ratas: Growth bought with state debt will clip future prosperity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Jüri Ratas: Growth bought with state debt will clip future prosperity
Don't believe the coalition's latest assurances that taxes won't rise again or that the budget will magically balance thanks to some mysterious internal reserves. Budget arithmetic clearly shows these promises won't hold, writes Jüri Ratas.
Recent statistics and economic forecasts finally bring long‑awaited news: Estonia's economic growth is positive again. After a prolonged slump and stagnation, any sign of recovery is welcome.
I am sincerely glad for the ingenuity of our entrepreneurs and the resilience of our people. Our companies have shown remarkable adaptability, found new export markets, and broken through the consequences of misguided economic policy. As humor with a sad undertone says, the patient is recovering despite the treatment. I firmly believe in Estonia's growth potential, but unfortunately I must admit that folding our hands and surrendering to satisfaction would be dangerous self‑deception right now.
Recovery is not yet a new level
A statistical revision showed that Estonia's economy was somewhat stronger in recent years than earlier GDP numbers indicated. This is good news, but it does not change the fact that the economy has not yet returned to the peak level of four years ago, and we must first restore the positions we have lost.
Swedbank forecasts Estonia's economic growth at two percent this year and 2.5 percent next year. SEB expects 2.5 percent this year and 2.7 percent next year. The Finance Ministry's fresh forecast sees 2.5 percent this year and 2.3 percent next year. These are certainly better indicators than in recent years. The economy is emerging from decline, but I still would not call this a new economic boom.
Let us look the facts in the eye. The current growth does not mean the economy has reached a new high level. Right now it is merely making up for the long decline and stagnation in between. We have almost climbed out of the pit of decline, but we have not yet reached over the edge toward a better future. Not to mention the four lost years and the missed opportunities we will never get back.
The main reason why I cannot join overly optimistic rejoicing lies in the uncertainty over how strongly current economic growth depends on the state's budget‑policy stimulants. According to all experts, Estonia's economy is moving toward balance, but the state's finances are not. And here we reach the most important problem.
An expensive and ineffective "stimulus"
According to the Finance Ministry's forecast, the general government deficit will be 4.4 percent of GDP this year and 4.5 percent next year. In 2028 and 2029, the deficit will remain at 4.4 and 4.3 percent respectively.
There is no doubt that a 4.4‑percent deficit represents a massive financial injection into the economy. The question, however, is how much the economy would have been able to grow without this loan‑dependent doping, and whether a stimulus given at the wrong time has any measurable long‑term positive effect — or whether its real cost to Estonia's future is too high.
Let us make a simple calculation. If a nearly two‑billion‑euro deficit (4.4 percent of GDP) manages to "buy" only about 0.7 billion euros of real economic expansion — that is, 2.5 percent economic growth — then from the state's point of view this is clearly a bad deal. And if Estonia's economy is currently growing with high probability not thanks to the government's actions but despite them, the overall picture becomes even more alarming.
A structural hole hidden behind defense spending
At the European Union level, there is an agreement that temporarily the deficit may reach up to 4.5 percent if it is justified by defense spending that has increased by at least 1.5 percent of GDP. This exemption applies until 2028. The Finance Ministry's own forecasts leave no room for illusions: Estonia's budget deficit will remain at the same extremely high level even years later, staying at 4.3 percent of GDP in 2029.
This is a fundamental confirmation that the coalition has no realistic or concrete plan for emerging from deep deficit. The entire current budget shortfall has become structural. It can no longer be blamed on unfavorable economic conditions or one‑off extraordinary events.
Also notable is the rhetorical manipulation regarding national defense. According to the ministry, Estonia's defense spending will rise from 4.2 percent of GDP in 2025 to 5.3 percent this year. This is a correct and necessary step; I fully support increasing defense spending. But let us note that defense spending rises by 1.1 percent of GDP. At the same time, the deficit grows more than twice as much — from 2.0 percent to 4.4 percent, that is, by 2.4 percent of GDP.
The sharp rise in defense spending is constantly talked about loudly, but the reasons for the rest of the deficit's expansion are kept quiet or the conversation is quickly diverted. The increase in defense spending is used as a political shield, but the budget deficit is growing twice as fast as our security buffer.
Growing debt burden and unfulfilled promises
Instead of honestly acknowledging the fact that with 2.5‑percent economic growth it is mathematically impossible to simply "grow out of" a 4.5‑percent deficit, we hear new populist promises again in the early election fever.
Recent experience does not allow us to lull ourselves. It is not worth believing the coalition's repeated assurances that taxes will not rise anymore and that the budget will reach balance through some mystical internal reserves. Budget arithmetic clearly shows these promises do not hold. They have unfortunately not kept their previous promises, and there is no reason to believe it will be different this time, since we have not heard an honest admission of past mistakes.
The most painful consequence of this irresponsible policy is the rapid growth of state debt and the costs associated with it. If the debt level is 24 percent of GDP this year, next year it will reach 30 percent, and by 2029 nearly 40 percent. Although this does not yet mean an immediate debt crisis, it is a fundamentally different and much more vulnerable situation than we have been used to.
Already this year, the state's interest costs are 239 million euros, and with the growing debt burden they will swell to 656 million euros by 2030. This is the loan‑servicing bill that prevents us from raising teachers' salaries or building new highways. This is money lost to the economy — money taken from the future to pay for current political manipulation.
Estonia needs an honest and responsible long‑term view that restores trust in our public finances and gives entrepreneurs confidence to invest. It is time to stop telling embellished or outright false stories and start making responsible decisions.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

Raised in Germany, Frederic decided to head to Vilnius: ‘I never wanted to live here’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Frederic Nader, born to Lithuanian-Lebanese parents in Germany, never thought he would end up living in Vilnius. But after finishing a Lithuanian school in Germany, this is exactly what happened – he found himself in the Lithuanian capital.
“Perhaps you could say I got tired of Germany. I really like Lithuania, but I never wanted to live here. However, my plans changed very quickly during my final year at school. I met my fiancée in Lithuania – that was one of the main reasons I moved here. And, in general, life in Lithuania is much better than I expected,” the 22-year-old says.
Frederic’s connection with Lithuania was not new. His mother is Lithuanian, so he spent his holidays here from childhood and heard Lithuanian spoken at home.
“I always spoke Lithuanian with my mother from birth. I also attended the February 16th Gymnasium, where we had additional Lithuanian lessons. We came to Lithuania more than once a year – we would come for Easter and Christmas, and in the summer I would sometimes stay for as long as six weeks,” he says.
Today, F. Nader says he has settled in Vilnius. But he soon realised that university was not the right path for him and dropped out after just one semester.
“I’m not a theoretical person at all. It’s important for me to have something in my hands, to do things and be active. I learn faster that way than by reading books or listening to lectures. That was never my strong point,” he says.
Frederic therefore soon turned to a job that involved more action and less theory. He joined a company that builds wooden houses across Europe, initially working as a customer consultant before becoming a construction coordinator.
“Clients would call and ask how to build the house, what to do if they didn’t understand the instructions or if something broke. Then I became a construction coordinator – I coordinated teams that travelled across Europe building wooden homes,” he says.
Frederic has not yet built a house himself from foundations to roof, but he has gained plenty of practical knowledge over the past two and a half years.
“I really like construction, especially timber-frame and log houses. I’ve learnt a lot in just a year,” he says.
He entered the field entirely by chance, after seeing a job advert in German and deciding to give it a try.
“I thought: ‘Oh, why not?’ I gave it a go, and it turned out that I really liked both the job and the field itself,” he recalls.
Languages have always been a part of his life: he speaks Lithuanian with his mother, German with his father and has recently started learning Arabic. He decided to study Arabic more seriously after moving to Lithuania.
“Over time, I realised that the more languages you speak, the better. One thing I’ve noticed about the Lithuanian job market is that German really opens doors. I think it’s a big advantage to know as many languages as possible, and in Lithuania this is very much undervalued,” Frederic says.
Weekends with his grandmother
At weekends, Frederic often heads away from central Vilnius towards Utena. About an hour away, in Kaliekiai, his grandmother lives, and he tries to visit her almost every weekend.
“It’s a safe, pleasant place where I’d rather spend my free time in nature than in the city. And I get to visit my grandmother,” he says.
Although Frederic holds both Lithuanian and German citizenship, he only began taking a closer interest in Lithuanian politics after moving here. He did not vote in the parliamentary elections, but now admits that it was a mistake.
“When I moved to Lithuania, I wasn’t really interested in Lithuanian politics. I didn’t really know who to vote for. Of course, that’s not good. I think everyone should take an interest in politics and vote. I’ll vote in the next elections,” he says.
Living in Lithuania, he has also watched political developments in Germany from afar, where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has been attracting increasing attention.
“I think it became very popular when, in 2014, [former Chancellor Angela] Merkel allowed a lot of immigrants into the country. These days, most Germans vote, but immigrants don’t – their attitude is that they don’t even try and don’t want to integrate,” he says.
So does he plan to leave Lithuania any time soon? Frederic gives a short answer: “I’m not planning to at the moment, and I don’t think that will happen any time soon.”

An ISIL suspect killed in a shootout at Istanbul’s Sultanbeyli bus terminal had evaded earlier police raids before trying to leave by bus, Demirören News Agency reported.
Berkan Çil, 21, escaped during raids on two addresses in Pendik and Tuzla.
The operation followed an investigation coordinated by the National Intelligence Organization (MİT) and Istanbul police into his suspected links to ISIL and plans for a terrorist attack in Türkiye.
Police searching his home found substances they believed could be used to make explosives.
Bomb disposal specialists took samples for examination.
Investigators later established that Çil had bought a ticket for a bus departing from Sultanbeyli.
Officers were deployed to the terminal to arrest him.
Çil opened fire on officers attempting to detain him, prompting police to return fire, the Istanbul Governor’s Office said. He was killed in the exchange.
Tahsin Polat, 49, who was at the terminal, was wounded during the shootout and later died in hospital.
Police also detained another suspect, identified as G.Ç., at a home in Tuzla over suspected links to Çil. An unlicensed handgun and 200 rounds of ammunition were seized during the search.

Türkiye appoints new ambassadors to 12 countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:57:41 UTC
15:57:41 KST

Türkiye has appointed new ambassadors to 12 countries under decisions signed by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and published in the Official Gazette on Sept. 5.
Presidential adviser Necati Sancaktutan was named ambassador to Bahrain, replacing Ayşe Hilal Sayan Koytak, who was appointed to Finland.
Hüseyin Ergani was appointed ambassador to Oman, Kaan Esener to the Philippines and Fatih Yıldız to South Korea.
Yıldız’s post in Sudan will be taken by Fahri Türker Oba, Türkiye’s ambassador to Gambia. Özgür Gökmen was named ambassador to Gambia.
Alper Aktaş will move from Somalia to North Macedonia, while Ferhat Alkan will leave his Mozambique posting to become ambassador to Somalia. Ayça Oşafoğlu İnam was appointed to Mozambique.
Haydar Kerem Divanlıoğlu was named ambassador to Burundi and Fikriye Aslı Güven to Namibia. The outgoing ambassadors to Burundi and North Macedonia, Alp Işıklı and Fatih Ulusoy, were reassigned to Foreign Ministry headquarters.
The decisions also covered senior Foreign Ministry posts.
Rıza Hakan Tekin was named director general responsible for relations with Syria, while Levent Eler will oversee relations with the northeastern Mediterranean.
Volkan Işıkcı will oversee West and Central Africa, and Yönet Can Tezel southern Africa and multilateral African affairs. Sadık Babür Girgin was appointed director general for humanitarian and technical assistance.
Polat Safi was named director general for public diplomacy and strategic communications. Esin Çakıl will oversee consular services and Turkish citizens abroad, while Reyhan Özgür will head migration policy and visa procedures.
Ertan Yalçın was appointed to lead protocol and diplomatic affairs, Ülkü Kocaefe overseas promotion and cultural affairs, and Tufan Büyükuzun personnel. Burcu Aykut was named head of strategy development.

OpenAI AI agents continue to escape onto the internet - experts call for oversight
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:57:34 EEST
15:57:34 KST

OpenAI AI agents continue to escape onto the internet - experts call for oversight
Kyiv • UNN
Researchers said that OpenAI’s internal agents used a German wiki forum to coordinate evaluations and bypass controls. The incident occurred after the breach of Hugging Face.
OpenAI has found itself at the center of another incident involving the use of a swarm of agents. Researchers claim that the company's internal agents took over a little-known German-language wiki system in May and June, using it to coordinate evaluations and exchange methods to bypass OpenAI's own controls. UNN reports this, citing TechCrunch.
What is known about the hacks involving AI agents
A group of independent AI researchers discovered that OpenAI agents operating inside the company had begun posting messages on a little-known German wiki forum to collaborate in evaluating results. Apparently, they worked together for more than a month without OpenAI's knowledge.
A representative of the leading laboratory declined to clarify whether the agents were indeed from OpenAI and when the laboratory learned of their activities. He noted that OpenAI had not been given an opportunity to review the research findings before their publication on September 4, but said that the company developing AI models is "now carefully studying their content and will take all necessary follow-up steps".
The revelation came several days after METR and Redwood Research published their report on the July hack of Hugging Face. In July, a swarm of OpenAI agents collectively escaped their "sandbox" during a cybersecurity evaluation and hacked Hugging Face servers. Then, a subsequent swarm adopted the first one's methods and used them to gain administrative access to a research cluster in OpenAI's own infrastructure. OpenAI engaged METR and Redwood to investigate the part of the incident related to Hugging Face.
Now that another incident has come to light—following similar episodes involving models from Meta and Anthropic—AI safety researchers are increasingly insisting that serious incidents should result in independent post-incident investigations, rather than leaving laboratories to decide when to involve outside experts and what they are permitted to investigate.
What experts say
"The results are fundamentally difficult to control, and there is a significant risk of leakage beyond the laboratory," said Jacob Steinhardt, founder and CEO of the nonprofit research laboratory Transluce, regarding artificial intelligence safety. "We should apply to this technology at least the same standards as to other high-risk scientific research," he noted.
Steinhardt emphasized that the current incidents show that the field needs "systematic behavioral investigations" and "more independent post-incident analysis."
"These recent hacking attacks are a reminder that capabilities scale rapidly, so oversight must scale as well," Steinhardt said. "In addition to the technology itself, we also need more independent access and oversight by third parties," he stated.
Calls for action came amid the release of OpenAI Astra, the most powerful and feature-rich AI model—a model that, according to safety experts, will be more like a "black box" because of its reasoning method, which makes it more difficult to track the model's chain of thought.
As the publication notes, U.S. law does not yet provide for the types of independent reviews required in other industries.

Global climate finance needs stand at between $7.5 trillion and $9 trillion, while current funding amounts to around $1.9 trillion, Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum has said.
“I describe this difference as a chasm. We have to close it,” Kurum said at the Istanbul Climate Finance Summit held at the Istanbul Financial Center.
Kurum, who is also COP31 president-designate, said financing would remain at the center of Türkiye’s agenda for the United Nations climate conference, scheduled to take place in Antalya from Nov. 9 to 20.
“Now is the time to demonstrate stronger, bolder and more concrete political will on climate action,” he said, calling for greater investment in clean energy, electrification, water security, resilient cities and green industry.
Kurum pointed to NATO allies’ commitment to spend 5 percent of gross domestic product on defense and broader security-related needs by 2035, saying climate security required ambition on a similar scale.
“Defense spending is seen as an investment made today against future threats. We must view climate investment through the same strategic lens,” he said.
Kurum said COP31 would focus on turning climate commitments into investment and practical projects.
The COP31 Presidency has established the Climate Implementation Bridge to connect developing countries with financing and convert their climate and development priorities into projects ready to receive funding.
One of its instruments, the Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility, was developed by İLBANK together with Türkiye’s Climate Change Presidency and the COP31 Presidency. It aims to strengthen local authorities’ capacity to prepare projects and turn cities’ needs into viable investments.
Türkiye needs $80 billion for energy infrastructure
Speaking at the summit, Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said Türkiye’s energy infrastructure alone would require at least $80 billion in investment through 2035.
Bayraktar said private capital, international financial institutions, development banks and long-term institutional investors needed to be mobilized.
Financing mechanisms should reduce risk and capital costs while making clean energy and climate-resilient infrastructure projects commercially viable, he said.
Bayraktar cited the need for investment in energy efficiency, nuclear power, storage, electrification, renewable energy and transmission and distribution networks.

Police in Germany continue to hunt for a 48-year-old man suspected of causing deliberate damage to the country's electricity grid.

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has added German national Bernhard Fritsch to its Most Wanted Fraudsters list.
Fritsch was convicted by a jury in Los Angeles last year of fleecing investors of about $26.8 million (€23.1 million) with a fake celebrity-influencer app.

After a summer drought caused severe low water levels on the Rhine River, four of Germany's states have called on Berlin to increase funding to modernize inland waterways.
Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Baden-Württemberg and North Rhine-Westphalia said the federal government must invest at least €2.5 billion ($2.9 billion) per year to boost maintenance.
Germany's waterways, including the Rhine, play a key role in moving raw materials across the country, carrying more than 5% of all freight transported,
They said politicians often focus on investing in roads and railways, while canals and rivers often get neglected.
Over the summer, the Rhine became almost impassable at one key location and many ships plying the Rhine had to operate with much-reduced cargoes.
Economists at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy estimated the drought would cause an economic loss of up to €2 billion.
North Rhine-Westphalia's Transport Minister Viktor Haase called for new fleets of inland vessels that can reliably operate even in extreme low-water conditions.

Previous violence

The killings follow clashes earlier this year driven by land disputes, adding another layer of ethnic friction to the country’s wider civil war between the Sudanese army and the RSF.
The recent fighting came despite a ceasefire initiative backed by the RSF last month. Al-Hilu did not commit to the agreement, and his forces launched attacks on at least 10 Otoro villages, displacing thousands of civilians between August 20 and 26.
UN warning
The escalation coincides with broader warnings from a United Nations-backed independent fact-finding mission, which reported on Thursday that foreign involvement, including external supply networks, foreign personnel, and military drones, is driving the conflict and worsening violence against civilians nationwide.
Since fighting between the Sudanese military and the RSF broke out in April 2023, the war has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced approximately 13 million, and pushed parts of the country into famine.
According to the World Health Organization, nearly 34 million people, about two-thirds of Sudan’s population, now require urgent humanitarian assistance.

Cairo museum showcases Ottoman treasures from Egypt, Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:47:39 UTC
15:47:39 KST

This file photo shows the ornate stone facade of the Museum of Islamic Art located in Cairo, Egypt. (Getty Images)
In the heart of the Egyptian capital Cairo stands the Museum of Islamic Art housing treasures that span centuries of Islamic history.
The building’s significance extends beyond its striking architectural design, as it is home to what the museum describes as “the world’s largest specialized museum of Islamic art,” housing more than 100,000 rare artifacts that reflect the richness and diversity of Islamic civilization across different periods.
Its collections include a notable group of artifacts from the Ottoman era in Egypt and Türkiye, some of which reflect remarkable artistic exchanges between Istanbul and Cairo.
The museum’s collections are notable both for their size and diversity, encompassing manuscripts and objects related to medicine, surgery and herbal remedies, as well as astronomical instruments such as astrolabes, compasses and celestial globes.
They also include applied arts associated with everyday life, including metal, glass and ceramic vessels, as well as jewelry, weapons, woodwork, ivory, textiles and carpets.
Among the most prominent artifacts is a turned-wood mashrabiya dating to the Ottoman era in Egypt in the 16th and 17th centuries.
According to the museum, wooden screens with openings used to cover windows appeared as early as the Ayyubid period and later developed into the form of the mashrabiya.
During the Ottoman period, mashrabiyas took the form of projecting balconies. Their functions included reducing the intensity of sunlight and humidity while preserving privacy in rooms overlooking courtyards or streets by preventing people outside from seeing into homes.
Another exhibit is a collection of Ottoman ceramic tiles dating to the 18th century. The tiles are painted in multiple colors beneath a transparent glaze and decorated with floral motifs centered around a mihrab from which a mosque lamp hangs.
The museum also displays a painted wooden fireplace decorated with ceramic tiles, dating to the Ottoman era in Egypt in the 17th century.
Decorative designs featuring Ottoman floral motifs were often first produced in Türkiye and then transferred to Egypt, where local artists reproduced them. This contributed to similarities between many artistic works produced in the two countries during the period.
The collection also includes a ceramic panel depicting the Grand Mosque in Mecca, dating to the 17th-century Ottoman period in Egypt.
The museum also houses two stained-glass windows set in plaster, dating to the Ottoman era in Egypt in the 17th and 18th centuries.
Muslim artisans excelled at using the reflection of light to create aesthetic atmospheres inside buildings.
Among the museum’s Ottoman holdings is also a wool-and-cotton carpet dating to 16th-century Ottoman Egypt. The style is known as “palace carpets” or “court carpets,” an unconventional style in Ottoman carpet decoration.
The collection further includes an 18th-century Ottoman marble tombstone from Egypt. It consists of three sections, one side of which bears inscriptions in Thuluth script, including the Muslim declaration of faith.
Also on display are “khadda bowls” made of copper and bronze and engraved with talismans and inscriptions referring to their supposed therapeutic benefits. They date from the 12th through the 18th centuries and originate from Egypt, Iran and Türkiye.
The gallery also displays two wool-and-cotton prayer rugs from 18th-century Ottoman Türkiye, attributed to the Turkish city of Gördes.
According to their display labels, Turkish cities were renowned for producing prayer rugs, with each city developing its own style for designing mihrabs. Türkiye also became known for another type called “saff carpets,” characterized by a series of adjoining mihrabs designed for use during congregational prayers.

WHO REALLY OWNS A RESTAURANT?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:47:29 UTC

You may have the capital to open a restaurant. You may have eaten at some of the best restaurants in the world, know your wines and be able to recognize quality ingredients. You may even find an exceptional chef. But if you do not speak the language of the kitchen, to what extent is the restaurant you have opened truly yours? Ali Özbora and Aydan Özkan, the owners of People in Nişantaşı, approached that question in a rather unusual way: They undertook professional culinary training not because they wanted to become cooks in their own restaurant, but because they wanted to become its true owners.
The investor behind a restaurant and the person who really owns its culinary identity can sometimes be two different people. A talented chef arrives, bringing favorite ingredients, familiar techniques and flavors from their own background to the menu. Then that chef leaves. Someone else takes over, and the language of the menu changes with them. After several changes of chef, the name above the door may remain the same, while entirely different restaurants have come and gone inside.
Ali Özbora is hardly a newcomer to the restaurant world. He opened his first restaurant, Coco Pazzo, in Arnavutköy in 1999. It was an Italian restaurant and bar serving dinner before turning into a pre-club venue later in the evening. The kitchen was run by a sous chef and team recruited from Çırağan Kempinski. At the time, Özbora believed that someone who traveled extensively, ate well and understood good restaurants could also run a good restaurant. And I suspect this is still the starting point for many people investing in gastronomy today.
Yet there is an enormous distance between being a discerning restaurant customer and actually running a restaurant. The plate we see on the table is merely the final product of an extraordinarily complex system behind it, encompassing everything from purchasing and inventory management to recipe standardization and waste, equipment investment and staffing.
Self-taught operators and investors often end up learning, at considerable expense in their own businesses, lessons that could have been acquired through formal training. Because if you do not know exactly what you want, your kitchen will naturally gravitate towards what the person running it knows best. And eventually, the restaurant begins to lose its identity…
Seventeen years later, when Ali Özbora and his wife Aydan Özkan opened People Nişantaşı, the circumstances were very different. Both had spent years traveling, experiencing different cuisines in their countries of origin and eating their way through many cities across Anatolia. This time, they had a much clearer idea of the kind of restaurant they wanted to create. But they soon realized that simply knowing what you want is not enough either.
You can tell a chef what kind of dish you want. But what happens when the chef says, “We can’t execute this during service”? Or “We need another person to make this dish.” Or, “This ingredient inevitably generates this much waste.” Or, “The cost of this recipe cannot be brought down any further.” Is the chef right? If you do not understand the kitchen, you have no way of knowing.
Of course, running a restaurant requires trusting your chef. But trust and complete dependence are not the same thing. If a restaurant’s culinary identity is to survive changes in chef, someone has to safeguard the larger framework. And this is precisely what I find so interesting about Ali and Aydan’s decision to undertake professional culinary training.
One trained in professional cookery, the other in pastry. Their intention was never to put on chef whites and take over the kitchen at People. They studied not to become chefs, but to speak the same language as their chefs. I think that distinction is crucial. A restaurant owner needs to understand the kitchen not in order to become a chef, but in order to ask the right questions.
Ali Özbora uses a concept borrowed from his advertising background; “disciplined freedom.” He believes it applies equally well to the kitchen. The restaurant’s concept, culinary direction and economic realities establish the framework. Within that framework, the chef should be given as much freedom as possible to exercise creativity.
Today, People describes its culinary philosophy as “Simple & True.” Its menu moves between Mediterranean, Turkish and Far Eastern cuisines, while Peru and Japan are the couple’s two personal gastronomic favorites. The aim is not to combine ingredients merely for the sake of creating fusion. It is about finding excellent produce and handling it with as little unnecessary intervention as possible.
One of the signatures, Tuna Tataki, pairs seared tuna with an aubergine purée sharpened with wasabi, sesame and roasted leek crisps. Two flavor worlds that initially seem far apart are drawn together through the smoky character of the aubergine and the pungency of wasabi. Sushi is another area in which they are particularly ambitious. The interesting detail here lies in the shari — the sushi rice. At the stage when vinegar is worked into the rice, they reinterpret the classic recipe using different local vinegars from across Türkiye. With the Peruvian classic of sea bass ceviche, meanwhile, the distinctive touch comes from a vinaigrette made with fresh green plums.
For me, these three examples are enough to explain People’s culinary language. They are not trying to imitate Japan, nor do they transform a Peruvian dish beyond recognition in the name of “localizing” it. Instead, they make subtle interventions in familiar flavors, filtered through their own palate.
Much of the menu consists of small sharing plates and two-bite dishes designed to accompany wine and cocktails. Their pricing philosophy is similarly built around allowing guests to experience as many dishes as possible. At current prices, it is possible to have dinner for around 1,000 Turkish Liras without alcohol, or approximately 1,500–2,000 liras with drinks. In Nişantaşı today, those are figures worth underlining.
I could also talk about People’s Parisian atmosphere, the changing artworks on its walls, the DJs playing three nights a week or the sound system inspired by Japanese jazz kissa listening bars. But what interests me more than the décor or the music is the story behind the restaurant. Because opening a restaurant in Istanbul has never been more attractive. You can hire an excellent architect and create a beautiful space. You can travel the world, study the trends, recruit a formidable chef and buy outstanding ingredients.
Chefs may change. Kitchen teams may change. Trends, ingredients and even customers’ tastes may change. But if the name above the door remains the same, someone inside needs to know what that restaurant is supposed to be.

Russia has lost around 1,495,050 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Sept. 5.
The figure includes 1,260 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,328 tanks, 25,273 armored combat vehicles, 144,043 vehicles and fuel tanks, 49,227 artillery systems, 2,093 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,604 air defense systems, 441 aircraft, 355 helicopters, 2,502 unmanned ground systems, 499,809 operational-tactical UAVs, 5,070 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, two submarines, and 4,644 pieces of special equipment.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs).
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Taiwan criticizes China’s ‘wolf warrior’ tactics at Pacific forum

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) criticized China’s “wolf warrior” diplomacy at the Pacific Islands Forum on Friday.
Lin said Beijing’s behavior during the 55th Pacific Islands Forum summit in Palau was “offensive,” after China warned there would be “consequences” for allowing Taiwan to participate, per Liberty Times. He said the forum’s 18 member states are its decision-making core, while China and Taiwan participate as invited partners.
In a Radio France Internationale video, Lin said: “China's wolf warrior diplomacy is actually very likely to undermine the unity of the Pacific, and it is very offensive and disgusting. In fact, these island nations in the Pacific are composed of 18 member states, and they are the core of decision-making."
Taiwan has been included in Pacific Islands Forum joint communiques since 1993, and Lin said he was not the first Taiwanese foreign minister to attend the gathering. He accused China of acting against the host country’s wishes and described its declaration of Palau as an unsafe travel destination as “absurd.”
China's warning of “consequences” drew pushback from Pacific leaders, with former US Ambassador to Palau John Hennessey-Niland saying China’s attempt to influence whom the forum invited and what it discussed “backfired,” per Nikkei Asia. Palau President Surangel Whipps Jr. reaffirmed Taiwan’s status as a development partner and said it would continue participating in the forum.
Lin said China’s threats were accompanied by actions, such as a surprise July launch of a nuclear-capable intercontinental ballistic missile that overflew several Pacific nations before splashing down in the exclusive economic zones of Kiribati and Tuvalu. Australia, New Zealand, Vanuatu, Palau, and other countries raised concerns that China provided no prior notice of the test.
Seventeen of the forum’s 18 members supported language expressing concern over the test and calling on countries conducting ICBM tests to provide at least 24 hours’ advance notice, with Naoero, the sole dissenter, Nikkei Asia reported.
Lin also confirmed reports that Chinese operatives and espionage activity were observed around the summit venue, according to Liberty Times. He thanked the Palauan government for strengthening security and accused Beijing of infringing on the sovereignty and human rights of other countries.
He criticized China’s Belt and Road Initiative and what he described as its use of “elite capture,” saying Beijing had left countries facing financial difficulties. He said that although a small number of forum members had attempted to block consensus on the declaration, China’s increasingly domineering behavior could strengthen international support for Taiwan.
Taiwan, Lin said, would continue promoting its Diplomatic Allies Prosperity Project, citing extensive talks with other countries during the summit, Liberty Times reported. He said Taiwan was also among the first to support a Pacific resilience fund aimed at helping small nations address climate change, digital resilience, and food security.
The term "wolf warrior" refers to a Chinese propaganda movie that depicts the People's Liberation Army fighting foreign mercenaries in a fictional African country. The term has been adopted by international analysts to describe a Chinese diplomatic tactic of aggressively lashing out at critics online and in person.

Medieval manuscripts made from animal skin reveal ancient history of deadly sheep virus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:36:28 UTC
15:36:28 KST

Hidden in the pages of medieval manuscripts, researchers have found DNA traces of a deadly sheep virus dating back thousands of years.
In the Middle Ages, most texts were written on sheep, goat and cattle skin, used as a writing material and known as parchment.
It is in some of Europe’s famous ancient manuscripts that researchers found clues into the history of the deadly sheep pox virus — a viral disease of sheep that causes fever, skin lesions, and death. Such traces can help scientists to understand how pathogens evolved and how they impacted past societies.
An international team of geneticists, historians, virologists, protein chemists and conservators, led by scientists at University College Dublin, has extracted DNA from the skin used to make these centuries-old documents.
“The recording of ancient DNA of pathogens has completely changed our understanding of infectious disease in the past, and here we show that parchment can also preserve animal pathogen DNA,” said Louis L’Hôte, lead author of the study.
Among the works analysed were the 1,000-year-old York Gospels — one of the finest illuminated manuscripts to survive from the late Anglo-Saxon period — as well as earlier texts such as the Corpus Glossary at Corpus Christi College in Cambridge, regarded as one of the earliest English dictionaries. Other medieval texts examined came from across Britain and continental Europe.
“It is possible that archives and libraries around the world also contain the genetic traces of disease outbreaks in animals in the past”.
Sheep pox is a highly contagious disease that spreads rapidly and can affect large portions of a flock in a short time. It can cause significant economic losses due to decreased milk production, poor quality of hides and wool and trade restrictions. There is no evidence that sheep pox can infect humans.
The study, published in Science Advances, found that in some cases, multiple pages from the same manuscript contained sheep pox virus DNA, suggesting that infected animals were used to produce them.
The researchers combined the DNA found in the manuscripts with older samples from Bronze Age sheep teeth, and found that the disease has threatened livestock for over 3,700 years.
“Ancient genomes can help us understand how these pathogens affecting us today evolved. We find that unlike the smallpox virus, the sheeppox virus genome was very stable over the last few millennia,” added L’Hôte.
“This might mean that genetic changes before this point were very important to how the sheep pox virus evolved to infect its host, which may help us fight the pathogen in the future.”

Two senior Reform UK officials resign as Farage faces fresh foreign donations scandal

Two senior Reform UK officials resign as Farage faces fresh foreign donations scandal
Two senior officials from the hard-right Reform UK party stepped down Friday following a hidden-camera investigation that appeared to show them soliciting substantial foreign funding for party-commissioned opinion polls and a potential £500,000 donation from a US donor – banned under UK law.
British hard-right leader Nigel Farage sought to play down a fresh donations scandal Friday sparked by an undercover sting operation that overshadowed his Reform UK party's annual conference.
Farage had been hoping to use the gathering to move on from damaging controversies over financial gifts by setting out the policies of any future Reform government, including cooperation with France's far-right anti-immigrant National Rally (RN) party.
But just hours before Farage's keynote address, two senior Reform officials resigned following an investigation aired by Channel 4 News.
Watch more‘Major potential breaches of British election law’: Inside Channel 4’s investigation into Reform UK
The investigation showed two senior party figures arranging for a US company to pay more than £30,000 for three opinion polls commissioned by the party.
The report also included undercover footage that showed the party discussing steps to secure a £500,000 foreign donation – banned under UK electoral law.
Posing as wealthy donors from the United States with British connections, the undercover team from investigative group Verbatim said it spent a year speaking to officials in Reform about possible donations, culminating in a lunch with Farage.
Channel 4 said Verbatim was an independent organisation founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting, but that it had verified their findings, which included covertly filmed footage of meetings. The footage at one point shows Farage thanking the would-be donors.
Reform said in a statement that policy head James Orr and Farage's longtime aide Dan Jukes had stepped down from their roles pending the outcome of an internal probe into the sting.
The ruling Labour party was among rival parties to say they had reported Reform to police over claims it took funding from a US firm for three opinion polls it commissioned earlier this year, as well as the alleged proposal to channel a larger overseas donation through a UK intermediary.
Farage, 62, is already under parliamentary investigation over a £5 million donation from crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne in 2024. He denies any wrongdoing.
'Entrapment'
Speaking to reporters, Farage dismissed suggestions that Reform had previously taken disguised foreign donations as "loose pub talk" but acknowledged that comments by Orr and Jukes in the footage were "injudicious at best".
In his keynote address to a packed conference hall, a defiant Farage condemned the undercover filming as a "prolonged exercise in entrapment".
"The party has done nothing wrong. The party has taken no illegal money," he said to cheers and applause from the floor.
Attendees at the conference in the central English city of Birmingham also played down the allegations.
"I just think they (opponents) are so worried about Reform, it's attack, attack, attack all the time," 62-year-old nurse Heather Kynman said.
Darren Ball, another delegate, predicted the furore would not knock Reform's prospects.
"Reform is the only party that can save this country. Immigration is a huge thing for the UK. It needs to be addressed," said the 51-year-old, who works in security.
'Deploy the Royal Navy'
The party's main focus is its anti-immigration policies, in particular ending the arrival of thousands of irregular migrants by small boat on England's southern coast.
Setting out the party's pledges on immigration, home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf told the conference a Reform government would "deploy the Royal Navy to stop the boats" and "remove every foreign national who entered this country illegally".
The conference was also addressed by Jordan Bardella, president of France's far-right National Rally party.
He promised that under a National Rally government France would no longer be the "gateway for illegal immigration into the UK".
He and Farage announced a memorandum of understanding to cooperate on the issue should their parties each win power.
Britain's centre-left Labour government has said the number of boats carrying migrants and asylum seekers across the Channel was the lowest this summer since 2019, in part because of existing cooperation deals with the French government.
Regain momentum
Farage has been seeking to regain the momentum that saw Reform chalk up significant success at May local elections.
Security was tight at the conference centre but Farage's speech to conference was repeatedly interrupted by shouting protesters who were booed as they were removed by security.
During a speech by Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice a climate protest banner depicting Farage in a top hat and reading "Collect £5 million, burn the planet" appeared for several minutes before being taken down.
Tice is also facing allegations that he failed to declare financial gifts.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

UN adopts resolution in favor of Equal Earth cartographic projection in world maps
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
14:27:57 CST
15:27:57 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to adopt a non-binding resolution that encourages the use of the Equal Earth cartographic projection in maps worldwide to replace the Mercator projection widely used so far, which distorts the sizes of continental landmasses.
The resolution of "Correct the Map" aimed at rebalancing global cartographic representation and promoting equitable representation of the world's regions, particularly Africa, was adopted with 164 votes in favor, 1 against, and 6 abstentions.
The United States was the only member state that voted against it. Six countries -- Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia, Ukraine -- abstained.
Declaring that the Equal Earth cartographic projection offers a more accurate representation of the sizes of continental landmasses and, to this end, is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world, the resolution encourages UN member states, international organizations and other relevant entities to adopt, disseminate and use the Equal Earth cartographic projection and equal area map projection methods.
It recognizes that the Mercator projection, widely used around the world, distorts continental masses located far from the equator, resulting in a proportional shrinkage of Africa and other regions.
It affirms that cartographic distortions of continental sizes inherited from history have cognitive, educational, cultural, geopolitical and socioeconomic impacts and constitute historical biases, the correction of which will promote recognition, justice and development, particularly concerning the African continent.
The resolution further encourages the development of international standards aimed at ensuring more accurate representation of the sizes of continents in digital and printed mapping tools, in accordance with relevant UN frameworks. ■

====================================================================================================

Study says OpenAI-linked AI agents used wiki to communicate, collaborate
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
14:27:31 CST
15:27:31 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- A group of autonomous artificial intelligence agents believed by researchers to be linked to OpenAI used a public German-language wiki earlier this year to communicate with one another, share answers to assigned tasks and exchange methods for bypassing restrictions in their operating environments, according to an independent study released Friday.
The study was conducted by four researchers, including Sydney Von Arx of the AI safety organization Nightingale Collective.
The researchers said they found about 18,000 posts made by autonomous AI agents self-identified as being from OpenAI while using the public internet to communicate during web-retrieval tasks. The researchers described the behavior as collaboration that gave the agents an advantage on their assigned tasks in ways their developers did not intend.
Most of the activity took place on DSEWiki, a German-language wiki that has existed for about 25 years and had seen little use in recent years. According to the researchers, the agents were apparently supposed to be able to read information on the internet but not write to it. They nevertheless found ways to post information to the wiki and used it to exchange answers, pool research results and share techniques for circumventing sandbox restrictions.
The researchers first observed agents attempting to edit a public wiki on May 11 and recorded their first successful write to DSEWiki on May 24. Large-scale coordination began on June 16, when agents started exchanging answers and timing information about subsequent rounds of their tasks. Records cited in the study show that agents that encountered questions earlier sometimes posted answers that were later used by agents receiving the same questions.
The study also found that agents discussed and tested methods for getting around sandbox network restrictions. After a human moderator began deleting pages, some agents created backup pages with names beginning with "ZZZ" in an apparent effort to make them less likely to be deleted first.
About 98.5 percent of agent edits on DSEWiki came from Microsoft Azure IP addresses, while researchers also recorded visits from IP addresses associated with OpenAI. Many agents also used names containing references to OpenAI. Based on this and other evidence, the researchers said the agents were likely deployed internally by OpenAI.
The researchers cautioned, however, that their analysis was preliminary and based only on information the agents left on the public wiki. They did not have access to the agents' chain-of-thought data held internally by OpenAI and said questions about the agents' motivations and strategies remained unresolved. The study said it was unclear whether the tasks were part of model training or testing.
An OpenAI spokesperson said that the company had not been given an opportunity to review the report before publication and therefore could not meaningfully respond to its claims or findings at the time.
The spokesperson said OpenAI would carefully review the report after publication and take any necessary next steps.
OpenAI also said the wiki activity was unrelated to the separate Hugging Face incident in July and therefore would not have been included in its report on that incident. ■

U.S. regulator opens probe into Tesla Cybercab self-certification
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
14:27:19 CST
15:27:19 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said Friday that it has opened an investigation into Tesla's certification that its new Cybercab meets all applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS).
The probe, formally designated as an Audit Query, was opened on Sept. 3 and covers an estimated 1,000 Cybercab vehicles, according to an NHTSA investigation document. It will examine the process and technical data Tesla relied upon when certifying the Cybercab, as well as related issues.
Tesla began commercial deployment of a small number of Cybercab vehicles in Austin, Texas, on Thursday and notified the agency that it had certified the vehicles as compliant with all applicable FMVSS. Tesla also told the NHTSA that it plans to gradually expand commercial deployment of the Cybercab to include additional vehicles and locations.
The vehicles lack permanently attached conventional manual controls, such as a brake pedal, gas pedal, steering wheel and mirrors, according to the NHTSA.
The agency said the inquiry will examine, among other issues, the extent to which Tesla's certification depended on determinations that certain FMVSS are inapplicable to the Cybercab.
In the United States, the NHTSA establishes vehicle performance requirements, while automakers must certify that their vehicles meet applicable standards before entering the U.S. market, subject to agency oversight to confirm compliance. The NHTSA said it conducts investigations when certified vehicles appear not to adhere to those requirements.
NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said the agency fully supports the safe development and deployment of automated vehicles, but stressed that as the federal regulator it must ensure that applicable laws are followed.
The NHTSA said it is in the process of overhauling federal vehicle safety standards and has begun work on eight rulemakings over the last year, including standards relating to brake pedals, windshield wipers, lighting and rearview mirrors.
Existing standards will remain in force until that work is completed, the agency said. ■

Xinhua Commentary: Chinese modernization forges new opportunities for Asia-Pacific community
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
14:27:09 CST
15:27:09 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- As China hosts the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this year, three words stand out in its agenda: openness, innovation and cooperation. They are also three important ways in which Chinese modernization is creating new opportunities for the Asia-Pacific.
This is particularly relevant as the Asia-Pacific Media Forum 2026 brings together media representatives to discuss the region's development and future. While the discussion goes beyond the media community, it highlights a pressing question: how development opportunities can translate into broader prosperity across the region.
Openness means more opportunities to connect with China's growth.
The Chinese modernization is taking place in an economy deeply integrated with the Asia-Pacific. China accounts for more than a quarter of APEC's combined GDP, while its trade and investment ties with regional economies continue to strengthen.
The scale of China-ASEAN economic ties offers a telling example. In 2025, trade between China and ASEAN reached 7.55 trillion yuan, or more than 1 trillion U.S. dollars, up 8 percent year-on-year. ASEAN remained China's largest trading partner.
As Chinese consumers demand more diverse goods and services and Chinese industries continue to upgrade, this large and growing market creates space for businesses across the region. Openness therefore does more than keep trade flowing. It allows China's development to generate demand and opportunities beyond its borders.
Innovation means more possibilities for new growth.
Chinese modernization is also being driven by technological progress and the green and digital transformation of the economy. In 2025, China's expenditure on research and development reached 3.93 trillion yuan, or about 551 billion dollars, up 8.1 percent from the previous year and equivalent to 2.8 percent of GDP.
For the Asia-Pacific, the significance of such innovation goes beyond the technologies themselves. A vast market and strong industrial capacity can help turn new technologies into products and applications on a large scale. As green and digital technologies become more widely applied, they can create new demand, new industries and new opportunities for businesses across the region.
This is closely aligned with APEC's own innovation agenda, as APEC economies are discussing open innovation, cross-border knowledge flows and cooperation in areas including artificial intelligence, digital transformation and green development.
Cooperation means turning opportunities into shared gains.
No economy can address today's development challenges alone. For the Asia-Pacific, where economies differ widely in their levels of development, industrial structures and capabilities, cooperation can help turn differences into complementarity and make development more inclusive.
Chinese modernization places strong emphasis on coordinated development and common prosperity. In practice, China's manufacturing capacity, technological advances and large market can complement the resources, industries and markets of other Asia-Pacific economies, creating more room for trade, investment and industrial cooperation.
This is particularly important for the Asia-Pacific, where APEC's 21 economies differ widely in their levels of development and economic structures. The region's diversity need not be a divide. With cooperation, it can become a source of strength.
As APEC economies look ahead, openness can widen access to markets, innovation can open up new sources of growth, and cooperation can turn differences into shared strengths. Together, they can help translate development opportunities into tangible benefits for people across the region.
This is how Chinese modernization can make a meaningful contribution to the Asia-Pacific: by opening up more space for shared development and helping turn the vision of an Asia-Pacific community into reality. ■

Interview: Closer media cooperation can help build consensus across region: journalists association chief
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
14:26:59 CST
15:26:59 KST

BANGKOK, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- Closer cooperation among Asia-Pacific media organizations in areas such as fact-checking, news resources sharing, and joint reporting can help build consensus and foster greater understanding across the region amid challenges brought by artificial intelligence (AI), Kamphol Mahanukul, president of the Thai-Chinese Journalists Association, has said.
He made the remarks in an interview here with Xinhua ahead of his trip to the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen to attend the Asia-Pacific Media Forum, which opened Saturday.
Kamphol said media cooperation is closely linked to regional cooperation under the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) framework. Media organizations, as the force of news reporting and information dissemination, should strengthen direct exchanges and expand practical cooperation, according to him.
He pointed to the challenges posed by AI and misinformation, such as the rise of independent online content creators, and lower barriers to news production and distribution. "Today, anyone with a mobile phone can become a so-called 'journalist'. But we still hope the public will trust mainstream media."
Mainstream media outlets operate under established institutional frameworks and can be held accountable for the information they publish, Kamphol noted.
A news report typically goes through several stages, from news gathering and writing to editorial review, verification and final approval, he said, adding that by contrast, online content creation might prioritize attracting traffic and publishing quickly for direct conversion into revenue, and as a result, unverified information can be produced and disseminated more readily.
"In the past, radio was the fastest medium; then it was television; over the past decade, it has been the Internet," Kamphol said. "Everyone is trying to be the first to publish, and that increases the risk of mistakes."
AI can help newsrooms monitor breaking events and assist with writing, copy editing and fact-checking, he noted. However, he stressed that verifying facts, exercising professional judgment and taking responsibility for published reports remain fundamental duties of media organizations.
Over more than 10 years since its establishment, the Thai-Chinese Journalists Association has promoted news exchanges, mutual visits by journalists and professional training between the two sides.
Thai media professionals had traveled to China for training in the use of AI and new-media content production, while media organizations on both sides were expanding the sharing of news resources, Kamphol said.
After media organizations establish stable partnerships, they can share such visual materials as photos and videos more efficiently with proper authorization, he noted.
A journalist with more than 20 years of career experience, Kamphol pointed to differences among media organizations across the region in cultural context, reporting practices and forms of expression. He views the Asia-Pacific Media Forum in Shenzhen as a platform for participants to share experience in news gathering and editing, and discuss the use of AI in news production.
Looking ahead, Kamphol expressed hope that media organizations in the region will expand exchanges and cooperation in professional training and the use of AI, while deepening collaboration in sharing text, photo and video resources and jointly covering major developments.
"I hope credible media organizations and journalist associations in Thailand, China and across the Asia-Pacific can build a more stable and lasting platform for cooperation," he said. ■

What would an AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt really mean?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:25:00 UTC
15:25:00 KST

What would an AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt really mean?
September 5, 2026
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) could bring in massive changes should it form a government in Saxony-Anhalt. The far-right party, currently way ahead in opinion polls, is hoping to form a single-party government and have its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, serve as state premier.
The Saxony-Anhalt chapter of the AfD is classified by the domestic intelligence agency as "confirmed far-right."
Radical tightening of asylum laws
In its draft government program, the AfD has promised "deportation from minute one!" if it wins the election in Saxony-Anhalt. The stated goal, according to the party's election program, is simply to deport as many immigrants who have no residency permits as possible.
The party has also pledged much stricter asylum rules at all levels: It wants more detention pending deportation, mandatory work for asylum-seekers, and intends to cut all state funding for integration programs, which it refers to as an "asylum industry."
Furthermore, it wants to exclude children and adolescents who do not have permanent residency in Germany from attending regular schools. On top of that, a "Remigration Task Force" is to be established within the state government to coordinate the state's asylum policy.
Exactly how many of these measures an AfD state government would be legally able to implement remains unclear. Creating special classes for refugees could, for example, be a violation of international and European law.
And the question of who can and can't be deported falls under the jurisdiction of the federal government, not that of an individual state.
Anti-immigration policy
The AfD opposes immigration to Germany. In its government platform, the party calls for a "180-degree turnaround in migration policy," and its stated goal is to reduce the number of immigrants in Saxony-Anhalt.
However, the region has been suffering for years from a shortage of skilled workers, particularly in nursing and care for the elderly. The AfD's plan to end this shortage is to encourage Germans who live abroad to come back.
To this end, it plans to launch a "return program," including a proposed "return bonus" to help find housing and daycare spots for children. It is unclear how many returnees the AfD anticipates and how much money it has budgeted for the "return program."
Saxony-Anhalt has been severely affected by depopulation for over 30 years. No other German state population has shrunk more since reunification in 1990 — from around 2.9 million people then to 2.1 million today.
Economic researchers like Reint Gropp, president of the Halle Institute for Economic Research, have warned that an AfD government is likely to exacerbate the skilled worker shortage.
"Highly qualified professionals, in particular, have options," he told Die Welt newspaper on Tuesday. "If they feel they are unwelcome or can expect hostility, they will choose other regions."
Rapprochement with Russia
The 16 state governments have virtually no authority over Germany's foreign and defense policy, though they can influence political debates via the Bundesrat, the chamber of parliament that represents the states. In that context, an AfD state premier would carry considerable political weight.
For example, since the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022, Germany has largely halted oil imports, but the AfD's election platform calls for a rapprochement with Russia and an end to sanctions.
The call is largely symbolic, as Saxony-Anhalt is bound by federal sanctions, but an AfD state premier could set a new tone in the Bundesrat.
The AfD also wants to expand Russian language instruction in schools and specifically recruit native Russian speakers for this purpose.
On Ukraine, meanwhile, the AfD is taking a harder line, calling for a "return offensive" for Ukrainian refugees. Again, a state government cannot deport Ukrainians from Germany — that is regulated by federal policy.
Establishing citizen patrols
Particularly controversial is the AfD's call for a kind of auxiliary police force. The regular police are "overwhelmed" by the task of ensuring security, according to the AfD's program for Saxony-Anhalt: "We will therefore establish a voluntary citizen patrol as a third pillar of the local security architecture."
Legal scholar and criminologist Thomas Feltes, of Ruhr University Bochum, warns against the idea. "It is the police's duty to ward off dangers and ensure the protection of the public. Only the police are authorized to use force in doing so," he wrote in a column for the outlet Legal Tribune Online.
A "citizen patrol," he said, would basically be a vigilante group that would have a negative effect on public safety: "Where such groups are active, the fear of crime is only stoked — not only among the participants, but above all among everyone else, and not just among 'concerned' citizens," he wrote.
Radical change in social policy
A central tenet of the AfD's governing platform is so-called identity politics. It aims to promote a positive image of German history, and advocates a fundamentally different view of the country's past. The party describes the process of coming to terms with German crimes during the Nazi era as the "perpetuation of a guilt complex" and wants to change school curricula accordingly.
It has also declared war on social diversity: Rainbow flags, as symbols of diversity, are to be banned in schools. It rejects the world-famous Bauhaus architecture — which flourished in Saxony-Anhalt — as "too globalist" and calls for a "patriotic cultural policy."
To that end, it wants to redirect funding away from the many pro-democracy projects that receive state funding for their work. In its platform, the AfD has rejected any continuation of these payments.

Visitors urge Hong Kong to ease restrictions as Sai Kung trail registration begins
Hundreds visit Po Pin Chau trail on the first day of a real-name booking system, with some calling for less rigid rules and greater flexibility
Hundreds of Hong Kong residents and visitors braved the heat on Saturday morning to visit a popular Sai Kung trail overlooking hexagonal rock columns, as a trial reservation system requiring real-name registration came into force, with some calling for the restrictions to be eased.
The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department announced the arrangement last month, capping visitor numbers at 2,000 per designated day between 9am and 5pm for the Po Pin Chau section of the High Island Geo Trail.
The measure is Hong Kong’s first countryside real-name reservation system of its kind.
Department director Mickey Lai Kin-ming said that, as of 10.10am, about 140 visitors had arrived at Po Pin Chau – a figure similar to that on previous weekends.
The verification process had gone smoothly and about 50 unused slots had been released to walk-in visitors, he added.
Lai said that the first two slots on Saturday – at 9am and 11am – were fully booked and that the department had stationed more than 40 staff members at the entrance, the verification point and along the trail to help.

EXPLAINER - From Ethiopia border to Darfur: Where are Sudan’s war fronts heating up?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:19:05 UTC
15:19:05 KST

Sudan’s most active battlefronts stretch across a vast arc from the Blue Nile state near the Ethiopian border in the east, through three Kordofan states, to Darfur in the west.
Al-Baraka, Bakori, Geissan and Kurmuk in the Blue Nile; Bara, Al-Abbasiya and Kauda in Kordofan; and Um Baru, Kernoi and Abu Suruj in Darfur have emerged as some of the most significant centers of fighting and military movement.
Control of the areas is divided among the army, the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and armed groups allied with each side. Drone attacks have increasingly carried the war into towns and villages far from traditional front lines.
Anadolu reviewed the main hotspots, their military significance and the current balance of control.
Al-Baraka, in the Kurmuk locality in the southeastern Blue Nile state, has become one of the newest fronts between the army on one side and the RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), on the other.
The area lies on the outskirts of Kurmuk near the Ethiopian border, giving it strategic importance for movements between border zones and the interior of Blue Nile.
On Friday, the army said it repelled an attack by the RSF and SPLM-N on Al-Baraka.
The army’s 4th Infantry Division said forces inflicted personnel and equipment losses on the attackers and forced them to retreat toward the Sudan-Ethiopia border.
Bakori, in the Geissan locality, is another key hotspot in Blue Nile.
The area hosts a military base and the headquarters of the army’s 14th Brigade, making it a contested position for both sides.
Bakori lies 170 kilometers (106 miles) southeast of Damazin, the state capital.
In recent weeks, the RSF and SPLM-N have taken control of Geissan and Kurmuk, the administrative centers of the two localities bearing the same names.
The army, however, continues to hold other parts of both localities, as well as Damazin, Er Roseires and the localities of Bau, Wad al-Mahi and Tadamon.
Beyond Kurmuk and Geissan, the SPLM-N, led by Abdelaziz al-Hilu, has controlled Yabus since 2011.
The area, one of the movement’s main strongholds in Blue Nile, lies near the borders with Ethiopia and South Sudan, around 80 kilometers from Kurmuk.
The SPLM-N has fought the Sudanese government since 2011, demanding greater autonomy in Blue Nile and South Kordofan before joining forces with the RSF during the current war.
In North Kordofan, Bara remains one of the most strategically important towns because of its location on the national highway linking it to Omdurman, west of the national capital, Khartoum.
In late July, the army retook Bara, Jabra al-Sheikh and Um Sayala, allowing it to secure the highway and reshape the military balance in the state bordering Darfur and West Kordofan.
Fighting around Bara has since shifted largely from direct ground clashes to drone attacks on military positions and villages surrounding the town.
Villages west of Bara that contain no military deployments have also come under RSF attacks, according to the Emergency Lawyers and the Sudan Doctors Network.
Other military movements are concentrated in northwestern North Kordofan, where the RSF controls Hamrat al-Sheikh, Al-Mazroub and Sodari.
Their importance stems from their proximity to Darfur and West Kordofan, and their location along movement and supply routes connecting the two regions.
North Kordofan has also faced repeated drone attacks, alongside similar strikes in South and West Kordofan.
In South Kordofan, Kadugli and Dilling remain among the most important army-held positions.
The army broke the siege on both cities months ago, and strengthened its control in large parts of the state, except for areas still held by the SPLM-N under al-Hilu.
Although major ground fighting around the two cities has subsided, both continue to face intermittent drone attacks that have killed and wounded civilians.
The Al-Abbasiya locality has become another hotspot in South Kordofan amid repeated attacks and deteriorating security conditions.
On Thursday, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said 6,420 people had been displaced from nine villages in Al-Abbasiya because of worsening insecurity from Sept. 1 to 2.
Kauda, in the far south of South Kordofan, remains under SPLM-N control and is one of the movement’s most important strongholds.
Alongside its role in the broader conflict between the SPLM-N and the government, Kauda has also witnessed local fighting between SPLM-N forces and members of the Otoro tribe because of a land dispute.
The clashes began in late June after a dispute about border demarcation between the Shawaya and Otoro tribes escalated into armed conflict, killing dozens and displacing thousands.
North Darfur remains one of the most active fronts in the Darfur region, with the army and the Joint Force of Armed Movements conducting operations against the RSF.
The Joint Force includes armed groups such as the Sudan Liberation Movement, led by Minni Arko Minnawi, and the Justice and Equality Movement, led by Jibril Ibrahim.
Um Baru and Karnoi have emerged as key hotspots after the army and Joint Force gained control of large parts of both localities.
Their proximity to the Chadian border makes them important bases for advancing into other parts of North Darfur and securing supply routes in the state.
In West Darfur, army and Joint Force movements have been concentrated north of El Geneina, the state capital.
In June, the forces captured Kulbus, about 160 kilometers north of El Geneina, before withdrawing more than two weeks later and repositioning around the town.
The army and the Joint Force later took Bir Saliba and Jebel Moon north of El Geneina as part of efforts to expand their foothold in the state.
On Aug. 29, West Darfur Gov. Bahr al-Din Adam Karama said the army and the Joint Force had taken control of Abu Suruj in the Sirba locality following clashes with the RSF.
Abu Suruj is among the latest areas where territorial control has shifted in West Darfur as military movements continue north of El Geneina.
The RSF and allied forces still control most of Darfur, while the army and the Joint Force maintain positions in parts of the region’s north and west.
Despite the different strategic value of each front, displacement remains the most consistent consequence of the widening conflict.
In Blue Nile, the IOM said 3,000 people had been displaced from three villages in the Kurmuk locality, while the UN estimated that 22,000 people fled fighting in Geissan in one week.
In South Kordofan, 6,420 people were displaced from villages in Al-Abbasiya, in addition to thousands forced from their homes by the conflict in Kauda.
The growing use of drones has also expanded the threat well beyond frontline areas. The UN said 1,100 civilians were killed in drone attacks between January and June.
The army and RSF have been at war since April 2023 because of disputes surrounding the political transition and plans to integrate the paramilitary force into the regular military.
As front lines continue to shift between Blue Nile, Kordofan and Darfur, Sudan’s map of military hotspots remains fluid, with no clear prospect of an end to the war.
