Lithuanian comedians take stage at Edinburgh Fringe: ‘Here you are naked’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Amid 4,000-plus shows at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, four Lithuanian artists took to the stage in theatre and stand-up shows, including award-winning actress Ingeborga Dapkūnaitė and rising stars of the British comedy circuit Evaldas Karosas, Justina Seselskaitė and Donatas Staneika.
In Scotland’s capital city, the world’s largest international arts festival was in full swing for three weeks from 7-31 August, with more than 61,000 performances taking place.
LRT met four Lithuanian artists performing solo Fringe shows.
Ingeborga Dapkūnaitė: a family history and the story of a nation on stage
With no props other than a single chair, Ingeborga Dapkūnaitė invites the audience to imagine her childhood apartment in Soviet-occupied Vilnius through storytelling and mime.
In four Christmas Eve scenes, she conjures her family around the dinner table, sharing kleckai dumplings, herring, as well as poppyseed milk with kūčiukai biscuits. While the number of people changes over time, the traditions remain.
Dapkūnaitė’s one-woman play, A Pebble in the Road, follows three generations of Lithuanian women and the turbulent history shaping the country around them.
Fond memories are interwoven with snapshots of dark history and double lives, of arrests, deportations, bullets and death.
The story was inspired by Dapkūnaitė’s grandmother Genovaitė – her beloved babutė –who was born in 1905 and lived to 103, spanning the final years of the Russian Empire, two world wars, Soviet occupation and the restoration of Lithuanian independence.
At the end of the show – just one of Dapkūnaitė’s 24 performances – a Lithuanian fan runs onto the stage with flowers. Soon after, she receives a second bouquet.
“My grandmother represents the 20th century of Lithuania for me,” Dapkūnaitė said. “But I realised that I couldn’t tell her story without my family story. Then I realised that my family story might be interesting not only to Lithuanians, but it reflects the story of a country. We cannot talk about anybody, in my view, in a vacuum.”
She recalls her Soviet diplomat father responding to the question ‘How’s life?’ with: “Like a pebble in the road, whoever isn’t lazy kicks me” – a response that speaks to the violence and upheaval inflicted on Lithuania throughout the 20th century.
Dapkūnaitė also echoes her grandfather Stasys, who said: “You should speak the languages of your neighbours because you never know who’s going to march in and when.”
Above all, it’s a story of resilience and the joy that can coexist alongside trauma.
“All of these people tried to survive in their own way, and as a family,” Dapkūnaitė said. “Life passes very quickly, and all you remember is the most vivid memories, whether it’s a hook that held granny’s door open, or the food you had.”
‘Close to home’
Many Lithuanians have come to watch the performance, including Lithuania’s ambassador to the UK, Asta Radikaitė and cultural attaché Ūla Tornau.
But in addition to the Baltic and Eastern European audience, for whom this history is so familiar, the show has opened the eyes of other visitors.
“A lot of Americans say: ‘Oh my God, we found out so many things that we didn’t know about,’” Dapkūnaitė said. “It’s educational.”
As Russia’s war in Ukraine continues and hybrid threats to the Baltic region persist, the history recounted in the play takes on contemporary significance. Dapkūnaitė left Moscow in 2022 and now lives in London.
“Many Ukrainians come, and they say very nice things, but also tell very painful things,” Dapkūnaitė said. “The show is very close to home for them.”
Dapkūnaitė has performed on some of the world’s biggest stages, from London to New York. On screen, she was the lead actress in the 1994 Oscar-winning film Burnt By The Sun and starred in Mission Impossible and Seven Years in Tibet. But the more intimate, intense Fringe theatre format provides a unique challenge.
“Here, you are naked,” she said. “People either come, or they don’t. You have ten minutes to get into the venue, ten minutes to get out, and you either connect with your audience or you don’t. You develop your show by listening to the audience.”
Evaldas Karosas: A very capable – and funny – man
Striking a different tone is 32-year-old Evaldas Karosas, who is performing a debut Fringe hour of comedy in his set A Very Capable Man. His show promises a dose of cynical objectivity applied to the art of Western stand-up and is billed as an “uncomfortably accurate” hour exposing unspoken thoughts.
After growing up in Antanašė and Rokiškis, Karosas gigged in Vilnius before moving to Manchester, England in 2018 and later settling in London.
In Lithuania's smaller comedy scene, he couldn't work jokes to their full potential: "If you've told a new joke even just 50 times in Lithuania, everyone and their mother has heard it.”
He became a full-time comedian three years ago and reached the finals of the BBC New Comedy Awards in 2025. Earlier this year, he signed with Off The Kerb, one of the UK’s top talent agencies representing some of the biggest names in British comedy.
Karosas previously performed at the Fringe five years ago in a split bill with another comedian. Like many Fringe acts, they struggled to attract an audience – the average Fringe audience is rumoured to be somewhere between six and 20 people in size, with many performances attracting fewer, or none at all.
“I have a documentary on my YouTube channel about doing the Fringe back then, and it’s fun to watch,” Karosas said. “We just kept cancelling shows because we had no audience.”
Comedy that crosses borders
On the evening of September 3, however, the seats in an underground vault in one of Edinburgh’s most iconic music venues are filled. Karosas delivers an energetic set, skewering themes ranging from culture clashes between the Baltics, Eastern Europe and the UK, to men’s mental health and dating.
The audience responds with belly laughs – even if Karosas claims that by performing in his second language, he’s only at sixty percent of his comedic power.
But Karosas doesn’t plan to gig in Lithuanian anytime soon. “Changing languages is like boxing and then changing to karate,” he explains. “It’s still another martial art, but you have to relearn, and even if you have the fitness, the moves are different.”
Karosas assumes that his audiences will know little about Lithuania – and perhaps even struggle to place it on a map. A friend made a video game for audiences to play on their phones, introducing them to his backstory while they wait for the show.
“You have to find a common denominator and talk about being from a small country, which immediately adds context to make it more relatable,” he said. “But I think we now live in such a globalised world that it’s no longer about where you’re from, it’s about how old you are.”
A testing ground for bigger ambitions
While most comedians place importance on winning one of the many Fringe awards, Karosas is not here for prizes.
“For me, the Fringe is more like a tool than the goal,” he said. “It’s the only place where I can do 30 hours in a month. It’s crafting the hour slowly, to be very precise about what you cut.”
Scottish audiences in particular respond well to Karosas’s comedy, and he is supporting acclaimed Glaswegian comedian Kevin Bridges in his 2026 international tour alongside more hour-long London gigs.
Reviews of Karosas’s Fringe show are overwhelmingly positive, but during the festival, he’s avoiding the critics and staying firmly in a bubble.
“I think I’m having a good run objectively,” he said. “But once I leave Edinburgh, I’ll allow myself to peer out of the bubble and read the reviews.”
Justina Seselskaitė: a Lithuanian with a northern English soul
Also making her solo Fringe debut, Justina Seselskaitė is performing in Settled, a 45-minute stand-up show exploring her journey as an immigrant in northern England. She jokes about locals mistaking her nationality and quizzes the audience on Lithuanian covers of British and American songs.
32-year-old Seselskaitė moved from Šiauliai to Manchester in 2014 and had made a name for herself in the city’s booming comedy circuit.
In 2025, she performed in a split-bill and became a finalist in the Fringe’s So You Think You’re Funny? newcomer competition – a launchpad for some of Britain’s top comedians.
‘Shock’ recognition
This year – on top of glowing reviews – Seselskaitė was longlisted for the ISH Edinburgh Comedy Awards for Best Newcomer, which she described as “a total shock.”
“When you’ve worked so hard on something, having that recognised really puts everything into perspective.”
Some audience members relate to her through Lithuanian acquaintances.
“They love telling me about every Lithuanian they’ve ever met,” she said. “I genuinely love it every time! It’s always really sweet.”
Seselskaitė will be back at the Fringe next year for a debut hour of stand-up, but before then, she’ll be “gigging as much as possible, all over the place” and working on her new podcast, The Favourites Pod.
Donatas Staneika: the prolific gigger
Also looking to fill seats and raise laughs is 27-year-old comedian Donatas Staneika from Vilnius, who is performing for 30 minutes in a split-bill stand-up show called 1 British, 1 Immigrant *Continental Breakfast, alongside British-born Bangladeshi comedian Ridwan Hussain.
Staneika is eager to make the most of the Fringe. He has performed at more than 100 gigs and smaller spots during the festival so far, and has done eight gigs in a single day.
“It’s a lot, I’m constantly moving,” he said. “Stand-up is my favourite thing to do, so just getting to do it is a reward. It gives very quick feedback – if you come up with a joke on stage and it doesn’t work, you know immediately.”
The experience has enabled him to practise crowd work, improvisation and refine his set, which pokes fun at everything from Eastern European stereotypes, British accents and immigrant life.
“If my family came to the UK to live with me, I would have them deported myself,” he joked.
‘I think of comedy in English’
Staneika moved to London in 2020 to pursue a stand-up career, having never set foot on stage in Lithuania. He performs observational stand-up across London’s comedy clubs.
This year is Staneika’s second Fringe visit. In 2023, he entered the So You Think You’re Funny? competition and made the semi-finals. He has since been shortlisted twice in the BBC New Comedy Awards.
In October, Staneika might be performing in Lithuania – in English: “The comedy scene in Lithuania is growing and a few clubs have opened, so there is more stand-up now than ever before.” Whether he ever performs in Lithuanian remains to be seen.
“I grew up watching American and British stand-up comedians, so even though I have my own style, I think of comedy in English,” he said. “I feel like English is made for stand-up, as you can play on words.”
Between his Fringe gigs, he’s enjoying connecting with performers and visitors from all over the world.
“Comedy is universal,” he said.

Details

The Williams sisters have won 14 Grand Slam doubles titles and 3 Olympic gold medals together—in 2000, 2008, and 2012. At the US Open, they won the doubles title in 1999 and 2009.
Serena, 44, returned to professional tennis this year after a lengthy break, while Venus, 46, continued competing on tour. Earlier this summer, the sisters also lost in the deciding tiebreak of a doubles match at the tournament in Cincinnati.

Argentina sanctions 45 firms, individuals over UK-linked Falklands oil drilling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
04:57:23 UTC
13:57:23 KST

Argentina initiated on Friday sanction proceedings against 45 individuals and companies suspected of carrying out unauthorised hydrocarbon exploration and exploitation on the Falkland Islands, which Buenos Aires calls Islas Malvinas.
President Javier Milei's office announced that the legal measures target not only active oil firms but also "their shareholders and companies that have been providing services" to facilitate the operations.
It said those trying to profit by violating Argentinian sovereignty "will find in the Argentine State the full force of the law."
The government reaffirmed its claim on the Falkland Islands, South Georgia, and the South Sandwich Islands and their "corresponding maritime and insular spaces," declaring they are Argentine "by history and by law" and that there is "no question about it."
Milei warned earlier that the Sea Lion oil project, a major offshore hydrocarbon development near the Falklands operated by British firm Rockhopper Exploration and Israel-based Navitas Petroleum, poses an imminent threat.
He noted that without swift action, foreign entities will "appropriate the oil reserves that lie beneath our sea" and deepen their "occupation."
Falkland dispute
London dismissed the sanctions as domestic politics, asserting its commitment to the islands, while Navitas and its partners said they expect to proceed with drilling under UK licensing.
The long-standing sovereignty dispute between Buenos Aires and London was recently reignited as offshore projects move toward active drilling.
The Falklands are a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic, about 300 miles (483 kilometres) east of the Argentine coast, with a small population. 
Argentina argues that it inherited sovereignty from Spain, and Britain has “illegally occupied” the islands since 1833; it calls the islands Islas Malvinas and rejects the residents’ right to self‑determination as decisive.

Arieh Warshel first Nobel Prize winner to receive Taiwan Employment Gold Card
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
04:56:41 UTC
13:56:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Chemical scientist Arieh Warshel has become the first Nobel Prize winner to receive an Employment Gold Card, a milestone the National Development Council said underscores the nation’s growing appeal to elite global scientists.
NDC Minister Yeh Chun-hsien (葉俊顯) presented the card to Warshel at a National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University (NYCU) hosted ceremony, CNA reported Friday. Yeh described the move as a new benchmark for Taiwan’s efforts to attract and retain major talents.
Warshel is the first person with a Nobel Prize to obtain Taiwan’s Employment Gold Card since the program launched in 2018. The NDC commented that the award demonstrates Taiwan’s ability to draw talent, particularly in fields tied to semiconductors, AI computing and biomedicine.
Yeh described the Gold Card as a “Taiwan VIP pass,” saying it makes coming to Taiwan “as easy as going home” for top-tier experts like Warshel, per Liberty Times.
Warshel, a professor at the University of Southern California and member of the US National Academy of Sciences, shared the 2013 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Martin Karplus and Michael Levitt for the development of multiscale models for complex chemical systems.
In the 1970s, he pioneered methods combining quantum and classical mechanics to simulate biological processes such as enzyme catalysis. His work became foundational for computer-aided drug design, enzyme research and protein engineering — earning recognition as a pioneer of computational structural biology.
Warshel accepted an invitation earlier this year from NYCU’s International Graduate Program of Semiconductor Technology to serve as an honorary professor, CNA further reported. It is a role the NDC said will deepen cooperation in talent development, semiconductors and other key technologies.
The Employment Gold Card combines a work permit, resident visa, Alien Resident Certificate and re-entry permit. Key benefits include freedom to seek employment, change jobs or start a business without needing an employer-sponsored work permit. It also provides a shortened path to permanent residency.
Liberty Times reported the NDC as saying that attracting talent is not just about bringing people to Taiwan but ensuring they stay.

Interview: Australia-China PV collaboration powers world: Australian solar pioneer
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
12:44:44 CST
13:44:44 KST

Scientia Professor Martin Green of the University of New South Wales introduces solar modules in Sydney, Australia, Aug. 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Gong Bing)
SYDNEY, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- The winter sun shined bright outside the window of Scientia Professor Martin Green's office at the University of New South Wales (UNSW), Sydney, a quiet reminder of the very element he has spent a lifetime converting into energy.
The energetic 78-year-old engineer from UNSW's School of Photovoltaic and Renewable Energy Engineering is a leading pioneer in modern photovoltaics thanks to his decades of relentless innovation that changed the way the world harnesses solar power.
Green and his team have made pioneering contributions to the advancement of photovoltaic (PV) technology, particularly in improving the performance of silicon solar cells. The two technological pathways they pioneered have both become fundamental to modern silicon solar cell design.
Yet "an even more important achievement" and "the most exciting stuff" is "helping to get the PV industry established in China through the researchers and engineers that we had trained, who did so well in setting up a very competitive industry in China," Green told Xinhua just weeks after returning from Beijing, where he received the China International Science and Technology Cooperation Award for the year 2025.
The contact with China all started in 1981. Green's lab welcomed its first Chinese visiting researcher, and batches of them were trained here over the following decades. Some of them founded China's earliest PV companies.
In 1984, Green published a paper on the fundamental efficiency limit of silicon solar cells -- around 30 percent. That same year, he visited China for the first time, invited to lecture at Huazhong University of Science and Technology. He sensed the country's unmistakable potential as it was just beginning to modernize.
In Green's view, mainly with solar and batteries, China's green development has made a massive contribution to the world's green transition. It was the combination of China's massive manufacturing scale and Australia's continuous technological advancement that drove photovoltaics to become one of the world's cheapest sources of electricity.
"Without China's involvement, we definitely wouldn't have solar cells as cheap as now. It could be 10 times the price that they are now. Solar would still be an interesting technology for the future rather than the best option for now."
According to a report Green released in 2016, the flow-on economic benefits to Australia from decades of local photovoltaic research were worth well over 8 billion Australian dollars (about 5.74 billion U.S. dollars), heavily underpinned by the solar manufacturing industry in China.
"If I did the calculation again now, it would be hundreds of billions that it saved Australia by providing a cheap way of generating electricity and avoiding the imputed costs of all the carbon dioxide that we would have been emitting," he told Xinhua,
A frequent visitor to China's PV research institutes and manufacturers, Green observed that they are evolving rapidly. "All the companies are continually building new production lines to accommodate the improved equipment that's going to be available as well as the improved cell technology."
Today, silicon solar cells are approaching the fundamental efficiency limit of around 30 percent. To go further, Green said, the industry must stack new materials on top of silicon. The next chapter of solar power will be defined not by efficiency records, but by whether new cell technologies can stand the test of time in the real world. That is where his latest collaboration with China comes in.
"China dominates the industry, so that makes the collaboration sort of unique," Green said. "Working with China, we feel we're in a position to improve the solar performance more quickly."
"We've just started a big project using AI to find other candidates for stacking onto silicon," Green said. "With AI, it might provide a more systematic way of finding such new materials."
China, he noted, has been pushing hard on AI development, and that makes it an even more attractive partner for this next phase of discovery. "The more China improves AI, the more options we'll have using different AI to explore the available space and see if they can come up with ideas for new compounds," he said. ■

JAKARTA, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- Mount Anak Krakatau in Indonesia's South Lampung regency continued erupting Saturday morning, with booming and rumbling sounds heard from a nearby volcano observation post, authorities said.
The eruption began at 11:07 p.m. local time Friday, with lava fountains observed between midnight and 6 a.m. Saturday. The volcano remains at Level III, or Alert status, with authorities imposing a three-kilometer exclusion zone around its active crater.
Indonesia's Geological Agency said the volcano's structure, rebuilt following its 2018 eruption, remains relatively small and is currently not considered capable of collapsing on a scale that could trigger a tsunami.
"People do not need to panic, but they must remain vigilant," the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) said in a statement.
Authorities urged residents and tourists not to enter the restricted area or approach the volcano to watch or record the eruption. People in coastal areas of Banten and Lampung were also advised to follow official updates from the Geological Agency, BNPB and local authorities rather than unverified information. ■

Researchers in Australia develop new approach to deliver cancer drugs into brain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
12:44:32 CST
13:44:32 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia are developing a new class of cancer drugs that can break through the blood-brain barrier, a protective shield that currently blocks most drugs from ever entering the brain.
The national project, which has received 18.8 million Australian dollars (about 13.54 million U.S. dollars) in government funding, aims to develop brain-penetrating drugs that can overcome one of the biggest barriers to brain cancer treatment, according to a statement released recently by Australia's Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research (WEHI).
The blood-brain barrier strictly controls what can enter the brain to prevent toxins and infections from passing through, blocking around 98 percent of cancer drugs from reaching brain tissue, essential to maintaining the brain's overall health, the statement said.
Researchers plan to "hijack" the blood-brain barrier's natural nutrient delivery pathways to "smuggle cancer-killing molecules into the brain," said lead investigator Associate Professor Jim Whittle, a WEHI laboratory head.
The brain relies on the natural delivery systems to transport essential nutrients such as iron and glucose from the bloodstream. Cells in the blood-brain barrier contain specialized "docking stations" that recognize and actively draw these nutrients into the brain, according to researchers.
The approach could unlock a new class of brain-penetrating drugs and create an opportunity to test existing cancer drugs that have previously failed to reach the brain, Whittle said.
The researchers said the team will initially target high-grade gliomas, including glioblastoma in adults and diffuse midline glioma in children. ■

Seattle Times, Newsday sue OpenAI, Microsoft, alleging copyright infringement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
04:35:00 UTC
13:35:00 KST

Seattle Times, Newsday sue OpenAI, Microsoft, alleging copyright infringement
NEW YORK - The Seattle Times and Newsday sued OpenAI and Microsoft on Sept 4, alleging in federal court that the US tech companies copied the US newspapers’ journalism without permission to train their AI systems.
The suit in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York alleges that OpenAI and Microsoft scraped the newspapers’ websites, including content behind paywalls, and incorporated articles into datasets used to train and operate products including ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Bing’s AI features.
The newspapers, based in Seattle and Long Island, New York, said the companies’ AI products can reproduce passages from their reporting, closely paraphrase articles and provide users with answers that reduce the need to visit their websites or buy subscriptions.
“We feel strongly that we must defend our content - which we spend millions of dollars a year to produce - from being used without our consent or compensation,” Seattle Times President and CEO Alan Fisco wrote to employees, according to the newspaper.
A spokesperson for San Francisco-based OpenAI said its models are trained on publicly available data and grounded in fair use, without commenting specifically on the lawsuit.
A spokesperson for Microsoft, based near Seattle in Washington state, said in an email: “While we’re surprised by the lawsuit, we appreciate the importance of local journalism and we’re always happy to sit down and explore solutions to this type of dispute.”
The Seattle Times and Newsday are seeking an order requiring the destruction of copies of their works as well as training datasets or AI models incorporating them.
The lawsuit echoes a case filed by the New York Times in 2023, which accused OpenAI and Microsoft of using millions of newspaper articles without permission to train OpenAI’s popular chatbot. 
The case is ongoing, and is one of dozens brought by copyright holders against tech companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta for what they say is misuse of their material to train AI systems. REUTERS

‘Mini-dictatorship’: students slam far-right turn at Argentina-run residence in Paris
Residents allege surveillance and far-right meetings as they claim Argentina House at Cite Universitaire has become ‘a space of fear’
Weeks before President Javier Milei visits France, scrutiny has grown around an Argentina-run university residence in Paris supposed to promote peaceful coexistence but which activists say instead restricts lodger freedoms and hosts European far-right figures.
Paris city officials have demanded the foreign ministry investigate Argentina House, one of dozens of homes run by foreign nations or French institutions on an international campus in the French capital.
The Cite Universitaire campus, or Cite U, was set up after World War I as lodgings for youth to form lasting connections with their peers across the globe.
But campus sources and former house residents, most speaking anonymously for fear of reprisal, say that the one run by Argentina had gone awry since a Milei appointee, fervent Catholic lawyer Santiago Muzio, became its director in 2024.
“The house used to be a space for community, culture, and art. Today it’s a space of fear, control, surveillance, cameras,” said an Argentine who lived there during the last academic year.
Residents said their access to common areas such as the lounge or the outdoor barbecue – an epicentre for socialising in Argentine culture – had been restricted.

Japan has advanced a $550 billion investment deal in the U.S. in exchange for a 15% tariff. The new package will focus on AI and chips.
Japan and the United States have made progress in implementing a large-scale $550 billion investment deal, which became a key part of the agreement to reduce U.S. tariffs on Japanese goods. Artificial intelligence and semiconductors may now play an increasingly important role in new projects, Bloomberg reports, writes UNN.
Details

With the growing presence of the artificial intelligence and semiconductor industries, we continue to develop and implement projects that promote mutual benefit
Why the $550 billion deal matters
The investment mechanism became a central part of the trade agreement under which U.S. President Donald Trump agreed to impose a 15% tariff on Japanese goods and reduce the tariff on automobiles – an export sector that is critically important to Japan's economy.
The first package provides for $36 billion in investment in oil, gas, and raw materials projects in the United States. The second – another $73 billion in nuclear power and gas-fired power plants.
The parties are now working on a third package. Akazawa did not disclose its parameters, but noted that AI and semiconductors would carry "very significant weight" in the negotiations.
For Japan, there is another important outcome of the negotiations: the parties confirmed that the United States would not impose additional tariffs on Japanese goods beyond those already provided for by the trade agreement.

Country diary: The wild, riotous sounds of otters in battle | Cal Flyn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
04:30:26 UTC
13:30:26 KST

I hear them before I see them: a wailing, or something more like ululation. High-pitched, repeated vocalisations that are neither man nor cat, but somewhere in between. I throw open the cabin door, unsure what to look for, and for a moment see nothing new: only the rocky strand and the sweep of dark wrack high above the shoreline.
The strange, warbling sound comes again. Ai-ai-ai-ai. Not quite screaming, not quite howling, not quite trilling, but all of those things at once.
A flash of movement in the water, perhaps 50 metres out. A small, dark body leaps from the surf, followed smartly by another. My eyes struggle to understand what I’m looking at. Tiny figures catch a millisecond of clear air, then slice back through the surface, like dolphins or porpoises. But the silhouette is all wrong. And there, again – two small heads pop up, turn to one another, and seem to wrestle.
Ai-ai-ai-ai. Are they playing? Fighting? Their forms are slick and dark. When one launches again from the water, I see it clearly: four limbs, and a long tail – two otters, locked in battle. Over a fish perhaps, or one of the crabs we were watching earlier from the rowing boat as we drifted on the breeze, hands trailing through saline, watching the tiny creatures on the seabed below like tourists from a cable car.
They tussle and twist. Then one breaks free and makes a dash for the shoreline. The other shrieks and follows, both now skimming over the surface like stones.
What drama! You would hear them a mile away. The otters disappear behind a boulder, and for a moment all is silent but for the wash of the waves.
It has gone 8pm. The sun is lowering in the sky, ready for bed. The wind ruffles the heads of the trees on the island in the bay. A pair of little egrets pick their way through the shallows, pause to examine their surroundings, then move on, feet lifted high and deliberate. Then the voices come again. Ai-ai-ai-ai. The soap opera continues unseen.

‘I could not save the rest’: Hero nurse remembers Pakistan’s nursery fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
04:29:33 UTC
13:29:33 KST

‘I could not save the rest’: Hero nurse remembers Pakistan’s nursery fire
The PIMS nurse who saved one newborn recalls the fire, the screams and the 14 babies she could not save.
Islamabad, Pakistan – Staff nurse Razia Noreen was at a medicine cupboard on the nursery ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), Islamabad’s largest public-sector hospital. She was two doors from the babies in her care, preparing the morning’s injections.
As she shut the cupboard door, she saw through the nursery’s glass panel a light too sharp and too red to be anything ordinary. She did not wait to understand what it was.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Locked inside: Grief and anger as Pakistan hospital fire kills 14 newborns
- list 2 of 3At least 14 babies killed in Pakistan hospital nursery fire
- list 3 of 3Pakistan suspends eight officials over hospital fire that killed 14 babies
It was 6:38am on Wednesday, August 26. Elsewhere in the ward, her colleague, Sister Nasreen, was already running out, shouting for help.
At 56 seconds past 6:38am, according to security camera timestamps later logged by a government inquiry committee, Noreen rushed into the nursery.
Eight seconds later, she emerged carrying a baby. She tried to go back in. She could not. By 6:40am, the room was gone, swallowed by smoke so thick that the security cameras could no longer see through it.
Noreen was recalling this eight days later, in a plain office beside the hostel warden’s room at PIMS, dressed in a pale pink shalwar kameez, her dupatta loose over one shoulder.
“There was a proper blast,” she told Al Jazeera. “Everything turned to smoke.”
Fifteen newborns had been in that nursery. Fourteen died. The baby Noreen carried out was the only one who lived.
On Thursday, Noreen was given an award by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif for her courage. But for the nurse, the trauma of that Wednesday morning was still raw.
Barely two hours after meeting the prime minister, she sat down and talked, at length, about what happened inside.
‘Save the babies’
Noreen had been on duty since 8pm the previous night, working a routine dawn medication round with Sister Nasreen, with less than two hours left before the end of her shift.
When she saw the light through the nursery glass, she says she did not stop to work out what it was.
“I just told my sister nurse, save the babies,” she told Al Jazeera. “I went in. I didn’t think about what would happen next.”
Noreen said the fire was coming out of the side of the air-conditioning unit facing her.
“The AC was right in front of me, and the fire was coming out of its side,” she said. “We don’t know what was happening behind it. That’s just what I saw.”
The government’s interim inquiry, submitted on August 28, states that the precise cause of the fire “is not yet conclusively established”, with evidence pointing variously to the air conditioner, an incubator or an electrical short circuit.
Inside the nursery, Noreen reached the nearest baby. There was no time to choose between 15. She carried the infant out and handed her to Dr Abdul Rehman, a doctor who had been inserting a feeding tube in the next room and emerged into the corridor moments after her. Then she turned back.
“I thought I’d get five, six, seven, eight more of them out,” she said. “But the fire was moving faster than I was.”
A second doctor, Dr Rimsha, who had been doing rounds nearby and saw the same light Noreen had, followed her in.
The two of them, and later Sister Nasreen, tried to crawl back through the smoke below the worst of the heat. A sudden loss of power plunged the room into darkness. They could not get through.
Noreen’s phone, left behind on the medication table when she ran in, sat inside the burned ward overnight. Hospital guards found it and returned it to her the next afternoon. Its case is still scorched and cracked.
Noreen, Dr Rimsha and Sister Nasreen instead moved to where a separate rescue team was lowering babies from an adjoining gynaecology ward. They stood there catching newborns and running them to the neonatal intensive care unit until the smoke became too thick to remain.
The government’s inquiry later found that the available evidence “does not support generalised allegations that front-line medical and nursing staff simply abandoned the newborns”.
Ask Noreen what a nurse is to a newborn separated from its mother, and she has one answer: its first mother.
“A mother who gives birth endures a pain no one else can stand in for,” she said. “But once a baby is in our hands, no one else is watching over it the way we are, checking their oxygen, their feeding, whether they’re breathing right, every two hours, whatever else is happening around us. That is why we are their first mother.”
‘I am very happy with the children’
Noreen, 38, has spent 21 years in government nursing, the last 17 of them at PIMS. She trained in Karachi right after school, at the age of 17, before a transfer brought her to PIMS in 2009. She has never married.
“Thank God, I am very happy with the children,” she said, when asked about it directly.
Born in Punjab’s city of Sahiwal, she was one of seven children. Her father, Victor John, was a pastor; he died when she was in the eighth grade. Two of her sisters have died; a third, also a nurse, lives in Lahore.
Her mother, 83, a retired government school teacher who is hard of hearing, lives in Lahore with one of Noreen’s brothers.
Noreen herself has lived in the PIMS staff hostel, across from the ward where she works, for most of the past two decades.
With her own phone trapped inside the burning ward, Noreen could not call her family herself.
Noreen’s niece happened to be staying with her that week. It was the niece the warden found, and who got word to the family in Lahore: Noreen was safe.
‘It’s always the two of us’
On the morning of the fire, Noreen and Sister Nasreen were the only two nurses on duty in a nursery holding 15 babies, backed by two doctors, one of them two rooms away. She says it was not an unusual night.
“Sometimes there are 20 babies, sometimes 25,” she said. “It’s always the two of us.”
Doctors on her ward work 36-hour shifts, she said, arriving at 8am and going off duty at 2pm the following day.
Handover between nursing shifts, checking each baby’s medication, feeding and vital signs, takes roughly 45 minutes given the numbers involved. The cost of drugs can also run to tens of thousands of Pakistani rupees per injection, all provided by PIMS to its patients.
“Sometimes we get a break, sometimes we don’t,” she said. “When the workload is heavy, even the water we carry with us goes back home untouched.”
No fire drill had been run in the nursery before August 26, not even after an earlier fire at a nearby PIMS hostel in July.
Asked what is required after an incident like this, she does not hesitate.
“We should all have proper drills. If a fire starts, everyone needs to already know what to do.”
She lists what should follow: extinguishers within reach, cross-ventilation to clear smoke, and a rehearsed evacuation route for babies who cannot walk or call out for help.
‘Golden letters in history’
Until the fire, almost nobody outside her own ward knew her name, Noreen says.
“I have almost no presence in the main hospital,” she said. “Nobody there knows who I am. I work in the nursery, in my own department. I never imagined that saving one baby would take me this far.”
She travelled on Thursday to meet the prime minister in a car the government sent.
During the meeting, Sharif called her “the nation’s daughter” and said her act would be remembered “in golden letters” in Pakistan’s history.
He confirmed Noreen will formally receive the country’s Sitara-i-Khidmat (Star of Service) award at a ceremony on March 23, and handed her a cheque for 10 million Pakistani rupees ($36,000).
She used the meeting to say what she had already told her own colleagues privately.
“My fellow nurses work with just as much dedication,” she said. “This was a very heartbreaking incident.”
‘I haven’t slept since that day’
Eight days on, Noreen is unwell. She has had a fever of 102 to 103 degrees Fahrenheit (38.9C to 39.4C) on and off, and a cough she says came from smoke she breathed in from the fire that morning — a morning she will never forget. She takes an antibiotic and sleeping tablets at night. Neither has worked as it should.
“I haven’t slept, not since that day,” she said. “I take the tablets, I drink the cough syrup, but sleep doesn’t come. I close my eyes, and I open them again.”
Asked whether the same dawn shift keeps replaying in her mind, she did not need the question finished.
“The whole incident. The same babies. The mothers’ screams, and the babies’ screams, how they must have screamed. Those are the things that don’t let me sleep.”
She was signed off on medical rest only the day before this interview. Colleagues have been steadying her since.
“I would just start crying, sitting there,” she said. “They supported me like I was a child.”
But the nights are still hers alone.
“It comes back to the same thing,” she said. “When I’m in the hostel, when I’m alone, it all comes back.”
‘That, I regret’
The baby Noreen carried out — she hasn’t been named yet, according to the nurse — remains in the neonatal intensive care unit a week on.
Born preterm at just over a kilogramme (2 pounds, 3 ounces), the baby was already unwell before the fire. She remains critical.
Noreen met the baby’s parents for the first time the day before the meeting with the prime minister.
“She [the baby’s mother Asifa] hugged me and thanked me, and cried, and I cried with her,” Noreen said, “because for the rest of the children, my heart is still exactly where it was.”
She has told the mother the same thing she tells herself.
“I said, look, your child survived such a huge storm, she will survive what comes next, too. You pray, and I will pray.”
Asked what she would tell other nurses, Noreen urged them to work with honesty and without conditions.
“When you work somewhere with honesty, the reward comes eventually,” she said. “It came to me after 21 years. Work with the same loyalty. That is our real strength.”
Then, unprompted, she returned to the 14 babies who died.
“I do regret it,” she said. “I could not save the rest of the children. That, I regret.”

Quantum oscillations defy expectations in this exotic material
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
04:18:12 UTC
13:18:12 KST

Quantum oscillations defy expectations in this exotic material
Under extreme magnetic fields, scientists discovered electrons in a topological material behaving in a way conventional theory says should not happen.
- Date:
- September 5, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered an unusual form of electron behavior in zirconium pentatelluride, a quantum material that can act as both an insulator and a conductor. Under temperatures near absolute zero and magnetic fields reaching 60 tesla, electrons produced quantum oscillations that continued even after conventional physics predicted they should disappear.
- Share:
A study published in Nature Communications has revealed an unusual form of quantum oscillation in a three-dimensional topological insulator. The findings show that electrons in zirconium pentatelluride (ZrTe5) can behave in unexpected ways when exposed to temperatures close to absolute zero and extremely powerful magnetic fields.
The research was led by scientists from the University of São Paulo (USP) in Brazil, Los Alamos National Laboratory, the University of Washington, and other U.S. institutions. The team combined electrical transport experiments performed in magnetic fields as strong as 60 tesla and at temperatures near 0.7 kelvin (-272.45 °C) with detailed theoretical calculations.
"This work expands our understanding of electron transport in exotic phases of matter and suggests that topological insulators support the transport of not only electric charge, but also another fundamental degree of freedom: electron spin," says Julio Larrea Jiménez, a professor at USP's Physics Institute (IF) and co-founder and director of the Laboratory for Quantum Matter under Extreme Conditions (LQMEC).
Larrea served as the doctoral advisor of Cauê Kaufmann Ribeiro, the study's first author. Ribeiro carried out a large portion of the experimental work during an internship at the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory in Los Alamos, United States, supported by a FAPESP Research Internship Abroad. While there, he was co-advised by Johanna Palmstrom and Sean Thomas.
A Material With Two Electronic Personalities
Topological insulators have an unusual combination of properties. Their interiors behave as electrical insulators, while their surfaces can conduct electricity. This behavior arises from the topology of their electronic bands, which describes broad features of the quantum structure of electronic states that are protected by crystal symmetries.
ZrTe5 is especially valuable for studying this type of physics because it sits close to the boundary separating different topological phases. Small changes in temperature, mechanical deformation, chemical composition, or magnetic field can significantly alter its electronic behavior. That sensitivity has made ZrTe5 an important material for investigating topological phase transitions and relativistic quasiparticles in solids.
When electrons move through a magnetic field, their possible energies no longer form a continuous range. Quantum mechanics restricts them to specific energy values known as Landau levels, named after the Soviet physicist and mathematician Lev Landau (1908-1968).
In very pure metals, these Landau levels can repeatedly pass through the Fermi level, the energy boundary between occupied and unoccupied electronic states. Each crossing can produce an oscillation in electrical resistance. These effects, known as Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations, normally follow a predictable periodic pattern in 1/B, where B represents the magnetic field.
Quantum Oscillations That Refused To Disappear
The researchers found that ZrTe5 did not follow this familiar pattern. Its magnetoresistance oscillations were not conventionally periodic in 1/B, and they continued well beyond the quantum limit.
That result was surprising because, beyond the quantum limit, electrons should be restricted to the lowest Landau level. Under conventional expectations, the familiar oscillations should therefore disappear.
"In materials near topological phase transitions, electrons may cease to behave like ordinary particles within a metal. Their electronic excitations begin to behave like quasiparticles similar to Dirac fermions -- that is, relativistic particles. In our work, we show that the spin of these quasiparticles plays a central role: when we apply strong magnetic fields, the interaction between spin and the magnetic field profoundly alters the energy levels of the electrons. As a result, Landau levels that would normally move away from the system's relevant energy can 'return' and cross it again. This unusual behavior is what we call reentrant Landau levels," says Kaufmann.
To explain the effect, the researchers propose a process known as the "back-bending" of Landau levels. Rather than changing their energy in a simple, straight progression as the magnetic field increases, some Landau levels can bend back toward the Fermi level and cross it again. Those renewed crossings generate additional oscillations in a regime where conventional theory predicts that oscillations should already have vanished.
Electron Spin Changes the Picture
The unusual behavior emerges from the interaction between two different physical effects. One is cyclotron energy, which comes from the orbital motion of electrons through a magnetic field. The other is the Zeeman effect, which describes the coupling between the magnetic field and electron spin.
In a material such as ZrTe5, where spin-orbit interaction is strong, these two contributions cannot be considered independently. Electron spin and orbital motion become coupled, causing the energies of the Landau levels to evolve in a nonlinear way as the magnetic field changes.
A major goal of the study was to determine which of two possible mechanisms was responsible for the anomalous oscillations. One possibility involved many-body effects produced by collective interactions among numerous electrons. The other involved intrinsic topological properties associated with the material's electronic structure.
The researchers found that interactions among many electrons were not required to explain the behavior observed in their sample. Instead, a single-particle model based on a three-dimensional Dirac Hamiltonian and including strong spin-orbit coupling was able to reproduce the experimental regimes.
"What we saw is that the effect doesn't stem from many-body interactions, but rather from a nontrivial topology of the electronic bands," Larrea summarizes.
Resolving Conflicting Results in ZrTe5
The findings may also help clarify a long-running debate surrounding experiments with ZrTe5. Different samples of the same material have produced apparently different kinds of quantum oscillations.
Some samples display conventional oscillations that are periodic in 1/B. Others show oscillations that are not periodic in 1/B. Still others produce signals that seem to have logarithmic periodicity in B.
According to the new results, those differences may not require separate physical explanations. Instead, all of these behaviors could arise from the same underlying Dirac electronic structure, with the outcome largely determined by the carrier density and the size of the Fermi surface in each sample.
"In samples with low carrier density, such as the one investigated here, the Zeeman and cyclotronic effects become comparable in experimentally accessible magnetic fields. That favors the re-entry of Landau levels and makes the anomalous oscillations visible. In samples with higher carrier density, the conventional term dominates, and the oscillations retain their usual periodicity of 1/B," Larrea comments.
Two Spin Channels Interfere
The researchers also identified two separate contributions to the quantum oscillations that are linked to spin-separated states. These two contributions have different effective masses and can interfere with each other.
That interference helps explain another unexpected feature in the measurements. According to the conventional Lifshitz-Kosevich model, the amplitude of quantum oscillations should steadily decrease as temperature rises. Instead, the researchers observed a local minimum in the oscillation amplitude across certain temperature ranges.
The result indicates that two electronic channels are interfering with one another rather than simply fading in the standard way.
Measurements of angular magnetoresistance provided additional information about the material. Under low magnetic fields, the Fermi surface appeared to be three-dimensional and roughly ellipsoidal.
The researchers calculated a very low carrier density of approximately 1016 per cubic centimeter. That value is consistent with ZrTe5 being positioned extremely close to a topological phase transition.
Testing Matter Under Extreme Conditions
The experiments were performed at the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory in Los Alamos, one of only a small number of facilities worldwide capable of combining pulsed magnetic fields reaching 60 tesla with temperatures below 1 kelvin.
"This type of experiment can only be performed in a few places around the world. Access to those facilities is highly competitive," Larrea notes.
Beyond explaining the unusual quantum oscillations themselves, the findings strengthen the case for using ZrTe5 as a platform for exploring additional topological phases of matter.
The researchers suggest that carefully adjusting factors such as symmetry, carrier density, mechanical stress, temperature, and magnetic field could produce even more exotic electronic states. These could include phases involving Weyl quasiparticles.
"Our experiment provided the first empirical demonstration of a process that had previously been shrouded in controversy," Larrea summarizes.
The research was also supported by FAPESP through a Young Investigator Grant awarded to Larrea. Additional funding came from U.S. institutions including Los Alamos National Laboratory, the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, the National Science Foundation, and the U.S. Department of Energy.
Story Source:

Journal Reference:
- C. Kaufmann Ribeiro, J. C. Mutch, Q. Jiang, J. P. Ayres-Sims, K. Rubi, C. A. Mizzi, E. A. Peterson, D. Bulmash, J. Singleton, N. Harrison, P. F. S. Rosa, J. X. Zhu, J. H. Chu, J. Larrea Jiménez, S. M. Thomas, J. C. Palmstrom. Reentrant Landau levels in a Dirac topological insulator. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-72885-9

Match report: Swans rally for Mills in AFL finals upset over Lions
Logan McDonald has fired an understrength and injury-hit Sydney to a thrilling 53-point qualifying final upset over a lacklustre Brisbane.
McDonald brought the energy with a career-best six-goal haul at the SCG to lift the Swans to a 21.15 (141) to 13.10 (88) triumph after captain Callum Mills went down with a knee injury in the opening quarter on Saturday.
Charlie Curnow and Tom Papley also kicked five goals each in a near-complete Swans performance against the reigning back-to-back premiers in front of 37,261 fans.
Bracing for scans to confirm the dreaded ACL tear for Mills, Sydney will host either Fremantle or Geelong in a preliminary final in their improbable premiership push.
The Swans are already without vice-captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey, who are among five players serving club-imposed suspensions.
Brisbane will return to the Gabba and host either the Western Bulldogs or Adelaide in a semi-final, as they continue their pursuit of a third consecutive flag.
Papley had shaken off a left calf issue — picked up during warm-up — to pull off an equal career-best haul, leading alongside midfielder Errol Gulden (34 disposals).
Brisbane's usual stars struggled to fire, with Lachie Neale (18 disposals) kept quiet by Swans midfielder James Rowbottom.

The Professor Molchanov remains detained at Barentsburg in Norway’s Svalbard archipelago under a court order connected to Naftogaz’s effort to enforce a $4.22 billion arbitration award against Russia for assets illegally seized following Moscow’s 2014 annexation of Crimea.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Norwegian authorities are doing what we can to protect Russian citizens who have found themselves in a difficult situation in Svalbard now,” Norway’s Foreign Ministry told Reuters, adding that Oslo was fulfilling its international obligations.
The seizure left passengers and crew aboard the vessel unable to continue their journey and raised questions about supplies reaching Russia’s isolated settlements on the Arctic archipelago.
Norway’s government said Russian companies are regularly granted exemptions from sanctions to allow food and other essential goods to reach the settlements.
Barentsburg, where the Professor Molchanov is being held, and another Russian settlement on Svalbard have a combined population of 392, compared with 2,914 people across the archipelago, according to Statistics Norway.
The new statement underscores Oslo’s position that enforcing the Ukrainian compensation award does not mean abandoning its responsibilities toward civilians living on Svalbard.
Will Russia Honor Zelensky’s Proposed Truce for US Envoys?
Ship seized over Russia’s seizure of Ukrainian assets
As Kyiv Post reported earlier this week, Norwegian authorities seized the Professor Molchanov in Barentsburg after the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court issued an order on Aug. 31 at Naftogaz’s request.
Naftogaz said the action forms part of a broader international campaign to recover compensation from Russia for the unlawful expropriation of the Ukrainian company’s assets in Crimea.
A Hague-based arbitration tribunal ruled in favor of Naftogaz and other companies in the group in 2023.
The award has been recognized as enforceable in Norway, and Naftogaz says Russia’s outstanding obligation amounts to approximately $4.22 billion, excluding additional interest and costs.
The Professor Molchanov is owned by the Russian Federation and is used for both scientific expeditions and commercial cruises, according to Naftogaz.
The 71-meter vessel can accommodate up to 32 crew members and 52 passengers and includes a library, sauna, bar and two restaurants.
Although the value of the vessel represents only a fraction of Russia’s outstanding obligation to Naftogaz, its seizure is significant because Kyiv has increasingly sought to turn arbitration victories into the actual confiscation or sale of Russian assets abroad.
Naftogaz has said it intends to continue pursuing Russian property internationally until Moscow pays the compensation awarded over its Crimea losses.
Moscow cries ‘piracy’
Russia reacted angrily to the seizure.
As Kyiv Post reported on Sept. 4, Moscow demanded that Norway immediately release the Professor Molchanov and ensure the safety of its passengers and crew.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry summoned Norwegian Ambassador Heidi Olufsen in protest, while Russian officials accused Oslo of undermining Moscow’s presence in Svalbard and described the seizure as “piracy.”
Russia has said it will appeal the Norwegian court decision.
Norwegian authorities have rejected Moscow’s attempt to portray the case as a political action by the government.
Oslo says the governor of Svalbard was legally required to execute the Norwegian court order and that the government itself is not a party to the underlying dispute between Naftogaz and Russia.
Svalbard adds sensitive Arctic dimension
The dispute has also drawn attention because of Svalbard’s unusual legal and geopolitical status.
Under the 1920 Svalbard Treaty, Norway exercises sovereignty over the archipelago while citizens and companies from treaty signatory states are granted equal rights to engage in certain commercial activities there.
Russia has maintained a presence on the islands for decades and operates a coal mine at Barentsburg.
Moscow has argued that Western sanctions and restrictions threaten its ability to maintain its settlements, while Norway maintains that the treaty does not exempt Russian citizens, companies or state property from Norwegian law.
Norway’s announcement Friday seeks to separate two issues increasingly intertwined by Moscow: enforcement of a Ukrainian legal judgment against Russian state property and the provision of essential goods and assistance to civilians living in Svalbard.
For Naftogaz, the ship remains another Russian asset caught in Kyiv’s widening international effort to make Moscow pay for property seized after the occupation and illegal annexation of Crimea.

The company is also facing a shortage of construction talent in both Taiwan and the US, Hou said. When demand nearly doubles over a short period, shortages of workers and other resources can become major bottlenecks throughout the supply chain.
He said the challenge extends beyond TSMC, with suppliers across the industry needing to accelerate capacity expansion while continuing to invest in research and development, according to Rti.

‘Then who or what did we cremate?’ Daughter’s horror at finding bones in British wildfire victims’ car
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
04:00:26 UTC
13:00:26 KST

When Danielle Gillam-Kirton’s parents, Pete and Fran Gillam, were killed in July’s Spanish wildfires, she felt her nightmare could get no worse. The much-loved couple had built their home in Bédar in Almería after retirement, becoming part of a tight-knit community. Fran, a former headteacher, loved to organise quiz nights to raise money for the local school and the couple enjoyed playing padel at a nearby sports club.
Spanish police told Gillam-Kirton that the vehicle in which her parents died had been “inspected meticulously” and no possessions had been found. But Gillam-Kirton, an assistant headteacher from Nottinghamshire, was sure her parents must have been wearing their wedding rings when they died.
She was invited to search the vehicle herself, which was parked in a police compound in Mojácar. “You won’t find anything,” she was told.
She describes crying out in shock when she looked through the door of the burnt-out car. On the front seats were what appeared to be a human hip bone. “I honestly can’t describe what that felt like. I remember staring at what was in my hand, and the slow realisation of what I thought I was looking at hit me. I shouted out in shock,” she says.
She and her partner searched the car and found more bones, which appeared to be the remains of the couple. They also found her parents’ mobile phones, sets of keys, jewellery, money and other personal effects.
The Gillams were among 14 people killed in the fires, including Belgian, French, American and Spanish nationals. Some of the bereaved families are now searching for answers and claim the Bédar authorities have botched the investigation into their deaths.
There has already been a funeral for the Gillams. “It makes you wonder: who or what did we cremate?” Gillam-Kirton says. She is demanding answers from the Spanish government and asking the UK Foreign Office to hold the authorities to account.
The bones she found have been sent for DNA testing after weeks of delay from the Bédar local authority. Forensic scientists who have looked at pictures of the bones have told Gillam-Kirton they appear to be human.
“The whole sequence is incredibly difficult to understand. We were told there was nothing left, and yet when we were finally able to look ourselves, we found significant personal belongings and what appeared to be human remains,” she says.
“We were initially told it was probably animal remains.” She says she had to push the Spanish authorities to send them off for DNA testing. “The bones were big. I can’t see how a large animal like a cow would have climbed into the passenger seat of the vehicle during a fire.”
Gillam-Kirton says she helped another family who were told their loved ones died while attempting to escape the fires on foot and that their remains had been cleared by a forensic team. She arranged for a search party – including a police officer and one of the victim’s relatives – to travel to the hillside on which they died. There they found what appeared to be human bones lying in plain view along with various personal belongings.
“These were people who were caught in the same horrific fire as my mum and dad,” she says. “They lost their lives in terrifying circumstances and they deserved dignity and respect, in the way they were treated at the time and afterwards. And for us and the other families, those personal belongings aren’t just objects. They’re the last physical things connecting us to the people we have lost.”
Gillam-Kirton has previously criticised the Spanish authorities for failing to alert her parents to the danger of the fire in good time. Though the fire alert came at 4.30pm, the evacuation order did not come for another three hours and was delivered by a lone police officer, who was “frantically driving from house to house”. Thirteen residents from the Gillams’ village died.
Gillam-Kirton says she wants the UK government to “keep pressing the Spanish authorities for proper answers”. She adds: “Eight British people died in this fire, including my mum and dad, so I think it is really important that the UK government continues to take an interest in what happened. After all, we are talking about the treatment of British nationals – the deceased and the living.”
She and the other families are asking the Spanish authorities for “a proper, thorough and transparent investigation … and I mean the whole thing, not just what caused the fire, but what happened during the emergency response, what warnings were given, when they were given, who received them, what evacuation arrangements were in place and what happened to the victims afterwards”.
Initially, the Spanish authorities blamed the victims for not understanding or following the evacuation instructions. However, it later emerged that no such instructions were given.
“I think that’s one of the things we’ve found hardest,” Gillam-Kirton says of the police response. “At the beginning, there seemed to be a lot of emphasis on the idea that the victims had ignored instructions or hadn’t evacuated when they were told to. And that was incredibly painful for us. And now, months later, we’re still asking basic questions.”
She adds: “That, along with what appears to us to have been a lack of proper search-and-preserve procedures at the scene, has left us feeling that there has been a real lack of empathy towards the victims and their families.”
The families hope that if there is a proper investigation into the deaths of their relatives and the behaviour of the authorities afterwards, others will not have to go through the unbearable situation they have had to face.
“Wildfires are becoming more frequent and more severe, and communities are going to face these situations again,” Gillam-Kirton says. “There will be another fire somewhere, and there will be other people who need to be evacuated.
“If you don’t properly investigate something, you can’t learn from it. We don’t want Mum and Dad to simply become two names in a list of people who died in a wildfire. We want to understand what happened to them, and if something went wrong, we want the lessons to be learned.”
The Foreign Office said that any investigations were the responsibility of the Spanish authorities. A spokesperson said: “We are supporting the family of a British couple who died in Spain, and our thoughts are with those affected by the devastating wildfires.”
The Bédar local government has been contacted for comment.

Expert Insights: Networking in Denmark – What psychological safety actually looks like on the ground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

The author: Marianne Danling is a Danish intercultural communication expert who has called Berlin home for over 31 years. With a background in Cultural Studies and three decades of experience working with leaders and organisations across Europe, she brings both personal and professional perspectives to the conversation.
Last month I promised to look at what psychological safety actually means in a Danish context. I had planned to start with theory. Instead, I want to start with a text message.
A cleaning employee, who does not speak Danish, texts her manager that her bil is broken, her car. The manager, confused about how a broken car connects to that day’s job, asks her to explain. It turns out she does not mean car. She means the floor-scrubbing machine. Same instinct, wrong word, easy to imagine how it could have gone differently: a manager who assumes rather than asks, an employee who stops texting rather than risk being misunderstood again.
That small exchange, and the way it was handled, is a better definition of psychological safety than most of what gets written about it. The term comes from Harvard researcher Amy Edmondson, who defined it as a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, that you can ask a question, admit an error, or say “I don’t understand” without fear of being punished or humiliated for it. It sounds abstract until you see it in a text message about a car that turns out to be a floor scrubber.
A different kind of workplace to learn from
Most of what gets discussed under diversity and inclusion in Denmark centres on the same group: highly educated, often white-collar internationals, the ones this column has focused on too. So, when I went looking for a concrete example of psychological safety in practice, I deliberately looked somewhere else.
TRASBO A/S is a family-run cleaning and facility services company based in Skibby, with around 100 employees. Sixty-six percent of them are international, representing 21 different nationalities, the highest share the company has ever had. Thirty-three percent are Danish, 13 percent Nigerian, 10 percent Ghanaian, 8 percent Polish, 6 percent Nepali, spanning three continents. Few of these employees hold formal qualifications in the sector. Most communicate in a mix of broken Danish, broken English, and whatever else works.
If cultural fit and structured onboarding were only possible with a highly educated, fluent workforce, TRASBO should not function. Instead, it offers a useful, unglamorous test case for what inclusion looks like when it has to work on a cleaning trolley, not in a seminar room.
Trust, built without a shared language
TRASBO’s answer to the language barrier is not a policy document. It is a smile, body language, visualisation, translation apps, videos, and each other. New employees are paired with a buddy, an existing colleague who shows them the ropes. The company runs its own internal mentoring programme alongside one in partnership with the local municipality, and it deliberately promotes international employees into middle-management roles, in part because they understand the barriers a new arrival is facing from the inside.
“At TRASBO we have a flat structure. That means there isn’t far from a service employee to the director’s office, and everyone has the chance to talk to the top director. We’re not afraid to go the extra step for our employees, whether that’s help with a residence or work permit, interpreting at a doctor’s appointment or at the municipality, or simply paying attention to each other in everyday life,” the company explains.
Building trust across very different starting points on hierarchy and authority takes longer than a company handbook. “It requires patience, praise, listening with both your ears and your body, and being the first to show trust. It requires spelling out the frame clearly, so an employee is in no doubt that questions, input and feedback are very welcome, in fact necessary, for us to get even better,” TRASBO says.
When things go wrong and nobody gets blamed
The floor scrubber was not the only misunderstanding TRASBO shared with me. A manager once ordered chicken-bacon sandwiches for a multinational, multi-faith cleaning team. Everyone said yes. When the sandwiches arrived, one employee was upset to find bacon in hers, she doesn’t eat it for religious reasons, and simply removing the bacon wasn’t enough, since it had touched the rest of the sandwich. The manager apologised, rushed out for a replacement, and, in the company’s words, learned that food is also a point of cultural attention.
Employees have also shown up to work on Danish public holidays they didn’t know existed, Denmark has an unusually large number of them, genuinely unaware the day was not a working day. The fix was not a memo about cultural awareness. It was communicating ahead of each holiday, removing the task from the schedule, and explaining, plainly, what the day is.
None of these are dramatic stories. That is rather the point. What makes them examples of psychological safety is not that misunderstandings never happen, they clearly do, constantly, but that when they happen, the instinct on both sides is to stop, ask, and explain, rather than to assume, blame, or go quiet. That instinct doesn’t appear by accident. It has to be built.
Trust without titles
I asked TRASBO what it makes of leading a multicultural team where most employees have limited formal education, a very different story from the “highly qualified professional” narrative that usually dominates this conversation.
“A big strength is that our employees bring a work ethic and a willingness to learn that doesn’t necessarily come from an education, but from life experience. Many of our employees have a resilience and adaptability that is worth its weight in gold in our industry,” they told me. “We also find that when you can’t lean on a formal title or education, the relationship and the trust between leader and employee often become stronger, you have to see and understand each other as people first. It isn’t about their academic background, but about their service instinct, their attitude, their good mood, their willingness to work and learn.”
That said, TRASBO is candid about the trade-offs. Employees typically need more concrete, hands-on instruction than a trained professional would, which means training has to be shown repeatedly and rethought as more practical. “It requires leaders to be clearer in their communication, and not assume something has been understood just because someone nodded,” the company says. And relatively few employees pursue further qualifications or move into leadership roles within the industry, which means TRASBO has to work harder at encouraging and informing people about internal opportunities, a process that takes longer when basic requirements, like learning Danish or getting a driving licence, haven’t yet been met.
Why this matters beyond one company
TRASBO does not present itself as a diversity case study. It presents itself as family-run and warm-hearted, and most of what it described to me, the weekly shared breakfast and lunch, the summer party, celebrating every five-year work anniversary, celebrating a completed language course or a new driving licence the same way, reads less like HR strategy and more like how a family keeps track of each other.
But that is precisely why it is worth paying attention to. Psychological safety is usually discussed as something knowledge workers negotiate in meetings and performance reviews. TRASBO is a reminder that the same underlying mechanism, can I ask, can I admit I don’t understand, can I tell you something is wrong without being punished for it, matters just as much, arguably more, on a cleaning shift where a missed instruction has immediate, physical consequences.
“When you work with people the way we do at TRASBO, where the employee’s work is our product, the soft values matter enormously,” the company reflects. “But the whole effort around an inclusive mindset also has to be anchored in leadership. Our work here isn’t finished, inclusion is a journey you have to keep buying into as a company.”
Denmark does not lack talent, in the office or on the cleaning trolley. It may still be learning, sector by sector, how to build the conditions that let people speak up when something has gone wrong, and stay, once they have.

Global food prices climb to highest level since 2022 amid Black Sea strikes, UN reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
03:56:31 UTC
12:56:31 KST

Global food prices climb to highest level since 2022 amid Black Sea strikes, UN reports
Food prices across the world reached a four-year high in August, in part driven by disruptions to grain export amid Russia's war against Ukraine, the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said in a report published Sept. 4.
The report follows weeks of intensified Russian attacks on shipping corridors in the Black Sea, including deadly strikes on civilian grain ships. The campaign has led to declining exports, rising costs, and a shrinking number of vessels willing to dock at Ukrainian ports.
The FAO Food Price Index (FFPI) averaged 133.3 points in August 2026, its highest since March 2022, the FAO said in its monthly report. Prices rose across all commodity groups, though the total index remained about 16% below the peak attained in the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Grain prices went up 2.5 points from the previous month, partly due to "continued uncertainty surrounding Black Sea export flows," the agency said. The cost of wheat, corn, sorghum, barley, and rice increased worldwide. Disruptions to Black Sea shipping was repeatedly cited as a contributing factor.
Weather concerns, including heat and dryness, and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz also contributed to the rise, according to the report.
Prices of vegetable oil, dairy products, meat, and sugar also increased globally in August, the report said.
The FAO also decreased its forecast for world grain production in its August report, bringing the number down by 3.4 million tons from its July prediction. According to the FAO, grain production in 2026 is expected to fall by over 61 percent from the previous year, representing "the largest annual decline since 2018."
The agency noted, however, that the output still marks the second-largest recorded harvest.
Throughout July and August, Russia stepped up its attacks on Odesa's seaports and civilian vessels in a bid to choke Ukraine's key trade route. Some 90% of the country's agricultural goods are exported via the Black Sea, accounting for 20% of the country's gross domestic product (GDP) before the full-scale invasion.
Ukraine's exports fell to just 30% of its target in the first two weeks of August, Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky reported.
Russia has rejected the idea of reinstating the 2022-2023 Black Sea grain initiative, instead ramping up strikes on ships and port infrastructure — leaving Ukraine to respond in kind.
The conflict in the Black Sea has sparked fears of a global food crisis. In July, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that Russia was "holding global food security hostage" by continuing to attack export corridors.

White House reviews candidates to replace Hegseth deputy Feinberg, sources say
