The White House has reviewed candidates to replace US Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg, three people familiar with the discussions told Reuters, signaling that more leadership change could come for a Pentagon already facing unusually high staff turnover.
The effort, which was under way in June, has included conversations with senior lawmakers in the Senate about whether the administration's picks would have enough support to be confirmed, said two of the people, one of whom added that the review was still going on as of late August. Reuters could not determine when the White House began considering candidates.
The three sources said no decision had been made to remove Feinberg from his post. They did not say why the White House was reviewing potential replacements and did not specify which candidates the White House was considering.
"These so-called anonymous 'sources' have no idea what they are talking about," said White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly.
"[US] President [Donald] Trump appreciates the work of [US Defense] Secretary [Pete] Hegseth, Deputy Secretary Feinberg, and the entire Department of War, whose record of success in Operation Epic Fury, Operation Absolute Resolve, and Operation Midnight Hammer speaks for itself," she said, referring to US military operations in Iran and Venezuela.
The Pentagon denied that it was pursuing a process to replace Feinberg. Asked for comment by Reuters, Hegseth said in a statement that Feinberg has his full support and “isn’t going anywhere.”
The Pentagon did not provide a comment from Feinberg and declined to make him available for an interview.
Feinberg's departure would be most senior Defense Department staff change
Feinberg's departure, the billionaire co-founder of private equity firm Cerberus Capital Management, would be the most senior staff change in a department that has already seen a string of high-profile departures under Hegseth.
US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned this week following months of tension with Hegseth, according to a source familiar with the matter. The US Army has declined to comment on the reasons for his departure. US Navy Secretary John Phelan and several senior army leaders have also departed in recent months.
Feinberg, who vowed to accelerate US munitions production, has not yet met that goal, according to analysts who say that the US industrial base cannot ramp up quickly. Some defense industry executives say his task has been complicated by the slow pace of Congress appropriating funds despite immense pressure from the administration.
Feinberg "has worked tirelessly to rebuild our Defense Industrial Base and ensure our military has everything it needs to win, and I look forward to continuing to work with him," Hegseth said in his statement to Reuters, adding, "He’s doing a tremendous job for President Trump, for the Department, and for our warfighters."
Frustration over the Iran war
Trump has increasingly expressed frustration with the lack of progress in the conflict with Iran, which has settled into a costly standoff between the US and Iran.
One of the costs has been a drawdown of US weapons stockpiles. Reuters has reported that the US military faces significant shortages of certain munitions, alarming Congress and military leaders.
Trump has dismissed the concerns, saying the US has "far more munitions than anyone in the world."
But in an exchange with Trump at Camp David earlier this month, Hegseth blamed Feinberg for letting stockpiles of long-range guided missiles and air-defense interceptors shrink, according to the Washington Post.
The White House has called the report "fake news." In a statement to Reuters, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said: "Secretary Hegseth did not mislead anyone about our munitions posture, and he did not blame Deputy Secretary Feinberg."
Appointed by Trump last year, Feinberg has attempted to reshape the Pentagon by ramping up the US military's direct investments in companies and delivering loans to military contractors through multiple offices inside the department, including the Office of Strategic Capital and the newly created Economic Defense Unit.
In an August 18 memo he sent to defense firms, which Reuters saw, Feinberg called on contractors to speed up production and provide more transparency around pricing. The Pentagon did not respond to a question about the memo.
Feinberg has also come under scrutiny on Capitol Hill, where Democratic US Senator Elizabeth Warren has raised concerns about whether his former firm Cerberus could benefit from the Pentagon's spending on its Golden Dome missile defense program.
“There are no conflicts of interest between Deputy Secretary of War Steve Feinberg and Cerberus," said Parnell. "He has completely divested from Cerberus and has recused himself from any conversations or business relationships between the Executive Branch and Cerberus."

Malaysia declares emergency in Sarawak as haze from Indonesia worsens
Country implements state of emergency in Sarawak’s Serian district after air pollution reaches ‘hazardous’ levels.
Malaysia has declared a state of emergency in a district in Sarawak state after haze caused by wildfires in neighbouring Indonesia increased air pollution to “hazardous” levels.
King Sultan Ibrahim “has consented to the declaration of emergency throughout Serian Division, Sarawak, following haze conditions that have reached air pollution levels hazardous to public health and safety”, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s office said in a statement on Thursday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Malaysia’s former PM Ismail Sabri charged with concealing assets
- list 2 of 3Malaysia to return 1,500 Rohingya refugees next month, despite safety fears
- list 3 of 3Indonesia battles haze as wildfires rage across South Sumatra forests
The declaration followed a formal request from the Sarawak Disaster Management Committee after the region’s Air Pollutant Index reached levels warranting consideration of a local emergency.
Under the order, 647 schools in Serian will close from Monday until at least the end of next week, alongside government and private offices, plantations, construction sites and quarries, with only essential services continuing to operate.
The state’s disaster management authorities said a three-day cloud-seeding operation launched on Thursday would be extended to at least Monday, citing forecasts of “more conducive cloud formations” during that period.
Sarawak State Disaster Management Committee chairman Douglas Uggah Embas, speaking at a news conference in Kuching, stressed that the emergency applied only to Serian, not the entire state, but urged residents there to take the situation seriously.
“Please minimise outdoor activities and avoid strenuous activities outdoors,” he said.
Sarawak, in the northern part of Borneo island, has been heavily affected by haze for weeks, as have the neighbouring states of Sabah and Peninsular Malaysia.
Other Southeast Asian countries like Brunei have also reported smoggy conditions. Singapore announced it would start providing daily haze advisories from Friday evening, after the 24-hour air quality readings entered the unhealthy range, the first since 2023.
It has also hit the Philippines, where President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ordered the suspension of classes in the capital region, Metro Manila, as well as more than a dozen provinces on Friday.
This year’s transboundary haze, which originates from fires burning across Indonesia, particularly the Kalimantan region and Sumatra island, is part of a wider seasonal wildfire crisis in the archipelago country.
Scientists say temperatures are expected to peak this month, potentially intensifying the fires by bringing hotter and drier conditions across the region.

A Russian operative positioned within five kilometers of central Kyiv may have helped guide the Shahed drone that struck the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) on Friday, according to a Ukrainian electronic warfare expert and presidential adviser.
Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said he believes the drone may have been controlled in real time through a portable Mesh radio repeater connected to the internet and briefly activated near the target.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“My personal opinion: the Shahed was controlled and guided online via a Mesh radio repeater with internet access, which a Russian agent switched on somewhere nearby – within 5 km – for a short period during the attack,” Beskrestnov said.
He added that such a repeater could be roughly half the size of a school backpack, making it relatively easy to transport and activate temporarily.
Beskrestnov also pointed to the fact that no other Shahed drones were in the air at the time of the strike. In his assessment, that meant the aircraft could not have been controlled through a relay chain involving other drones stretching back toward Russian-controlled territory.
His account has not been independently verified, and Ukrainian authorities have not announced the identification or detention of an operative suspected of helping guide the drone.
If confirmed, however, the assessment would raise fresh concerns about Russia’s ability to combine long-range drone attacks with covert activity inside Ukraine to improve the precision of strikes against sensitive targets.
Russian Attack Sets Nine-Story Residential Building Ablaze in Boryspil
Drone aimed at SBU chief’s office
The Russian drone struck the SBU’s central headquarters on Volodymyrska Street in the heart of Kyiv on Sept. 4, directly across from the historic St Sophia Cathedral.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the drone had been deliberately directed at the office of acting SBU chief Oleksandr Poklad. Poklad was not in the office when the drone hit and was unharmed.
The SBU also said the drone deliberately struck Poklad’s office but failed to achieve its intended objective.
At least 12 people were injured in the attack, according to Kyiv authorities, with seven hospitalized. The strike also damaged the exterior of the SBU building.
Zelensky subsequently instructed Poklad to prepare an appropriate and tangible response to the Russian attack, including, where possible, a symmetrical one.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the strike as a major escalation amid renewed diplomatic efforts aimed at ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Strike comes ahead of US envoys’ visit
The attack came as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner prepared to travel to Moscow and Kyiv for another round of US-led diplomacy.
Zelensky said Ukraine would refrain from conducting aerial strikes against Russia during the negotiations to ensure the envoys’ safety and urged Moscow to reciprocate.
Separately, Ukrainian troops were ordered to observe a temporary halt in fighting from Sept. 5 through Sept. 8, according to Ukrainska Pravda, citing military sources. No formal bilateral ceasefire agreement had been announced as of Friday night.

Tunisia: Judge orders arrest of journalist Mohamed Yousfi
September 5, 2026
A judge in Tunisia ordered the detention of prominent journalist Mohamed Yousfi on Friday. Police had taken him into custody as he arrived at a radio station to give an interview, according to Zied Dabbar, president of the journalist syndicate SNJT.
Dabbar said it was unclear why Yousfi was detained outside Radio Express FM, but he believed it was related to Yousfi's criticism of the authorities.
The judge ordered Yousfi detained on charges of illicit enrichment and money laundering, the state news agency reported, citing a judicial source.
No reason provided for detention
Yousfi, editor-in-chief of investigative news website Al-Qatiba, has been an outspoken critic of President Kais Saied. Al-Qatiba is known for investigative reporting and coverage of political, economic, social and environmental issues.
Radio Express FM host Walid Ben Rhouma said no reason was given for Yousfi's detention.
"He was barred from entering to participate in the program as a guest and was taken away for questioning, according to those who stopped him," Rhouma said in a Facebook post.
The SNJT said Yousfi's detention shows the erosion of press freedoms in Tunisia, where reporters, lawyers, opposition figures and activists have recently faced prosecution.
Attack on freedom of the press
SNJT called Yousfi's arrest not only an attack on him but also on all journalists and Tunisians' right to a free and independent media.
Rights groups warn of efforts to close Tunisia's remaining independent voices since Saied suspended parliament in 2021 and dissolved it in 2022. Saied says he will not be a dictator and that freedoms are guaranteed in Tunisia.
In August, protesters took the streets to demonstrate in support of jailed activists and journalists, as well as to call for Saied's removal from power.
Media figures jailed this year include Zied Heni, Mourad Zghidi and Borhen Bsaies. Khaoula Boukrim was sentenced in June to four years in absentia.
On Thursday, lawyer Ghazi Mrabet, known for handling politically sensitive and civil liberties cases, was arrested and placed in custody, according to local media reports.
The case reportedly involves alleged drug trafficking, although there are conflicting accounts of the circumstances.

Israel Aerospace Industries' first cargo-converted Airbus aircraft completes first flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
03:21:19 UTC
12:21:19 KST

Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) completed the first successful flight of an Airbus A330-200 converted into a cargo aircraft, marking a milestone in the company’s expansion into Airbus aircraft conversions.
The flight, which took off from and landed at Ben-Gurion Airport on Friday morning, was part of the aircraft’s certification process and marks a significant step toward delivery to customers and entry into service.
The flight followed the completion of the aircraft’s main structural conversion phase and an extensive series of ground tests, during which the aircraft and its systems were examined under a range of operating conditions.
The Airbus A330-300BDSF was designed for cargo operations on regional routes and medium-range flights. It offers cargo operators a competitive solution, with capacity for up to 30 cargo containers and a payload of up to 61 tons. The aircraft features an electric cargo-loading system and optimized cargo-flow capabilities. The forward placement of the main deck cargo door enables faster loading and unloading while improving operational efficiency.
First Airbus cargo conversion for IAI
Until now, IAI has converted only Boeing aircraft for cargo operations, aerial refueling, and VIP aircraft such as Wing of Zion, which is used by the prime minister and president. This is the first time IAI has converted an Airbus aircraft, after receiving approval from the European manufacturer.
The project extends IAI’s Boeing 777-300ERSF conversion program, which has already received dozens of orders. The 777, and now the A330, are being given a second life after serving for around 20 years as passenger aircraft and no longer meeting airline standards because of fuel-consumption requirements.
Both aircraft types are now being retired from airline service and are available for conversion. A converted aircraft costs tens of millions of dollars, including the purchase of the aircraft itself, compared with more than $250 million for a new cargo aircraft of the same model directly from the production line.
IAI CEO: New Airbus program strengthens company's abilities
"This milestone reflects the continued investment of Israel Aerospace Industries in advanced aviation technologies and industrial and engineering capabilities, while strengthening our position in the global air cargo market," said IAI CEO Guy Bar Lev. "The A330-300BDSF aircraft conversion program expands our comprehensive conversion portfolio and strengthens our ability to provide our customers around the world with flexible and reliable long-term solutions."
IAI Executive Vice President and General Manager of the Aviation Group, Yaakov Berkovitz, who carries out the conversions, said that "through decades of engineering and operational experience, we provide a solution with advanced and competitive capabilities designed to address the evolving needs of the global cargo market."

Iranian leadership considers escalation as US officials fear military, cyberattacks - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
03:20:58 UTC
12:20:58 KST

Iran may be considering a significant escalation in its war with the United States, having grown more confident in its ability to attack targets in the Middle East, The New York Times reported on Friday, citing recent US intelligence reports.
Throughout the war, Iran gained a better understanding of its military strengths and confidence regarding its capabilities, leading to a reluctance among Iranian leaders to make any sort of agreement to fully end the war, according to the report.
In recent weeks, Iran has resumed strikes against US targets in the Middle East and the US has resumed strikes within Iran, but US officials fear that Iran may intensify their attacks both within the Middle East, targeting more ships in the Strait of Hormuz and US infrastructure in the region and within the cybersphere, mounting cyberattacks on essential US domestic systems, the NYT wrote.
Cyberattacks believed to have been perpetrated by Iran-linked hackers
According to the report, US officials believe Iran-linked hackers were behind cyberattacks on more than 100 water systems across the US in July.
While no systems were degraded to the point of making water unsafe to drink, the attacks caused disruptions that required manual overrides and precautionary boil-water advisories.
US oil and gas infrastructure may also be on the hackers' target list, current and former US officials told the NYT, although those systems are more protected.
It is unclear whether any energy systems have been breached, the NYT wrote.
In addition to any actual disruptions to US systems, former intelligence officials and security experts told the NYT that Iran may use the opportunity to increase the unpopularity of the war.
“Even if such attacks fail to meaningfully unsettle the American public, they can still play into a broader effort to exhaust domestic patience with this administration’s handling of the conflict,” Alex Orleans, a former US government cybersecurity contractor who specializes in tracking Iranian hacking groups, told the NYT.
Iran has also gained a more precise understanding of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, and believes that US forces will not be able to sustain major new strikes due to dwindling munition stockpiles, according to the report.
Iran focuses on US elections
Additionally, knowing the war is unpopular, in part due to high gas prices, Iranian leaders may want to drag the war out until at least the midterms.
“The Iranians think they have maximum leverage,” the NYT cited Representative Josh Gottheimer, Democrat of New Jersey, as saying. “So, from their perspective, why not keep sticking it to the president?”
Signs of Iran spreading propaganda against Trump have emerged, with Meta releasing a report highlighting a network of Facebook and Instagram accounts originating in Iran and focused on US politics, including "anti-Republican views."
Domestic media in Iran has also published more than 1,200 Persian-language articles within the past two weeks about Trump and the midterm elections, according to threat intelligence company Alethea.
While the Trump administration has focused on economic sanctions, one member of the Intelligence Committee told the NYT he expected Iran to endure the measures.
“Because the Iranian government does not care much about the suffering of its people, it has been able to withstand both punishing economic sanctions and military bombardments,” he was cited as saying.

Nazi-looted painting must be returned to Jewish art dealer’s heir, Argentina court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
03:13:46 UTC
12:13:46 KST

Argentina must return to the rightful owner’s heir an 18th-century painting stolen by Nazis from a Dutch Jewish art collector, a judge has ruled.
Portrait of a Lady by Italian baroque painter Giuseppe Ghislandi was missing for eight decades before being photographed in 2025 hanging in the home of the daughter of a senior Nazi officer who had fled to Argentina after the second world war.
“An order will be issued for the painting to be returned to the heir” of art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, judge Santiago Inchausti declared on Friday after an agreement reached between the concerned parties.
The painting was first recognised by the Dutch newspaper AD in photographs of a house for sale in the seaside resort of Mar del Plata.
It was hanging above a green sofa in the living room of Patricia Kadgien, whose father, Friedrich Kadgien, was a financier for the Nazi SS paramilitary organisation.
He was one of several high-ranking Nazis to escape to Argentina after the second world war.
Patricia Kadgien, who clutched a rosary during the hearing in Mar del Plata, was charged with concealment and placed under house arrest along with her husband when the artwork was identified.
The pair agreed to return the painting to Goudstikker’s daughter-in-law and sole heir, Marei von Saher, and give about $3,200 to local hospitals.
Portrait of a Lady was among more than 1,000 artworks stolen from Goudstikker’s collection after the Nazi invasion of the Netherlands in 1940.
Goudstikker fled his country days after the invasion, leaving behind many works which were divided up by top German officials.
After the war the Dutch state retrieved about 300 works from the collection, most of which it later returned to Goudstikker’s heirs. But more remain scattered around the world.

US intelligence: Iran determined to continue war, weighing major escalation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
03:09:36 UTC
12:09:36 KST

Iran has emerged from six months of intermittent war with the United States more confident in its ability to inflict damage across the Middle East and increasingly convinced that it can sustain the conflict for months, according to recent U.S. intelligence assessments cited by The New York Times.
Officials familiar with the reports say Tehran now has a clearer understanding of both its own military capabilities and the limits of American power. That confidence is feeding concerns in Washington that Iran’s leadership may be prepared to escalate after weeks of renewed fighting.
The shift has become visible on the ground. Over the past week, Iran has targeted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and American forces in the region, while the United States has carried out strikes inside Iran that killed military personnel and civilians.
The latest exchanges have remained relatively limited. But officials who reviewed the intelligence said the assessments indicate that Iran’s hard-line leadership may be considering a broader confrontation.
The reports also suggest that a comprehensive agreement ending the war remains difficult to imagine. U.S. officials see little indication that Tehran is preparing to make major concessions, while some believe Iran is content to prolong the confrontation and deepen President Donald Trump’s political problems ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump is not currently pursuing negotiations. Instead, he has argued that economic pressure will eventually force Iran to make concessions over the Strait of Hormuz and perhaps, later, its nuclear program.
In the short term, however, officials who reviewed the intelligence believe additional sanctions could have the opposite effect and prompt further Iranian escalation.
U.S. officials say Tehran could soon repeat some of the tactics it used in July, when Iran attacked American military bases across the Middle East, killing three Americans in Jordan, struck shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and targeted infrastructure in Kuwait and elsewhere.
Cyberattacks remain part of Iran’s arsenal
Washington is also closely watching Iranian cyber activity.
U.S. officials believe Iran-linked hackers were most likely responsible for cyberattacks against more than 100 American water systems in late July. None of the attacks is known to have made drinking water unsafe, but some caused disruptions that required manual intervention and precautionary boil-water advisories.
Iranian hackers have also shown interest in U.S. oil and gas infrastructure, according to current and former officials, although such systems are generally considered more difficult to penetrate. It remains unclear whether any energy infrastructure has actually been breached.
There are indications that Iranian hacking groups have regrouped after suffering losses early in the war.
Even when cyber operations fail to cause major physical damage, former intelligence officials and security experts say Tehran may see them as a useful way to increase public anxiety and weaken American support for an already unpopular conflict.
Alex Orleans, a former U.S. government cybersecurity contractor who tracks Iranian hacking groups, said Iranian cyberoperators are likely feeling more confident.
“Even if such attacks fail to meaningfully unsettle the American public, they can still play into a broader effort to exhaust domestic patience with this administration’s handling of the conflict,” he said.
Vice President JD Vance also acknowledged Thursday that Iran was likely to continue trying to disrupt the United States, although he played down the scale of the threat.
“If you look at the Iranian ability to disrupt the normal lives of Americans, I think it is quite limited,” Vance said. “It’s not zero, but it’s quite limited. I’d be much more worried about cyberattacks from other actors.”
Iran believes it can absorb the damage
Trump predicted a swift and decisive victory when U.S. and Israeli forces launched the war on Feb. 28. Six months later, critics of the administration argue that Washington underestimated Iran’s ability to absorb military and economic punishment.
Representative Jason Crow, a Colorado Democrat who sits on the House Intelligence Committee, said Tehran appears increasingly confident in its position.
“Iranians are feeling pretty bullish about their position,” Crow said. “They have taken substantial damage, but that has always been built into their system. They understand they can take damage, and they are playing a much longer game here.”
Crow declined to discuss classified assessments directly, but said several factors appear to have strengthened Iran’s sense of leverage.
Iran’s leadership, previously divided by internal rivalries, is now more unified, he said, while domestic opposition has been largely silenced. Tehran also continues to hold significant stocks of missiles and drones despite months of attacks.
Just as importantly, Iranian leaders now appear to have a better understanding of how much pressure they can exert through the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway that carried about one-fifth of the world’s oil before the war.
“They have always known the strait was a big bargaining chip, but have come to realize to a greater degree the leverage that gives them,” Crow said.
Iran may believe US military options are narrowing
Officials briefed on the intelligence also say Tehran may believe the United States will struggle to sustain another large wave of strikes as American weapons stockpiles are depleted.
That perception may be encouraging Iran to extend the conflict.
Current and former U.S. officials say there are signs Tehran intends to keep fighting at least through the midterm elections, calculating that the war and the high gasoline prices caused by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz are damaging Trump and the Republican Party politically.
“The Iranians think they have maximum leverage,” said Representative Josh Gottheimer, a New Jersey Democrat and member of the Intelligence Committee. “So, from their perspective, why not keep sticking it to the president?”
Iran has additional tools beyond military pressure.
U.S. officials see indications that Tehran is again trying to influence American political debate, building on interference efforts seen during the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections.
Meta said last week that it had removed a small network of Facebook and Instagram accounts originating in Iran that focused on U.S. politics. Some of the material was generated with artificial intelligence, and Meta said the accounts promoted “anti-Republican views.”
Threat intelligence company Alethea also found that Iranian domestic media published more than 1,200 Persian-language articles over a two-week period referring to both Trump and the midterm elections. According to the company, the dominant message was that the war had become a political liability for the president.
A war with no clear end
Gottheimer, who said he initially supported the war, argued that the Trump administration has failed to establish a coherent strategy for ending it.
He said Iran’s government has so far been able to absorb both military attacks and economic sanctions despite the damage inflicted on the country.
“Because the Iranian government does not care much about the suffering of its people, it has been able to withstand both punishing economic sanctions and military bombardments,” he said.
The emerging U.S. intelligence picture suggests that endurance itself has become a source of confidence for Tehran.
After months of strikes, sanctions and military losses, Iranian leaders appear to believe they have identified where the United States is vulnerable: regional bases, global shipping, American infrastructure, domestic political opinion and the economic pressure created by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
That does not mean Iran is stronger in every military sense. It has sustained heavy losses and remains under enormous economic pressure. But U.S. officials increasingly believe Tehran now understands the battlefield better than it did at the start of the war and sees fewer reasons to compromise quickly.
That calculation could make the next phase more dangerous.
Rather than pushing Iran toward a settlement, six months of conflict may have convinced its leadership that it can absorb American pressure, prolong the war and wait for the political and economic costs in the United States to rise.

After Pretoria peace deal, old enemies in Ethiopia’s Tigray find new ground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
03:05:28 UTC
12:05:28 KST

After Pretoria peace deal, old enemies in Ethiopia’s Tigray find new ground
The 2022 peace deal ended the war but left key disputes unresolved, giving the TPLF room to regroup as tensions return.
Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – When Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) signed the Pretoria Agreement in November 2022, it was meant to end two years of devastating war.
The agreement called for a permanent cessation of hostilities, the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of Tigrayan forces, political dialogue and the return of displaced people. Article 7 also required the TPLF to refrain from conscription, training, deployment and mobilisation of military forces, as well as preparations for renewed conflict.
Nearly four years later, the large-scale war has ended, but many of the disputes that fuelled it remain unresolved.
More significantly, the period since 2024 has seen the TPLF reposition itself politically and organisationally while retaining military leverage and developing new relationships.
The sequence is striking: TPLF contacts with Eritrean officials, including reported meetings in Dubai and Zalambessa; a renewed struggle over political control in Tigray; reports of recruitment and mobilisation; new clashes involving Tigrayan forces; and the emergence of Tsimdo, a loose convergence of groups opposed to the federal government.
Taken together, the developments raise a question over whether Pretoria became less a completed transition to peace than a period in which the TPLF could regroup and reposition itself while the underlying conflict remained unresolved.
There is no evidence that the TPLF entered the agreement with a predetermined plan to use it as a tactical pause. But the events since 2024 suggest that the movement has retained an organisational and security role that Pretoria was supposed to diminish.
What happened to disarmament?
Article 6 established the process for disarming, demobilising and reintegrating TPLF fighters. Tigrayan forces handed over heavy weapons after the agreement, and thousands of former combatants have entered demobilisation programmes.
But the process did not fully dismantle the region’s military structures.
In 2026, reports emerged of renewed recruitment and forced mobilisation in Tigray. If confirmed, such activity would go beyond the incomplete implementation of the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration (DDR) process and directly challenge Article 7’s ban on conscription and mobilisation.
The distinction between organised mobilisation and the views of Tigray’s civilian population is important.
There is no basis for assuming that Tigrayans as a whole support a return to war. Many are still living with the consequences of the last conflict.
A civilian source in Tigray, who spoke to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity, said: “The people of Tigray want peace; we don’t want a second war.”
For those civilians, reports of recruitment carry a simple implication: the possibility of being pulled back into a conflict they believed had ended.
How did the TPLF reposition itself?
The change was not only in the military.
From 2024, the TPLF was increasingly consumed by an internal struggle over its direction after the war. The internal meetings and political manoeuvring formed part of a wider contest over the movement’s future.
The struggle eventually reached Tigray’s political institutions.
Getachew Reda was removed as head of the interim administration in 2025 and replaced by Lieutenant General Tadesse Werede.
Then, in May 2026, the Tigray regional council was reinstated and elected Debretsion Gebremichael as president, strengthening the position of the faction around him.
The developments showed that the TPLF remained a powerful political force in Tigray. Instead of a settled post-war political order emerging, the region was again caught in a struggle over authority while the security question remained unresolved.
When did politics turn back into fighting?
By early 2026, political tensions were accompanied by military developments.
Tigray Defence Forces-aligned troops crossed the Tekeze River into the disputed Tselemt district in January and clashed with Ethiopian federal forces. Later, TDF-aligned fighters took control of Alamata and Korem after a federal command post withdrew.
By August, fighting had again broken out in western Tigray near the Sudanese border, in another serious breach of the peace agreement.
The federal government and the TPLF blamed each other for the escalation, while responsibility for initiating the clashes remained disputed.
But the renewed fighting demonstrated that organised armed forces were still capable of mobilising and contesting territory.
The incomplete disarmament has therefore become more consequential as the political disputes left unresolved by Pretoria have begun to coincide with renewed military activity.
Why are former enemies finding common ground?
The repositioning has extended beyond Tigray.
Eritrea and the TPLF fought a devastating border war from 1998 to 2000. Eritrean forces later fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal government against the TPLF during the 2020-22 Tigray war.
Yet the post-Pretoria period has brought reports of closer contacts between Eritrea and elements of the TPLF.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF and using it as a proxy. Eritrea rejects that characterisation.
A broader realignment is reflected in the emergence of Tsimdo, a loose convergence of groups opposed to the federal government.
Recent reporting has identified cooperation involving the TPLF, Fano, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) and other armed groups. Fano leader Zemene Kassie has confirmed the existence of such a coalition while saying Eritrea is not currently part of it.
The significance of Tsimdo lies not simply in whether its members share the same political programme, but in what they appear willing to put aside to cooperate.
Major disputes remain unresolved: displaced people have yet to return to some contested areas, including Welkait, while territorial claims continue to divide Tigray and Amhara actors.
Yet groups that once fought on opposing sides now appear willing to set aside some of those differences when cooperation can increase pressure on the federal government.
That raises a further question about the TPLF’s post-Pretoria strategy. The organisation appears to be rebuilding its political influence while retaining links to military structures, even as many Tigrayans remain displaced and fear renewed mobilisation.
The emerging convergence points to a potentially widening gap between the strategic calculations of political and armed actors and the immediate interests of civilians still dealing with the consequences of war.
The groups have different histories and political ambitions, and their cooperation may not last. But their willingness to find common ground against Addis Ababa matters.
For the TPLF, Tsimdo offers another arena in which to build political and strategic relationships beyond Tigray.
What did Pretoria leave unresolved?
The war displaced about 1.9 million people. Many remain unable to return, particularly to disputed areas including Welkait, Tsegede, Humera and Raya.
Those territorial disputes remain closely tied to the return of displaced Tigrayans, while the political relationship between Tigray and the federal government remains unsettled.
The federal government has also failed to deliver on important elements of the post-war settlement. But those failures do not erase the TPLF’s commitments under Pretoria.
Article 6 envisaged the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of its fighters. Article 7 banned conscription, mobilisation and preparations for renewed conflict.
The record since 2024 does not prove that Pretoria was deliberately used by the TPLF to buy time.
It does, however, show a movement that has remained politically organised, fought to regain control of Tigray’s institutions, retained links to armed structures and found new potential partners as the settlement stalled.
Pretoria ended the large-scale war. It did not settle the struggle over power, territory and security that lay beneath it.
For Tigrayans, however, the calculations are simpler.
A young man from Tigray, who spoke to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity, said: “The fear of being drafted is what’s making many youth lose hope.”

Southeast Asia’s extreme heat exposes holes in safety net for outdoor workers
Many Southeast Asian cities lack adequate heat risk assessments, and have weak regulations protecting outdoor workers, a report says
Oil palms younger than three years offer little shade, so he tends them in the early mornings and evenings, spraying pesticide, applying fertiliser or weeding. “We try our best to avoid going to the plantation around noon,” Chung said.
He carries extra drinking water and, as a smallholder, decides when to slow down or change his hours.
But not everyone shares that luxury. Many construction, agriculture and platform workers across Southeast Asia lack that flexibility because employers or output determine their schedules.
Southeast Asia is getting hotter, with the annual mean temperature rising by 0.14 degrees Celsius (0.25 degrees Fahrenheit) to 0.2 degrees per decade since the 1960s, according to an Asian Development Bank report in June.
Many Southeast Asian cities lacked adequate heat risk assessments, and regulations protecting outdoor workers from extreme heat were either weak or unenforced, the report said.

After 66 years, Kau Kee’s first shop offers fish balls ‘every Hongkonger has eaten’
Second-generation owner Anita Lee has modernised the family business so customers can now directly buy the products once supplied only to industry
Anita Lee Yan-kwan grew up around a traditional business that supplied fish balls to Hong Kong’s street food stalls and eateries. But for decades, Kau Kee Food Factory’s signature product was known only among industry operators until Lee, a second-generation owner, opened the company’s first retail store late last year.
Kau Kee has operated as a silent giant in the food industry for 66 years, supplying its fish balls to nearly 1,000 eateries and snack stalls across the city. But it finally opened its first bricks-and-mortar shop in Mong Kok last December.
“Before opening the retail shop, if you were to ask people about Kau Kee on the street, they would probably not know about it,” Lee said. “Yet it’s likely almost every Hongkonger has eaten our fish balls.”
The 30-year-old politics graduate and former civil servant made a career pivot during the Covid-19 pandemic and took charge of the family business even as mask mandates and social distancing rules crippled the street food scene.
It left Kau Kee, which was relying solely on manufacturing and wholesaling at the time, in a precarious position as orders from food stalls dropped drastically.
“Our business took a really big hit and was severely affected. Since everyone was wearing masks, they stopped eating fish balls on the street. With the economy being so poor, people were spending less money overall,” Lee said.

Top 10 movies set in Australia's creepy outback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
02:59:33 UTC
11:59:33 KST

It's one of the biggest streaming hits of the year so far.
Netflix original action thriller Apex is one of the most-watched movies on the steaming service.
Released in late April, it quickly racked up 2.54 billion minutes viewed and peaked at number one on Netflix's Global Top 10 English movies list, capturing fans obsessed with the Australian wild.
Starring Academy Award-winner Charlize Theron, Welsh star Taron Egerton who nails a "gnarly" Australian accent, and Australian star Eric Bana, Apex is about a grieving woman who seeks solace in the wilderness, only to become ensnared in a deadly game of cat and mouse with a serial killer.
When asked why he decided to set and shoot the film in Australia, director Baltasar Kormákur said the film was actually set in the United States in the script, but they needed a warm climate at a specific time of year.
"As I started looking into it I felt it was actually a great idea to locate the film here and really use Australian nature, which is unique, and build the film around that more,"
Australia's outback is a backdrop that has found favour in both Hollywood and homegrown hits, with the bush and sometimes the wildlife being characters in themselves.
It's become a go-to setting for horror movies but other genres have also benefited from the world's anxious relationship with rural Australia.
Here's our list of top 10 movies set in Australia's creepy outback.
10. Rabbit-Proof Fence (2002)
A film that opened many people's eyes about the Stolen Generations and the role that state governments had in taking children from their families.
Yet another warning that the most dangerous creatures in the outback might wear a uniform and act in the name of the law.
9. Road Games (1981)
Director Richard Franklin was an Alfred Hitchcock super fan and used Rear Window as the inspiration for this cross-country thriller set in a truck.
Two imported American stars, Stacy Keach and Jamie Lee Curtis, encounter a serial killer on the long road across the continent.
It's a warning to be careful about who you run into on the Nullarbor.
8. Quigley Down Under (1990)
Magnum PI TV star Tom Selleck came to Australia to make a revisionist Western that revealed a harsh side of the outback.
The story saw local landowner Alan Rickman using a hired gunman to exterminate the local Indigenous population.
It pulls no punches and proves yet again that the most dangerous creatures in the outback are the humans.
7. Burke & Wills (1985)
An ambitious production shot by future Oscar-winner Russell Boyd with Jack Thompson as Robert O'Hara Burke and Nigel Havers as William John Wills, it told the most famous cautionary tale of colonial Australia.
Two ill-prepared explorers aim to cross the continent from south to north and back again, only to die of thirst on the way home in a Greek tragedy of mammoth proportions.
If they'd only taken the advice of the local Indigenous people, Burke and Wills might have made it home to become living legends — rather than dead ones.
6. Razorback (1984)
The movies love it when animals go rogue.
Sometimes it's a shark, or killer bees, or a bear, a crocodile, or piranhas. But in the Australian outback it's a wild pig, a razorback.
Best known for his music video clips, Russell Mulcahy's film is wildly over the top and often very funny, shot by another future Oscar-winner Dean Semler with music by Iva Davies.
It has all the ingredients of a classic genre film in the Ozploitation tradition.
5. Walkabout (1971)
Strangers in a strange land, two English children wander the outback in their school uniforms before being rescued by a local indigenous man played by David Gulpilil in his film debut.
Like other great films about Australia it was made by a foreign director, Nicolas Roeg, who had an eye for the details of what makes this country distinctive. They are things that local filmmakers might, perhaps, take for granted.
4. Evil Angels (1988)
Based on possibly the most famous legal case in Australian history, a family goes camping at Uluru only to have their daughter taken by a dingo.
A baby's cry in the dark that August night in 1980 has echoed down the decades and Fred Schepisi's film, fiercely in Lindy and Michael Chamberlain's favour, used members of TV's Comedy Company as a kind of Greek Chorus repeating the many wild, and untrue, rumours about the case.
3. Picnic At Hanging Rock (1975)
Not quite the outback but still a cautionary tale about going into the bush, only this time there's no wild pig or serial killer waiting. Just a mysterious rock.
One of the classics that revitalised the Australia film industry, superbly directed by Peter Weir with the greatest use of panpipes in the history of the movies, four schoolgirls in 1900 go on a picnic and don't return for their afternoon classes.
And not even an extra chapter of the original novel released decades later satisfactorily explained what happened.
2. Wolf Creek (2004)
Inspired in part by killers Ivan Milat and Bradley Murdoch, this film did more to scare potential tourists from Australia than just about any other.
Which is why it is so high on this list.
John Jarratt as Mick Taylor created a legendary character, but the film is torture porn of the worst kind. It seems to relish depicting the violence dished out to his victims, and the ending of the film leaves us in no doubt that a sequel was on the way. And about that film the less said the better.
1. Wake in Fright (1971)
Regarded by many as the greatest Australian film of all time, it tells the story of a teacher from the city working at an incredibly isolated outback school.
Staying overnight in a town very much like Broken Hill, he sees the chance to win enough at the local two-up school to buy his way out of his teaching contract and go home to his girlfriend in Sydney.
Needless to say, it doesn't work out that way and he is forced to confront his own demons as well as the locals who introduce him to the many terrors of the outback, including a notorious and horrific kangaroo shoot.
Wake in Fright was renamed Outback internationally.

11:57:00 KST

by sportswriter He Leijing
NANJING, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- As the new school year begins, fifth-grader Wang Xuan is looking forward to more than just seeing his classmates again. He is hoping to find someone to play pickleball with.
For the young sports enthusiast who picked up the fast-growing sport during the summer vacation, that may not be difficult. His school in Suzhou New District is just a short distance from a newly opened pickleball complex that drew scores of teenage players during the season.
"We had never played before, but pickleball is easy to pick up," said Wang's mother, Li Shuang. "I played with him, too, and it was such a relaxing way to have fun."
The family lives nearby and often comes to the courts to work up a sweat. During the summer, the venue offered four hours of play for just 29.9 yuan (about 4.4 U.S. dollars), further lowering the threshold for newcomers.
The 23-court facility, featuring a 1,600-square-meter central court, is the largest pickleball base in Jiangsu Province. Yet its growing popularity is more than a local phenomenon.
Across China, a new generation of sports is rapidly moving from niche pastime to mainstream leisure, transforming how people exercise, socialize and spend their free time.
Data from Douyin E-commerce show that sales of pickleball products surged 229 percent year-on-year over the past four months. On Xiaohongshu, a lifestyle-focused social media platform, more than 1.2 million posts about the sport have been published, while related topics have accumulated 820 million views.
"Ten minutes to get the hang of it, half an hour to get hooked," said Zhang Bingcheng, deputy general manager of Suzhou River Sports, capturing the sport's appeal in a nutshell.
With a session costing only a few dozen yuan, pickleball combines elements of tennis, table tennis and badminton. Its relatively gentle pace and easy-to-learn rules allow beginners to find their rhythm quickly, while its built-in sense of rally and interaction keeps them coming back.
Its appeal also finds unlikely new settings. On the 51st floor of a shopping mall in Nanjing, 11 standard pickleball courts offer players a game with a panoramic view of the city. The courts are often packed at night, with young people emerging as the driving force behind the summer boom.
"Playing pickleball this high above the ground while taking in the city view is such a unique experience," said pickleball enthusiast Zhang Ying.
And pickleball is only one piece of a much larger sporting mosaic taking shape across China.
This summer, as people sought ways to beat the heat while staying active, paddleboarding, kayaking and indoor skiing also gained traction, turning exercise into a form of leisure, socializing and escape from the heat.
At dusk, paddleboarders can be seen gliding across some waterways in Beijing and across lakes in cities such as Suzhou and Chengdu, their silhouettes drifting through the evening breeze.
"We have seen around 100 paddleboarders a day on average this summer, up 400 percent from a year earlier. Many visitors have also come from other cities specifically to try it," said Wu Yan, a manager at a water sports base in Jiangsu's Huai'an.
At Wuxi's Lihu Lake water sports base, daily visitors have topped 300, with revenue exceeding 20,000 yuan, while weekend traffic has doubled.
"After inflating the board for about five minutes, you can stand on the water. I was nervous the first time, but after paddling a few dozen meters, I was hooked," said paddleboarder Wang Xin.
The sport can be enjoyed by people ranging from children as young as six to those in their 80s, said paddleboarding coach Sun Qihai. "Beginners often fall into the water, but that's precisely part of the charm. It leaves room for mistakes, allowing people to unwind and let go of pressure while playing with the water."
Experts say easy access and affordable prices are the most visible reasons for the rise of these emerging sports. But behind the boom lies a deeper shift in what people expect from exercise.
"People's demand for sports has gone beyond simply staying fit. They are increasingly seeking stress relief, social interaction and ways to express themselves," said Lu Yulin, an organizer involved in promoting pickleball in Jiangsu.
The blend of fitness, fun and social connection is helping turn once-niche pursuits into new consumption engines.
In Suzhou, the pickleball base run by River Sports plans to host more than 90 competitions a year and expects them to generate around 220 million yuan in consumption. In Yangzhou, a flag football tournament attracted about 600 players, and after the games, athletes and their families explored local tourist spots, turning a sporting event into a gateway to tourism and culture.
The boom is also rippling through manufacturing. In Hebi, Henan Province, the city's established rubber and plastics manufacturing base is being leveraged to develop pickleball equipment. Nearly 1,600 courts are being built across the city, making it one of China's most densely equipped cities for the sport.
In Weihai, Shandong Province, orders for water sports equipment have surged, helping create an industrial chain spanning raw-material research and development, mold design, assembly manufacturing and cross-border sales.
Traditional commercial spaces are adapting as well. "As shopping increasingly shifts toward experience-driven consumption, such sports are an ideal vehicle for blending different scenarios and activities," said Niu Yong, an executive at a department store.
"Since our pickleball venue opened two months ago, players from several banks, insurance companies and technology firms have already used it as a place to socialize and build business connections," Niu said.
In some cities, meanwhile, unused or underused urban spaces are being converted into facilities for new sports, offering more options for public fitness while giving a second life to dormant corners of the city.
"These sports are not simply creating new ways to exercise," he said. "They are also helping cities rethink how public space can be used and how sports can become part of everyday life." ■

Australian former number one overall draft pick Ben Simmons has taken a significant step towards resurrecting his NBA career, agreeing to a one-year deal with the Sacramento Kings.
The Melbourne-born guard returns on a $US3.5 million ($4.9 million) contract after sitting out the entire 2025-26 campaign while rehabilitating back and leg injuries that have hampered him in recent years.
Simmons, who last played with the Los Angeles Clippers in April 2025, celebrated his Kings deal on social media on Saturday morning (AEST) by posting a photograph of himself wearing a team cap.
While reigniting Simmons's NBA career, his latest move is also a step towards possible Australian Boomers selection for next year's FIBA World Cup in Qatar and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
The Boomers, under Washington Wizards assistant and former NBL guard Adam Caporn, are chasing a podium return after a breakthrough bronze medal at the Tokyo Olympics five years ago.
Simmons spent his year out of basketball rebuilding his body and gathered momentum in his comeback bid during a Boomers mini-camp in Melbourne last month.
The former Philadelphia 76ers (2017-21), Brooklyn Nets (2022-25) and Clippers (2024-25) guard also reportedly attracted serious attention from the reigning champion New York Knicks and Golden State Warriors before he signed with Sacramento.
Simmons was drafted as the No.1 overall by Philadelphia in 2016, but missed his entire first season with a foot injury before establishing himself as one of the league's brightest young stars.
He claimed 2017-18 rookie of the year honours and was a two-time All-Defensive pick before further injuries derailed his career.
Simmons has not played more than 58 games in a season since 2018-19.
He has averaged 13.1 points, 7.4 rebounds, 7.2 assists and 1.5 steals in 383 career games (344 starts) with the 76ers, Nets and Clippers.
Sacramento open the NBA preseason at home against the Los Angeles Lakers on October 5, and visit the Clippers for their regular-season opener on October 21.
The Kings were 22-60 last season, finishing 14th in the Western Conference, and have only reached the playoffs once since 2006.

‘To challenge deadly blockade’: New flotilla mission sets sail for Gaza
Human rights advocates call for diplomatic measures to guarantee flotilla safety and end Israel’s deadly Gaza blockade.
The Freedom Flotilla Coalition (FFC) has announced that a new international mission is under way, with vessels stopping at European ports ahead of its attempt to reach Gaza’s shores in October.
The coalition said in a statement that the mission to “challenge Israel’s illegal and deadly blockade of Gaza” would go ahead despite the violence Israeli forces inflicted on flotilla volunteers and activists, such as documented cases of severe beatings, repeated tasering and sexual assault.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Boat sets sail from Bristol, aiming to break Israel’s siege of Gaza
- list 2 of 3Four Gaza aid flotilla activists released from Libya detention
- list 3 of 3‘Active in BDS’: Document reveals how Israel scrutinised global NGOs
It added that “action is needed now more than ever as much of the world has moved on from Gaza” since the announcement of a ceasefire in October 2025.
According to the statement, two vessels have already set out. Handala II sailed around Scandinavia in June and July, stopping in Norway, Sweden and Denmark, while the ship Kate departed Bristol, UK, earlier this month and has since called at ports in Ireland, Germany and France.
Stops in Spain, Portugal and Italy are planned before the flotilla continues towards Gaza, the mission added.
Demands and calls
“The Freedom Flotilla sails again because our governments continue to fail to uphold their obligations,” said Zohar Chamberlain Regev, an FFC Steering Committee member.
“At every port, we will carry the demand that Palestinians be free to live with dignity,” he added.
Human rights advocates, peace activists, elected representatives, journalists, medical professionals and advocates for Palestinian rights have joined the new flotilla.
The coalition is calling on governments to guarantee safe passage for the flotilla, press Israel to end its obstruction of food, water and medicine into Gaza, declare that any attack or seizure of the vessels will trigger diplomatic consequences and use diplomatic and economic measures to end the blockade.
“We know that sailing toward Gaza carries serious risks,” said Edward Digilio, an engineer from Maryland taking part in the mission. “But silence and inaction carry a much greater cost for Palestinians and the world.”
Pattern of Israeli interception and abuse
The coalition traces its roots to 2010, when Israeli forces killed 10 activists on board the Mavi Marmara during a flotilla attempt, and to the Free Gaza Movement’s first voyages in 2008.
Israeli forces intercepted the Global Sumud Flotilla twice within the past year, detaining more than 450 participants in October 2025 — including South African author Zukiswa Wanner and Nelson Mandela’s grandson, Mandla Mandela — and about 175 more in April 2026.
Amnesty International said it documented sleep deprivation, denial of water and medical care, and other ill-treatment of activists held by Israel after intercepting and storming the ships.
Two activists, Thiago Avila and Saif Abukeshek, were held incommunicado for days in April this year and had their detention extended partly on secret evidence before being deported.
Humanitarian conditions in Gaza
The mission joins many other aid groups who have described Gaza’s humanitarian situation as reaching crisis levels despite the ceasefire.
UNICEF estimates that more than 82 percent of families remain water insecure and roughly 90 percent of water and sanitation infrastructure is destroyed.
Israel has continued to target hospitals, aid warehouses and medical supply sites in Gaza in recent weeks.
Gaza’s Health Ministry has recorded more than 1,300 deaths from Israeli fire since the truce took effect in October, alongside thousands still missing or believed trapped under rubble.

Serena and Venus Williams knocked out of US Open women's doubles by Maya Joint, Hao-Ching Chan
Australian Maya Joint has again spoiled the part for the legendary Williams sisters, teaming up with Hao-Ching Chan to knock Serena and Venus out of the first round of the US Open women's doubles.
In front of a packed and passionate crowd at Arthur Ashe Stadium, Joint and Chan came from 0-5 down in the deciding 10-point tiebreaker to down the legendary sisters 6-3, 6-7 (6/8), 7-6 (10/7).
This is the second consecutive grand slam that Joint has played spoiler, knocking Serena out in the first round of the Wimbledon ladies singles on Centre Court.
After losing the second set in a tiebreaker, Joint and Chan were in control of the third set with a 4-1 lead, before the Williams sisters fought back.
Serena and Venus looked set for a dream comeback win when they held a huge 5-0 lead in the first to 10.
But both sisters double-faulted as Joint and Chan won 10 of the final 12 points to take the match.
The Williams sisters were supposed to make their grand slam doubles return at Wimbledon, but had to pull out after Serena hurt her knee.
That delayed their return to the Grand Slam stage until New York, where they won in 1999 and 2009 and are now 27-8 in their 10 appearances.
The match got a spot in the night session in Arthur Ashe Stadium — practically unheard of for first-round doubles.
The sisters were once dominant in women's doubles, teaming to win 14 grand slam titles along with Olympic gold medals in 2000, 2008 and 2012. They shared the number one ranking in women's doubles for eight weeks.
It appeared a first-round loss in 2022 was their last time together, with Serena stepping away from tennis that year after winning 23 Grand Slam singles titles. She came back this summer and now has two heartbreaking defeats with her older sister. They also lost in a match tiebreaker at the Cincinnati Open.
Venus Williams also lost in the first round of singles.

Trump sends envoys to Moscow and Kyiv with new plan to 'end the war'
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are travelling to Moscow and Kyiv this weekend with what US President Donald Trump says is a new proposal to end the war in Ukraine. Despite Trump's promises to resolve the conflict, Washington's efforts to broker a peace have so far come to nothing.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
US President Donald Trump said Friday he is sending envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv with a plan to end more than four years of war in Ukraine.
The move marks Washington's latest bid to break a diplomatic stalemate in Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
A senior Ukrainian official told AFP the envoys were due in Kyiv on Sunday.
US outlet Axios reported they would meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday, and then President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv on Sunday.
While the Kremlin declined to comment, a business jet believed to be carrying Witkoff and Kushner touched down in Moscow on Saturday, Russia's Interfax news agency reported, citing aviation sources.
Read moreUkraine warns Russian airspace ‘not safe’ in message to UN aviation watchdog
Trump told reporters that the two negotiators would seek to gauge whether progress towards peace was possible.
Peace efforts have stalled due to Washington's war with Iran, while Moscow and Kyiv have intensified long-range attacks, driving up civilian casualties to levels not seen since the start of fighting.
'An idea for peace'
In late August, Central Intelligence Agency Director John Ratcliffe travelled to Moscow in part to press counterparts there to consider a settlement, Reuters and several other media outlets reported. US media also reported that Ratcliffe warned Russia against any attack on NATO member states.
Earlier this week, the United States welcomed the Russian finance minister at a G20 gathering in North Carolina.
"I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators. They've done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done. And there may be a good chance that we'll do it," Trump said.
"They're bringing with them a proposal to end the war," he said.
The US president would not say whether the plan involved Ukraine ceding territory as he has previously suggested, but added: "We have an idea for peace."
It will be the first time that Trump's businessman friend Witkoff and son-in-law Kushner have visited war-torn Kyiv since Trump returned to office last year with a pledge to resolve the conflict.
Witkoff and Kushner, who have been involved in negotiations for ceasefires in Gaza and Iran, have travelled repeatedly to Moscow in previous attempts at diplomacy.
'No air strikes on our part'
The renewed push for diplomacy comes as Russia and Ukraine pummel each other with long-range missile and drone attacks.
Just hours before Trump's announcement, a Russian drone struck the headquarters of Ukraine's SBU security service in central Kyiv, according to Zelensky.
The strike, which Zelensky said was aimed at the office of the agency's acting chief, was the first on its headquarters since the start of the invasion.
Despite the unprecedented nature of the strike, the Ukrainian president proposed observing a ceasefire with Russia for the duration of the US envoys' trip.
"There will be no air strikes on our part, and Russia must reciprocally ensure a ceasefire – without its own air strikes – for the duration needed to conduct these talks," he said in his evening address.
Russia did not immediately comment on the proposal.
Zelensky on Saturday accused Russia of hitting Ukraine's airports in Kyiv and the nearby town of Boryspil overnight ahead of Witkoff and Kushner's visit.
Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. But Zelensky said that officials discussed the possibility of the two peace negotiators using a plane for their expected visit to Kyiv on Sunday.
"Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport," Zelensky said on the Telegram app.
"Russian-Iranian Shaheds (drones) in response to American diplomacy."

Hours later, Oleksandr Ganzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk regional military administration, said a Russian strike killed four people and wounded five in the southeastern city of Kamianske.
Zelensky had said on Wednesday that Russian airspace would be "completely unsafe" and filled with Ukrainian drones as long as Moscow continued its war.
Putin said Zelensky's comments amounted to "state terrorism" and said that Moscow would head off any disruption to civil aviation.

- UN experts warn the blockade violates international law and is causing a humanitarian crisis threatening health, food, and development rights in Cuba.
AI generated
HAVANA - The US embassy in Havana issued a health alert for Cuba on Sept 4, warning travellers and residents of a spike in intestinal illnesses and diarrhoea caused by failing water and electricity supply, even as the Trump administration continued to hold back fuel shipments necessary for power generation on the island.
“The US Embassy has noted a significant increase in diarrhoea illness across Cuba, associated with the continuing degradation of the water and energy infrastructure,” the alert stated.
“This degradation affects water supply, and food storage and temperature control.”
The US warning comes nine months after the Trump administration imposed a fuel blockade on the communist-run island, contributing to a sharp spike in power cuts and complicating refrigeration and sanitary measures in homes and businesses.
UN-appointed human rights experts have called the Trump fuel blockade a violation of international law.
A team of UN experts in August warned of a growing risk of disease outbreaks on the island as the US has tightened sanctions.
“The humanitarian consequences are already unfolding into a full-blown crisis, threatening the rights to health, to life, to food and to development,” the experts said.
The Trump administration says sanctions are necessary to force a change in the island’s government, a decades-long aim of the US following Fidel Castro’s 1959 revolution.
Trump has called Cuba a national security threat to the United States.
Residents throughout Cuba have for months complained of rampant illnesses that cause several days of diarrhoea, fever and body aches, leaving many bedridden.
During the Caribbean’s sultry summer, sleep without air conditioning or a fan often becomes impossible, as does food preservation without refrigeration.
Blackouts spanning days have become commonplace amid the US fuel blockade.
The US health alert on Sept 4 advised travellers and residents in Cuba to “be cautious of... perishable foods that may have been inadequately stored,” and warned against eating “foods that appear to have been sitting at room temperature for extended periods.” REUTERS

Romanian prosecutors have officially indicted social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate with a range of trafficking and sex offences.
They are accused of making more than $1.2m (£888,000) by coercing a girl to perform sex acts on video chats, according to the Romanian Directorate for Investigating Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT).
Andrew, 39, is charged with trafficking minors, money laundering and having sex with a minor. Tristan, 38, is charged with complicity in trafficking in minors and money laundering.
The Tates - currently in a Miami jail fighting extradition to the UK over separate charges - deny all the allegations.
- Will the Tate brothers be extradited from the US to the UK? 
  - Published21 July
The brothers - former kickboxers with dual US and British citizenship - have been under criminal investigation in Romania since December 2022.
They have been mainly based there since 2017, drawing a large social media audience - many of them young men - through misogynistic messages and images of a luxury lifestyle.
Romanian prosecutors described a case as centring on a vulnerable female who was 15 at the time of the alleged offence, in information released on Friday.
She is alleged to have been recruited by Andrew and housed in a building in Luton, Bedfordshire, so he could sexually exploit her. Tristan is alleged to have been an accessory, prosecutors say, using physical aggression to coerce the victim.
DIICOT investigators allege Andrew controlled her through surveillance and physical aggression, and coerced her to perform sex acts on video chats for his financial gain.
Andrew is also accused of moving her to Romania to carry on exploiting her in two of his homes.
He is separately charged with having sex with a minor, who was 15, in Romania.
Prosecutors have also requested four of the brothers' luxury cars worth £710,000 be confiscated. They believe money was laundered through their purchase.
The two brothers were previously indicted in Romania on trafficking charges, but in 2024 an appeals court in Bucharest sent the case back to prosecutors after deeming some evidence inadmissible.

"DIICOT has now chosen to file a new indictment. We will examine every aspect of it with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process.
"Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them. They have the right to the presumption of innocence, the right to properly examine the evidence relied upon against them and the right to mount an effective defence."

Some defence industry executives say his task has been complicated by the slow pace of Congress appropriating funds despite immense pressure from the administration.

One of the costs has been a drawdown of US weapons stockpiles.

Lubomyr Horbach, Head of the Pamiat (Memory) Society for Searching for War Victims, told Ukrinform.

According to him, search teams initially use machinery to remove the top layer of soil from the grave pit and then work by hand, carefully clearing the remains of soil. The remains are then photographed before the bones are recovered and the soil is examined for personal belongings, buttons and other items.
During the exhumation at the Holosko Cemetery, the team found a military identification tag belonging to a Polish soldier and three belonging to German servicemen, uniform buttons bearing the Polish coat of arms, various fasteners, hooks and rings characteristic of Polish military equipment, as well as a Catholic rosary and a small mirror.
Horbach said the Polish identification tag contained the soldier’s first and last name, year of birth, religious affiliation and the locality where he was drafted. German tags contain only a personal identification number, military unit and blood group. However, he added, German archives contain extensive records on military units, meaning there is a good chance the servicemen can be identified.
As Ukrinform reported, on August 25, around 30 specialists from Ukraine and Poland began search and exhumation work at the Holosko Cemetery in Lviv. The operation is scheduled to continue until October 2. The exhumation studies are being carried out pursuant to agreements reached through the work of the Ukrainian-Polish Working Group on National Memory.
The search and exhumation work is being conducted on the Ukrainian side by the Pamiat Society for Searching for War Victims, and on the Polish side by specialists from the Institute of National Remembrance of the Republic of Poland and Wroclaw Medical University.
Search operations conducted in 2010 and 2019 identified 110–120 individual graves of Polish Army soldiers at the cemetery who were killed in battles against German military units that surrounded Lviv from the west and south in September 1939.

A Russian ‘dispute about love’: The story behind the viral video
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
02:18:37 UTC
11:18:37 KST

A loud argument between Russian intelligentsia over Schubert, Bach, and the merits of a fugue has delighted millions of viewers far beyond the Russian-speaking internet.
Here’s the background.
St. Petersburg, 2019. Three old friends are bantering around a table when the topic naturally turns to Franz Schubert, as it does, and things get emotional.
Esteemed musicologist Natalia Entelis is at a post-lunch table with friends; former orchestral violinist Emil Finkelstein and his wife Elena Fradkina, who was celebrating her 80th birthday. Their daughter, pianist Polina Fradkina, who – possibly knowing what was coming – recorded the video, posted it online recently in connection with comments over the merits of an online music course, and it has struck a chord.
Finkelstein opens with a demand for an inquiry, into how Schubert could have written such brilliant music without knowing the work of Johann Sebastian Bach.
Opposite and stoic in her resolve, Entelis observes that fugues are almost entirely absent from Schubert’s masses and, as you would, points instead to the Italian tradition he studied.
The best video you'll see all day pic.twitter.com/PMkiUnn63G
— Joan Cook from PBS (@MissPavIichenko) September 2, 2026
Tip: a fugue is more or less a form in which one musical voice introduces a theme and others pick it up. Bach used them.
Meanwhile, birthday girl Fradkina drops a bomb, asking if writing one is “some f***g mark of quality?”
Voices rise and hands fly, of course. Italian polyphony – always the first to go – is dismissed as “bullsh*t.”
Beethoven’s preference for Handel over Bach enters the fray, obviously, before Fradkina declares: Schubert’s songs were works of genius; everything else was “crap.”
The argument ends with one final disagreement:
“Schubert, as a person, is my favorite composer,” Entelis says.
“No,” Finkelstein corrects her. “Bach is your favorite composer.”
Finkelstein, now 85, told the St. Petersburg publication Paper that Entelis was working on an academic article about Schubert at the time.
“I once got to perform a mass by Schubert, a religious work, that is terribly boring, to my taste,” he recalled. “I did not like her writing about bad music.”
He described the exchange as something more personal. “It was a dispute about who values which music, and who loves which music,” he said. “A dispute about love, if you like.”
An online course on medieval and Renaissance music by popular lecturer Anna Vilenskaya had come under fire from specialists over factual errors, prompting a wider argument about accuracy in popular education.
Fradkina said she shared her family video to explain why professional musicians can react so strongly to an apparently small mistake.
“Understanding how music works is not a collection of correct dates and terms,” she wrote. “Facts are needed to see the process behind them.”
In late Soviet life, private flats – and kitchens in particular – were gathering places where friends could spend hours arguing about everything from politics and history to books, music and everyday life.
“I grew up in a family of musicologists,” Fradkina wrote on Facebook, recalling how everything at home revolved around music: “from family squabbles over a missing slipper to fierce discussions about the roots of antisemitism, from Slavophiles and Westernizers to the proper way to make Olivier salad. Somehow, sooner or later, it all came back to music.”
With English subtitles, the clip became a hit on X. One widely shared upload has received more than five million views and thousands of comments.
Viewers called it “the most intellectual argument” they had seen on the platform and said they would watch five seasons of the discussion. Some joked that the scene explained Russian classical literature; others described it as “a breath of fresh air” and even a video that “heals the nervous system.”

The reactions sometimes romanticized three individuals as representatives of an entire culture. But they also recognized something genuine: in an internet full of anger without intimacy, this was an argument that became heated because everyone at the table cared.
So while some might be surprised at the emotionality of Russians engaged in a passionate discussion of pinnacles of European culture, here's the reality.
Finkelstein says he and Entelis are still friends and still meet for coffee.
