That viral 'bulls***' moment and how football saved Awer Mabil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
02:18:28 UTC
11:18:28 KST

Socceroo Awer Mabil on his response to Pauline Hanson's monoculture comments
In short:
Socceroos star Awer Mabil says he was being himself when he called Pauline Hanson's plan for a monoculture in Australia "bulls***".
He says it's important to celebrate multiculturalism because that's what makes Australia great.
What's next?
Mabil is looking forward to putting down roots in Australia after spending more than a decade playing in Europe.
Awer Mabil will never forget his first football, because he made it himself.
"We used to collect plastic bags and then tie them up into a ball shape," he tells triple j hack.
"It was pretty cool."
Loading...
Mabil is remembering his childhood in the Kakuma Refugee Camp where he was born in north-western Kenya.
"Football was 100 per cent an escape for us," he says.
"If you're hungry, you don't feel hungry because you're just playing for the moment with your friends.
"Then when I came to Australia, I was like, 'oh … I don't have to make the balls from the scratch.'"
Mabil and his family arrived in Australia as refugees when he was 10-years-old.
Since then he's established himself as one of Australia's most well-known football players, representing the nation at two World Cups, and being recognised as the Young Australian of the Year in 2023.
Now 30, Mabil is back in Australia after a decade playing in Europe, achieving his dreams.
Earlier this year, the Socceroos star signed a three-year deal with Melbourne City and says he's looking forward to putting some roots down here.
"I can finally buy furniture that I can keep," he laughs.
"I also want to play in front of my family and friends ... I didn't take advantage of it when I was here before and now I get that chance again."
'We're all proud'
Returning to Adelaide from the Socceroos World Cup campaign in July, Mabil made headlines when he was asked about One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's calls for a "monoculture" in Australia.
"It's just all bulls***," Mabil told waiting reporters.
Now with a few months distance, the football player says he's still surprised by how much traction his response got.
"To be honest, it just came to my head," he tells hack.
"I was just being myself.
"I feel passionate about including everybody because that's what makes Australia great.
"So if there are people that try to divide what Australia is then that's not good."
Mabil says it's important to not only tolerate other cultures in Australia, but celebrate them.
"My little brothers were born here and they're more Aussie than anybody else.
"But everybody's got different flavours."
Mabil says many have thrown their support behind his defence of multiculturalism in recent months, but concedes there has been hate as well.
"I don't let that energy get to me."
"I've learned that being genuine, being pure to yourself and honest is best.
"Don't take in negativity."
Returning to Kakuma
One of Awer Mabil's biggest focuses in life, away from sport, is charity.
After a trip back to the camp where he was born, he and his brother started the charity Barefoot to Boots which supports refugees living in camps around the world by supplying them with football boots and equipment.
"It's very humbling," he says.
"Every time I go back it brings me back to appreciating the life that I have, that we have here in Australia, because people are struggling with the basic stuff there."
Barefoot to Boots has expanded its scope in recent years, funding sanitary products for girls, hospital equipment, teaching supplies and building public bathrooms.
"We went into the hospitals and realised the premature born kids didn't have a chance.
"So we donated three incubators and to be honest that's the best thing we've ever done because that's saving lives."
'Learn to love yourself'
Mabil says a bit of time has helped him better appreciate the Socceroos' effort at this year's World Cup, after the Australian team was beaten in a Round of 32 clash against Egypt.
It was just the third time the Socceroos had reached the knockout stage of the tournament.
"We were so close to making history," he says.
"We should be proud as a team.
"The future is looking great and I'm very optimistic about Australian football."
Asked what his future holds after football, Mabil smiles.
"It's an interesting question.
"I enjoy media a lot and could go down that path.
"But whatever I choose next … I'll put the same discipline into it that I did towards my football career."
His advice for other young Australians who may be struggling with identity or feeling different is simple.
"Learn to love yourself.
"Remember … I'm created perfectly the way I am."

Muhammed Yasin Güngör

US investigators in August administered polygraph tests to 50 military officers and civilian officials following leaks concerning depleted American munitions stocks, according to multiple media reports on Friday.
The probe targeted personnel with the Joint Staff, a group of senior military leaders advising the president, focusing on leaks regarding shortages of long-range missiles and Patriot interceptors due to the war with Iran, The New York Times reported.
A CBS News report revealed that the FBI was not involved in conducting the tests, as the military utilized its internal investigators. Not all senior leaders were tested, with the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine being excluded from the sweep.
US President Donald Trump is said to be furious about the unauthorized disclosures.
No officials failed the polygraph questions designed to determine if they leaked information to the media, according to CBS News. Investigators were also concerned about whether a government official was potentially operating as a foreign spy because access to the specific munitions data was highly restricted, it said.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the agency "does not comment on internal personnel or investigative matters" but takes classified leaks "extremely seriously and investigates accordingly."
Trump denied the reported strategic shortages, insisting the military possesses "massive amounts" of weaponry. Trump labeled the disclosures as "treasonous statements" and "fake news," warning that those responsible would be "hunted down" and face severe prison sentences.
The polygraph sweep followed separate unauthorized disclosures, including a leaked portion of the Secretary of Defense Orders Book. The document showed six four-star leaders formally expressing dissent about extending large-scale operations against Iran, warning the war is "unsustainable" and erodes global readiness.
Parnell condemned the leak as a "crime" and "a betrayal of the force" and said much of the reporting was inaccurate.

The Times reported that the leak investigations have contributed to an atmosphere of distrust inside the Pentagon under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has also restricted journalists' access to the department. The Times is challenging those restrictions in court.

temporary pavilion uses cedar, cypress, and reclaimed CLT for japan’s forest festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
02:10:29 UTC
11:10:29 KST

Three Rotating Planes Define Onodatesho Pavilion’s Form
Crafted from regional cedar and cypress, the Onodatesho Pavilion was designed as the ceremonial structure for Japan’s annual National Tree-Planting Festival, hosting the Emperor and Empress during the day-long event dedicated to forest appreciation and preservation. Since 1950, Japan has commissioned a temporary piece of state architecture for the festival, with the ceremonial pavilion traditionally dismantled shortly after the event.
For the pavilion in Ehime, Yano Aoyama Architecture Design developed a timber structure that combines large-scale cross-laminated timber (CLT) panels with a simple structural system and an approach centered on reuse. The largest CLT panels transportable in Japan, measuring 12 by 2.3 meters, are kept substantially intact. Instead of relying on extensive cutting to define the overall form, the geometry is produced through six operations: tilt, rotate, lean, taper, shift, and cut. These operations are coordinated through a single joint detail repeated throughout the structure.
The pavilion comprises three principal asymmetrical planes that rotate around an imaginary axis. One of the main wooden masses leans ten degrees toward the audience, referencing the profile of nearby Mt. Ishizuchi and supported by slender steel rods. The planes are positioned according to ceremonial sightlines and requirements for sun protection, while their arrangement reflects the festival’s theme of renewal: plant, grow, use, repeat.
Timber Reuse Extends the Pavilion Beyond Its Temporary Life
The structure was developed in collaboration with local carpenters, CLT manufacturers, and drafters, combining regional timber traditions with contemporary timber production. Cedar and cypress sourced from Ehime establish a direct material connection with the region’s forests, while the use of large CLT panels reflects developments in local timber technology.
Material reuse extends throughout the temporary construction by Yano Aoyama Architecture Design Studio. Cut-offs from the primary CLT panels are incorporated into secondary elements, including the stage stairs. Following the festival, the main panels can be unbolted and repurposed within the regional school network as custom furniture. The pavilion’s temporary lifecycle therefore forms part of its architectural strategy, with its timber components designed for subsequent use after dismantling.

BERLIN, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Defending champion the United States opened its FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup campaign with a 94-61 victory over China as all four groups tipped off with eight matches in Berlin on Friday.
Caitlin Clark registered 14 points and 11 assists without committing a turnover as the United States took control early, leading 27-14 after the first quarter. Paige Bueckers and Rhyne Howard also scored 14 points apiece, while Luo Xinyu led China with 13 points and six rebounds.
Gong Luming, head coach of the Chinese women's basketball team, said he was unsatisfied with the team's performance as the players had failed to get their mindsets in the best possible shape.
"On the defensive end, we were not resolute enough when containing their outside shooters. On the offensive end, we also failed to give full play to our inside advantage," he commented. "The players will go back to watch game footage, draw lessons from this contest and strive for a better performance in the next match."
In Group D's other game, Italy claimed its first Women's World Cup victory in more than three decades, beating Czechia 63-54.
Spain also made a strong start in Group A, cruising past host Germany 83-53 after establishing an early double-digit advantage. Awa Fam scored 17 points for Spain, while Leonie Fiebich led Germany with 13.
"The start was very difficult. Spain made everything and we couldn't stop them or react," said Germany coach Olaf Lange. "We never really found solutions. We must look at it, learn from it and move forward. Our goal now is to finish second in the group."
Saki Hayashi scored 27 points through a World Cup-record nine 3-pointers as Japan rallied in the fourth quarter to edge Mali 102-97 in the other Group D game.
In Group B, South Korea pulled away in the fourth quarter to defeat Nigeria 99-81. France recorded the biggest winning margin of the opening day with a commanding 99-53 victory over Hungary.
In Group C, Belgium registered an 89-75 victory over Türkiye, Australia won 70-54 over Puerto Rico. ■

TOKYO, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- Japan's weather agency on Saturday issued a Level 5 emergency warning for landslides, its highest-level alert, for Yakushima Town in Kagoshima Prefecture, southwestern Japan, as Typhoon Krovanh and an autumn rain front combined to bring record-breaking rainfall to the region.
The Japan Meteorological Agency said it was highly likely that serious landslides had already occurred in the area and urged residents to remain on maximum vigilance and take immediate action to protect their lives.

====================================================================================================

Uruguay declares health emergency for avian influenza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
02:01:45 UTC
11:01:45 KST

Muhammed Yasin Güngör
05 September 2026•Update: 05 September 2026
Uruguay declared a nationwide health emergency on Friday after the discovery of the highly pathogenic H5 avian influenza in backyard poultry, according to officials.
The Livestock, Agriculture and Fisheries Ministry, through the General Directorate of Livestock Services, confirmed the outbreak in Colonia, a department in the southwest. That was after a health concern triggered by bird mortality. Although an initial rapid test yielded negative results, subsequent official laboratory analysis confirmed the presence of the virus.
Authorities ordered a nationwide "interdiction of the affected establishment" alongside strict movement restrictions on non-commercial birds.
The emergency directive restricts all domestic movement of backyard and uncontrolled birds, while exempting those registered under the official Poultry Monitoring System.
The resolution also suspends fairs, auctions and public exhibitions related to avian species. Authorities ordered that free-range and backyard poultry must be confined to "enclosed, covered facilities" to prevent contact with wild birds.
Sanitarians have initiated the slaughter and safe disposal of all exposed birds at the affected site, alongside extensive cleaning and disinfection of potentially contaminated materials. For poultry producers, the ministry recommended "extreme "biosecurity measures, such as restricting the entry of unauthorized people or vehicles, protecting water and food sources from wild birds, and reinforcing disinfection protocols.
Officials emphasized that consuming poultry meat or eggs does not pose any risk to human health, though agricultural teams are coordinating with health authorities to monitor exposed individuals.
Avian influenza A(H5N1), a highly pathogenic subtype that primarily infects birds but can rarely transmit to humans via close contact, carries a high mortality rate in humans, though sustained human-to-human transmission has not been recorded. The public is urged not to handle dead or sick birds.

Police said more than 50 people were injured and dozens of homes damaged, largely by windows shattered in the blast.

====================================================================================================

The lonely crusader against Gianni Infantino
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
02:01:00 UTC
11:01:00 KST

Years before Europe soured on him, Norway's Lise Klaveness was already fighting FIFA's president. Now she's laying out how to rebuild FIFA without him.
Lise Klaveness was calling out Gianni Infantino before it was cool.
The president of Norway’s soccer federation has been a longtime thorn in the side of FIFA’s president, pushing vociferously for more transparent governance at the summit of global soccer. Her concerns, which date back to the World Cup in Qatar in 2022 and its questions about migrant labor and human rights, found a much wider audience this summer after Infantino’s secret plot to sell off parts of the tournament exposed the risks of FIFA’s highly centralized leadership.
The 45-year-old former international soccer player, attorney and judge recently told POLITICO that not only must Infantino depart FIFA but the system he constructed be totally rebuilt. Sipping black coffee recently in Le Café Lacoste at Monaco’s tony Méridien Beach Plaza hotel, the flame-haired Klaveness outlined five areas where that should start, including committee reform and reducing the president’s executive power.
Advertisement
A wave of European nations have now followed Norway in calling for Infantino to go, after his aborted commercial sell-off to private investors including Joshua Kushner’s firm Thrive Capital. Political heavyweights, including British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Canadian premier Mark Carney, have also called for the president’s exit. But Klaveness said she’s not resentful about how slow reinforcements were to arrive. “I think it’s very bad to be passionate about something and then when it happens you are sort of bitter that it didn’t happen before,” she said.
Our expansive conversation with Klaveness about the intersection of global soccer governance and politics took place during UEFA’s season-opening competition draw in Monaco. Just hours after the death of Norway’s King Harald, Klaveness saw her Monaco itinerary upturned as she faced a whirlwind round of meetings with domestic soccer officials about postponing the weekend’s fixtures.
Lise Klaveness, at the women’s Champions League final on May 23, 2026 in Oslo. | Maja Hitij/Getty Images
But she still found time to discuss, beyond Infantino, Russia and Israel’s place in world soccer, why she feels sorry for FIFA’s staff — and which two men she credits with saving the World Cup from Infantino and Kushner.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
POLITICO: Do you believe FIFA’s problems can be solved by removing Gianni Infantino, or has the organization become incapable of governing football well?
Klaveness: So is it an individual problem or is it a structural problem? Right now it’s both. We are very clear that, first of all, we have over time been very worried about how Gianni Infantino has conducted his leadership, distancing himself more and more from his own reforms. And it started even before power would corrupt. So it seemed like that was his modus [operandi], to be elected on one agenda and then rule on another agenda. We desperately need a leader who puts compromises above himself, that puts the sport above himself, that gathers everyone. And we can all see that’s not happening. It’s polarizing.
Advertisement
But even if he leaves, we still think it’s also a structural problem, which needs to be fixed. I would not say FIFA is ungovernable. I think good governance is fully possible. But it needs to be a passion, and we all thought it would be after 2015 with the crisis, and that’s why he was elected.
So of course it’s a bit depressing that it didn’t happen, and it’s easy to think that that will just reproduce. The next leader coming in needs to understand that leadership is not just one person — it’s all of us — and we all need to be accountable for these systems.
With all good governance, the process is also part of the aim. The process in itself makes people accountable. So that it’s not a bureaucracy, but it’s necessary to do it and to have a FIFA Congress next year that — regardless of Infantino or anyone else taking over — needs to decide changes to the structures.
Infantino, standing next to the World Cup trophy on January 29, 2026 in Washington. | Alex Wong/Getty Images
POLITICO: Imagine it’s 2031 and FIFA has successfully rebuilt trust. What are three things that are different from today?
Klaveness: We have many committees doing checks and balances today, and those people should be selected more independently. They are officially selected by the Congress, but they are mainly appointed by the president. And the people there should have a proven record for governance — not critical journalists, on one hand, or loyal soldiers to the president on the other. Normal people that have competence with governance. Because if you put those people in such chairs, my experience is that they will not be corrupted.
I guess it’s not popular to say, but we need to reduce the number in the Council to a third, or at least half. When you have a Council of 37 people it is inefficient and then one person will take over. If you have a fully functioning FIFA in five years that has changed.
Advertisement
And, thirdly, you need a good, implemented and checked regulation between the administration and the president. The president should be more nonexecutive and the general secretary should run the administration and that should be regulated and tested by these committees.
FIFA also very strongly needs to move away from the strategy of growing, growing, growing commercial revenues. So you’re governing the laws of the game, you’re governing the laws of transfers, you are governing the international periods, you’re governing the World Cup, but you’re not first and foremost a business entity.
POLITICO: Thank you for four ideas, not just three.
Klaveness and UEFA President Aleksander Čeferin in Bodoe, Norway on May 8, 2025. | Stian Lysberg Solum/NTB via Getty Images
Klaveness: Yeah, it should actually be more. I would say the fifth thing is that we actually make a review of the reforms Infantino was elected on and implement them. We have to do the analysis, which is now a bit outdated, but I think we went through it in 2015. Then I was following as a nerd, but I liked them and I thought they were good changes.
POLITICO: Do you think football should look outside the football industry for a future leader?
Klaveness: It’s difficult for me to answer that, to be honest. To me, it’s not a yes or no question. I think when we work in football, we all have experienced people from outside football that really lift your organization, really have a very valuable add to your organization. We have all experienced the opposite also, that you come in — for example, business people — and underestimate certain parts of football, that it’s not only a product.
Advertisement
But I think we football people have a tendency to say that it should be football people, and people in the organization — who have come a bit more from outside football — have a tendency to say it should be people coming from outside football. So we all see it from where we are.
And I’m from football, so it would be easy for me to say that is an advantage. I played, but I do not rule out that you can have good leaders [from outside], of course you can. But you need football people in the close team at least. I do think sometimes it’s an advantage to educate players after they’re done and to really make them come back to the game because it is a super power to know how the locker room works.
POLITICO: In light of the Trump-Infantino-Balogun issue that marred the World Cup, what is the red line beyond which political influence becomes unacceptable interference in football?
Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino at the World Cup final trophy ceremony on July 19, 2026 in New Jersey. | Carl Recine/Getty Images
Klaveness: We have been worried about two particular points with the current leadership for almost five years. We have protocol worries about the lack of implementation of very reasonable reforms and very necessary safeguards toward corruption and conflicts of interest. Secondly, the lack of arm’s-length distance to state leaders. And we have repeated this worry for almost five years — before Trump, with different state leaders.
Many people have told us that it’s pragmatism. We all know that if you organize something, you need to cooperate very well with the state leader, which we should all respect. You cannot expect to have a good World Cup and antagonize any state leader. You need access to airports, you need access to city people. Police should keep the streets open. So it’s a state matter.
Advertisement
But for us, at least, it’s been clear over these four years that this arm’s-length distance is not kept, and then you come into very difficult situations, because politicians and state leaders, if they are not kept at arm’s length, they will ask you for political favors — directly or indirectly — which are not yours to give.
It’s been, in our assessment, political interference with FIFA at an unacceptable level, at least for the four years I’ve been following this. Over time, this political influence, too many wanted to see it as pragmatism but I think in all honesty, we all knew that it went too far.
POLITICO: You have been maybe the clearest voice in football talking about these issues for the last five years. Do you feel any sort of vindication … or exasperation?
Klaveness talks to journalists after the 47th UEFA congress in Lisbon on April 5, 2023. | Patricia de Melo Moreira/AFP via Getty Images
Klaveness: First and foremost, I feel very relieved that the UEFA president [Aleksander Čeferin] takes such strong leadership in this, which is not easy; without him the FFE project [to sell of parts of the World Cup] would probably live on.
If UEFA didn’t go so hard against it and [FIFA’s then-Chief Operating Officer, who was fired from the organization] Kevin Lamour didn’t call it out, I think it would have been very difficult to stop it. So I think we have to thank these two, because you had an administrative guy telling the truth and you had a confederation president going very clearly in one direction. That was a huge relief.
I think it’s very bad to be passionate about something and then when it happens you are sort of bitter that it didn’t happen before. No, it is what it is and I also have to respect that we are a smaller country, I have a membership and a board that expects this from me. We have been equally disturbed by this for four years, and not just me, my whole board. And my congress has asked me for this several times. So, transparency drives behavior also.
Advertisement
POLITICO: In terms of the current structure of FIFA, do you think the structure is strong enough to resist potential political interference or do you think the structures need to be toughened in 2027?
Klaveness: I think both. I honestly think that it’s easy to say that power corrupts and that goes for everyone — but I’ve met so many people in power that are not corrupted by power. They are decent, concentrated, checked and balanced every day because they also have people around them every day. They hire people that are strong CEOs or general secretaries or advisers. So it is an individual crisis, we have to be honest that he was not what he promised to be, he was a legal officer, he was portraying himself as a governance guy. But when in position — listen to his speeches …
Should we, for example, have external members in the FIFA Council? I would say definitely, but it needs to be thoroughly assessed because it cannot be like whistleblowers. It needs a trusted environment where we all work together. Maybe supervisory board, and maybe external members; definitely a Council culture, where you ask questions every Council meeting. And, not to be rude, but where you also allow — it sounds banal — but where we decide now that in every Council meeting it should be fully OK that we ask questions.
Spain’s captain Rodri is presented with the World Cup winner’s trophy by Infantino and Trump. | Dan Mullan/Getty Images
POLITICO: Infantino built a system where that sort of scrutiny is not welcome?
Klaveness: No, and I think that is a general football thing, when you want a leader gone, then you speak; but when you support a leader, then you don’t speak, because then it’s seen as taking a position.
Of course I come from a country where it’s not like that, so it’s easy for me. At all my meetings, people will discuss everything. And also at Congress people go to the stage and maybe a hundred people could come — I’m not exaggerating, it goes for two days — and some of them are really angry at some cases, but I still have their trust, it’s not a personal thing.
Advertisement
What we need to remember is that FIFA does a lot of great stuff — you’ve got to remember this. They have the World Cup now. We work with FIFA, with our team. I was the head of delegation with my team. I was there from June 1 till we went out. And all interaction we have with FIFA on an operational level was excellent, beyond excellent.
POLITICO: But this makes it even worse for all those hundreds of staff who work for FIFA, right?
Klaveness: I feel so bad for them, after the World Cup, honestly. I really want people to know that when we meet them it’s not like arrogant people. They’re really de-escalating, really knowledgeable, really patient and I think really sad for this happening.
Klaveness and Secretary-General of Norway’s football association Karl-Petter Loken on October 10, 2025. | Fredrik Varfjell/NTB via Getty Images
They don’t say it necessarily and I don’t put them on the spot, but it’s between the lines that they don’t like it and Kevin Lamour was one of the guys really building bridges. Always interpreting discussions not as opposition but as constructive. He would say, ‘yeah, this is a reasonable thing, I will bring it up, maybe they will not be happy, but then we can have a meeting.’ So those have been good things the last four years, but lack of implementation of reforms and lack of arms-length distance from state leaders, without fail, we will have a crisis.
POLITICO: Where does Norway stand on any move to bring Russian teams back into international competition, and should there be sanctions against Israeli teams?
Klaveness: Such difficult, sensitive cases. I think boycotting countries should be the last resort. It’s not something we should think is a victory, especially from kids. To punish kids for the state leader’s choices, to take them away from football, I really don’t like it.
Advertisement
That being said, it’s impossible now to bring back the Russian teams. Because of the way they are used, the national teams, it’s so hard to separate from the propaganda. But that is a failure, I’m not happy to say that it’s impossible; it’s sadly so, even though we are in 100 percent solidarity with Ukraine. It’s never good to make kids never play with each other. That is the aim, that they could play with each other and not be affected by the war. But that’s not possible now, football would stop and Ukraine would not play. So then we are there, and that’s a sad situation, but happening because of war.
When it comes to the Israel situation, we have always said, and we will always say, when you have a breach of FIFA statutes, it needs to be treated. It was delayed, delayed, delayed for many years, that they play with teams from [settlements in] Palestinian territories, which is not allowed by FIFA statutes. And then it’s politically very difficult, but legally not so difficult. So then you need sanctions, and then what the sanctions should be. You’ve got to look at precedents. Do you have any similar cases where you play in other people’s territories? What about Crimea? What about former Yugoslavia? Maybe you have some precedent. What’s the sanction? If it’s not changed, you increase the sanctions, because you need a rules-based system. And you need territory lines.
Klaveness at a press conference in Oslo on August 7, 2026. | Terje Bendiksby/NTB via Getty Images
When we played Israel, we gave the money to the victims of Gaza, not because we did not want to give to the victims of October 7th, but because there were ongoing attacks on the kids in Gaza, and they were poor, they needed the money.
In the end, it’s all about having bridges that are actually working when this is over, when people come to terms, you need to be effective bridges that speak to both sides. For us, we have had projects in Palestine for very many years, decades, educating girls and women there to be coaches; also in Jordan, in this area. So it’s an area [where] we know how difficult it is, how many good people live there on both sides. You know, in Israel, Jordan, everywhere. So we feel very connected to the region because of these projects.

‘Can’t live without fighting’: Myanmar youth find solace in bareknuckle lethwei
Amid five years of devastating conflict, young fighters embrace the traditional bloodsport as both self-defence and refuge
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
In a country consumed by conflict, a sport defined by brutality dominates: Myanmar’s lethwei martial art, where headbutts are encouraged and knockout blows are the aim of the game.
“I can’t live without fighting,” said 19-year-old Su Luck, who enters the ring under the paradoxical pseudonym “Peace Prize”.
“I have never once considered giving up this passion,” she said.
Lethwei is traditional Burmese boxing, distinct from Thai kickboxing because head blows are permitted and fighters compete bareknuckle, fists protected only with wraps of thin gauze.
It is known as the “Art of Nine Limbs” because each contender’s two fists, elbows, knees, feet and head are considered viable weapons to take down opponents.
In a country where many have been dragged into the five-year-old civil war, the popularity of a tooth-and-nail national sport is obvious to some.

US reportedly put 50 military and civilian officers on lie detectors over Iran war leaks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
02:00:10 UTC
11:00:10 KST

US investigators in August administered polygraph tests to 50 military officers and civilian officials following leaks concerning depleted American munitions stocks amid US war on Iran, according to multiple US media reports.
The probe targeted personnel with the Joint Staff, a group of senior military leaders advising the president, focusing on leaks regarding shortages of long-range missiles and Patriot interceptors due to the war with Iran, The New York Times reported.
A CBS News report revealed that the FBI was not involved in conducting the tests, as the military utilised its internal investigators.
Not all senior leaders were tested, with the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine being excluded from the sweep.
US President Donald Trump is said to be furious about the unauthorised disclosures.
Those subjected to polygraphs were questioned on whether they leaked information to journalists regarding critical ammunition shortages amid tensions between the US and Iran.
No officials failed the polygraph questions designed to determine if they leaked information to the media, according to CBS News.
Pentagon refuses to speak on probe
Investigators were also concerned about whether a government official was potentially operating as a foreign spy because access to the specific munitions data was highly restricted, it said.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the agency "does not comment on internal personnel or investigative matters" but takes classified leaks "extremely seriously and investigates accordingly."
Trump denied the reported strategic shortages, insisting the military possesses "massive amounts" of weaponry.
Trump labelled the disclosures as "treasonous statements" and "fake news," warning that those responsible would be "hunted down" and face severe prison sentences.
The polygraph sweep followed separate unauthorised disclosures, including a leaked portion of the Secretary of Defense Orders Book.
The document showed six four-star leaders formally expressing dissent about extending the war against Iran, warning it is "unsustainable" and erodes global readiness.
Parnell condemned the leak as a "crime" and "a betrayal of the force" and said much of the reporting was inaccurate.

Ecuador defends US sinking of vessels as joint anti-drug operation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ecuador defends US sinking of vessels as joint anti-drug operation
Relatives of detained crew say US forces acted without evidence, claiming the men were fishermen, not smugglers.
Ecuador has defended a US operation this week that sank three vessels accused of sustaining drug-trafficking operations in the Eastern Pacific.
Ecuador’s government said on Friday the interception and sinking of the Ecuadorian vessels were part of joint investigations with Washington targeting drug-smuggling activities linked to criminal gangs.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4US strike on an alleged drug boat in eastern Pacific kills two
- list 2 of 4Civilians faced attacks, abuse in joint US-Ecuador operations, HRW says
- list 3 of 4US military says strike on alleged drug-smuggling boat kills two
- list 4 of 4A year into Trump’s boat strike campaign, families search for answers
Ecuadorian Interior Minister John Reimberg told broadcaster Teleamazonas the vessels were refueling points for speedboats that move drugs north towards Mexico and the United States.
“This is work carried out through international cooperation,” Reimberg said.
The US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) reiterated Reimberg’s claim, saying it “successfully interdicted a vessel operating as a floating refueling station in support of illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations”, linked to the Los Choneros gang.
“Individuals removed from the vessel will be safely transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. Once cleared, U.S. forces sank the vessel,” SOUTHCOM posted on X on Thursday.
A video accompanying SOUTHCOM’s post showed US forces approaching and boarding a vessel before it was blown up at sea. The time and location of the video have not been independently verified.
Relatives of some crew members accused the US military of acting without evidence and said the men on the boats were fishermen. The wife of one crew member told the Reuters news agency in a phone interview that the men had been fishing when US forces boarded and that no drugs were found. Her account has not been independently verified.
The Ecuadorian navy said that it received 28 crew members from that vessel and another boat that was sunk on Wednesday and that they arrived in Manta, the country’s main fishing port, on board a local coastguard vessel.
On Friday, a group of people waited for news of their relatives who, they said, were traveling on the boats targeted in the past two days, the AFP news agency reported.
The incidents are the latest in the Trump administration’s campaign against maritime drug trafficking that has drawn concern in Latin America over the use of air attacks and lethal force on international waters.
SOUTHCOM confirmed a previous attack on a “low-profile” vessel that killed two people on August 23. Another US strike killed four people two days later. No victims were identified in either attack.
Trump has claimed the US is in a “non-international armed conflict” with drug-trafficking organisations in an unreleased memo obtained by US media.

Opponents seek to block US from starting work on Trump arch in Washington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
01:38:00 UTC
10:38:00 KST

Judge reinforces order barring immediate work on Trump arch in Washington
- A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to give 48 hours’ notice before any work on the planned Trump arch near Arlington National Cemetery, except for archaeological testing.
- The administration claims a 1925 law authorises the arch, but opponents argue it violates federal law and lacks Congressional approval.
- The arch project faces legal and planning challenges, with concerns over historic site impact and ongoing court disputes delaying construction.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - A federal judge on Sept 4 ordered the Trump administration to give 48 hours’ notice before engaging in any activity on the site of a triumphal arch it wants to build near Arlington National Cemetery, except for work to identify underground cultural artifacts.
The ruling by US District Judge Tanya Chutkan came a day after the US Interior Department announced plans to move forward soon with work for the 76m arch despite legal challenges and the lack of final approval from a government planning authority.
In a US District Court filing on Sept 4 seeking a temporary restraining order, lawyers for a group of three military veterans and an architectural historian said the administration has “no legal basis for the construction work.”
They said the arch violates federal law and needs approval from Congress.
The administration has argued a 1925 law that authorised a now-defunct commission to build Washington’s Arlington Memorial Bridge provides congressional approval for the arch, which the opponents dispute.
Despite Sept 3’s announcement on X by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum of work starting after “a very long wait,” the government said in a court filing on Sept 4 the planned excavation work at the arch site was “not construction, or demolition in preparation for construction, of an arch.”
The government added in its court filing that it plans to dig four “test pits” to assess if any artifacts or cultural materials are present, starting on or after Sept 21. It said it would restore the site by Oct 31.
Chutkan in April sharply questioned Trump’s authority to build the arch and the government in April agreed to provide 14 days’ notice before starting construction.
The Interior Department reiterated that notice plan on Sept 4.
In her latest ruling, Chutkan ordered the administration to provide the court at least 48 hours’ notice before “engaging in any activity” at the site, except efforts to gather information on archaeological resources beneath subsurface fill materials as required under the National Historic Preservation Act.
She also reiterated that any construction or demolition in preparation for construction before the National Park Service issues a final authorisation, or without providing 14 days’ notice, would violate Sept 4’s order and her previous consent order.
The arch is part of Trump’s broader effort to leave his architectural mark on America’s capital city, with projects including a new White House ballroom, renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and redevelopment of a golf course in East Potomac Park.
With a design evoking Paris’ Arc de Triomphe, the monument would rise near the Arlington National Cemetery, a military burial ground, which supporters say would honour the sacrifice of American veterans.
Opponents say the arch would destroy the cemetery’s carefully designed historic sight line between Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House.
The project also has yet to receive final approval from the National Capital Planning Commission, which is considering whether to grant an exception to the 40m building height limit that applies to most of Washington.
In the Sept 4 court filing, opponents of the project pointed to Trump’s construction of a ballroom on the White House grounds as a “cautionary tale,” saying the government proceeded with construction even though a District Court found it unlawful and the Circuit Court affirmed the ruling.
The US Supreme Court last week in a 5-4 ruling let ballroom construction continue while Trump challenges a judicial order that would halt much of the development, with Chief Justice John Roberts in a dissent calling the project “likely unlawful.” REUTERS

Air Force Coalition identifies five areas of support for Ukraine
According to Ukrinform, the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine reported this.
Representatives of Ukraine, the Kingdom of the Netherlands, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada took part in the meeting.
The participants discussed the Coalition’s achievements, Ukraine’s current needs, and further steps to develop the country’s aviation capabilities. They also met with Ukrainian Deputy Defense Minister Serhii Boiev and a working group led by Lieutenant General Anatolii Kryvonozhko, Commander of the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
The Coalition is focusing on five areas of support for Ukraine:
- development of aviation infrastructure;
- personnel training;
- maintenance of existing aviation capabilities;
- development of the helicopter component;
- scaling up defense-industrial and military-technical cooperation.
The participants also discussed establishing an Air Force Capabilities Coalition Fund. The fund will improve coordination in developing aviation capabilities and help attract financing to accelerate the implementation of priority projects.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukraine is being moved from the status of a country waging war through reliance on external supplies to that of a European defense hub.

John Malkovich to return to Israel with satirical theatrical-musical show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
01:30:39 UTC
10:30:39 KST

Two-time Oscar nominee and Emmy Award-winning actor John Malkovich is scheduled to return to Israel on April 13 to star in the satirical theatrical-musical production The Music Critic at the Charles Bronfman Auditorium (Heichal Hatarbut) in Tel Aviv.
The Music Critic – written and conceived by Russian-German Jewish violinist and composer Aleksey Igudesman – blends classical masterpieces with some of the most scathing historical reviews ever written about them.
On stage, Malkovich embodies an “evil critic” who insults iconic composers, declaring that Robert Schumann merely “fancies himself a composer,” Johannes Brahms is a “giftless bastard,” and the works of Ludwig van Beethoven and Frédéric Chopin are simply tedious.
A live ensemble, featuring Igudesman and pianist Hyung-ki Joo, fights back against Malkovich’s verbal assaults by performing live renditions of the disputed music by Bach, Mozart, Debussy, and Prokofiev.
Malkovich reads a real, brutally harsh critique written about his own career
The performance culminates in a grand finale titled “The Malkovich Torment,” where the actor reads a real, brutally harsh critique written about his own career.
The show has previously toured extensively across Europe and the United States and has been released as an official album.
The announcement comes at a rare time for international bookings in the country, which have faced widespread disruptions and cultural boycotts amid the ongoing regional conflict.
In a statement regarding his upcoming tour, Malkovich shared his excitement about returning to the region:
“I am thrilled to return to Israel and look forward to meeting the warm Israeli audience once again, to whom I feel a strong closeness and solidarity. I hope to find you happy and optimistic! Sending you much love.”
Israeli producer Alon Yuryk expressed optimism that the booking would signal a broader return for major global performers.
“It is deeply moving to see Malkovich’s heartwarming responsiveness to performing here,” Yuryk said. “I view this as a trust-building step toward reviving major international performances in Israel.”
Malkovich's third time back since being guest of honor at the 2008 Jerusalem Film Festival
The April 2027 performance will mark Malkovich’s third professional visit to Israel. He first visited the country in July 2008 as a guest of honor at the Jerusalem Film Festival. He returned for his first stage performance in April 2013, headlining the musical drama The Infernal Comedy: Confessions of a Serial Killer, at the Eilat International Chamber Music Festival and the Tel Aviv Museum of Art.
The 72-year-old actor remains best known for his acclaimed screen roles in Places in the Heart, In the Line of Fire, Dangerous Liaisons, Con Air, and Being John Malkovich.
When asked in a 2020 interview with Walla which characters align most closely with his actual personality, Malkovich remarked that he shares very little in common with the serious or intellectual archetypes he usually plays.
He suggested that his roles in Of Mice and Men or the borderline-clownish showman in The Great Buck Howard felt closer to his true nature.
“In real life, I’m not a serious person,” he said.

What to watch this week: Gal Gadot speeds through The Runner, Hearsay delivers gripping thriller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
01:30:17 UTC
10:30:17 KST

It’s exhausting watching Gal Gadot sprinting for about 95% of the time during The Runner, her new movie directed by Kevin Macdonald, which just became available to stream on Prime Video from Amazon.
The movie is just what the trailer promises: an action-packed thriller featuring Gadot as Maia, a lawyer and single mom in London, who gets a phone call from a man with a scary voice and learns that her son has been kidnapped as she goes for a run in the park before a big trial.
The little boy, Noah (Rory Wilmot), is diabetic, and the caller (Damian Lewis, who played Brody on Homeland) says he has messed with her son’s insulin, and she can see for herself through an app on her phone that he has gone into a coma.
The menacing, all-knowing caller threatens to let her son die unless she goes to the hotel suite where her star witness is holed up, waiting to testify in a murder trial, and kills him.
Without this witness’s testimony, the murderer will walk free, of course.
Maia protests that she can’t kill anyone, and the scary voice says, “Oh, I think you can.”
He tells her to run all the way across town to the hotel, and gives her an hour to do the deed.
If any actress could convince us that she has a shot at outfoxing this guy, it’s Gadot, who has never looked more intimidatingly fit than she does here.
Most of the movie shows her running across the city, bumping into people, narrowly avoiding cars, and giving us glimpses of postcard-perfect London.
All the while, the caller keeps up a steady stream of malevolent chitchat as he strips her bare psychologically at her most vulnerable moments, the way mysterious movie villains tend to do.
There’s a twist about her background that provides one of the movie’s two or three most predictable moments, which you will probably see coming from a mile off, but much of The Runner gets pretty wild.
There are a few especially good action sequences, which are right up there with the car chase through Paris in The Bourne Identity.
While Mark Gibson’s script throws in a cliché or two (or three), it’s fun if you watch it with the right mindset.
Gadot radiates tension effectively and generally seems more relaxed than she has in any movie since Wonder Woman.
The Runner may be enhanced if you see it as a metaphor for the impossible life of a single mother, who tries to please everyone as she races from one obligation to another. Most working mothers will identify with Maia as she becomes progressively more disheveled and desperate as the day goes on and the clock ticks down.
Director Macdonald, who won an Oscar for his documentary about the Munich Olympic massacre, One Day in September, and who also made The Last King of Scotland, comes from British-movie royalty, as his grandfather was Emeric Pressburger, a Hungarian Jew who worked in the German and French film industries until he fled to England rather than Hollywood, as many of his contemporaries did.
With his writing/directing partner Michael Powell, Pressburger made some of the greatest and most quintessentially British classics of all time, including The Red Shoes, The Life and Death of Colonel Blimp, and I Know Where I’m Going!
Two of his films, One of Our Aircraft is Missing, a World War II military thriller, and A Matter of Life and Death, a World War II romance with supernatural elements, are available to stream in Israel on Apple TV+.
Macdonald has always been proud of this legacy and made a documentary about his grandfather, The Making of an Englishman.
Macdonald is also known for his music documentaries, such as Whitney, Marley, and One to One: John & Yoko.
Two Blondie songs feature prominently in The Runner, one of which, of course, is “Hanging on the Telephone.” Kevin, if you’re reading this, please make a documentary about Blondie and/or Debbie Harry.
New psychological thriller: Hearsay on Hot 3
A TERRIFIC new series, Hearsay, just started running on Thursday nights on Hot 3, and it is also available on Hot VOD and Next TV.
It’s a dark, psychological thriller/crime drama, set in Jerusalem, about a troubled police detective who discovers that widespread sexual abuse of children is taking place in an ultra-Orthodox neighborhood.
It’s disturbing but gripping, and it’s the best dark drama on Israeli television since Bad Boy.
Oshri Cohen, who has always been engaging, has matured as an actor in recent years, and he plays Moshe, a detective who is transferred from youth crimes to a precinct in Geula, a promotion arranged by his father-in-law. But Moshe is not particularly happy about it.
He is anxious now that his wife is pregnant with their first son, after having two daughters, and has been wetting the bed.
Reluctantly, he begins therapy with a gruff psychologist, played memorably by Menashe Noy, who opens their first session with an old joke: An atheist puts up a mezuzah, and someone asks him why; he replies that he heard it brings good luck even if you don’t believe in it.
Moshe does not believe that exploring his psyche will solve any problems, even as he begins having nightmares that intensify.
The more he learns about multiple cases of child abuse that may be linked to a Christian pedophile ring, which are being covered up by the rabbinic authorities in the neighborhood who want to handle them on their own, the more he makes enemies and feels threatened wherever he goes.
The series was created by Nimrod Eldar, who made an excellent movie a few years ago called The Day After I’m Gone.
The cast includes Sasson Gabay as Moshe’s father, Shmil Ben Ari as his uncle, Aleeza Chanowitz as a child psychologist, and Seymor Daniel as his quirky office mate. I binged all the episodes I received from Hot, but if you watch them one episode at a time, the suspense will build slowly.
Looking forward to what Hanoch Daum would say
AFTER THE year we’ve had, I was looking forward to what Hanoch Daum would have to say in the new season of his often funny series Life is a Difficult Age, which features a fictionalized version of his schlubby self, a guy who never found an awkward situation he couldn’t make more awkward.
While the promos looked good, the first episode, which premiered on Keshet on Tuesday (and is available online), was a disappointment.
The first episode focused on how Daum and his wife, Efrat (played by Alma Zak of Eretz Nehederet), a computer programmer, created an app to help wounded IDF soldiers navigate the bureaucracy to receive all the benefits due to them.
It makes sense that the characters would do just that, and the episode brings attention to the wounded soldiers and features many of them, spotlighting some of the issues surrounding their recovery.
What this isn’t, of course, is funny, so Daum brings his trademark irreverent humor to the situation. Occasionally, he gets a genuine laugh, but much of it is repetitive, and some of it is truly cringe-inducing.
Much is made of him buying basketballs in the rehab center gift shop and forging the autographs of famous basketball and soccer stars on them. It’s not a spoiler that he gets caught, or that one of the real players arrives to give him hell.
Are Daum and the series running out of decent jokes and funny situations? We’ll know more next week, after an episode that features his daughter (Neta Roth, a scene-stealing actress).

10:29:58 KST

Some 170 notable Jewish personalities have released an open letter defending actor and producer Mark Ruffalo, who has been accused of antisemitism for his comments on Paramount Skydance’s pending acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.
Entertainers, rabbis and a physician who is featured in a new documentary about doctors treating Palestinians in Gaza signed the letter released Wednesday, which called the attacks against Ruffalo a “false and dangerous weaponization of charges of antisemitism.” George Clooney also defended Ruffalo on Thursday.
Signatories of the pro-Ruffalo petition include “Broad City” creators Abbi Jacobson and Ilana Glazer; celebrated filmmakers Joel Coen, Jonathan Glazer and Todd Haynes; Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Tony Kushner; and actors including Hannah Einbinder, Joaquin Phoenix and Debra Winger.
In late August, Ruffalo, the award-winning actor and progressive activist, went on social media to link Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison, the chief driver of the looming Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, to tech giant Oracle, which Ruffalo claimed is responsible for “an apartheid system of oppression” in Gaza.
Oracle is owned by Ellison’s father, Larry Ellison, one of the world’s richest men; both Ellisons are Jewish and prominent supporters of Israel. Oracle also owns a stake in the social media network TikTok’s US operations, and has long been a target of progressives who point to the company’s links to, and public support for, Israel.
“Larry Ellison will own most of ‘Para Bros,’” Ruffalo wrote in the post, which is no longer available, according to a screenshot reproduced by the Hollywood Reporter. The Spotlight and Marvel star also called Larry Ellison a “classic oligarch” who is “crushing workers and consolidating the wealth of the world for their own power and concentrated dominance.”
The $110 billion merger is under adjudication in federal court in California following an antitrust lawsuit filed by 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America. As backlash to the merger has steadily grown across Hollywood and in political and media spaces, Paramount, at least since June, has pushed the idea that opposition to the merger has an antisemitic element.
Ruffalo’s comments expose his 'true motivation,' Paramount says
The company seized on Ruffalo’s comments, immediately releasing a lengthy statement to the media after his controversial social media post that accused the actor of invoking “antisemitic tropes,” adding, “This simply exposes the true motivation of some who have advocated opposition to this transaction.”
Several leading Jewish groups have also said his post stepped beyond legitimate criticism of the merger and into classic antisemitic rhetoric about Jewish wealth and power.
In an August statement, the head of the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles said the actor’s comments “combined Jewish wealth, media control, secret technology and sinister global power,” drawing on “recognizable antisemitic tropes with a long and dangerous history.” Other LA-based Jewish activist groups, including Creative Community For Peace and the Simon Wiesenthal Center, have also condemned his comments.
Speaking amid the unfolding controversy about Ruffalo and his use of the word genocide to describe Israel’s campaign in Gaza, “Fauda” co-creator Avi Isaacharoff called him “a rare combination” of “ignorant” and “stupid.”
The Jewish Telegraphic Agency has reached out to Shani Rosenzweig, Ruffalo’s agent and a prominent Jewish entertainment figure in her own right, for comment and a Ruffalo interview request. Rosenzweig did not respond to either request.
Several Jewish progressive figures support Ruffalo
Ruffalo has found support from several progressive Jewish figures beyond the entertainment industry, including IfNotNow co-founder Simone Zimmerman, Israeli Holocaust historian Raz Segal and Jewish Currents editor Peter Beinart.
In their open letter defending Ruffalo, the progressive Jewish cohort argued the actor was right to draw links between Israel’s behavior and the merger.
“Pointing out the crucial connections between what is happening in Gaza and what is happening in Hollywood is the exact opposite of antisemitism,” the letter reads. “It is, for us, the very essence of Jewish ethical duty.” The letter points to specific statements from Larry Ellison and Oracle executives, describing their surveillance and artificial-intelligence technological ventures and their positive relationship with Israel.
Other entertainment figures have tried to thread a more careful needle. Oscar-winning filmmaker Kenneth Lonergan, who has directed Ruffalo in two movies and was at one point developing an American remake of the hit Israeli TV series “Shtisel,” defended the actor from antisemitism charges this week while also noting, “I disagree profoundly with many of his positions on the Middle East, Israel, Gaza, and Iran’s constellation of fanatical Islamist fundamentalist proxies.”
“But Mark and I have been friends for over 30 years,” Lonergan continued in his letter to the Hollywood Reporter. “The notion that he is antisemitic is overtly preposterous, and the accusation itself a cynical and disgusting lie.”
Ruffalo is soon scheduled to attend the Toronto International Film Festival for the Sept. 10 premiere of the biopic Being Heumann, about Jewish-American disability rights activist Judy Heumann, in which he co-stars.
Opposition to David Ellison’s bid to combine two historic media giants, each having recently weathered smaller mergers of their own, has grown considerably in recent months. Those objections have come from both Hollywood rank-and-file concerned about further industry consolidation and political and media figures voicing concerns about Ellison’s close ties to US President Donald Trump and his intentions for Warner’s flagship news property, CNN.
The merger was initially expected to be finalized this fall with Trump’s blessing. The president has publicly championed the merger, and his Justice Department approved the deal in June. But talks have stalled following the antitrust lawsuit. The fate of the merger is now in question, with Paramount having agreed to a trial in March 2027 and on the hook for a $7-million-per-day “ticking fee” it had previously agreed to pay out to shareholders if the deal failed to close by this October.
Prior to Ruffalo’s post, Ellison himself published a New York Times op-ed defending his merger plans.

A workshop focusing on confronting antisemitism and amplifying Jewish pride, joy, and resilience through the use of artificial intelligence and social media was held at the Congregation Etz Hayim synagogue in Queens, New York, on Thursday.
The workshop, titled "Digital Defender 102," was run by IMPACT, a nonprofit organization founded after the October 7 massacre to organize, empower, and mobilize the Jewish community and its allies, according to the organization's CEO and co-founder Aaron Herman, who led the event.
About sixty people participated in the workshop, designed for those aged 55 and up, a group Herman described as an "underserved yet incredibly motivated part of our community."
"They have valuable experience, the desire to make a difference and an eagerness to learn," he said. "Through our training programs, we have seen how strongly they want to find their voices, speak up and take meaningful action."
Digital Defender 102 is the second of three such workshops developed by IMPACT; the first introduces participants to the organization's mission and the modern social media landscape, while the third explores advanced social media training and group organization within the IMPACT app.
"Through rewards, incentives, and gamification, we are creating a dynamic and engaging experience that motivates people to participate, have fun, and mobilize around shared goals," said Herman. "Participants can create and share meaningful content, take action in their communities, and inspire others - transforming individual voices and everyday actions into collective impact."
Herman: Workshop participants' growth, progress 'inspiring'
Herman noted the inspiration of watching program participants progress "from not even having a Facebook account to regularly liking, sharing, and engaging with meaningful content."
"That is what IMPACT is all about," he emphasized. "Giving people the tools, confidence, and community to transform small actions into meaningful change."
IMPACT also runs a program for high school students known as their "Learn, Lead, Do" model, designed to empower them to "stand up, speak out and make a meaningful difference online and in their communities."
"Students complete dynamic missions ranging from civic action and community service to creating content and making their voices heard on social media," Herman said. "The program gives young people the knowledge, leadership skills and confidence to turn their values into action."

US envoys to visit Russia, Ukraine with plan 'to end war'
September 5, 2026
US President Donald Trump said he was sending his son-in-law Jared Kushner and businessman Steve Witkoff to Moscow and Kyiv with a proposal to end the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"They're bringing with them a proposal to end the war," Trump told reporters Friday when asked about the pair's trip. Kushner and Witkoff have served as Trump's envoys to lead peace efforts in the Middle East as well as Ukraine.
The US president did not provide any details on the potential plan, including whether it involved Ukraine giving territory to Russia as he has previously suggested, instead, he said, "We have an idea for peace."
Kushner and Witkoff's first trip to Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that Kushner and Witkoff would travel to Ukraine on Sunday following talks in Moscow.
Recent media reports have questioned whether the pair would indeed travel to Ukraine. Despite trips to Moscow to meet with Russian officials, the US envoys have not visited Kyiv since Trump's reelection last year.
Trump had promised to end the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, on his first day back in office, but has more recently commented that bringing an end to the war was more complicated than he expected. In the past, he has blamed Ukraine for the Russian invasion and a "personality problem" between the countries' leaders for the continued fighting.
Zelenskyy vows to pause air attacks during talks
Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram that Ukraine would halt airstrikes during the negotiations and called on Moscow to do the same so talks could proceed safely.
"As with previous diplomatic visits by the American side, we will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace so that the negotiators can arrive safely. We are concerned about their safety, not about Russia," Zelenskyy said.
Russian presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov did not confirm reports that US officials would visit Moscow, saying only that the media would be informed if such a meeting took place. Kushner and Witkoff were last in Moscow in January for a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
On Wednesday, Putin described negotiations as "frozen."
Drone strikes continue

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the strike "a major escalation" of the war.
"Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace — laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy," he wrote on X.
Zelenskyy said he ordered "an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike."
Ukraine has also launched repeated drone strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and the retail giant Wildberries.

Argentina initiates sanction process against 45 entities over Falklands oil exploration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
01:26:22 UTC
10:26:22 KST

Muhammed Yasin Güngör
05 September 2026•Update: 05 September 2026
Argentina initiated on Friday sanction proceedings against 45 individuals and companies suspected of carrying out unauthorized hydrocarbon exploration and exploitation on the Falkland Islands, which Buenos Aires calls Islas Malvinas.
President Javier Milei's office announced that the legal measures target not only active oil firms but also "their shareholders and companies that have been providing services" to facilitate the operations. It said those trying to profit by violating Argentinian sovereignty "will find in the Argentine State the full force of the law."
The government reaffirmed its claim on the Falkland Islands, South Georgia, and the South Sandwich Islands and their "corresponding maritime and insular spaces," declaring they are Argentine "by history and by law" and that there is "no question about it."
Milei warned earlier that the Sea Lion oil project, a major offshore hydrocarbon development near the Falklands operated by British firm Rockhopper Exploration and Israel-based Navitas Petroleum, poses an imminent threat. He noted that without swift action, foreign entities will "appropriate the oil reserves that lie beneath our sea" and deepen their "occupation."
London dismissed the sanctions as domestic politics, asserting its commitment to the islands, while Navitas and its partners said they expect to proceed with drilling under UK licensing.
The long-standing sovereignty dispute between Buenos Aires and London was recently reignited as offshore projects move toward active drilling.
The Falklands are a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic, about 300 miles (483 kilometers) east of the Argentine coast, with a small population. 
Argentina argues that it inherited sovereignty from Spain, and Britain has “illegally occupied” the islands since 1833; it calls the islands Islas Malvinas and rejects the residents’ right to self‑determination as decisive.

Former senator to take 'independent' look at sexual violence in the ADF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
01:16:33 UTC
10:16:33 KST

Natasha Stott Despoja to take 'independent' look at sexual violence in the Australian Defence Force
In short:
Former senator Natasha Stott Despoja has been appointed to lead an inquiry into sexual violence within the Australian Defence Force (ADF).
The inquiry was a key recommendation from The Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide, which found the problem was "systemic" within the ADF.
What's next?
The inquiry is due to begin public hearings next year, and victim-survivors have been told non-disclosure agreements made with the ADF will not be enforced for the purposes of the inquiry.
Former senator Natasha Stott Despoja will lead a new inquiry into sexual violence within the Australian Defence Force (ADF), arguing her independence from the military provides a "fresh" perspective on the issue.
The inquiry was a key recommendation of The Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide, which found sexual misconduct was a "systemic issue" within the ADF.
Ms Stott Despoja will lead a one-year inquiry looking at issues such as prevention and reporting of sexual violence in the military, and how the ADF is managing efforts to tackle the problem in the wake of the royal commission.
The former senator has pursued a career centred on issues such as social justice and gendered violence since leaving politics, including leading South Australia's Royal Commission into Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence.
She does not have a military background, which she said was a key factor in her appointment.
"I understand from the minister and from the [Defence and Veterans' Services Commission] that it was a very purposeful, deliberate decision to have someone who was completely independent in relation to this specific, dedicated inquiry dealing with sexual violence," she said.
"I think the idea was to ensure that they felt that there was someone who would come to this independently and listen to their concerns, take on board the previous reports and the evidence base that's been provided and do so in a way that was very informed, trauma-informed and victim-centric."
In the five years leading up to the royal commission's 2024 final report, there were 800 reported sexual assaults within the ADF.
But the final report noted that figure was in the context of an estimated 60 per cent under-reporting rate, meaning the true number of assaults was likely much higher.
It argued the ADF needed to implement "deep, systemic reform" to tackle the issue, including recommendations such as the mandatory discharge of any members convicted of sexual offences.
Ms Stott Despoja said there are specific issues the royal commission wanted this inquiry to address, including around the effectiveness of the military justice system and barriers to reporting sexual offences.
"This will be — I believe and hope — a once-in-a-generation opportunity for defence to make some changes," she said.
"And what do I want from that? Meaningful change that leads to a workplace that should be equal, ethical, healthy and respectful.
"We respect our military. We know that men and women in uniform deserve to have a safe working environment, given the sacrifices and the challenges and the risks that they already have to face in the context of their job.
"They shouldn't be dealing with sexual violence as part of those risks and challenges."
Inquiry to hear from some previously silenced
Following pressure from legal groups and victim-survivors, the government recently agreed not to enforce non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) for those giving evidence to the looming inquiry.
Some victim-survivors are bound by non-disclosure agreements or non-disparagement agreements as part of legal settlements agreed with Defence.
There had been fears some of the worst-affected victim-survivors would be effectively barred from giving evidence to the inquiry by the legal orders.
Ms Stott Despoja said the agreement means some people can tell their stories for the first time.
"There'll be people who previously couldn't tell their stories because of the NDAs," she said.
"We don't know who those people are, but I'm hoping they will feel able to come forward in an environment that is sensitive, that will provide wellbeing and legal support, but I would like them to come forward if they feel they can to tell those stories that we haven't had the opportunity to hear."
The inquiry is expected to start accepting written submissions later this year, and hold public hearings early next year.
It is due to report by the end of next year.

The fund's money could potentially have gone, among other things, toward payments to participants in the January 6, 2021, Capitol riot who were pardoned by Trump, NBC News reports, writes UNN.

Today's order to disclose the information is a significant step in investigating the secret fund
Nearly $1.8 billion was planned to be allocated to the fund

What is celebrated on September 5 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
04:01:22 EEST
10:01:22 KST

What is celebrated on September 5 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
September 5 marks the International Day of Charity, Beard Day, and commemorative dates in various countries. Believers honor Zechariah and Elizabeth.
On September 5, the world celebrates the International Day of Charity, established in memory of Mother Teresa; India celebrates National Teachers' Day, while according to the new church calendar, believers commemorate Saint Zechariah the Prophet and Righteous Elizabeth, UNN writes.
International Day of Charity
An official UN observance established by the General Assembly in 2012 at Hungary's initiative. The date was chosen to commemorate the death of Nobel laureate Mother Teresa (1997), who devoted her life to helping the underprivileged. The observance is intended to raise awareness of the role of charity in overcoming poverty, engage citizens and organizations in volunteer activities, and support humanitarian initiatives around the world.
World Beard Day
An unofficial holiday traditionally observed on the first Saturday of September. The event brings together bearded people from around the world, promotes the culture of grooming and barbering, and, according to an old humorous tradition, bearded men are exempt from doing any heavy housework on this day.
Teachers' Day in India
A national holiday celebrated since 1962 in honor of the birthday of the prominent philosopher, statesman, and country's second president, Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan. On this day, senior students traditionally switch roles with teachers, conduct lessons in their place, and organize ceremonial events to honor the importance of the educational mission.
Amazon Day in Brazil (Dia da Amazônia)
A state commemorative date established to mark the creation of the Province of Amazonas by Emperor Pedro II in 1850. The day aims to draw public attention to the preservation of the world's largest tropical rainforest, the fight against illegal logging, and the protection of the unique biodiversity of the Amazon River ecosystem.
Knowledge Day in Vietnam
The official beginning of the new academic year for all schools in the country, when millions of schoolchildren return to classes after the summer holidays as part of a unified nationwide ceremonial event.
Remembrance Day of Saint Zechariah the Prophet and Saint Righteous Elizabeth
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Saint Zechariah the Prophet and Saint Righteous Elizabeth—the parents of Saint John the Baptist (Forerunner). According to the Gospel, they remained childless for a long time, but after the Archangel Gabriel appeared to them, a son was born to them who foretold the coming of the Messiah. This day also commemorates the killing of Blessed Prince Gleb—one of the first Old Rus saints who suffered martyrdom.
According to the old calendar, believers celebrate the Leave-taking of the Feast of the Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos and also commemorate Saint Luppus of Thessalonica, who was a faithful servant of Saint Demetrius of Thessalonica and suffered execution for preaching Christianity. In the folk calendar, this day was called "Lup the Lingonberry Gatherer," because by this date lingonberries in the forests usually ripened fully and the first autumn frosts began.

Palestinian football returned on Friday with a club competition in the occupied West Bank, the Gaza Strip and refugee camps in Lebanon after a nearly three-year suspension due to Israel’s genocidal war. 
The Palestinian Football Association organized the competition, “Thousand Martyrs Cup,” with opening matches held simultaneously in the three areas. 
Jabal Al-Mukaber faced Shabab Al-Khalil at Faisal Al-Husseini International Stadium in the town of Al-Ram, north of Jerusalem, while Khadamat Rafah played Shabab Rafah at Ittihad Deir Al-Balah Club’s stadium in the central Gaza Strip.

The association named the competition in memory of Palestinian athletes killed by Israel during its war on the Gaza Strip. 
Return after lengthy suspension

The tournament was named after the martyrs of the sports movement, honoring their loyalty and their sacrifice, said Siyam. Its launch represents “a message that sporting life is returning, even if only in a limited way.” 
Sport amid death, destruction

10:00:07 KST

How some grey-market crypto ATMs in Hong Kong can turn users into fraud victims
Tucked away in laundromats and arcades, machines offer easy access to crypto, but coming regulations will protect consumers, experts say
Inside a tiny self-service laundromat in Quarry Bay in the east of Hong Kong Island, next to a wall of washing machines, stands a waist-high cryptocurrency terminal with signs reading “Elon Musk recommends Dogecoin” and “Buy bitcoin in one minute”.
In order to obtain Dogecoin through the ATM, customers feed Hong Kong dollar notes into a slot and scan a QR code. The equivalent amount in cryptocurrency is then credited into their digital wallet.
Such machines have proliferated across the city in recent years as interest in cryptocurrencies has risen. Many are installed at 24-hour unstaffed shops such as laundromats and claw-machine arcades.
As of 2024, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) found about 200 virtual asset retailers in the city, which included such ATMs.
According to Coin ATM Radar, a global geographical tracker, there are currently 236 crypto ATMs in Hong Kong – concentrated in Mong Kok, Tsim Sha Tsui, Wan Chai and Quarry Bay – offering a dozen different types of cryptocurrencies.
However, these ATMs operate in a legal grey area, with the city still in the process of setting up a regulatory regime for over-the-counter cryptocurrency trading.
