EXPLAINER - How the White House turned its deportation policies into online arcade games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
23:03:14 UTC
08:03:14 KST

“Build the Wall.” “Rio Run.” “Supply Line.” “Flappy Bill.” “Trump Savings Tycoon.”
On the White House website, they are the names of five games in which players stack bricks against a border “horde,” round up pixelated migrants, remove unhealthy food from school lunch lines, keep legislation in the air and catch money for children’s savings accounts.
Behind the deliberately nostalgic graphics are policies, parts of which have faced declining public support, with real consequences for migrants, families and children, cast as targets in a game to capture and points to accumulate.
The online “Arcade,” launched Thursday, packages parts of US President Donald Trump’s political agenda as low-resolution entertainment, drawing criticism from a state lawmaker and social media users who say the administration is trivializing immigration enforcement and stripping it of its human cost.  
How are migrants depicted?
Two of the games focus directly on Trump’s border and deportation policies.
“Build the Wall,” presented with “Zombie Border Siege” imagery, copies the mechanics of Tetris. Players arrange falling blocks to construct a barrier while the game instructs them to “protect the border from the coming horde.”
“Rio Run” adapts the Snake format, placing a pixelated likeness of Trump’s border czar, Tom Homan, on a grid representing the Rio Grande. Players direct the character toward people depicted as border crossers, collecting them one by one while being warned not to double back.
The migrants, shown as small figures with different skin tones, effectively become collectibles in a game built around an administration policy that has resulted in mass arrests, detention and deportation.
The other titles give similar treatment to domestic initiatives.
“Supply Line” asks players to knock products containing seed oils, coloring or additives off a school-food conveyor belt under the banner of the administration’s “Make America Healthy Again” campaign.
In “Flappy Bill,” a bald eagle carries legislation through obstacles above Washington’s monuments, while “Trump Savings Tycoon” has players swing a net at falling cash and gold bars to fund “Trump Accounts,” the administration’s investment program for children born during Trump’s second term.
The White House promoted the arcade through videos imitating the loading screens of major gaming consoles, including one that transformed the Sega logo into “MAGA,” an abbreviation of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” slogan.
It later posted “CAN’T STOP WINNING” on X alongside a link to the games. 
How popular are the policies behind the games?
The arcade also arrives as public support for Trump’s immigration agenda has weakened, particularly over deportations.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll published in February found that 38% of Americans approved of Trump’s handling of immigration, down from 50% shortly after he returned to the White House.
Polling by the Pew Research Center has shown a similar shift on deportations.
In February 2025, 44% of Americans said the Trump administration was doing “too much” to deport immigrants living in the US illegally. By April 2026, that figure had risen to 52%.
Over the same period, the share saying the administration was doing “about the right amount” fell from 47% to 31%. 
Why has the arcade drawn criticism?
The arcade was launched as Trump faces criticism over rising living costs and the economic fallout from the war on Iran, which has disrupted global energy and fertilizer supplies through the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Connecticut state Sen. Matt Lesser pointed to the contrast between the website and the financial pressure facing households, noting that heating-oil prices were near record levels while the administration offered a game featuring Homan.
“Heating oil is near an all-time high but hey you can play Border Czar Tom Homan in a video game. #outoftouch,” Lesser wrote on X.
Adam Cochran, a professor, policy consultant and independent journalist, described the launch on X as “a pathetic and shameful moment in American history.”
The White House defended its approach as a way to communicate Trump’s record and contrast its culture of “fun and winning” with its political opponents. A White House official made the remarks to the Washington Examiner.
The arcade was launched as Trump faces criticism over rising living costs and the economic fallout from the war on Iran, which has disrupted global energy and fertilizer supplies through the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

- A federal judge again blocked the U.S. Postal Service from enforcing President Trump’s sweeping new mail ballot rules.
- California has led the legal charge against the rules, arguing they could cause chaos and disenfranchise millions of voters.
- Judge Indira Talwani’s ruling follows a whistleblower’s claims that USPS is rushing out untested and flawed computer systems to implement the new rules.
A federal judge again Friday blocked the U.S. Postal Service from enacting President Trump’s sweeping new mail ballot rules for the November election, finding that the Postal Service lacks such authority over elections and that neither it nor states such as California are capable of implementing the changes without causing chaos and disenfranchising voters.
U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani noted that election officials from across the country told the court that it is “likely impossible” to comply with the rules, which “makes disenfranchisement more than likely, if not probable” if the Postal Service were to proceed with them.
Talwani’s order — her latest of several halting the plan this summer — came after a Postal Service whistleblower alleged the agency’s new computer systems for the project are fundamentally flawed, a top Postal Service official acknowledged a key online portal was unfinished and the Trump administration filed an emergency petition asking the U.S. Supreme Court to allow the plans to proceed anyway.
All this unfolded this week as some of the first mail ballots of the election cycle started to go out.
The new rules — which Trump required in a March executive order — would require states to submit complete voter lists to the Postal Service and to adopt new ballot envelopes with individualized voter bar codes designed by the Postal Service, and empower the Postal Service to reject any mail ballots that don’t match those lists.
Trump’s executive order also required the Department of Homeland Security to develop its own lists of eligible citizen voters, ostensibly to be compared against the state lists.
Trump has said the changes are necessary to combat widespread voter fraud, including by noncitizens, though independent election experts say there is no evidence that such fraud exists in large numbers.
The effort is part of the implementation of President Trump’s executive order limiting mail voting and has been temporarily halted by a federal judge. The ruling is being appealed by the administration and the directive may ultimately end up back before the U.S. Supreme Court.
Leading Democrats and elections officials in California and other states say the new rules constitute an unlawful federal overreach into state-run elections and a thinly veiled effort by the Trump administration to suppress the vote in a midterm election the GOP is expected to lose.
Talwani, an appointee of President Obama, agreed, finding that the states and voting rights groups are likely to succeed in their claims that the U.S. Constitution reserves the right to regulate elections to the states and Congress — not the executive branch.
Talwani issued her order after holding a contentious hearing in federal court in Boston on Thursday, where she questioned the Postal Service and the dozen conservative-led states supporting it on their ability to implement the changes in time for the Nov. 3 elections. She also heard from California, other liberal-led states and voting rights groups that it would be impossible.
California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta, whose office is helping lead the states’ challenge, hailed Talwani’s order as a crucial reprieve.
“We’ve now secured longer-term relief that will keep the USPS changes blocked while our case moves forward,” Bonta said in a statement to The Times. “We will continue to take all steps to stop the Trump Administration from trampling on voting rights and restricting mail voting.”
Bonta’s office also criticized Department of Justice attorneys for rushing to the Supreme Court before Talwani could issue her order or the U.S. 1st Circuit Court of Appeals could weigh in on an appeal the department had already filed on the matter.
Walter Garcia, a Bonta spokesperson, said the Justice Department had “flouted standard procedural rules” by approaching the high court before the lower courts had weighed in, despite the fact that the Postal Service acknowledged Thursday that it was not ready to launch its new portal.
“It defies common sense that they would seek emergency relief from the U.S. Supreme Court when USPS is unprepared to implement the rule now,” Garcia said.
State law requires that all registered voters be sent a ballot in the mail, and more than 80% of California voters have used those ballots to vote in recent elections.
President Trump has spent months waging an unusually aggressive campaign to reshape how states run elections.
In its emergency petition to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration argued that an earlier temporary restraining order by Talwani to halt the new rules from taking effect was “baseless” and would cause “serious irreparable harm” to the federal government, states and voting public.
“To forestall those harms and protect the public interest, this Court should grant an immediate stay, making clear to States that they should begin efforts to comply if they have not done so already,” wrote Solicitor Gen. D. John Sauer.
The swirl of litigation has created uncertainty around the Nov. 3 election. It also reflects the Trump administration’s desperate race to get the lower court orders lifted and the new rules implemented in time for that election — the rushed nature of which was a prime focus of the whistleblower.
The unidentified Postal Service employee alleged in a statement released Tuesday by congressional Democrats and submitted in court by Bonta’s office that the agency has been rushing to implement the changes — in defiance of an earlier court order — using “an entirely new and untested set of IT systems” that could cause “catastrophic problems” and disenfranchise millions of voters nationwide.
The Postal Service in a statement Friday said that while its system was developed on an “accelerated schedule,” quality and security standards “were not compromised,” and the agency stands behind “both the rigor of our process and the resulting system.”
At Thursday’s hearing, Talwani appeared frustrated when a Justice Department attorney was unable to tell her the status of the portal.
In a subsequent declaration hours later, Steven W. Monteith, the Postal Service’s chief customer and marketing officer, said officials were still making “refinements” to the portal, but anticipated being able to make it available “for voluntary use by sometime next week.”
Talwani previously issued an order blocking the Postal Service changes from being implemented in California and more than 20 other states suing in June. The Trump administration appealed that decision to the 1st Circuit, which declined to lift it, and then on an emergency basis to the U.S. Supreme Court. In early August, Talwani issued a second ruling for the League of Women Voters and other voting rights groups, blocking the changes nationwide.
On Aug. 24, the Supreme Court set aside Talwani’s order in the states’ case, finding that the states’ challenge was essentially premature because the Postal Service had yet to formally initiate the changes or require state compliance. However, the court explicitly noted that it was not reaching any conclusions as to the legality of the pending rules themselves. “On that score, time will tell,” it said.
The states and voting rights groups promptly filed new lawsuits challenging the legality of the rules, which the Postal Service formally issued Aug. 21. And it is in those cases that Talwani issued her ruling Friday.
She wrote that the voting rights groups had standing to challenge the Postal Service rules nationwide in part because the “chaos” created by the rules’ stiff deadlines significantly interfered with their mission to provide voters with accurate and reliable information about how to vote — and whether to use mail ballots to do so.
David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, said in remarks prior to Talwani’s Friday order that he was “very, very confident” that the Postal Service changes will be blocked for the upcoming elections, and that “mail voting is going to go forward as conveniently and securely as it always has.”
That’s in part because election officials nationwide are “telling the courts that even if they wanted to, they could not implement it,” he said — including in a legal filing Becker helped nearly 100 local elections officials from red and blue states file in separate litigation challenging the rules.

Mock Republican convention website tops Google, redirects to Epstein files
Democratic lawmakers poke fun at prank website, while Republicans slam ‘fake news’ and redirect users to real one.
A mock website that directs users to the Epstein Files appears to be the primary search result on Google for the Republican Party’s upcoming midterm convention in Dallas, Texas.
For hours on Friday, the website gopdallas2026.com soared to the top of the search results, with preview text that offered viewers the chance to “discover details about the 2026 RNC [Republican National Committee] Midterm Convention”.

But users who clicked on the website were immediately taken to the Department of Justice’s website for the files about notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The Republican Party quickly denounced the website on social media, pointing visitors instead to GOPConvention.com for the official site.
“FAKE NEWS!” the party wrote of the reports circulating on social media that the fake website was the real one.
Democratic lawmakers used the prank to revive discussion of the Epstein Files, which has been a long-running source of criticism for the administration of President Donald Trump, a speaker at the two-day convention.
Trump officials have been accused of mishandling the files’ release, which was mandated within 30 days under November’s Epstein Files Transparency Act.
Some critics have pointed out that certain records published by the Justice Department appear unnecessarily redacted, while others reveal the identities of victims.
Trump has also faced scrutiny for his personal relationship with Epstein, which he says ended decades ago.
There has long been speculation, however, that powerful figures in Epstein’s orbit turned a blind eye to his crimes. He was convicted in 2008 of soliciting a minor, and he faced sex-trafficking charges at the time of his death in 2019. His victims are thought to number in the hundreds.
Democratic lawmakers like Representative Ted Lieu of California seized on reports of the purported convention website. He shared a message from reporter Jake Lahut saying that “something funky is going on”.
“I just tried the website and the below description, as of right now, is accurate,” Lieu said in response to Lahut. “Sort of awesome.”
According to documentation from the Internet Archive, which captures snapshots of past websites, gopdallas2026.com used to include a background photo displaying the American Airlines Center in Dallas, the site of the upcoming midterm convention.
The centre of the website prompted users to input their contact information to “get exclusive updates”.
But, in small text at the bottom, the website included a caveat that it was not the official source for information related to the midterm convention.
“This website is an independent informational resource and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or operated by the Republican National Committee (RNC), the 2026 RNC Midterm Convention, the American Airlines Center, or any official convention entity,” it said.
“For official convention information, please visit the appropriate official websites.”
This month’s event is the first-ever midterm convention hosted by the Republican Party.
It is slated to take place from September 9 to 10. A press release from the Republican National Committee indicates that the event is expected to be the party’s largest convention since 2016.
Trump is reportedly slated to speak on both nights, as he tries to rouse enthusiasm for his party ahead of the November midterm elections.
Republicans hope to hold onto their majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate as Trump’s popularity slides to new lows amid continued fallout from the war on Iran.
“Never before in history has any major party held a midterm convention, and President Trump wants to focus in on that and open this up to the American people, because all of his work has been about improving their lives,” RNC spokesperson Zach Kraft said in an interview with CBS Texas.
Democrats, however, held national midterm party conferences in 1974, 1978 and 1982.
“So, he wants them to be able to have an opportunity to attend this event and hear from him directly.”

Chants, applause, and hundreds of supporters: A report from the Moscow courthouse where children’s hospice founder Lida Moniava faced a charge of spreading ‘fakes’ about the Russian military
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
22:42:39 UTC
07:42:39 KST

Chants, applause, and hundreds of supporters: A report from the Moscow courthouse where children’s hospice founder Lida Moniava faced a charge of spreading ‘fakes’ about the Russian military
On the evening of September 3, Simonovsky Court placed Lida Moniava, founder of Dom s Mayakom (“Lighthouse Charity Foundation”), under a set of restrictions in a criminal case accusing her of spreading “fake” information about the Russian military. Moniava is one of the leading figures in contemporary Russian philanthropy: she founded the Dom s Mayakom charity and its hospices for children with severe and incurable illnesses. Dozens of people came to Simonovsky Court in Moscow to support her. The news outlet Bereg recounts what happened — and shows how Moniava’s supporters celebrated her release. Meduza is translating the report in full.
A hearing on pretrial restrictions for Lida Moniava, founder of the Lighthouse Charity Foundation, is scheduled for 5 p.m. on September 3. A full hour before the hearing, Muscovites who have come to support Moniava are already gathering outside the Simonovsky Court building.
Police searched Moniava’s home early on the morning of August 2 as part of a criminal case over spreading “fake” information about the Russian military, then arrested her. The case stems from a post Moniava published on her Telegram channel to mark the first anniversary of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “For a year now, my country has been sending missiles, tanks, and soldiers into Ukraine. For a year now, innocent people have been dying because of it,” she wrote.
A short young woman named Nadezhda stands in the parking lot reserved for official vehicles directly in front of the courthouse. She is visibly nervous. She introduces herself as Moniava’s goddaughter.
“I’m waiting for justice. If someone like Lida is sent to prison, something truly terrible will happen to the world,” Nadezhda says.
A mixed crowd gradually gathers by the parking lot: young people who might be described as part of the alternative scene, middle-aged people, and elderly members of the support group. Some call themselves Moniava’s friends and acquaintances; others, like red-haired Makar, dressed all in black, learned about her from recent news coverage.
“When I read about Lida, I realized she’s just an incredibly good person — kind, with the noblest intentions,” Makar tells the independent Russian outlet Bereg. “Of course, it’s a real shame things turned out this way.”
Makar says he is trying not to get his hopes up that the charges against Moniava will be dropped or that she will be released from custody, “so I don’t end up disappointed.”
Mikhail, an acquaintance of Moniava’s, is also there to support her. He speaks about her much as dozens of others have in Facebook posts supporting her over the past day.
“I admire what she does, what she stands for, and the fact that she’s open about it. That’s genuinely brave,” Mikhail says. “You can do charity work and still be a conformist because you think charity makes up for everything. But Lida did good work without becoming a conformist just to keep doing it.”
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moniava stayed in the country and continued helping children with incurable illnesses. She also set up a fund to help refugees from Ukraine and Nagorno-Karabakh, as well as residents of the Kursk region’s border areas affected by the Ukrainian military’s incursion in August 2024.
While helping people affected by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Moniava also wrote antiwar posts on Facebook. In February 2026, Russian authorities fined her 45,000 rubles for “discrediting” the Russian military over those posts. She wrote about children killed in a Russian missile strike on Kryvyi Rih and the deaths of the Martynenko family — a father, a mother, and their 11-year-old son — in a strike on Sumy.
After the February hearing at which a judge imposed the fine, Moniava thanked her followers for their support and said in a post that she had “received a lot of advice to leave Russia”:
When Center E is banging on your apartment door, it’s scary, of course. But look at this photo — Anya and I are having such a great time on our shift [at the hospice]. She’s a girl who spent 19 years behind the walls of a residential institution. If I leave, children in palliative care will spend more time in residential institutions and intensive care units. I doubt I could live happily in some other country knowing that. So emigration isn’t in the plans.
In the same post, Moniava added: “I also can’t stay silent as if there’s no war. Trying to live honestly comes first for me.”
Natalya, who came to Simonovsky Court, does not know Moniava personally but has long followed her work. “I’m just in shock over what’s happening,” she says. “It’s probably to be expected, but it’s still very hard for me to accept. I’m an outsider looking on, and I simply respect her work, so I came here to support her. Lida is a wonderful person who helps others live and survive. That’s very important in our world. In turbulent times, we need to support each other somehow and do something.”
Others who came to support the Dom s Mayakom founder included Nobel laureate Dmitry Muratov, former editor-in-chief of the independent Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta; Nyuta Federmesser, founder of the Vera Fund, which helps people with incurable illnesses; actress Tatyana Drubich, co-chair of the same fund; and Daniil Maksimov, a Vera Fund employee and founder of an inclusive magazine about sex for people with disabilities.
Maksimov, a blogger, writes on social media about living with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) and the problems wheelchair users face. Several people in motorized wheelchairs gathered outside Simonovsky Court on the day of Moniava’s hearing.
The Lighthouse Charity Foundation needs support. In recent days, it has lost many donations and some of its donors. You can donate from Russia in rubles on the foundation’s website.
Shortly before 5 p.m., a prison transport van parked outside the courthouse pulls away. By now, around 200 people have gathered. Someone in the crowd says, “This one’s probably leaving now, and the next one will have Lida in it.” When another prison van drives onto the court grounds soon afterward, people start chanting, “Lida! Lida!”
The van’s barred windows make it impossible to see who is inside. The van pulls into the garage.
People line up to enter the courthouse, and the line moves very slowly. One woman in a blue jacket stands out among the crowd, holding a copy of Viktor Vilisov’s book Nas Vsekh Toshnit (We’re All Sick to Our Stomachs) with a bright orange cover. Off to one side stands Yekaterina Duntsova, head of the Rassvet (“Dawn”) party; somewhere in the same crowd are Tatyana and Valery Yashin, the parents of convicted politician Ilya Yashin, who was sent to Germany in a prisoner exchange.
“So many people showed up. This is a really high-profile case,” someone in the crowd says.
“Yeah, this isn’t Remeslo.”
Forty minutes later, the line still has not cleared. Two young men carrying tripods come out of the courthouse toward the line. Someone in the crowd asks hopefully:
“So, any news?”
“No, nothing at all.”
It is a little after 5 p.m. when Nyuta Federmesser, who had entered the courthouse near the front of the line, comes back outside. “Lida hasn’t arrived yet,” she says. “We came down because it’s impossible to breathe in there. There’s no point in standing here anymore because they’ll start kicking everyone out soon. The court closes at 6 p.m.”
Some of those who came are in no hurry to leave, even though it is very stuffy inside. Dmitry Muratov takes a spot right by the courtroom entrance. One woman who came to support Moniava offers people postcards to write warm messages on, which will later be delivered to Moniava. A police officer comes upstairs and asks everyone to leave the building: the court has closed for the day.
Everyone heads down to the courtyard, which is packed with people. In the middle, a group shares a pie. Police soon drive everyone out of the courtyard as well, and the gates close. Now everyone waits for Moniava by the fence.
Traffic police officers watch the crowd from cars with their emergency lights on. One of them approaches the crowd. What he says is familiar from rallies and pickets:
“Citizens, do not obstruct the passage of other citizens!”
“We’ve heard that one before,” a woman over 60 says. “I’m so sick of you!”
Word eventually spreads that Moniava has been brought to the courthouse after all and that the hearing has begun. The press is not allowed to attend.
“I know Lida personally,” says Fatima, who came to Simonovsky Court to support her. “Lida is a wonderful person. She’s done a lot in our country to help children with severe and incurable illnesses, and she built a palliative care system. Of course, it’s pretty horrifying that she’s inside the Simonovsky Court building at all.”
Neither Fatima nor Mikhail, who respects Moniava for refusing to conform, expects “anything good” to come of the judge’s decision.
Half an hour later, the crowd starts to stir. The courthouse doors open, and two security officers appear in the doorway. Several people start chanting “Lida!” but she is nowhere in sight. A few men come out, followed by a woman. “The workday is over,” someone in the crowd says.
As they wait, someone starts singing, but the words are impossible to make out.
Finally, Moniava’s defense attorney, Mikhail Biryukov, says from inside the courtroom that the court is releasing Moniava from custody and placing her under a “ban on certain activities.” While the investigation continues, she is barred from going outside between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m., communicating with witnesses, or using the internet.
Sometime between 8 and 9 p.m., Moniava and Biryukov emerge from the courthouse. The people waiting behind the fence chant Moniava’s name and applaud. Once outside the gates, she tells the crowd: “I thought I was going to get 10 years in prison. Some kind of miracle.”
She says investigators spent “many hours” trying to persuade her to admit guilt: “For some reason, it’s very important that the defendant say they feel guilty. I don’t feel guilty. I want the war to end as soon as possible.”
“Is there anything you want to do right now?” journalists ask Moniava.
“See my friends,” she says with a smile.

At least 26 killed, dozens injured in two attacks in Sudan's South Kordofan

Unknown Publisher

06:39:12 CST
07:39:12 KST

KHARTOUM, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- At least 26 people were killed and dozens injured in two separate attacks in Sudan's South Kordofan State, multiple sources said on Friday.
The Sudan Doctors Network, a volunteer group, said in a statement that more than 21 people, including women and children, were killed and others injured on Thursday afternoon in an attack by forces of the Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), an ally of paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), on Debi and Luwairi, south and west of Kauda.
In a separate incident early Friday, five people, including a child, were killed and others injured in artillery shelling by SPLM-N forces that struck the city of Dilling, the network said in a separate statement.
The network condemned the attack on Debi and Luwairi as a violation of a ceasefire agreement reached in late August and accused SPLM-N of targeting civilians.
A medical source at a rural hospital in Debi told Xinhua that more than 20 bodies and 11 injured had arrived at the facility, with civilians fleeing the area amid fears of worsening humanitarian conditions.
In Dilling, an eyewitness told Xinhua that artillery hit residential neighborhoods, killing about five civilians and injuring more than seven.
SPLM-N has not commented on the allegations.
SPLM-N, established in 2011, controls parts of South Kordofan and Blue Nile State.
Sudan's Kordofan states have witnessed fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) on one side and the RSF and SPLM-N on the other, as part of a broader conflict that began in April 2023.
Now in its fourth year, the conflict has killed thousands and displaced millions inside and outside the country. ■

LOS ANGELES, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Hurricane Lowell, located several hundred miles south of the Hawaiian Islands, has been rapidly strengthening, prompting Hawaii Governor Josh Green to declare a statewide emergency on Thursday to support preparations for potential impacts from the storm.
Hurricane Lowell has strengthened back to Category 4, with sustained winds of about 240 kilometers per hour and a central pressure of 926 millibars. It was located about 985 kilometers south of Lihue, Hawaii, as of Friday morning local time, according to an update of the U.S. National Hurricane Center on Friday.
Lowell, which was briefly a Category 5 on Wednesday, was forecast to strengthen further Friday afternoon, according to the U.S. National Weather Service (NWS).
The latest forecast track shows Lowell will remain near major hurricane strength as it moves closer to the western Hawaiian Islands late Monday and Monday night. Weather impacts such as high surf and heavy rain may extend hundreds of miles from the center of Hurricane Lowell, according to the NWS.
Green signed an emergency proclamation on Thursday covering the entire state to support preparations for and potential impacts from Hurricane Lowell, Hurricane Karina, Tropical Storm Marie and any additional storms that could affect Hawaii.
The proclamation allows state and county agencies to mobilize personnel, equipment and resources more quickly as Hawaii continues recovering from Tropical Cyclone Lala.
"This proclamation gives our agencies and counties the flexibility to move people, equipment and resources quickly so we can protect communities across every island. We encourage everyone to remain prepared and continue following official weather updates," Green said. ■

LOS ANGELES, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- The United States had recorded 3,134 confirmed measles cases this year as of Thursday, with the nationwide total continuing to rise amid declining childhood vaccination coverage, according to data released Friday by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
The figure has already surpassed the 2,289 confirmed cases reported for the whole of 2025. The 2026 total is the highest annual number recorded in the United States since 1991, according to the CDC.
Of the cases reported this year, 3,118 were identified across 47 U.S. jurisdictions, while 16 were among international visitors. A total of 248 people have been hospitalized, accounting for about 8 percent of confirmed cases, and 38 measles outbreaks have been reported so far this year.
About 94 percent of confirmed cases involved people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown, the CDC said. The agency recommends two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine as the best protection against measles.
The CDC said measles vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners fell to 92.4 percent in the 2025-2026 school year, down from 95.2 percent in the 2019-2020 school year. About 280,000 kindergartners did not have documentation of completing the MMR vaccine series.
The agency has said that when more than 95 percent of people in a community are vaccinated, most people are protected through community immunity. ■

Spanish far-right activists use Nazi-style salutes in anti-migrant protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
22:29:30 UTC
07:29:30 KST

Dozens of far-right activists raised their arms in Nazi-style salutes and sang a Spanish fascist anthem in the heart of Madrid on Wednesday, amid protests against the government’s handling of migration.
Between 60 and 70 members of Núcleo Nacional, an ultra-nationalist anti-immigrant group, participated in Madrid during mass demonstrations across Spain, a spokesperson for the group told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency. The protests followed an influx of migrants from Morocco into Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa.
The broader demonstrations in Madrid were called by Spain’s conservative People’s Party and far-right Vox party, drawing about 50,000 people to the streets, according to government estimates. The protests were planned for Ceuta Day, a holiday marking the Portuguese conquest of Ceuta from the Marinid Sultanate of Morocco in the 15th century, beginning centuries of Portuguese and later Spanish rule.
Núcleo Nacional activists were shown on video making the outstretched-arm gesture associated with neo-Nazi movements and chanting, “Ceuta is not for sale, Ceuta will defend itself.”
They also sang the song “Cara al Sol,” a fascist anthem from 1935 that became central to the regime of former Spanish dictator Francisco Franco, who ruled from 1939 to 1975. Núcleo Nacional denied a link between their gesture and Nazi history.
The demonstration ended in clashes between protesters and police, with four people arrested and four police officers injured, according to local authorities. Protesters were also shown on camera grabbing, pushing and cursing at multiple journalists who were covering the rally.
Francisco Martín Aguirre, the delegate of the Spanish government in Madrid, condemned “the violent acts that occurred at the end of the gatherings in Madrid.”
“All respect to those who legitimately and peacefully protest for the cause they deem fit,” he said on X/Twitter. “Violence is never the way, and those who daily incite it are also responsible.”
Núcleo Nacional spokesperson: Salute was 'Iberian or Roman,' not Nazi
A spokesperson for Núcleo Nacional told JTA that the group was not performing a Nazi salute, but an “Iberian or Roman salute.”
“It represents our ancestors,” the spokesperson said. They added that the group was protesting to “support the people of Ceuta.”
The outstretched arm salute in Nazi Germany was inspired by a gesture popularized in the 1920s in Italy’s fascist movement, which later allied with the Nazis. The Italians called it a Roman salute, though researchers say there is no evidence linking it to ancient Rome. Franco also instituted the gesture in 1937, then instructed Spaniards to abandon it in 1945 after the Axis powers lost World War II.
More than 72,000 Moroccan migrants crossed into Ceuta between July 30 and July 31, with at least 100 people dying in the attempt. Most have returned to Morocco, but some 5,000 remain in makeshift shelters or on the streets and beaches, inflaming tensions between migrants and local residents and heaping pressure on the left-wing government of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
Núcleo Nacional's 2,000 members include those from neo-Nazi, Francoist groups
Núcleo Nacional has about 2,000 members, many from neo-Nazi and Francoist groups that lost their capacity to mobilize, according to the Global Network on Extremism and Technology. The group has grown rapidly and opened four regional branches since its founding in 2024. Earlier this year, it registered a political party as Noviembre Nacional.
The group pledges to defend the white race, Christianity, the Spanish nation and Europe against foreign and domestic enemies, including migrants, internal independence movements and “multicultural globalism.” Spain’s Civil Guard last year opened an investigation into Núcleo Nacional after it posted a video calling for groups to “actively defend” the streets and “jointly fight against the invasion” of immigration.
Núcleo Nacional leaders have also denied the Holocaust and suggested that Israel orchestrates migration to Europe, according to the Observatory of Antisemitism, a Spanish watchdog organization. Núcleo Nacional said in a 2024 statement, “Any Spanish patriot should not forget that it is Israel that is financing the Maghrebi invasion to which all of Europe is being subjected.”
On Núcleo Nacional’s social media channels, it has claimed that it is targeted by “the Jewish-Zionist lobby in Spain” and accused the “international Jewish-American financial elite” of “buying up Spain at bargain prices while ruining us.”

Because supplies will arrive gradually, the vaccines will initially be administered at major clinics and designated vaccination centers. The campaign will later be expanded to all Clalit clinics nationwide.
Meuhedet has also ordered approximately 250,000 vaccines, similar to last year. These include a high-dose vaccine for people aged 65 and older, which will be administered to at-risk populations; an inactivated injectable vaccine; and, later, the FluMist nasal spray vaccine for people ages two to 49. Deliveries to clinics will continue gradually until Sukkot.
“The vaccines are arriving in Israel and at clinics gradually this year, and it is recommended to schedule an appointment in advance to get vaccinated,” said Hagar Wexler, director of Meuhedet’s Nursing Division.
“We expect vaccination on a more significant scale to become possible during October,” she said.
“It is important to remember that the flu is not a mild illness, and last year we saw significant morbidity and a heavy burden on hospitals. The goal is to enter flu season protected, so once the vaccine is available at the clinic, there is no reason to wait,” she added.

Scientists overturn a theory about this shark’s strange head
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
22:24:32 UTC
07:24:32 KST

Scientists overturn a theory about this shark’s strange head
Bonnethead sharks change head shape as they grow, overturning a long-held theory and leaving scientists with a new evolutionary mystery.
- Date:
- September 4, 2026
- Source:
- University of Miami Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric, and Earth Science
- Summary:
- Scientists have overturned a leading explanation for why male and female bonnethead sharks have differently shaped heads. Instead of males developing a pointed snout at maturity, both sexes actually begin with more pointed heads that become rounder with age, particularly in females.
- Share:
A new study of bonnethead sharks (Sphyrna tiburo) in Florida is challenging a previous explanation for how males and females develop their distinctively different head shapes.
Researchers from the University of Miami Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric, and Earth Science and collaborating institutions found that the sharks' shovel shaped heads become more rounded as both males and females grow older, with the change especially pronounced in females. Earlier research had suggested that males developed their more pointed snouts when they reached sexual maturity.
Tracking Bonnethead Head Shape
The research is the first detailed investigation of both head shape and diet in bonnethead sharks from Biscayne Bay. Scientists also included sharks from Tampa Bay to see whether the same developmental patterns appeared in populations living on opposite sides of Florida.
Bonnetheads are small relatives of hammerhead sharks and are the only shark species known to show clear sex based differences in head shape. Males usually have a more noticeable point along the front edge of the head, while females tend to have a smoother and more rounded outline. Scientists describe this type of physical difference between males and females as sexual dimorphism.
"Our findings show that the pointed head shape is not a feature that develops in males when they reach maturity," said Kathy Liu, lead author of the study, which she conducted while earning her master's degree at the Rosenstiel School. "Younger males and females both had more pointed heads, but the head became rounder as the sharks matured. That change was much greater in females."
Diet Does Not Explain the Difference
The researchers also tested whether males and females might develop different head shapes because they eat different foods or forage in different ways. Their results showed that bonnetheads in Biscayne Bay and Tampa Bay occupied distinct food webs and experienced dietary changes as they grew. However, males and females living within the same bay depended on many of the same local food sources.
"Our findings provided no evidence that differences in diet or foraging were driving the development of the sharks' sex-specific head shapes," said Liu.
"This study helps narrow the drivers of a biological trait that has puzzled scientists," said Catherine Macdonald, a co-author of the study and an associate professor in the Department of Environmental Science and Policy and the director of the Shark Research and Conservation Program at the Rosenstiel School. "By examining body shape and diet in the same animals, we were able to assess whether diet and morphological changes co-occur. Our results suggest there is another cause behind the differences in head shape between male and female bonnetheads."
Measuring Sharks Across Florida
Between May 2022 and May 2023, the team sampled 105 bonnethead sharks in Biscayne Bay and another 39 in the Tampa Bay region. Scientists used research longlines to capture sharks in Biscayne Bay, while sharks in Tampa Bay were collected primarily with scientific gillnets.
Each shark was measured, and a small muscle sample was taken. Researchers then photographed both sides of the animal's head against a specially designed grid board before quickly releasing the shark.
The team used ImageJ software to analyze the photographs and precisely compare the curvature of each shark's head. This technique allowed researchers to collect detailed measurements while keeping handling time as short as possible.
Chemical Clues Reveal Different Food Webs
Scientists also analyzed muscle tissue from 137 sharks for carbon and nitrogen isotope signatures. These chemical markers can reveal where an animal has been feeding within a food web and provide a broader view of long-term diet than simply examining recently eaten prey.
The isotope signatures of sharks from Biscayne Bay showed little overlap with those from Tampa Bay. That suggests the two populations were feeding within ecosystems that had different environmental signatures.
The researchers cautioned that this does not necessarily mean the sharks were eating completely different prey species. The same or similar prey can carry different isotope signatures depending on the ecosystem where they live.
Why Do Bonnetheads Have Pointed Heads?
Scientists still do not know what advantage the bonnethead's pointed head provides.
One possibility proposed by the researchers is that the shape could help younger and smaller sharks swim more efficiently. As females grow larger to support reproduction and gestation, that potential benefit may become less important.
Future research on swimming performance and embryonic development will be needed to test that possibility. Such work could also reveal when the differences between male and female head shapes first begin to appear.
Expanding the Research Beyond Florida
The researchers said the same photographic technique could be used to study bonnethead sharks in other parts of their range. Comparing populations from different regions could reveal additional variation in head shape and help scientists better understand how local populations differ.
Those comparisons could also have conservation value by helping researchers identify biological and ecological differences that may be important when developing region-specific management strategies.
By combining measurements of body shape with information about diet, scientists can test competing explanations for how unusual biological traits develop and evolve. Studying bonnetheads across a wider geographic range could also reveal population differences that might otherwise remain hidden.
The study titled: "A Head of the Curve: Bonnethead Shark (Sphyrna tiburo) Cephalofoil Morphology and Trophic Ecology," was published in the journal Integrative Organismal Biology.
The authors are Kathy Liu; University of Miami Rosenstiel School and Field School, Jasmin Graham; Minorities in Shark Science, H Ro and S L Kim; University of California, Merced, T. R. Wiley and J.M. Gardiner; Havenworth Coastal Conservation, L.J. Baker; California State University, Monterey Bay, C. Macdonald; Rosenstiel School and Field School.
The research was supported by the Field School and the University of Miami Shark Research and Conservation Program. Tampa Bay fieldwork was supported by the Tampa Bay Environmental Restoration Fund and Disney Conservation Fund. Stable isotope analysis was supported by the University of California, Merced, and partial project support was provided by the Maxwell/Hanrahan Foundation.

Five Great Reads: After the flood, leaving Maga, and sex doll ethics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04

Hello and welcome to the weekend.
This week, we have selected stories that will move you. A dispatch from a disaster zone, where rescue teams are sifting through scattered, buried remnants, a feature about walking away from a community that once welcomed you, and a piece on running just to see how far you can go.
Enjoy.
1. After the flood
In the aftermath of the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster, thousands remain missing and access to aid remains hindered by treacherous conditions. On the ground in some of the worst-hit areas, our south Asia correspondent, Hannah Ellis-Petersen, and journalist Gaurav Pokharel write that while the scale of the damage caused by the flood is unfathomable, so too is the human suffering as communities almost wiped out of existence reckon with what comes next. 
   Notable quote: “Even now, I cannot believe that she is gone. That’s why I keep walking around looking for her. I still feel as if she might be walking around somewhere here. I keep getting this feeling that she might still be here, looking after the chickens and the goats.”
Scattered fragments: The ruins of the lives of thousands are now buried in and among the debris. “Kettles, teddy bears, a record-keeping book, saucepans, medicine packets, a pair of glasses” remind rescue teams of the hundreds still missing.
How long will it take to read: Three-and-a-half minutes.
Further reading: Trapped workers could still be alive, families hope DNA can be used to find their loved ones, and desperate relatives of the missing fear attention is already drifting away from the ongoing crisis.
2. Walking away from the cult of Trump
Donald Trump and his “Make America Great Again” (Maga) base of supporters have come to dominate American politics. For many Trump followers, the movement built on lies and conspiracy theories offered a shared identity. For others, it became something closer to religion. But after more than 10 years, some devotees are finally walking away, making amends, and offering support to others who are reckoning with their role in Trump’s America.
What drew people into the Maga “cult” and why did they leave? Rich Logis found a second family in the Maga community. He found belonging, camaraderie and a common enemy. But after the politicians he lionised platformed Covid anti-vaxxers he started to diversify his news sources. Logis slowly began to realise that what he believed was false and he had been “complicit in dividing this country”.
Notable quote: “My loyalty wasn’t to Trump. My loyalty was to God and the church.”
How long will it take to read: Four-and-a-half minutes to read, and less than one minute to share with a friend who has fallen down a rabbit hole.
Further reading: You can learn more about Life after Maga, and how the non-profit Leaving Maga is fighting Trumpism like a disease.
3. Freddie Mercury’s one-time girlfriend on the Queen frontman’s untold story
Mary Austin was the quiet girlfriend of rock band Queen’s flamboyant figurehead. They dreamed of marriage until they both finally spoke the unspoken. Thirty-five years after his death, Austin’s new book lays out Mercury’s life in lyrics.
‘No, Freddie, I think you’re gay’: Austin and Mercury had been living together for four years when they both realised Mercury was only attracted to men. But rather than destroying their relationship, Austin says the revelation felt like a relief. They continued living together for the next 18 months and, as Queen and Mercury became a global phenomenon, Mary and Freddie became better friends.
Mercurial money: Austin has inherited half of Mercury’s estate (now estimated at about £150m). Asked where the money will go when she dies and if much of it will go to charity, she said, “It’s going to go to my children.”
How long will it take to read: Just over 13 minutes. Enough time to listen to Bohemian Rhapsody two times through.
Further reading: Check out Freddie Mercury’s “splendid things”, or pick up a copy of Mary Austin’s book from the Guardian Bookshop.
4. The ethics of sex dolls
On a quiet country road south of Sydney, two distressed citizens stumbled across what they assumed was the mangled corpse of a woman stuffed into a suitcase. But the woman was not a woman at all and, after forensic analysis revealed it was a sex doll, questions about the booming sex doll industry have garnered global attention.
A flourishing trade: Estimates show that the global sex doll market is valued at more than US$6bn. But as the industry grows, Madison Griffiths asks, does it matter how these dolls get treated?
How much? Lifelike sex dolls are now increasingly customisable and you can walk away with one for about US$1,790. But Caitlin Roper, the Australian author of Sex Dolls, Robots and Woman Hating: The Case for Resistance, calls these kinds of dolls “replica female sex slaves”.
How long will it take to read: Just under four minutes. 
Further reading: The rise of “sex robots”, how police mistook a sex doll for a “body”, and what can we learn about male desire in a sex doll factory?
5. A week-long run in the park
In a remarkable feat of physical and mental endurance, the Australian endurance athlete Phil Gore ran 6.71km every hour for an entire week just to see how far he could push himself.
Finding your limit: Having already set the world record in 2025, Gore knew he had “a lot more left to give”. But the rules of backyard ultra running require the final runner to stop one lap after the second-place runner drops out – limiting the potential boundaries of the winner. Gore wanted a challenge that would push him further. This time around, competing only against his own body and mind, Gore says, “that’s what I’ve done. Maybe [there is] a little bit of disappointment that I wanted my limit to be a bit further away.”
Fuel fit for a champion: Running for a week straight requires calories. A steady stream of “speckled snakes and Nerd clusters, jelly cups, custard pouches, simple sugars like that” kept Gore going for days.
How long will it take to read: Just over two minutes.
Further reading: What happens when you don’t finish a race, and why would anyone run an ultramarathon anyway?

Mexican ruling-party lawmaker found dead with gunshot wound, a year before elections
MEXICO CITY, Sept 4 - A member of Congress from Mexico's ruling Morena party was found dead from a gunshot wound in the eastern state of Veracruz on Friday, less than a year before local and federal elections.
Zenyazen Escobar, a federal legislator representing the coastal state — home to some of the country’s oil complexes — was found dead inside his car with at least one gunshot wound.
“The investigation file is being compiled,” state Attorney General Lisbeth Jimenez told reporters, without providing further details.
The secretary general of Veracruz, Ricardo Ahued, said the lawmaker's vehicle showed no signs of violence.
Mexico's lower house of Congress expressed its condolences to Escobar's family and friends and urged judicial authorities to conduct a "thorough investigation into the facts."
The death occurred as the country prepares to hold elections on June 6 to renew mayoral, state legislative, city council and gubernatorial positions.
In previous elections, various regions have experienced incidents of violence linked to organized crime groups seeking to co-opt political figures and consolidate territorial control.
According to the human rights organization Data Civica, in July alone there were at least 30 incidents of "political-criminal violence" across 11 states in Mexico, 14 of which were homicides.
The states with the highest registered cases were Zacatecas, with 10 cases; Michoacan and Quintana Roo, with four each; Oaxaca, with three; and Baja California and Veracruz, with two each.
Data Civica describes political-criminal violence as threats, murders, armed attacks, assassination attempts, disappearances, and kidnappings.
The national electoral body INE has warned that organized crime represents one of the most serious concerns for democratic processes.
According to the INE, court rulings have in the past documented the presence of armed individuals seeking to intimidate or coerce the public into voting a certain way, as well as acts of theft and the burning of election materials. REUTERS

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 5, 2026

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 5, 2026
UN adopts new world map showing true scale of continents; only US votes against it
The United Nations General Assembly voted on Sept 4 for a resolution spearheaded by several African countries to adopt a map that makes their continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe - aiming at “a more accurate representation” of world geography.
The resolution was backed by 164 countries while the United States voted against it and six other states abstained.
The new map - known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection - “offers a more accurate representation of the sizes of continental landmasses and to this end is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world,” the resolution says.
It urges member states to adopt the new map in place of the traditional Mercator projection, which was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569.
US midterm elections begin with chaos over mail-in voting crackdown
America’s midterm elections opened on Sept 4 in a fog of confusion over mail-in voting, with ballots already going out as President Donald Trump presses courts to let him impose sweeping new restrictions on how they are handled.
North Carolina became the first state authorised to begin sending out ballots, formally launching an election season that culminates on Nov 3 and will determine control of Congress for the final two years of Trump’s term.
Yet voters and election officials still do not know what rules may govern millions of mail-in ballots, as Trump asks the Supreme Court to revive curbs blocked by a federal judge and as states scramble to prepare for changes that could come after voting has begun.
Trump says envoys Witkoff, Kushner heading abroad to discuss Ukraine peace
US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, are heading abroad to attempt to forge a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, the US president told reporters on Sept 4.
During comments in the Oval Office, Trump suggested the US had a fresh concrete proposal aimed at ending the war, which is now in its fifth year.
He did not, however, elaborate on what that proposal would be, nor did he say if Witkoff and Kushner would be travelling to Ukraine, Russia or both nations.
EU to help cities clamp down on tourist rentals
The EU is set to lay out rules helping European cities to curb short-term rentals such as Airbnb in a bid to tackle rising house prices, according to plans seen by AFP on Sept 4.
The European Commission is expected to unveil next week a legal proposal setting out the conditions under which authorities can restrict the provision of short-term tourist lets.
Such rentals have increasingly come into the crosshairs of local authorities in tourist hotspots such as Florence and Barcelona, as residents complain about being priced out by visitors.
Air India A320 issued stall warning when seatbelt signs off, injuring 24, investigators say
An Air India A320 flying from Phuket to New Delhi in August issued a stall warning when seatbelt signs were off, while a rapid pitch up and then down threw passengers and cabin crew against overhead bins and injured 24 people, Indian investigators said.
The Airbus plane, cruising at 36,000ft, initially ascended 372 feet (113m) and then fell to 292 feet (89m) below it, according to a preliminary report released on Sept 4.
The two-second stall warning came after the flight control system detected the loss of all three of the aircraft’s hydraulic systems within four seconds, disengaging the autopilot and setting off a continuous cockpit alarm.

Who really benefits from the CIA chief’s Moscow trip?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
22:04:01 UTC
07:04:01 KST

Who really benefits from the CIA chief’s Moscow trip?
Speculation abounds over the reason for CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s recent trip to Moscow. Which probably could have been an email. Or a social media post. Just like everything else this administration does.
Oooh, don’t tell me! He went to demand that Russian President Vladimir Putin not help Iran! Or he went to ask whether they’re still up for more speed dating to talk peace in Ukraine! Or maybe just to talk about swapping prisoners. Which happens fairly regularly. And doesn’t require a personal visit. Or maybe Ratcliffe just had a jonesing for that ice cream at the GUM mall in Red Square. Who really knows.
So I’d like to personally take the opportunity to add to the theories, which can only really be evaluated sometime down the road in hindsight.
The thing that strikes me the most about this trip is the sudden secrecy. Specifically from an administration with a penchant for blabbing about everything. If Trump wanted to tell Putin or Russian intelligence something, he’d do it himself on Truth Social Instead, he was uncharacteristically vague, calling the trip semi-routine. When is this guy tight-lipped about anything? It’s so far out of character for the American President that one is almost obligated to look for a motive for the secrecy.
So with that in mind, it seems reasonable to ask whether there is any financial or political constituency that stands to benefit from the message being sent by this unusually secretive trip.
Well, it turns out that it just happened to take place at the same time as the European Union was meeting to set its new 7-year budget, and Eastern European Baltic nations were making a massive push for cash from Brussels.
You know what they say: if you have a pet that starts in with some nasty habits, like chewing the furniture to get your attention, then you really have to nip that in the bud real quick. Otherwise, there’s a risk that, next thing you know, your other pets will learn from it and start gnawing on the couch or the table legs, too.
So here you have Europe, that’s been sitting there while Kiev says 'gimme money', and 'I deserve it because I’m defending all of Europe for you. Oh, and even better, actually, defending DEMOCRACY for you lazy bums'. And instead of whacking it on the nose and going, 'NO, BAD! Brussels just goes, 'Wanna treat?'
So now, what do you know, here comes Latvia, who’s been watching this whole charade, seeing that Ukraine goes from begging to getting tossed a bone every single time, and now they too are like, 'Woof, woof, I’m defending all of Europe for you. Where’s my money? 7 BILLION EUROS, specifically'.
And it’s not like Latvia is even bothering to come up with its own twist on Ukraine’s pitch. It’s not like they’re saying, 'Ukraine’s pitch to Brussels is, ‘Look, we’re being invaded. You’d better give us what we want because we’re the only thing standing between Putin showing up in Europe with a neck pillow for an Interrail tour of Europe.’ So we, Latvia, need to come up with something else. Especially since we aren’t actually being invaded – we just need some emotional-support money'.
No, instead, they’re just basically saying the exact same sort of thing minus the existential threat – that Latvia is the bouncer at the Baltic door keeping Putin on the other side of the velvet rope.
Surely it can’t possibly have anything to do with the fact that Latvia’s economy could use the kind of economic boost that can only come from having Brussels dump a ton of cash into its defense industry, right? Because everything’s going so well for Latvia economically, ever since this conflict in Ukraine went hot in 2022 and Riga cut itself off from Russian trade: from just over €2 billion a year back then, to just €193 million last year – an almost 90% reduction in the value of trade between the two countries, according to Latvia’s own foreign affairs ministry.
And now energy prices are going back up again, too – an 83% spike in gas prices since the beginning of this year in Latvia, and 24% over just the past month. An established trend since the EU cut everyone off from Russian fuel and now Trump’s cutting everyone off from fuel from the Middle East with his apparently endless 'mine’s bigger' standoff with Iran.
Oh look, here comes Lithuania now, too. What a surprise! Another guy watching from the cheap seats and going: 'Hang on. We’re also next to Russia. We have security problems, infrastructure costs, and defense bills. Where is OUR cash handout?'
Turns out that Lithuania has just gone directly to Brussels with the invoice, essentially saying: You keep telling us the eastern flank is crucial to European security. Wonderful. Please prove this commitment using the traditional European unit of measurement: euros.
When it comes to Eastern Europe, the EU’s seven-year budget plan is starting to look like a group dinner where everyone suddenly remembers that the guy at the end of the table has a corporate credit card.
But the real question is whose bills would Brussels ultimately be paying? Surely it’s just a mere coincidence that major beneficiaries of Latvian and Lithuanian defense spending include Trump’s America, as the largest supplier of major conventional arms to Latvia and Lithuania, according to the most recently available Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) arms transfer data.
All this comes after the western press reported that the CIA director flew to Moscow this week to tell Russia not to attack NATO countries. Which is actually great marketing for the cause of Eastern European countries shaking down Brussels and basically launching a grant program. They’re behaving now as though a potential future hypothetical Russian attack on NATO is serious enough to justify enormous new expenditures, but the benefit of Brussels’ largesse risks going to Washington as the top weapons supplier.
The trip is remarkably convenient for governments seeking to turn fears about Russia into a case for vastly increased European defense spending – and for the American defense industry that stands to benefit from a big chunk of that spending.
But hey, who really cares if everyone’s barking out for treats when you’re Brussels and all you ever need to do is reach into the pockets of the taxpayer. Even if you then run straight back to Uncle Sam with it and drop it in his lap.

Study reveals a double standard in how we view AI-assisted communication
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
22:00:52 UTC
07:00:52 KST

People expected others to use AI-assisted communication tools more often than they would use them themselves, according to a study published in the British Journal of Psychology. The research also discovered that people viewed openly disclosed AI use more favorably than secret use when the two options were directly compared.
AI-mediated communication includes technologies that assist in communication by changing or generating part of a message. Examples include writing assistants, tools that improve the sound of someone’s voice and video software that changes a person’s appearance or facial expressions. These technologies can make communication faster or more polished, but they may also raise questions about whether a message is authentic.
The researchers were interested in the social rules people apply to these tools. Individuals often hold ideas about the acceptability of behavior, and beliefs about what others are likely to do, but those two judgments do not always match.
Led by Zoe A. Purcell of Université Paris Cité in Paris, the team conducted two online studies. Study 1 included 477 UK adults (mean age 48.48 years; 200 males, 266 females, and 11 participants in other categories). Study 2 included 765 U.S. adults (mean age 45.47 years; 379 males, 375 females, and 11 participants who were nonbinary or preferred not to say).
Participants viewed examples involving text, audio and video. In Study 1, they rated both openly disclosed and secret AI use on a five-point scale. They also rated how likely they would be to use the technology and how likely they thought other people would be to use it. Study 2 used a preregistered design in which participants were placed into separate conditions and rated acceptability and likelihood on a scale from zero to 100.
In Study 1, participants rated open AI use as more acceptable than secret use, with average scores of 3.41 and 2.72 out of 5, respectively. They also expected others to use AI communication tools more than themselves, with average likelihood ratings of 3.73 for others and 2.80 for themselves.
Study 2 produced a more nuanced result. When participants were not shown open and secret versions side by side, the difference in acceptability was small and not statistically significant. Open use received an average rating of 56.87 out of 100, compared with 53.62 for secret use. Transparency also did not change expectations about use. However, the self-other difference remained strong: participants rated the likelihood that others would use the tools at 71.41, compared with 40.44 for themselves.
Participants also considered AI use slightly more acceptable when judging other people than when judging themselves. Acceptability was more closely connected to expected behavior when people considered their own use than when they considered others’ use.
Additionally, greater familiarity with AI was associated with higher acceptability and greater expectations of use. By contrast, people who believed AI communication caused information loss or revealed something negative about a user’s character tended to rate it less favorably. These results suggest that concerns regarding AI-assisted communication may ease as these tools become more mainstream and individuals become more accustomed to them.
Purcell and colleagues summarized their findings: “Self-other differences are a central factor for understanding people’s attitudes and expectations for AI-mediated communication.”
Some limitations are to be noted. For instance, the word “others” was deliberately broad and did not specify whether participants were thinking about friends, colleagues, strangers or family members. In addition, data were collected in 2021 and 2022, before many current AI communication tools became widely used.
The study, “People have different expectations for their own versus others’ use of AI-mediated communication tools,” was authored by Zoe A. Purcell, Mengchen Dong, Anne-Marie Nussberger, Nils Köbis, and Maurice Jakesch.

US midterms kick off as North Carolina starts sending out ballots amid mail-voting chaos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
22:00:11 UTC
07:00:11 KST

America's midterm elections have opened in a fog of confusion over mail voting, with ballots already going out as President Donald Trump presses courts to let him impose sweeping new restrictions on how they are handled.
North Carolina became the first state on Friday authorised to begin sending out ballots, formally launching an election season that culminates on November 3 and will determine control of Congress for the final two years of Trump's term.
Yet voters and election officials still do not know what rules may govern millions of mail ballots, as Trump asks the Supreme Court to revive curbs blocked by a federal judge and as states scramble to prepare for changes that could come after voting has begun.
The dispute has been compounded by whistleblower allegations that a new Postal Service verification system was rushed, inadequately tested and could delay or even disqualify entire batches of ballots because of a single barcode problem.
A federal judge weighing whether to extend the temporary block on Trump's plan warned on Thursday that hurried changes could cause widespread disruption.
"We're not playing an intellectual puzzle game," Judge Indira Talwani reportedly told a lawyer defending the restrictions, in remarks widely picked up by US media. "We're talking about people's right to vote."
Trump's March executive order would require states to provide the US Postal Service with lists of eligible mail voters through a new federal portal.
Rules in limbo
Ballot envelopes would also need individual barcodes and other design features, with USPS empowered to refuse mailings that fail to meet its requirements.
The administration says the rules are to protect election integrity, although it has produced no evidence of significant fraud through mail voting.
Trump has repeatedly denounced the practice as corrupt while using it himself — including to vote in Florida's Republican primary just last month.
The uncertainty comes on top of a voting system that already differs dramatically from state to state.
Some automatically send ballots to registered voters, others require voters to request them, while identification requirements, return deadlines and rules for counting late-arriving ballots vary across the country.
Election officials now face the additional prospect of federal requirements changing while voting is already underway.
"The states set the time, place and manner of elections in this country, not the president," Marc Elias, the founder of voting rights platform Democracy Docket, said on his YouTube show.
"In fact, the Congress can override the states in many instances, but in no instance can the president. The president is given no power over federal elections."
North Carolina officials said Friday's mailings would proceed normally and that the state has no plans to use the federal portal at the center of the dispute.
But time is rapidly running out for any nationwide overhaul.
'Rushed, chaotic'
Friday marks 60 days before Election Day — the deadline Trump's order itself envisioned for states to submit voter information — while another 18 states are expected to begin distributing ballots roughly 45 days before November 3.
That leaves little room for officials to redesign envelopes, update computer systems, train workers and upload voter data if the courts suddenly allow the restrictions to take effect.
Concerns intensified this week after an anonymous USPS whistleblower alleged that the ballot portal had been developed through a "rushed, chaotic, and fundamentally flawed" process.
The official warned that under a proposed "zero-percent failure" policy, one barcode that fails to scan or match could result in an entire batch containing thousands of ballots being rejected until it is checked again.
USPS told AFP no mandatory verification procedures were being performed and that election officials would initially use its portal only voluntarily.
The fight — alongside disputes over partisan redistricting in around a dozen states — comes with high political stakes.
Republicans hold narrow congressional majorities, but Democrats are favoured to capture the House as Trump's approval ratings remain weak and voters voice frustration over living costs and the continuing war with Iran.
A new Cornell University forecast gives Democrats an eight-in-10 chance of taking the chamber, projecting a roughly 226-209 majority.
