Food has returned to Gaza’s markets, but most people still cannot afford to eat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:54:55 UTC
04:54:55 KST

In a tent in Tal al-Hawa, west of Gaza City, 39-year-old Iman Abdel Karim, a mother of six, hands pieces of bread to her hungry children, some of whom are too young to have grown their teeth. Around her are a few empty cooking pots. At the entrance to the tent, the stove has not been lit either yesterday or today.
Abdel Karim and her family live on a single meal a day, usually eaten around noon. When available, it comes from a communal kitchen. When there is no food from the kitchens, they eat bread alone. Sometimes they manage to get a meal from a neighboring tent, or they cook lentils – long among the cheapest foods in Gaza, though even lentil prices have risen beyond what some families can afford.
“My children see some vegetables and fruit with the neighbors, and they start asking me for some,” Abdel Karim says. “But even though some fruit, vegetables, and other foods are available in the markets, we cannot buy anything. We have been living in tents for more than two years. We have spent all our money trying to stay alive, and we have nothing left.”
Food is visible in Gaza’s markets for the first time in years, but hunger is not gone. According to the August 2026 IPC report, more than 1.4 million people, or two-thirds of Gaza’s population, are projected to face Crisis conditions or worse through December 2026. The presence of goods on shelves has not translated into food security for the majority of Gaza’s population, whose purchasing power has been destroyed by more than two years of war, displacement, and economic collapse.
Prices have fallen noticeably compared with last year, when famine was ravaging the population. At the peak of the crisis in mid-2025, a kilogram of flour could cost around 250 to 300 shekels ($70 to $90) in some parts of the Strip. According to a WFP report, wheat flour was being sold at a price 4,900 percent higher than pre-October 2023 tags. Today, a 25-kilogram bag of flour costs around 30 shekels ($10).
Tomato prices have fallen by approximately 81 percent since the ceasefire, potatoes by around 70 percent, and rice by approximately 73 percent, according to a UNICEF humanitarian situation report covering the period from October 2025 to June 2026. Accumulating humanitarian supplies – including commodities such as legumes and flour, which can spoil when stored for long periods in Gaza’s summer heat- drives merchants to sell them fast.
But falling prices have not reached all goods equally. Milk, protein, and fish, which people need, remain difficult to obtain. Cooking gas is regulated by Gaza’s Ministry of Economy, with families allocated an estimated eight kilograms of cooking gas every six months — a quantity far below weekly household needs. And electricity remains unavailable across much of the Strip, making food storage nearly impossible for families and merchants alike.
Abdel Karim remembers the famine with particular pain.
“During the famine last year, I could hear my children crying from hunger day and night, moaning, and there was nothing I could do for them. I could not go to the aid trucks that they described as the road to death. My husband could not either. He has had an injury to his foot since the beginning of the war.
“So instead, I sold my jewelry so I could bring bread to my children. And I was not alone. Many women did the same.”
‘A political game’
Rami Oweis, 56, a father of eight and a retired employee, sees the gap between what is visible and what is accessible as deliberate — part of what he calls “a political game” in which Israel has become highly adept at creating the appearance of normality.
“You see the markets filled with fruit and vegetables in every color and shape,” Oweis says. “But who can afford to buy them every day? Who can bring enough food for himself and his family back to a tent that becomes like an oven in the summer?”
Storage is its own problem. “There are no refrigerators in the tents. Even if there were, there is no electricity to run them.” Cooking what can be brought, he explains, requires firewood, which takes hours to gather and fills the tents with smoke.
“All of this is part of the policy,” Oweis told Mondoweiss. “You see the pictures, but only those who live among the people of Gaza and under the conditions of Gaza know the hell they are living through.”
In Gaza, Oweis says, the markets reflect these contradictions.
A kilogram of meat, which during the Israeli-engineered famine could cost 400 or 500 shekels when it could be found at all, now sells for around 40 shekels.
Potatoes cost around six shekels per kilogram, tomatoes eight, onions six, and cucumbers 12. By pre-war standards, these would be manageable prices. But purchasing power has collapsed.
More than one-third of Gaza’s bread needs are covered by WFP-supported bakeries, where bundles of eight to nine pitas are sold at a capped price of around $1. But the WFP has been forced to reduce flour supplies to bakeries due to Israel’s import restrictions, pushing many families who relied on these bakeries to look elsewhere.
“We no longer have money,” Oweis says. “We are no longer able to buy things the way we did before the war. This war drained everything we had saved for the future, and then destroyed the future itself.”
Permanent state of emergency
Merchants are caught in the same bind. They struggle to store what they buy, watching perishable goods deteriorate in the heat without electricity to refrigerate them, and find themselves forced to sell at reduced prices, sometimes at a loss, to move stock before it spoils..
Abdel Aziz, a small-scale merchant in Gaza who declined to give his full name, says that whenever vegetables and fruit become available, merchants rush to buy them – knowing these are foods Palestinians have deeply longed for. But demand remains limited, even at ordinary prices.
“People are afraid to buy,” Abdel Aziz says. “They always try to keep some cash in their hands in case of an emergency. And Gaza has become a permanent state of emergency.
When people do buy, they buy as little as possible. “Instead of buying two kilograms of potatoes, for example, a father might buy only two potatoes for the family to eat that day.” Families no longer cook full meals every day. They eat at aid kitchens or have sandwiches with cheese or jam instead of preparing a full meal, he adds.
On how the war has impacted Gazans’ eating behaviors, Abdel Aziz describes this as “politics”. “Deliberate politics, so that people remain in a state of need. Even if goods are available, people will not be able to buy them.”
 “The Israeli occupation tells the world that it is bringing food into Gaza,” Abdel Aziz says. “The world can see it. But the world does not know how those who survived in Gaza managed to survive, what exhausted them, or what they sacrificed to reach this point, where they can no longer afford to buy vegetables and fruit for their families.”

The UN General Assembly approved a resolution on a new world map: what makes it special
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
22:53:18 EEST
04:53:18 KST

The UN General Assembly approved a resolution on a new world map: what makes it special
Kyiv • UNN
164 countries supported the use of Equal Earth maps, which more accurately represent the sizes of the continents. The United States voted against the resolution.
The UN General Assembly approved a reform of the use of world maps with more realistic proportions. The relevant resolution was supported by 164 countries on Friday; the United States voted against it, and six countries abstained, UNN reports, citing DW.
Details
The resolution was introduced by Togo and the African Union, calling on international organizations and states to use Equal Earth maps in the future. This type of world map reflects the actual sizes of the continents more accurately: Africa appears larger on it, while the United States is reduced in size.
This map is intended to replace the so-called Mercator map, which is associated with the cartographer Gerardus Mercator, who was born in Flanders in 1512. The Mercator map was developed for maritime navigation and artificially enlarged areas at high latitudes.
"Maps shape our understanding of the world," Togo's Foreign Minister Robert Dussey said at the UN General Assembly. "But they are never neutral." There is a risk that they "present a distorted picture of our planet and reinforce misconceptions passed down from generation to generation."
We would add
The Equal Earth map was created in 2018 by a group of geographers to ensure that the depiction of the continents corresponds as closely as possible to their actual sizes. As a result, Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania are shown as significantly larger than on conventional world maps.

The court was hearing the students' plea seeking release of their re-NEET results
NEW DELHI: Delhi HC has directed National Testing Agency (NTA) to declare within 24 hours the NEET-UG re-examination results of two candidates, whose results were withheld over allegations linking them to the question paper leak. Justice Jasmeet Singh pointed out the candidates had not been named as accused by CBI in its chargesheet.While CBI told the court that it did not make them accused, though they had paid money to get question papers, the judge observed that at this stage, it was just an allegation and "therefore, the petitioners cannot be treated as persons against whom criminal culpability has been established or as having been found guilty of any illegality".
The court was hearing the students' plea seeking release of their re-NEET results and permission to participate in the ongoing counselling. The CBI chargesheet named the two petitioners as witnesses, and not accused. NTA, however, issued show-cause notices to them and withheld their results.During the hearing, NTA submitted that it withheld the results after CBI informed it that several candidates had allegedly received or shared the question paper of the May 3 examination.
On its part, CBI submitted that the petitioners had received the question paper and had the "mens rea" (intent) to commit the illegality, since money had been paid by them for obtaining the question paper.HC observed that the petitioners were at a "nascent stage of their academic careers", and withholding their results merely on the basis of allegations that were yet to be tested would cause serious prejudice to them.
"The petitioners ought to be permitted to know their results and, subject to the outcome of the proceedings, participate in the further rounds of counseling conducted by the NTA," Justice Singh said. The order recorded denying them an opportunity to participate in counselling at this stage could result in consequences that may not subsequently be adequately remedied.

Queers for Palestine? The complicated politics of being LGBTQ in Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:36:15 UTC
18:36:15 KST

Political stickers, flyers and other ephemera from Israel's LGBTQ community, with slogans ranging from "Queers Against Genocide" to "Proud to Serve in the Reserves."
With a fateful election looming in under two months, we spoke to LGBTQ Israelis of every stripe about how their identities shape – or possibly clash – with their politics, how Oct. 7 and the Gaza war affected them, and what they fear most during this turbulent campaign season

Marking record tenure, Meloni hails Italy’s turn to stability
- Italy's government under Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has achieved a record period of stability, surpassing previous postwar tenures.
- Political stability has improved Italy's financial reputation, lowering borrowing costs despite ongoing economic challenges.
- Critics highlight stalled reforms and slow economic growth, with upcoming elections showing a tight race between Meloni's coalition and the centre-left opposition.
AI generated
ROME – A record period of government stability has strengthened Italy, which is no longer viewed within the European Union as “a case to monitor”, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Sept 4 as her administration became the longest-serving of the postwar era.
In a country notorious for political volatility, Meloni’s right-wing coalition has surpassed Silvio Berlusconi’s 2005 record, passing more than 1,400 days in office since taking power in October 2022.
Speaking at an event in the southern city of Bari to mark the milestone, Meloni listed what she described as her government’s key achievements. Delivering lasting political stability in a country that had had 68 governments in 80 years was itself a major accomplishment, she said.
“Stability is the first major reform we have delivered to this nation. Thanks to that stability, Italy has stopped being a country under watch in Europe,” she told supporters.
Financial discipline
During a tumultuous global period of conflict and economic shockwaves, Italy has appeared steadier than some nearby countries, including France, which has had five prime ministers since autumn 2022, and Britain, which has had four.
Meloni said political stability had reassured financial markets about Italy’s handling of its public finances and high debt pile, helping soften borrowing costs on government bonds.
“Having the public accounts in order means fewer constraints. Those who keep their finances in order get to decide where to spend their money,” she said.
Analysts broadly agree that Meloni’s strongest achievement has been restoring confidence in Italy’s finances, but critics say little has been done to overhaul the inefficient public administration, healthcare and education systems.
The government’s main institutional reforms, including plans to strengthen the prime minister’s powers, have stalled, while voters this year rejected a government-backed referendum on judicial reform.
The centre-left opposition on Sept 4 accused the government of failing to address Italy’s longstanding problems.
“Four years of inactivity and inertia are not a badge of honour but an aggravating factor,” said Giuseppe Conte, a former prime minister and leader of the 5-Star Movement, pointing to the country’s persistently sluggish economic growth.
A demonstration was staged in Bari against the rally organised by Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party.
With elections due in 2027, Meloni is expected to lead her coalition into the campaign.
In opinion polls, the centre-left bloc holds a narrow lead over Meloni’s alliance, whose support has been eroded by Futuro Nazionale, a far-right movement that has tapped into concerns over immigration, security and cultural change. REUTERS

Ukraine’s R-2200 Keeps Battlefield Networks Running When LTE and Starlink Fail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:47:48 UTC
04:47:48 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine’s R-2200 Keeps Battlefield Networks Running When LTE and Starlink Fail
An unnamed Ukrainian military technology company has developed a broadband radio station designed to keep battlefield communications running where satellite and cellular networks fail, Oboronka reported on September 4.
The system, designated the R-2200, has passed experimental operation with units of Ukraine's Armed Forces in both its stationary and mobile configurations, according to the outlet. Both variants have been codified and assigned NATO Stock Numbers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Oboronka informed that the R-2200 works across the 2202–2602 MHz band and delivers several core functions:
- reliable links over at least 10 kilometers, or about six miles, in line-of-sight conditions;
- integration into a subscriber's local network through Ethernet and 802.11 Wi-Fi interfaces;
- relay and Wi-Fi mesh operation at up to 54 Mbit/s, and up to 100 Mbit/s in point-to-point mode;
- output power reaching 43 dBm, or up to 20 watts, per antenna connector.
The R-2200 is a digital broadband station built for both fixed and field networks serving military and civilian users. Its defining feature is the ability to hold a connection when LTE and satellite systems are jammed or unavailable, according to the source.
The station supports BPSK, QPSK, 16QAM, and 64QAM modulation and runs in point-to-point, point-to-multipoint, and decentralized relay modes. It carries frequency retuning to counter interference and pairs with omnidirectional antennas rated at 10 or 13 dBi.
Oboronka noted that the network self-organizes and self-heals, extending coverage for mobile command posts and for reconnaissance and fire-control systems operating at range. That design targets mobility on a front where Russian electronic warfare routinely severs conventional links.
Two versions are on offer. The stationary R-2200 runs as a network node on 220-volt alternating current, while the mobile R-2200-01 draws 12 or 24 volts from a vehicle's onboard supply.
The R-2200 fits a wider shift in Ukraine's defense industry, where the assumption of dependable satellite and cellular links has quietly collapsed.
As Russian jamming has spread across the front, developers have moved to build redundancy into everything from ground robots to tactical radios, layering MESH links, Wi-Fi fallbacks, and self-healing networks that keep operating when a single channel goes dark.
Systems are increasingly judged less by peak performance than by whether they can maintain a connection under sustained electronic attack. The station's emphasis on functioning without LTE or satellite reflects that reordering of priorities.

Smoking raises mortality risk by 55% for diabetics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:47:17 UTC
04:47:17 KST

Smoking raises mortality risk by 55% for diabetics
NEW DELHI: Smoking increased the risk of death from any cause by 55% among people with diabetes, according to evidence reviewed in a new international consensus that calls for smoking cessation to be treated as an essential part of type-2 diabetes care. Experts say patients who smoke should be offered medicines, intensive behavioural counselling and regular follow-ups instead of being given a one-time "quit smoking" warning.The recommendations, published in Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice, represent the first dedicated international consensus on smoking cessation specifically for people with type-2 diabetes. They were developed by 35 experts from 13 countries, including Indian diabetes specialist Dr Anoop Misra.
The consensus recommends varenicline as the first-line medicine where available, with nicotine replacement therapy or bupropion as alternatives when varenicline is unavailable or unsuitable. Medicines should be combined with structured, intensive behavioural support and repeated contact rather than brief counselling alone.The stronger approach reflects the added risk smoking poses to people with diabetes.
A meta-analysis of 48 studies involving 1.13 million people found a 55% higher risk of death, while another study of about 130,000 people with diabetes found 48% higher overall mortality and 36% higher cardiovascular mortality among smokers.
Doctors should review patients within two weeks of their quitting and again at four weeks, checking blood sugar, weight, blood pressure and medicines, as quitting can alter drug metabolism and sometimes require dose adjustments.Smoking is also linked to kidney damage in diabetics, with higher risks of albuminuria and diabetic nephropathy. A Japanese study of 2,490 people with type-2 diabetes found insulin resistance rose with cigarettes smoked per day and fell with time after quitting.Quitting, however, can be difficult. Some patients may not recognise the link between smoking and diabetes complications, while others fear weight gain or use cigarettes to cope with stress and anxiety. The experts recommend personalised quitting strategies and relapse prevention.

Andrew Tate indicted in Romania for trafficking minors, money laundering
The UK has requested that Andrew and his brother Tristan be extradited from the US, but it remains unclear whether Romania will follow suit.
Romanian prosecutors have indicted controversial social media influencer Andrew Tate on charges of trafficking minors, sex with a minor and money laundering.
The move on Friday piles further legal pressure on Tate, who along with his brother were jailed in the United States in July after prosecutors in the United Kingdom requested their extradition on rape charges.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Tate supporters rally for brothers ahead of bail hearing in Miami
- list 2 of 3Tate’s attorney says allegations ‘puts a target on their backs’
- list 3 of 3Tate brothers arrested in Miami as UK adds rape, trafficking charges
Romania’s anti-organised crime agency DIICOT said in a statement that Tate and his brother Tristan, who was indicted for complicity in the case, recruited their victims by falsely claiming to seek a relationship or marriage before forcing them to produce sexually exploitative content for a webcam business.
The Tate brothers have denied all wrongdoing.
DIICOT said one of Andrew Tate’s victims was 15 when he seduced her in Britain in 2012 before moving her to the Romanian capital Bucharest and using physical violence and psychological intimidation to force her into producing indecent images of children for social media.
Tristan was an accessory, the unit said, and used physical aggression to coerce the victim.
Prosecutors said the brothers kept $1.25m from the video chat income generated by the victim, or roughly 80 percent of her earnings. The brothers tried to launder the funds by buying four luxury cars, they added.
DIICOT alleges that the Tate brothers’ victims were paid or intimidated in a bid to coax them “not to give statements or to give false statements.”
Eugen Vidineac, a Romanian lawyer for the Tates, said in a statement that the brothers rejected the allegations.
“We will examine every aspect of [the indictment] with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process,” he said. “Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them.”
The Tates are former kickboxers with dual US and British citizenship who amassed a vast social media following worldwide, especially among young men. Their content frequently criticised gender equality and argued for male dominance.
They were arrested in Florida in late July after the UK requested their extradition. Andrew Tate’s official social media accounts have bemoaned the conditions of his Miami jail and alleged that the charges against him are persecution for his social and political views.
Romanian authorities first opened a probe into the brothers related to potential crimes including human trafficking in December 2022, around five years after they moved to the country. Andrew Tate had boasted in online videos that he had relocated to Romania because law enforcement was more lax.
It was not immediately clear whether DIICOT would seek their extradition.
Romanian law permits the prosecution of defendants in absentia, and the case is now bound for a preliminary court chamber for a judge’s review. While the law states that the preliminary chamber judge has 60 days to finalise its advancement, indictments routinely take significantly longer.
The brothers were previously indicted in Romania on charges of human trafficking, but in late 2024 the Bucharest court of appeals sent the case back to prosecutors after deeming some evidence inadmissible.

NEW DELHI: Broadening the definition of "property" under Prevention of Money Laundering Act, a special PMLA court in Mohali has ruled that seized bank cheques, even if not encashed, and narcotics both fall under the definition of "property" and constitute proceeds of crime under the money laundering Act.The judgement came Thursday, when ED launched a massive search operation at 30 premises across all zones of the southern region in different narcotics-related cases. The searches are being conducted under the mandate of Centre's 'Nasha Mukt Bharat' campaign with targets in the first phase spread across Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Telangana.The judge convicted two accused and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for three years, while rejecting the contention of the defence that their property and bank accounts were not attached and the seized contraband could not be considered proceeds of crime as no money trail had been brought on the record.
Special judge Hardip Singh also rejected the defence's argument that the cheques recovered from the accused were not encashed and thus could not constitute proceeds of crime. The judge noted that the cheques were exchanged for the purpose of purchasing the contraband and the accused could not provide any explanation to the contrary.Starting with the four southern states, ED Thursday began a crackdown on major drug syndicates operating across the country.
The drive has been launched as part of Centre's "drug-free India" campaign to attach properties of all those engaged in drug dealing and generation of "proceeds of crime". The ED's search covered targets involved in trafficking of illicit drugs like methamphetamine, marijuana, and MDMA. Over 20 foreign nationals are under scanner, an official said.Searches were conducted at premises in Chennai, Tirunelveli, Nagapattinam, Velankanni and Ramanathapuram in Tamil Nadu; Kolar, Malur (Kolar district) and Hoskote (Bengaluru North district); Serilingampally and Nanakramguda (Hyderabad) and Ranga Reddy district in Telangana; Kozhikode, Kannur, Malappuram and Thrissur in Kerala.ED is coordinating with other central agencies and state police forces that have registered cases of drug trafficking in the past few years to further investigate the money trail and track the proceeds of crime."The investigation prima facie discloses not merely trafficking of methamphetamine, but also the generation, receipt and movement of money arising out of this," a senior official said, adding that syndicates were using hawala and crypto currency dealers to further transfer the proceeds of crime outside the country to tax havens.
The money trail to uncover cash-based hawala settlements revealed "account details, transaction records, diaries, slips or tokens, mobile phones, electronic communications and digital devices, property documents and other financial records". Based on these findings, the agency ascertained the complete quantum and trail of the proceeds of crime, and the persons who received, possessed, transferred, concealed, utilised or invested such proceeds.Further these details help in identifying movable and immovable properties acquired and that leads to their attachments.

What the latest flare-up between the U.S and Iran means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:41:34 UTC
04:41:34 KST

The past few days have seen a flare-up of the war of choice that the United States launched against Iran. American forces launched a series of attacks against Iran, killing both military personnel and civilians. The latter included five people at a wedding, two of them children.
Iran responded by attacking American military locations in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, and, later, the United Arab Emirates.
While the mutual attacks, including the probable war crime by the U.S., represented a break in what had been a relative lull in fighting, they were also calibrated to maintain each side’s control over escalation. Neither side seeks an immediate escalation back to the all-out fighting of the spring months.
That, however, should not imply that both sides are equally reluctant to reignite greater fighting. Although Iran has much more at risk by a return to all-out war, it also has a greater incentive than the United States to end the current state of tension, which is primarily characterized by less firepower and more economic warfare.
The American strategy, to the extent that the administration of Donald Trump has one, is currently to focus on enacting ever-tighter sanctions on Iran, closing off alternative revenue streams, and hoping that the economic collapse does today what it has not done for forty-seven years and brings down the Islamic Republic.
Iran, conversely, is trying to hold on to control of the Strait of Hormuz while continuing to push the United States’ military farther away from the Persian Gulf region. Their increased focus on attacking the remaining American bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, and the UAE is coupled with their growing focus on American positions in Jordan. But they seem, at least for the moment, to have decided to refrain from further attacks on Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
That indicates that Iran is trying to promote a new regional security regime, diminishing the American role, thereby shifting the defense focus from Iran to Israel.
That reflects a more careful long-term strategy, which is sensible for Tehran as the United States is simultaneously making other moves that threaten to entrench this conflict for the long term, bringing a new “forever war.”
How does Trump intend to sell that war to his MAGA followers, who backed him based on “no forever wars”? The same way he always does: he’ll lie to them.
Media blackouts and disinformation
From the beginning of this war, both the United States and Iran have worked to hide information on the damage they have suffered. Iran has more incentive than the United States to broadcast damage, however, so we have had somewhat better views of some American actions, such as this week’s bombing of a wedding in the town of Sirik.
A Reuters investigation confirmed what was initially clear: the United States had directly attacked the wedding site. Obviously, Iran wants to let the world know about such crimes, and the United States, which does not risk its own civilians in this war, has no such temptation.
Of course, Iran has other reasons to conceal some data, such as the extent of the damage the U.S. has done to its missile and drone manufacturing capabilities. Whether those are as greatly diminished as the U.S. dubiously claims or remain largely intact, keeping that knowledge secret is advantageous to Tehran.
This week’s attacks illustrate that advantage. The American attacks, though the largest in many weeks, mostly targeted sites they had hit before, so they were not likely to have caused much more damage, given the mobility of Iran’s defensive systems.
On the other hand, the United States claimed that the Iranian strikes in response were all intercepted or landed in uninhabited areas. Other reporting disputes that, supporting Iranian claims of having hit American communication, radar, and hangar sites as well as the headquarters of an American commander.
There is no way to be certain where the truth lies, but earlier similar American claims have been shown weeks later to be false. The clampdown on reporting has only stiffened since then.
Damage assessments are not the only arena of disinformation. Both sides have an interest in giving the impression of total control of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran insists that the Strait is closed, but some ships are getting through, even without Iran’s permission. They are moving stealthily, often at night, and with their transponders turned off to avoid detection. They are accompanied by American naval and air forces, an expensive, provocative, and unsustainable operation, but one that has temporarily eased the global shortage of oil that has resulted from this war to some degree.
But this week’s claim from U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright that the United States was able to bring 17 million barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday — a figure nearly on par with pre-war traffic through the Strait — was met with widespread skepticism.
Commercial tracking agencies detected only a handful of ships transiting the Strait that day, nothing like the more than one hundred that would be required to match Wright’s claim. Those companies rely not only on transponder signals but also on satellite imagery to count traffic.
The oil market also does not seem convinced by the Trump administration’s claims.
It would take several weeks for shipments of crude oil leaving the Gulf now to hit the market, so we wouldn’t expect to see crude oil prices fall yet.
But if oil buyers believed these figures, we would expect to see an effect on the price of crude oil futures, which is based on the expected market, not the current one. But those prices, too, have not come down.
High oil prices hurt Trump’s claims of victory and of controlling the Strait. But he might still be able to deceive parts of the public if the shooting war does not heat up again.
Trump’s first attacks this week seem to have been intended to deter Iran from exercising more control over the Strait by laying more mines and positioning more launchers. It is unclear whether the American strikes were successful in doing that.
What is clear is that Iran is not likely to allow Trump to strangle the Iranian economy without a response. That was the message sent by Iran when they continued attacking American sites even after they had responded to the first American strikes.
That strategy is becoming even more imperative as the Trump administration, consciously or not, takes steps to prolong this war.
Entrenching the war in Lebanon and Saudi Arabia
There are two matters, beyond the direct confrontation between Iran and the United States in the Persian Gulf, that must be resolved for this war to end. Those are the Israeli invasion and occupation of Lebanon and the issue of Iran’s nuclear program.
The Israeli invasion of Lebanon must end for there to be negotiations with any hope of success. The nuclear issue will upend any deal that might be made if it is not resolved, and the future is currently very hard to see.
Events this week made both of those areas tougher to confront.
Iran had warned the United States not to allow Israel to attack the Ali Taher Ridge, which was a key Hezbollah outpost. The warning should not have been necessary since there is supposed to be a ceasefire, and both Israel and Hezbollah are supposed to be holding their positions until there is a resolution.
Even that unjust arrangement was not good enough for Israel, which, given the impunity it continues to enjoy, went ahead and took out the Hezbollah headquarters, without provocation. As always, a ceasefire means the other side ceases, while Israel fires.
Initial reports stated that IRGC personnel were also in Ali Taher Ridge, but reports after the operation claimed there were none. It is possible the Iranians evacuated to avoid the Israeli assault.
In any case, it remains to be seen if Iran will retaliate, but even if they don’t, there is little hope that Israel will withdraw from Lebanon in the foreseeable future. Talks in Washington between Israel and the Lebanese government, always a meaningless sideshow, have paused as even the Lebanese president has been unable to maintain credibility while engaging Israel.
The looming midterm elections certainly mean Trump will be even more reluctant to press Israel on Lebanon, and after them, it is entirely possible that a thoroughly lame duck Trump will embark on even more radical paths. That, of course, would free Israel even more to act as it wants. Israeli Prime Minister’s precarious position only makes him more inclined to naked aggression.
Even in the unlikely event that the Lebanon issue can be resolved and that terms for ending the war in the Gulf could be found and agreed to, neither Iran nor the U.S. can end the war without a deal on Iran’s nuclear program that lifts the economic sanctions on the Islamic Republic.
As if that wasn’t already difficult enough, the announcement this week was that the United States and Saudi Arabia had signed an agreement for the U.S. to help Saudi Arabia develop a nuclear energy program.
The deal will certainly make it harder for the U.S. to reach an agreement with Iran, and that difficulty is likely to persist beyond Trump’s administration.
The nuclear deal would allow Saudi Arabia to enrich up to 20%, a level the U.S. had cried foul about when Iran enriched to that figure more than fifteen years ago. Moreover, the deal would not require Riyadh to sign on to the Additional Protocol, which allows for much more intrusive inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency, and which Iran did sign on to as part of the JCPOA.
It’s a clear double standard and one that will make Iran even more reluctant than it already is to find common ground with the U.S. on the nuclear issue. This comes on top of the fact that the war itself increased the impetus for Iran to develop a nuclear weapon.
All these factors are coming together and pointing the conflict in a hopeless direction. The way out, however, is still clear: a negotiated settlement along the lines of the Memorandum of Understanding reached in June, combined with elements of the JCPOA and international guarantees for all of it.
Does that mean the United States would have to admit defeat? Yes. But that defeat is manifest already, and Iran is not going to allow the U.S. to prolong this war and the economic strangulation of the Islamic Republic indefinitely. There will, eventually, be blows in the region and possibly beyond that which dwarf what we’ve seen already.
This war has been calamitous enough. The longer it goes on, the harder it will be to end, and the more likely it becomes that a certain global disaster will result.

Outrage as Maltese tycoon acquitted in journalist's murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:31:00 UTC
04:31:00 KST

Outrage as Maltese tycoon acquitted in journalist's murder
September 4, 2026
"Murderer!" — "Scum!" — "Mafia!"
As Yorgen Fenech left the courthouse in Valletta on Wednesday evening, he was confronted by the furious crowd outside. The 44-year-old Maltese businessman pushed through, flanked by his security guards. Just minutes earlier, a jury had acquitted him of ordering the murder of the 53-year-old investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.
The verdict came as a shock to her family. Her son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, said it was a "terrible decision by the jurors that our country may never recover from." He later doubled down on his criticism, describing the verdict in a post on Facebook as "obscene" and saying: "Their decision flies in the face of all evidence, of all logic, of the truth."
Almost nine years after Caruana Galizia's murder, Malta is again confronted with the crucial question: Who was responsible for her death on October 16, 2017? The men who procured the bomb, placed it under the driver's seat and detonated it remotely have already been convicted. But the person who contracted them to do it has still not been legally identified.
A difficult trial
For years, Fenech was considered to be the central figure in the investigations. His arrest on the morning of November 20, 2019, was like something out of a movie. His luxury yacht, Gio, had just left harbor when it was stopped by a Maltese military patrol boat. Fenech was arrested on board and subsequently interrogated by the police.
Fenech's arrest, and suspicion that people in government circles were involved in the crime, sparked protests all across the country. Joseph Muscat, prime minister at the time, was accused of protecting political allies and stepped down in January 2020. Fenech spent more than five years in detention before being released on bail, under strict conditions, in early 2025.
His trial only began this summer, and the final verdict was decisive. Eight of the nine jurors rejected the prosecution's argument that it was Fenech who had ordered the journalist's murder.
Who was responsible?
The prosecution case relied above all on the testimony of Melvin Theuma, who confessed to being the middleman and testified that Fenech had contracted him to organize the murder. Theuma received a pardon in exchange for his cooperation.
But Fenech's defense called Theuma's credibility into question, highlighting contradictions in his testimony and false statements he had made previously.
Fenech's lawyers also sought to prove that evidence pointing to Keith Schembri, chief of staff to Muscat at the time, was not properly followed up. Schembri has denied any involvement in the murder, and the investigators did not charge him as a suspect in this case.
The public prosecutors' argument was that Caruana Galizia had been investigating Fenech, specifically his company 17 Black and the energy consortium ElectroGas, on suspicion of corruption. This, they said, meant Fenech had a motive for silencing her. She had not, however, been on the point of publishing anything that could have threatened him.
Open questions
Many in Malta are outraged by the not-guilty verdict. But there is no indication to date that Fenech did not receive a fair trial, or that the process was manipulated. For him to be convicted, Fenech's guilt had to be proved beyond reasonable doubt.
Caruana Galizia's family are therefore also focusing on institutional failures that they believe facilitated the murder. They complain that these have not been addressed, and necessary reforms not implemented. An official investigation already established, in 2021, that an "atmosphere of impunity" in Malta created conditions that made the murder possible.
Reforms in Malta
Since then, Malta has made progress with a series of reforms, but many say they do not go far enough. This is especially the case with regard to press freedom. In 2021, the committee of inquiry recommended that journalists be better protected against political and economic pressure and their role institutionally strengthened, yet the country is still waiting for comprehensive media reform.
Following years of discussion and a public consultation, the Maltese government brought the relevant bill before parliament in March 2026, but the legislation was not passed before early parliamentary elections in May.
In its latest Rule of Law Report, the European Commission only certifies limited progress made by Malta. It acknowledges that it has introduced some specific protection measures for journalists, but says core recommendations from the investigation into the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia remain unfulfilled.
Government sees progress
But the government paints a different picture. It has highlighted changes to the judiciary and anti-corruption measures, as well as better protection of journalistic sources, and additional measures to protect media professionals. This is what the EU Commission referred to as progress in specific areas.
The case has also shone a spotlight on the slow pace of the Maltese justice system. According to a report by the Daphne Caruana Galizia Foundation, 46% of homicide cases brought to trial between 2010 and 2020 had still not been concluded in mid-2025. The foundation regards this as a structural problem, and warns that when proceedings go on for so long, it compromises the chances of an effective prosecution.
Fresh investigation?
No decision has yet been made as to what will happen now, following Fenech's acquittal. Judge Edwina Grima has ordered that the evidence presented at trial be passed on to the chief of police, who will decide whether criminal proceedings should be brought against anyone else.
On Thursday, former PM Muscat said that, according to the public prosecutors, further investigations were ongoing.
The Institute of Maltese Journalists (IGM) has called on the authorities to pursue every line of inquiry that came to light during the trial — including, explicitly, those that lead to former high-ranking politicians. The acquittal must be respected as the outcome of the constitutional process, the IGM said, but it does not close the case.
The demonstrators outside the courthouse in Valletta are in no doubt. Someone must have issued a contract for the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia. And almost nine years after her death, still no one has been held responsible.
This article was originally written in German.

UN votes to adopt new world map that reflects Africa’s true size
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:25:08 UTC
04:25:08 KST

UN votes to adopt new world map that reflects Africa’s true size
The widely-used Mercator map is often criticised for visually exaggerating and centralising Western nations.
The United Nations has voted to adopt a new world map that more accurately reflects countries’ true sizes, a resolution sponsored by African states to right a centuries-old wrong.
The “Correct the Map” resolution adopted by the UN general assembly on Friday aims to address a colonial-era injustice that has visually shrunk Africa for 450 years, shaping how the continent is perceived in media, education and policy around the world.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘US, China, India can all fit into Africa’: On a quest to fix the world map
- list 2 of 3Apple changes name of Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ in maps app
- list 3 of 3Google Maps renames Lake Ontario after Trump’s decree on ‘Lake America’
The resolution, put forward by African Union (AU) member states and the Bahamas, was backed by a vote of 164-1 with six abstentions.
Togo led the AU’s campaign to limit use of the widely-used Mercator map.
Developed in the 16th century by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator, the projection distorts the relative size of land masses by expanding those nearer the poles. For instance, it makes Greenland appear roughly the same size as Africa, even though Africa is about 14 times larger.
Some critics of the Mercator map believe it remains widely used because it visually exaggerates and centralises Western nations, perpetuating ideas of European superiority.
“A fair world begins with a fair map,” Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told the Reuters news agency ahead of Friday’s vote.
The resolution promotes the Equal Earth projection, which more accurately portrays the size of the continents.
The resolution is not legally binding and it “in no way challenges the use of the Mercator projection for maritime and aerial navigation, for which it remains fully suited,” the Togolese ministry said in a statement.
The United States – the only country to vote against the resolution – said it promoted an “ideological agenda” and was a distraction from the “genuine problems of international peace, prosperity or good relations”.
Moky Makura, executive director of the advocacy organisation Africa No Filter that’s involved in “Correct the World” map campaign, hailed the vote, saying “now the real work begins”.
“We want to see accurate maps in schools, textbooks, newsrooms, businesses and on the digital platforms billions of people use every day,” Makura said in a statement.
“If we got something as basic as Africa’s size wrong for this long, what else about Africa have we simply accepted without questioning? Africa doesn’t need to be made bigger. It needs to be seen accurately,” she added.
‘Distortions eventually take root in perceptions’
Ahead of the vote, France, who co-sponsored the resolution, announced that it planned to abandon the Mercator map.
The foreign ministry “will abandon the Mercator projection in favour of map representations tailored to specific uses, more faithful to actual surface areas and in line with the recommendations of cartographers and scientists”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said in a speech at the Sorbonne University in Paris.
“The United States, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence compared to Africa, Latin America or southeast Asia,” Barrot said, adding that “distortions eventually take root in perceptions” and that “the time has come to correct them.”
The Mercator map remains widely used in classrooms, but Togo hopes to change its school geography materials by the end of the year, Dussey told Reuters.
Togo will press other governments, schools, international organisations and technology companies to move away from the Mercator map in favour of the Equal Earth one, Dussey said.
Dussey linked the campaign to adopt the map to wider African efforts to confront colonial-era legacies, while saying it was not an attack on Europe or any other civilisation.
The Mercator map’s widespread use is a consequence of colonisation, he said.
“The world is changing. Africa also is changing.”

Mistrial declared in Lindsay Clancy child killings case
Jurors could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether the former nurse was criminally responsible for the deaths of her three kids
A judge declared a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial on Friday after jurors said they could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for killing her three young children.
The mistrial, on the seventh day of deliberations, leaves the case unresolved and allows prosecutors to take the 36-year-old former labour and delivery nurse to trial again. Neither Clancy, her family nor the jury showed any emotion as the judge announced the mistrial.
The deliberations took a dramatic turn late in the week when Judge William Sullivan said he was going to declare a mistrial on Friday before suddenly changing course and giving her defence lawyer a chance to appeal to the top court in Massachusetts. The emergency appeal was quickly denied.
The trial has generated intense interest for more than a month, deeply dividing the public and drawing attention to issues around maternal mental health after childbirth. Clancy’s lawyer said she was suffering from a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she strangled her children, the youngest just eight months old, then tried to take her own life.
Prosecutors, who said Clancy knew what she was doing, now must decide whether to put Clancy on trial again, drop the charges or try to negotiate a plea deal with her lawyer.
Prosecutors said Clancy acted deliberately when she strangled five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson and eight-month-old Callan Clancy with exercise bands on January 24, 2023.

Trump says US might hit Pickaxe Mountain in Iran ‘very soon’

US President Donald Trump said Friday that Washington could strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain site “very soon,” while describing the ongoing conflict with Tehran as “small potatoes” and saying the US is carrying out intermittent strikes.
Asked whether the confrontation should be considered a war, Trump said he preferred to call it a “military conflict.”
“A lot of people don’t call it a war. I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us. It’s not a big thing,” he told reporters in the Oval Office.

Asked when the conflict would end, Trump said he could not give a timeframe but argued Washington had already achieved its main objective.

Trump added that even if the US withdrew immediately, “it would take them 25 years to rebuild their country.”

Police hunt German man who claimed sabotage of power substations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:17:39 UTC
04:17:39 KST

Ayhan Simsek
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
German police launched a manhunt Friday for a 48-year-old man who sent handwritten letters to newsrooms claiming responsibility for a string of sabotage attacks on electric substations, saying he acted to protest power generation from fossil fuels.
Media identified the suspect as Daniel V. from Gevelsberg in North Rhine-Westphalia. The letters were signed with his full name. Investigators said the descriptions of the devices matched finds at the scenes.
The writer said he acted alone and that left-wing groups and activists “had nothing to do with it.”
“Electricity generation from fossil fuels is a crime that brings unspeakable suffering,” one letter said. “Because the media don’t do a damn thing to convey the urgency of the situation and the state does not intervene to avert this suffering, I have to do it now.”
In another passage, he wrote: “I am not attacking the country but the fossil fuel industry, even if for some politicians that is the same thing.” He said he was “pleased that there were no power outages and yet coal-fired power plant units went offline.”
He also wrote that he would “not be sad” if Germany’s arms industry were hit by outages, “particularly as long as Germany supports the genocide in Palestine.”
The letters described the alleged method in technical detail, mentioning electric detonators, timers, pipes and a wire used to throw conductive material over high-voltage lines and cause short circuits.
Police units stormed the suspect’s home in Gevelsberg on Friday and later searched a truck found in woodland near Duren, close to the Hambach lignite mine. Officials said the man was not there. The search continued. North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said the suspect was now believed to be on foot.
Germany has witnessed three sabotage attempts on electric substations this week. The first attack struck Tuesday near the Jaenschwalde coal-fired power plant in Brandenburg, when homemade launch devices sent conductive material toward high-voltage lines. Hours later, a second strike hit a substation in Bergheim, west of Cologne. On Thursday evening, a walker found similar devices near a substation in Dormagen, and police said someone had apparently tried to cause a short circuit there, though no damage was reported.

UN adopts new world map showing true scale of continents; only US votes against it
- The United Nations adopted the Equal Earth map projection to show a more accurate size of continents, supported by 164 countries; the US opposed it.
- The new map corrects distortions of the Mercator projection, enlarging Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania while reducing North America and Europe.
- France supports the change to improve relations with Africa and calls the update "an act of truth," despite acknowledging that maps do not change reality.
AI generated
NEW YORK – The United Nations General Assembly voted on Sept 4 to adopt a new world map that makes the African continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe, drawing ire from Washington.
Aimed at “a more accurate representation” of continental landmasses, the resolution was supported by 164 countries, while the US voted against it and six other states abstained.
The new map – known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection – improves “the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world”, the resolution said.
It urges member states to use the new map in place of the traditional Mercator projection, which was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569.
Foreign Minister Robert Dussey of Togo, which sponsored the resolution, said maps “guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions”.
“They are therefore never neutral; when they present a distorted image of our planet, they risk perpetuating inaccurate representation that is passed down through generations.”
The US, however, slammed the resolution, saying such moves are “the reason this institution is losing its credibility”.
“Instead of focusing on genuine problems... this body is debating map projects from the 16th century and their role in promoting reparations and cognitive justice,” US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said ahead of the vote.
The Mercator projection focused on accurate depictions of the shapes and angles of land masses, but their relative sizes were often inaccurate – largely due to the challenge of rendering a 3D globe onto a 2D map.
It inflated northern regions and compressed equatorial ones, making Europe and North America appear much larger, while shrinking Africa and South America.
A group of cartographers launched the Equal Earth projection in 2018. It makes Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania appear much larger.
“Equal Earth preserves the relative surface areas of continents and, as much as possible, shows their shapes as they appear on a globe,” one of the cartographers, Bojan Savric, told AFP in 2025.
France – which co-sponsored the resolution in support of the new map – announced on Sept 4 that it would abandon the Mercator projection.
In that map, “the United States, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence compared to Africa, Latin America or South-east Asia”, while “Greenland appears almost as big as Africa,” Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said.
“Changing maps obviously doesn’t change the world,” he said. “But correcting a distorted representation is already an act of truth.”
The initiative comes as France is seeking to improve relations with Africa, particularly in former colonies with which it has prickly ties. AFP

Yemen: Fighting intensifies amid Houthi push in the west
September 4, 2026
Both sides in Yemen's long-running civil war have sustained losses in a new push from the Houthi militia to try to seize control of the gateway to the Red Sea in the west.
The Iran-backed Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of the country, launched a ground offensive against the Saudi Arabia-led coalition supporting Yemen's government-in-exile on Thursday.
No casualty numbers were formally announced but news agencies citing sources off the record concurred that both sides had sustained dozens of losses, as well as civilians who were killed amid the fighting. The AFP news agency tallied 129 deaths as of Friday.
Officials also reported shelling and artillery fire forcing hundreds of families to flee from a pair of coastal cities, Hodeidah and Mokha, one held by either side in the conflict.
Why are the Houthis pushing to control this territory now?
Yemen has been in a state of civil war for almost exactly 12 years, and a period of comparative calm broke down this July amid the war with Iran in the Gulf.
The Houthis are targeting ports and elevated terrain held by Saudi-led forces that would improve their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, where the Red Sea meets the Gulf of Aden, leading out into the Arabian Sea and open waters.
Always a crucial waterway, its significance has increased amid the restrictions to traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis declared a blockade on ships approaching the west coast of Saudi Arabia, with access to its eastern ports already impeded via Hormuz. But they are not ideally placed or equipped to enforce their stated desire.
Nevertheless they have already fired on several commercial vessels, causing severe damage and deaths in a few cases, even with their imperfect control of the relevant coastline.
What do we know about the intensified fighting?
Military sources speaking off the record told both the DPA and AFP news agencies that both sides had sustained multiple casualties. DPA put the figure in the dozens on both sides, AFP had a more precise estimate of roughly 60 on either side.
Exchanges of fire, on land as well as using rockets and drones, were reported in two southwestern provinces, Taiz and Hodeidah.
The Houthis control the major western port of Hodeidah further north, but large chunks of Yemen's southwestern tip in Taiz including the port of Mokha near the strait are controlled by Saudi-led forces.
"They are going for Bab al-Mandeb," Mohammed al-Basha of the US-based risk advisory Basha Report told the AFP news agency.
Fighting for the high ground, for instance on Mount al-Numan overlooking Mokha, was particularly fierce.
"The Houthis feel that if they capture Bab al-Mandab or Mokha port they will be in a better position of power to negotiate with the government and the Saudis," al-Basha said.

The escalation is among the most significant rounds of fighting in Taiz since a U.N.-brokered truce in 2022, amid U.N. warnings over the risk of Yemen sliding back into a wider conflict.
The Houthis have controlled the capital Sanaa and other cities since September 2014, while the internationally recognized government and allied forces control large areas in the south, east and west of the country.

Saxony-Anhalt: Small parties will be the kingmakers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:06:00 UTC
04:06:00 KST

Saxony-Anhalt: Small parties will be the kingmakers
September 4, 2026
It's rare that a state parliament election in Germany attracts as much media interest as this one in Saxony-Anhalt. On September 6, 2026, the 1.7 million eligible voters in the eastern German state will decide whether the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party can form a state government for the first time.
So far, there has not been a head of government who belonged to a proven far-right party in post-World War II Germany — at neither federal nor state level. That would change if AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund were to be elected to this position, since the Office for the Protection of the Constitution in Saxony Anhalt already classified the AfD as such in 2023.
Siegmund's chances of a historical triumph are high: For months the AfD has been comfortably leading the polls with well over 40% of the vote.
AfD, CDU and Left Party will get into parliament
Aside from the AfD, there are only two other parties who can count on being included in the next state parliament: The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of current State Premier Sven Schulze and the socialist Left Party, which is traditionally strong in eastern Germany, the former socialist GDR.
All other parties have cause for concern they could fail to reach the 5% threshold of votes necessary for entry into parliaments in Germany.
This even applies to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), who currently form part of the federal government coalition with the CDU and its Bavarian counterpart, the Christian Social Union (CSU).
SPD, Greens, FDP, BSW might not make the 5% mark
The SPD is losing popularity nationwide. In Saxony-Anhalt, they are polling below the 8% they won five years ago.
The third party in Saxony-Anhalt's current governing coalition, formed in 2021, has even fewer hopes: The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) are polling only about 3%. Following the FDP's failure in the Bundestag general election of 2025 and multiple defeats at the state level, supporters are bracing themselves for the next setback.
The environmentalist Greens are also concerned about returning to the state parliament. The party, whose core voter base is in wealthy western German cities, is vehemently rejected by many voters in rural areas because of its climate policies and multicultural vision of society.
Concern over Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW)
And then there is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), founded in 2024 by its namesake, a former Left Party co-leader. The party is economically left-leaning, but socially right-wing conservative and populist. This is its first time participating in a state election in Saxony-Anhalt.
After the BSW gained 6.2% of the vote in the European parliament elections in 2024 and won results of between about 12% and 16% in the eastern German states of Brandenburg, Saxony and Thuringia during its first year, it failed by only a few thousand votes to reach the 5% hurdle to enter German parliament in the 2025 general election.
The BSW never really recovered from this setback. They went on to be defeated in three further state parliament elections. The party also has cause for concern in Saxony-Anhalt, where it has been polling under 5%.
Should it win representation after all, Sahra Wagenknecht has already announced that her party's lawmakers would not vote an AfD premier into office, but abstain from the vote paving the way for him to win a majority in parliament and take office.
Considering the poor polling numbers for the BSW in Saxony-Anhalt, political scientist Oliver Lembcke speaks of an "endgame" for the party as a whole.
Small parties could prevent absolute majority for the AfD
The fact is: The more parties fail to reach the threshold, the higher the likelihood of the Alternative for Germany will be able to govern alone.
On the other hand, if aside from the AfD, the CDU, Left Party and SPD win representation in the next Saxony-Anhalt parliament, and those three parties together hold more seats than the AfD, the situation is complicated. This is because in 2018 the CDU adopted a so-called "resolution of incompatibility," which rejects cooperation with both the AfD and the Left Party.
If the CDU sticks to this, forming even a minority government would be very difficult, perhaps impossible.
Could the CDU form a minority government?
Political scientist Lembcke from Ruhr University Bochum in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia argues that the CDU should have adapted its incompatibility resolution to the changed conditions of the party systems and political landscape. Because it has failed to do so, this issue could now escalate drastically in Saxony-Anhalt.
The Left Party is prepared to support Premier Sven Schulze of the CDU to secure a second term.
"In recent years, we, the Left Party, have shown that we take responsibility for this country. Especially when it comes to inhibiting the AfD," Left Party co-leader Luigi Pantisano told television broadcaster ZDF.
He pointed to the states of Thuringia and Saxony, where the CDU leads coalition governments without a parliamentary majority and depends on the support of the Left Party.
Given the foreseeably complicated situation, one thing is clear ahead of the September 6 election: either Saxony-Anhalt faces an incredibly difficult coalition-building process, or the state will be governed by the AfD — if the party profits from the failure of many small parties and thereby receives an absolute majority in the state parliament.
This article has been translated from German.

Adelaide returns to scene of finals flop to face biggest test of growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:02:34 UTC
04:02:34 KST

analysis
Adelaide's elimination final against Western Bulldogs looms as its biggest test of growth
Every week it seems like there is history being written in the AFL.
Some of this is welcomed, memorable and celebrated, such as when Scott Pendlebury broke the games record earlier this year, or when Lance Franklin notched the 1,000-goal mark in 2022.
Moments like these are cherished throughout each club's fanbase and reflects the long history of the league and sport.
Other slices of history are far more trivial. Last week, Sam Walsh set the record for the most disposals in the Wildcard Finals round. While the stat is interesting, it is not necessarily illustrative of a feat of great importance.
Nonetheless, it provides colour to the rich tapestry that is Australian football.
And there are some feats that players and coaches avoid like the plague.
Many football fans know the tale of Kevin Murray. The former Roys stalwart managed to play 333 games, all without winning a single final — a league record.
While his career was rich and storied, eventually earning him Legend status in the Hall of Fame, the achievement underscored the futility of playing for Fitzroy through most of the second half of the 20th century.
Though never winning a VFL final, Murray did manage to play in a finals win during a lucrative mid-career stint at East Perth in 1966 on the way to a losing Grand Final against Perth.
This Saturday night Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks is set to, at least temporarily, claim his own slice of footballing ignominy.
Nicks will join Alec Hall as the coaches to steer their sides through the most VFL/AFL games without winning a final.
For those who don't immediately recognise the name Alec Hall, his last game as coach came more than a century ago.
Over the last two years Nicks's Crows have won the second most regular season games. Last year's minor premiership season was cut short with a straight sets exit.
This year the Crows are already on their last chance with a rampaging Bulldogs ahead of them.
Nicks has quietly rebuilt his side's biggest question mark. But in the Bulldogs, the Crows face a test designed to test this weakness in full.
Mayhem in the middle
Fresh in the mind of Nicks, and all Crows fans, is how their 2025 season came to an end.
Like all sides who fall short of their end goal, reflection on their failings quickly sets in.
For Nicks, the message on what went wrong was clear, and last year's disappointment has put them in a stronger place for this year.
"I think we're ahead of last year," Nicks said after their round 24 win over the Giants, despite being "a little lower on the ladder."
"We've been doing a lot of work around what it was we didn't get right last year. Under that immense pressure that Collingwood and Hawthorn brought last year we weren't able to execute and deliver our game on our game plan."
That pressure around the contest is arguably what brought their once-promising 2025 season undone. Against Hawthorn, the Crows struggled both at contests both at stoppage and in general play, with the Hawks midfield unit gaining control of the game.
Starved of opportunity with ball in hand, the Crows' defence could only do so much to hold the wave of Hawks back.
The Hawks ended that final with a six-clearance advantage and 20 more post-clearance ground ball gets. Starved of the ball, the Crows were left passengers in a finals series that they were meant to drive from the front.
At the most basic level, only part of the contest game needed adjustment from the outside. The Crows finished the 2025 season leading for post-clearance ground ball gets and contested possessions.
They were relatively weak at stoppage, however, with a negative clearance differential across the year.
But that hid a slide against the best of the best.
The Crows struggled more against good opposition midfields than most other contenders, perhaps the canary in the coalmine for their finals struggles.
This is despite their units at either end of the ground largely holding up their ends of the bargain.
The Crows defence in 2025 and 2026 has actually gotten stronger against the best sides in the league. They conceded just 1.47 points per inside 50 this year — better than any team's full season record.
The figures were even starker last year. While the Crows concede more in games against good sides, this has largely been down to an increased volume of inside 50s their defence has to protect against.
It's yet another mark of honour for the severely underrated Adelaide backline. Over the past two years the Crows defence has arguably been the strongest defensive unit in the league, despite the lack of individual acknowledgement.
Only one Crows defender, Wayne Milera, has made the All-Australian team in this time despite the depth and strength of their taller options.
While their forward line has had a rotating list of players contribute it has been a little stronger when it matters most.
The territory battle at the contest, particularly up the ground and at stoppage, is so important for one of the Crows' other weaknesses.
Despite their defensive miserliness, their backline has struggled to transition the ball from defensive 50 and the defensive half to create scoring opportunities.
It means the Crows can absorb the pressure of opposition attacks, but sometimes struggle to get the game back on their terms in this way.
Without the benefit of winning the territory battle, or control of the footy at the contest, it can make a spellbinding side look pedestrian at best.
The shift
This has spurred the Adelaide brains trust into action. Throughout this year Nicks has experimented with different looks up the ground.
Bodies have floated through the middle and up forward to try to execute when it matters most.
The highest profile change through the year was one involving a player who missed last year's finals altogether.
Since he entered the league with Gold Coast, Izak Rankine has long been viewed as one of the game's most damaging attacking players. He is the type of player that makes the hair stand up on the back of your neck, or your eyes quickly dart back to the TV if the commentator mentions his name in excited tones.
His 2025 season ended not due to form or injury, but rather as a consequence of using a homophobic slur towards a Collingwood player in round 23. Suspended for four matches, Rankine admitted his mistake and apologised publicly and privately.
It is always difficult to judge atonement and sincerity from a distance, but Rankine has made further efforts to build a relationship with the Rainbow Crows supporter group, which has in turn praised the progress made.
Some fans, both of Adelaide and the sport more broadly, may need more time to evaluate his response to the incident.
Others, particularly a large cohort of Crows fans, believed the punishment to be too severe from the outset.
Regardless of your stance, Rankine appears to be choosing his own course in making amends for his grave misstep.
Rankine's on field evolution in 2026 is far easier to evaluate than anything off field.
This year Rankine has been deployed full time in the middle of the ground for the first time in his career. The results have been dramatic.
Since the shift, Rankine has been about the most damaging player in the competition, with his previous skill in limited opportunities scaling up when foisted around the ball more often.
The tipping point for Nicks to throw Rankine through the middle more was making sure the young Crow fit with the defence first mindset of the side.
"I've always wanted to play midfield." Rankine told AFC.com.au earlier this month.
"I just had to fix up my two-way running, understanding the game, and when the opposition gets momentum against us how to mentally stay in the game and not get frustrated.
"I've found that the way I can get more of those opportunities is really delving into the defensive side of the game, getting back and helping the defenders, and being an option for them when they get stuck."
It's hard to overstate the growth in Rankine's game. Rankine has moved his predominantly front-half game to impact across the ground.
Defensively, Rankine has increasingly involved himself at contest and tracked his opponent while retaining that attacking flair that makes his game so appealing.
In that time, Adelaide has become even stronger at the contest without suffering on the defensive side. Rankine provides an explosive attacking strength that few other sides can boast, and his improved defensive effort has cost the Crows little the other way.
Rankine is not the only adjustment the Crows have made in the middle through the year.
The Crows have exposed players like Jake Soligo and Brayden Cook at the contest, with other experiments along the way. Instead of direct results on a week to week basis, it appears that Nicks is attempting to expose a wider group to action in the middle in order to maximise his options come September.
Perhaps the last shift might be their biggest, as over the past month the Crows have shifted recent draftee Dan Curtin to the guts in order to provide a vastly different look.
At 197cm and with the build of a key position player, Curtin may be the league's biggest full-time midfielder.
If it sticks, Curtin might provide a midfield option that few other sides have seen before.
"He's still got so much upside in his game. We haven't really scratched the surface there yet," Nicks said.
"I think we see Dan as a midfielder moving forward. We feel like he's got the football intelligence, the execution and the awareness that you need to be a midfielder.
"He's unique in that he's such a big body, so he's a tough match-up. He's still a very young player that's still learning a fair bit about the game. But it's exciting for us."
Curtin presents opponents a rare challenge of raw size alongside unquestioned footballing ability, similar to Patrick Cripps and experiments with ruck-mids such as Mark Blicavs and Luke Jackson.
Curtin's exposure to different roles across his short professional career has also gifted him with a sense of defensive responsibility when running through the middle — key to executing the Crows' game plan.
A meeting with the biggest midfield test
Given how much of their focus has been on building their game at the contest, it is somewhat fitting that their first finals test comes against arguably the league's most damaging contested side on their day.
While the Bulldogs are entering September with a depleted forward line and a defence with more questions than answers, few can question the raw ability and system of their midfield unit.
For a side entrenched in the mid-table hustle over the last two years the Dogs are a side few want to see when the footy starts to get serious.
It's that ability in the middle of the ground, led by All-Australian duo Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards, that is set to stress test Nicks's personnel changes.
While the Crows have improved their work at the contest as the year has progressed, the results across the whole year paint a similar picture to that of 2025.
Looking at the entire season likely undersells where they sit right now. While they lost the clearance battle to Fremantle in round 23, they dominated the post-clearance contested battle — crucial to maintaining field position.
Despite Adelaide's strong performances over the last two years, rumbling from Victoria has suggested that Nicks must steer the Crows to victory to retain his job.
"I understand the narrative, it's part of this industry, [but] it's probably not something I could talk to," Nicks said.
If, for whatever reason, the Crows do the unthinkable and remove Nicks from his post after the season, it would be a move without little recent precedent.
The most recent coach to lead his side to at least 33 wins over his last two seasons in charge before leaving his role was Mick Malthouse in his "negotiated handover" to Nathan Buckley at Collingwood.
Few, if any, coaches have been legitimately sacked in league history with so many home and away wins immediately prior to their removal.
While it is likely just a rumour spread wild, the game on Saturday night presents a chance to silence the speculation of the doubters.
