Stanford scientists discover a seafood that can reverse signs of aging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:29:06 UTC
21:29:06 KST

Stanford scientists discover a seafood that can reverse signs of aging
A compound found in sea squirts improved memory, rejuvenated brain connections, and even restored darker hair in aging mice.
- Date:
- September 4, 2026
- Source:
- Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University
- Summary:
- A substance found in edible sea squirts appeared to reverse several signs of aging in older mice. Plasmalogen supplements improved memory and learning, strengthened connections between brain cells, reduced inflammation, and even helped the mice grow thicker, darker hair. Researchers believe the compounds may encourage brain regeneration and protect aging synapses.
- Share:
Aging often makes itself visible in familiar ways, from gray hair and wrinkles to lapses in memory. That has fueled a longstanding scientific question: Could some of those changes eventually be slowed, prevented, or even reversed?
Research involving a group of scientists from Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, Stanford University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences points to an intriguing possibility. In experiments with aged mice, researchers found that dietary supplements containing compounds associated with Ascidiacea, commonly known as sea squirts, reversed several signs linked to aging.
An Unusual Source of Anti-Aging Compounds
Sea squirts are marine animals that are eaten in parts of Asia, including Korea (where it is known as meongge, or 멍게) and Japan (hoya, or ホヤ). They can be eaten raw and contain high levels of compounds called plasmalogens.
Plasmalogens are a type of lipid, or fat molecule, that forms an important part of cell membranes. They occur naturally throughout the human body and are especially abundant in the brain, heart, and immune cells. Their levels tend to decline as people grow older.
Reduced plasmalogen levels have also been observed in several neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease. That connection has led researchers to investigate whether restoring plasmalogens could help protect the brain from some of the changes associated with aging.
To explore that possibility, the team added plasmalogens to the diets of aged mice and examined how the supplements affected both their behavior and their bodies.
The results were striking. The treated mice showed substantial improvements in learning and displayed visible physical changes as well.
Professor Lei Fu, the corresponding author of the study, says: "Our research suggests that plasmalogens may not just stop cognitive decline, but may reverse cognitive impairments in the aging brain. Additionally, aged mice fed with the plasmalogens grow new black hair that is thicker and glossier than aged mice not fed the supplement."
According to the researchers, the work provides the first detailed look at how plasmalogens may influence the aging brain.
Aging Mice Show Improved Memory
To measure learning and memory, the scientists used a common laboratory experiment called the Morris water maze. In this test, mice are placed in a pool containing a hidden platform where they can rest.
Because mice generally prefer to escape the water, they gradually learn where the platform is located. After several days of training, younger mice typically remember its position and swim toward it quickly. Older mice often need more time to locate the platform, reflecting the decline in learning and memory that can accompany aging.
After five days of training, aged mice receiving plasmalogens performed much more like younger animals. They reached the platform significantly faster than aged mice that had not received the supplement.
The researchers then examined the animals' brains to determine what might explain the improvement.
They found that mice given plasmalogens had more synapses, and those synapses appeared to be in better condition than those in untreated aged mice.
Synapses are the tiny junctions through which nerve cells communicate. They allow signals to pass through neural networks and are essential for learning, memory, and many other brain functions.
Restoring Connections in the Aging Brain
Synapses are highly adaptable early in life. This ability to change and form new connections, often called neural plasticity, helps the brain learn new information and skills.
With age, however, synapses can become less numerous and less effective. Similar deterioration is also associated with neurodegenerative diseases and can contribute to declining cognitive abilities.
In the experiment, aged mice receiving plasmalogen supplements appeared better able to form new neural connections and learn new tasks than mice eating a normal diet. The findings suggest that increasing dietary plasmalogens may help protect synapses from some forms of age-related deterioration.
The researchers also identified another important difference between the groups: inflammation in the brain was substantially lower among mice receiving plasmalogens.
Inflammation is part of the body's normal immune response, but chronic or excessive inflammation in the brain can become harmful. As the brain ages, immune activity can become dysregulated, potentially damaging nerve cells and disrupting communication between synapses. Persistent inflammation is also considered an important contributor to several neurodegenerative disorders.
The reduction in inflammation seen in the plasmalogen-treated mice could therefore help explain why they performed better on tests of learning and memory.
How Plasmalogens Might Work
Scientists do not yet know exactly how dietary plasmalogens produce these effects. Professor Fu outlined several possible mechanisms.
"We found that plasmalogens significantly increase the number of molecules that aid the growth and development of neurones and synapses in the brain. This suggests that plasmalogens can promote neuroregeneration.
"There is also an increasing body of evidence that plasmalogens directly affect the structural properties of synapses. Plasmalogens may increase the fluidity and flexibility of synaptic membranes, affecting the transmission of impulses between neurones."
Neuroregeneration refers to the repair, renewal, or regrowth of nerve cells and their connections. If plasmalogens support that process, they could potentially help the aging brain maintain or rebuild some of the neural circuitry needed for memory and learning.
The researchers also believe the effects may not be limited to what happens directly inside the brain.
Professor Fu points to the gut-brain connection as another possible pathway.
"Some studies have shown that dietary plasmalogens affect the microorganisms in the gut. It has been widely reported that the connection between the organisms in our gut and our brain influences neurodegeneration. It may be the plasmalogen's effect on this connection that causes the improvements in learning and memory seen in this study."
The gut contains enormous communities of bacteria and other microorganisms, collectively known as the gut microbiome. Research increasingly suggests that these microbes can influence the brain through immune signals, metabolism, and other biological pathways. Scientists often refer to this two-way communication system as the gut-brain axis.
Could Plasmalogens Eventually Help People?
Professor Fu has such confidence in the findings that he personally takes a plasmalogen supplement every day.
"For the first time, we show that plasmalogen supplements might be a potential intervention strategy for halting neurodegeneration and promoting neuroregeneration.
"The oral intake of plasmalogens could be a feasible therapeutic strategy to improve cognitive function in older people."
The findings are intriguing, but they come from an animal model. Improvements observed in mice do not necessarily mean that eating sea squirts or taking plasmalogen supplements will reverse aging in humans. Additional research would be needed to determine whether similar effects occur in people, what doses might be effective, and whether long-term supplementation is safe.
Still, the results raise an unusual possibility. A compound found in an edible marine animal may offer scientists a new way to investigate how aging affects the brain and whether some of those changes can eventually be reversed.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Jinxin Gu, Lixue Chen, Ran Sun, Jie-Li Wang, Juntao Wang, Yingjun Lin, Shuwen Lei, Yang Zhang, Dan Lv, Faqin Jiang, Yuru Deng, James P. Collman, Lei Fu. Plasmalogens Eliminate Aging-Associated Synaptic Defects and Microglia-Mediated Neuroinflammation in Mice. Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences, 2022; 9 DOI: 10.3389/fmolb.2022.815320

U.S. Army seeks faster rail repairs to speed up deployments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:29:01 UTC
21:29:01 KST

- Army logistics leaders met at Anniston Army Depot, Alabama, August 25-27 to build a coordinated plan for the service's strained rail network.
- The Army is working with the Department of Transportation's Volpe Center to speed up rail repairs, cutting some procurement timelines in half through existing contract vehicles.
Army logistics leaders met at Anniston Army Depot in Alabama from August 25 to 27 to work through readiness problems across the service’s rail network, the system the Army relies on to move tanks, other heavy equipment and munitions to where they’re needed.
The summit brought together Army Sustainment Enterprise leaders and technical experts to build a shared plan for a rail system that has been strained by decades of heavy use. Aging locomotives, worn-out rail cars and deteriorating track at Army installations have created readiness gaps across the network, according to the Army.
“Rail directly impacts readiness and is an integral part of force projection,” said Mike Dusablon, the Army’s force projection lead. “Rail is readiness force projection. We as the rail experts must connect to it all, the training, the rail crews, safety, to be able to project forces effectively. It’s going to take the entire enterprise to change how the Army operates on a day-to-day basis.”
Rail matters to Army planners because it’s how heavy equipment gets from a base to a port or staging area during a deployment. Discussions at the summit centered on moving away from managing rail base by base and toward a single, coordinated approach tied to the Army’s broader effort to modernize its Organic Industrial Base, the network of 23 government-owned arsenals, depots and ammunition plants the service is currently upgrading under a 15-year, $18 billion investment plan.
“When the command talks about modernizing the Organic Industrial Base, rail falls right into that with infrastructure, locomotives and rail cars,” said Isis Green, lead traffic management specialist with Army Materiel Command’s G-3 Support Operations Division. “Two of the focus areas are rail safety and making sure that we are aligned across the enterprise.”
For commanders, how fast a combat unit can load up and move during a crisis depends directly on whether the rail network at their installation is ready to support them. Leaders at the summit reviewed plans to build real-time visibility into which tracks are usable, what shape the equipment is in, and whether rail crews hold current certifications.
“We are working through the whole maintenance process and documenting it to give it visibility,” said Dan Starkenburg, mobility chief for the Army Sustainment Command’s Transportation Readiness Division. “Ultimately, our goal at ASC is to be able to take a snapshot and look at an installation if we are ready. Do I have locomotives? Do I have the personnel to operate? And is my infrastructure ready to support the warfighter to launch them off the installation? Because we are the initial point where the warfighter launches from.”
Staffing was another focus area, with plans discussed for mobile training teams and retention efforts aimed at keeping rail crews qualified and available.
To speed up repairs and parts procurement, the Army is also leaning on a long-running partnership with the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Volpe Transportation Systems Center, which has supported Army rail operations for more than 37 years.
“The Volpe Center has been supporting Army rail for over 37 years. It’s a partnership that the Department of Transportation has had for over 50 years, we’re all in this together,” said John Wojtowicz, senior advisor for National Security and Critical Infrastructure Programs at Volpe.
That partnership includes indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contracts that let the Army draw from a pool of pre-approved vendors instead of starting a new contract from scratch for each repair job.
“For a contracting officer to do a separate requirement can take 12 to 18 months, which the mission just cannot wait for,” said Patricia Barnette, a contracting officer at the Volpe Center. “Starting an innovative IDIQ contract vehicle with a pool of pre-vetted vendors allows us to issue task orders against an existing contract, which cuts procurement lead time in half.”
“We’re making great traction bringing the stakeholders together and getting a singular way forward through the Army Rail Enterprise to receive guidance from the major commands on what they want us to do, and how we are moving forward with bringing Army rail into the 21st century,” said Brett Goertemoeller, supervisor of locomotive engineers at the U.S. Army Transportation School.

Kanyshai Butun and Burc Eruygur

A Ukrainian lawmaker said Friday that a Russian drone struck two Soviet-era passenger planes at Igor Sikorsky Kyiv International Airport ahead of a possible visit to the Ukrainian capital by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
 Oleksii Honcharenko, a member of Ukraine's parliament, said on Telegram that Witkoff and Kushner were expected to travel to Kyiv on Sunday after visiting Moscow on Saturday.
 “They were to arrive at Boryspil (International Airport) by plane. This was at the stage of an agreement. The Americans were skeptical, but they were close enough to agree,” he said.
 Honcharenko said that just a few minutes prior to his statement, two old Soviet Yak-40 passenger planes were struck at Kyiv International Airport, situated in the capital's Zhuliany neighborhood, adding that the aircraft “had not been flying even before the war.”

"In essence, Putin is sending a signal to the Americans -- I do not want to negotiate and I will not. Otherwise, why this demonstrative strike? It is unclear," he said.

 Separately, citing sources, the Axios news website and Russian state news agency Tass also reported Friday that the two US envoys will visit Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday that he expected US President Donald Trump's envoys in Kyiv “in the coming days.”
The trip would mark the first visit to Kyiv by Witkoff and Kushner, who have made several trips to Moscow as part of US efforts to broker an end to the Russia-Ukraine war.
Their last visit to Moscow took place on Jan. 22, when they met Putin at the Kremlin.
Moscow and Kyiv last held peace negotiations under US mediation earlier this year, when they held three rounds of peace talks in January and February.
Negotiations have since been paused, with Moscow and Kyiv attributing the halt to the US war on Iran, which began in late February.

Rare repair job finished on U.S. nuclear missile system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:26:01 UTC
21:26:01 KST

- The 583rd Missile Maintenance Squadron completed its first full removal, refurbishment and reinstallation of a Minuteman III suspension system on August 18 near Minot Air Force Base.
- The all-civilian squadron employs 196 people across five bases and is the only Department of War unit authorized for depot-level Minuteman III maintenance.
Air Force maintenance crews completed a first-of-its-kind overhaul of a Minuteman III missile suspension system on August 18, removing the component from a launch facility near Minot Air Force Base, North Dakota, shipping it to California for a full refurbishment, and reinstalling it back at the same site.
The work was carried out by the 583rd Missile Maintenance Squadron, a unit better known by its historical name, Rivet MILE, short for Minuteman Integrated Life Extension. The squadron handles depot-level maintenance across the Air Force’s fleet of Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missiles, the land-based leg of the U.S. nuclear triad.
“The suspension system that was removed from one of the launch facilities earlier this year was the first operation site at Minot AFB to be removed, transported to Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, refurbished and returned to be reinstalled,” said Roy Ring, 583rd Missile Maintenance Squadron production superintendent.
Inside a Minuteman III launch facility, the suspension system helps hold and protect the missile within its silo. Routine upkeep on the system is normally handled on-site through preventative maintenance rather than by removing and rebuilding the entire assembly. A complete overhaul, like the one just finished, happens rarely across the Minuteman III fleet.
“The complete overhaul of a suspension system does not happen often across the Minuteman III fleet,” Ring said. “Since the creation of the Depot Maintenance Teams in the mid-1980s, known as Rivet Mile and now the 583rd Missile Maintenance Squadron, mechanics have been routinely inspecting and repairing the suspension systems.”
The squadron is the only one in the Department of War authorized to perform this level of maintenance on Minuteman III facilities, both underground and above ground, according to KyAnn Betz, the squadron’s director.
“We have a full maintenance shop at each missile wing for local manufacturing and repair,” Betz said. “We also assist with field-level maintenance if needed.”
Unlike most Air Force squadrons, the 583rd has no active-duty service members. It is staffed entirely by civilian employees, with more than 250 combined years of Minuteman III experience at each base where it operates. The squadron employs 196 people across five separate units at Minot Air Force Base, Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, F.E. Warren Air Force Base in Wyoming, Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, and Hill Air Force Base in Utah.
The Air Force has operated the Minuteman III since 1971, and roughly 400 of the missiles remain deployed at bases in North Dakota, Montana and Wyoming. The squadron’s approach traces back to a Minuteman maintenance and service-life program the Air Force launched in 1985, which formed the basis for what eventually became the 583rd.
By completing the full removal, refurbishment and reinstallation cycle at an operational site, the squadron demonstrated that major structural components of the missile system can be taken off-site for a complete rebuild rather than repaired in place. The Air Force has not said whether it plans to repeat this approach at other launch facilities or how often future full suspension system overhauls might occur.

U.S. Army’s special forces command holds first drone competition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:21:24 UTC
21:21:24 KST

- 1st Special Forces Group (Airborne) won the first Best Drone Team Competition held by 1st Special Forces Command, beating 14 other teams in Alabama.
- The five-day event, held August 24-28 at Fort McClellan, tested how Special Forces teams integrate small drones into rural and urban tactical scenarios.
Green Berets from 1st Special Forces Group (Airborne) won the U.S. Army’s first-ever Best Drone Team Competition organized specifically for special operations units, beating 14 other teams during a five-day event held August 24-28 at Fort McClellan and the Clarke Range Complex in Anniston, Alabama.
The competition, run by 1st Special Forces Command (Airborne), tested how well Special Forces teams could work small drones into realistic combat scenarios, including rural and urban tactical problem sets. Fifteen teams from units across the command took part, combining Special Forces operators with soldiers focused on robotics and unmanned systems.
The competition follows a broader Army push to formalize drone skills testing across the force. The service held its own inaugural Best Drone Warfighter Competition in Huntsville, Alabama, in February, drawing more than 800 participants from active duty, National Guard and Reserve units. This August event was the first version built specifically for Army special operations formations.
1st SFG(A)’s preparation began well before the competition itself. The unit selected an Operational Detachment Alpha, the basic 12-soldier team structure used by Army Special Forces, and started training at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Washington. During that process, the team identified gaps in its equipment, and staff officers at the group level pushed through last-minute procurements to get soldiers the gear they needed in time.
“We wouldn’t have been successful without the last-minute procurements Group pushed through for us,” the team sergeant said after the competition, according to 1st SFG(A).
Judges evaluated teams on more than just flying ability. Competitors had to read changing conditions, figure out which of their available systems fit the problem in front of them, and fold that into their broader tactical decisions, rather than treating the drone as a separate task from the mission.
Col. Ronald J. Hudak, commander of 1st SFG(A), described the winning team as “good people taking disciplined initiative and getting results” in guidance issued after the event.
“These are some of our best [Soldiers],” said Brig. Gen. Joseph Wortham, commander of 1st Special Forces Command (Airborne). “They stare at the UxS problem day in and day out and they do so in a very tangible, tactical way.”
1st SFG(A) says it now plans to fold what the winning team learned into training across the wider group, rather than keeping that knowledge with the individual soldiers who competed. That includes developing hands-on instructional materials and looking at ways to raise baseline drone proficiency across the formation, not just among specialized operators.
The unit has not said whether 1st Special Forces Command plans to hold the competition again next year or how it intends to measure whether the post-competition training changes have taken hold across the group.

US Unpredictability Is Giving Its Asian Allies New Reasons to Cooperate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:20:00 UTC
21:20:00 KST

When U.S. President Donald Trump abruptly ordered the Pentagon to substantially reduce joint military exercises with South Korea, officials in Seoul were caught off guard. The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield drills still went ahead, but were cut short on Trump’s order. The episode was a reminder that even one of Washington’s closest allies can find the assumptions of its security policy changed with little warning.
That uncertainty is why, across the Indo-Pacific, several of the United States’ closest partners are investing more heavily in relationships with one another – and, increasingly, with Europe. South Korea and Japan are expanding cooperation on supply chains, energy and advanced industries. Japan and Australia are linking economic security more closely to defense production and military operations. All three are also building more structured ties with the European Union.
Of course, these efforts are not an attempt to replace the United States. China’s growing power, North Korea’s weapons programs, Russia’s war in Ukraine, and repeated disruptions to energy and supply chains were already pushing like-minded countries closer together. But Trump’s second term has added another incentive: the need for relationships that remain useful when U.S. policy changes suddenly, including toward its own allies.
South Korea and Japan offer the most politically unlikely example. Their relationship has repeatedly been derailed by disputes over Japan’s colonial rule, wartime labor and historical memory. The rapprochement begun under former South Korean President Yoon Suk-yeol and former Japanese Prime Minister Kishida Fumio therefore looked vulnerable to political turnover.
Instead, it has continued under progressive President Lee Jae-myung and conservative Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae. In his August 15 Liberation Day address, Lee pointed to a year of shuttle diplomacy with Japan and highlighted cooperation in supply chains, energy, and advanced industries. The setting was just as important as the message: a South Korean president was emphasizing the practical value of ties with Tokyo on the day commemorating Korea’s liberation from Japanese colonial rule.
The substance has become harder to dismiss as symbolism. In March, Seoul and Tokyo signed a Supply Chain Partnership Arrangement that created mechanisms for information sharing and consultation during disruptions. Their industry ministries also established a regular policy dialogue covering trade, economic security, supply chains and mineral resources. At the Lee-Takaichi summit in May – their third in seven months – the two governments moved further into energy security, agreeing to explore emergency cooperation involving crude oil and petroleum products while strengthening supply-chain resilience.
SK Hynix is now considering a large memory-chip manufacturing investment in Japan. The project may never materialize, but its consideration is telling given the history of rivalry and trade friction between the two countries’ semiconductor sectors.
Washington once provided much of the external pressure encouraging Seoul and Tokyo to overcome their differences. Under the Biden administration, the Camp David summit in 2023 made improved bilateral ties a central part of a U.S.-led trilateral strategy. Under Trump, the logic is becoming more complicated. The United States remains indispensable to both countries, but uncertainty over U.S. trade and alliance policy is also increasing the value of a relationship that does not depend on Washington to function. The Trump administration today isn’t playing the same mediating role as its predecessor did, and yet Japan-South Korea relations are arguably closer than ever.
Japan and Australia show the same trend in a more mature form. In May, Prime Ministers Takaichi and Anthony Albanese signed a Joint Declaration on Economic Security Cooperation, committing their countries to consult during economic-security contingencies and deepen cooperation on energy, critical minerals, resilient supply chains and critical technologies.
Their defense relationship is advancing even faster. Australia is acquiring Japan’s upgraded Mogami-class frigates, while both governments are working to establish sustainment and shipbuilding capabilities in Australia. In August, they announced successful field trials of their first jointly developed defense-technology project: Boobook, a laser-based surveillance system. They are also developing arrangements for Japan to use Australian test ranges for long-range weapons, including systems linked to Japan’s hypersonic missile program. Japanese F-35s have spent weeks training in Australia, and the two militaries are expanding information sharing and operational coordination.
It would be a mistake to recast every new Australia-Japan initiative as a reaction to Trump; China is the clearest strategic driver of this partnership. Yet Tokyo and Canberra’s ability to work directly with each other is more valuable at a time when neither can assume that U.S. priorities, trade policy, or diplomatic tactics will remain consistent.
The search for additional options extends beyond Asia. South Korea and Japan both established Security and Defense Partnerships with the EU in 2024, and Australia signed its agreement with Brussels in March. Seoul and the EU are expanding cooperation on maritime security, cybersecurity, space, and defense industry policy. Japan and the EU held their second Security and Defense Dialogue in May. Australia’s new partnership with the EU spans maritime security, cyber, emerging technologies, and support for Ukraine, while Canberra and Brussels have also concluded negotiations on a free-trade agreement.
These relationships are modest compared with U.S. alliances. Europe cannot provide South Korea or Japan with extended nuclear deterrence, or replace the operational reach the United States provides Australia. But replacement is not the point. More partnerships mean more channels for coordinating supply chains, technology, energy and security when governments face a shock.
That matters because uncertainty from Washington is no longer confined to defense policy. Trump’s trade agenda has applied pressure to allies as well as competitors. In July, the administration imposed new Section 301 tariffs covering South Korea, Japan, and Australia, as well as the European Union, though applicable rates differ under existing trade arrangements. The measures reinforced a message allies had already absorbed: close security ties with Washington do not guarantee insulation from U.S. economic pressure.
For South Korea, Japan, and Australia, this makes economic resilience and strategic flexibility increasingly difficult to separate. Cooperation on critical minerals can reduce vulnerability to supply disruptions. Energy arrangements can provide alternatives during crises. Deeper technology and defense industrial ties can spread capacity across trusted partners. None of these measures protects them from every shift in U.S. policy, but they reduce the cost of having too few alternatives.
Obviously, there are limits. Seoul, Tokyo, and Canberra do not share identical threat perceptions, and historical disputes can still disrupt Japan-South Korea ties. Their relations with Europe are far less consequential militarily than their alliances with the United States. In many cases, stronger cooperation among these countries reinforces rather than competes with U.S. strategy.
But there is a difference between depending on the United States for security and depending on Washington for every form of cooperation. That distinction is becoming more important in Trump’s second term. Washington’s Asian allies are not preparing for a post-American Indo-Pacific, and there is little evidence that they want one. They are preparing for an Indo-Pacific in which the United States remains indispensable but can no longer be assumed to be predictable. The response is not to leave the United States behind, but to make sure they have more options when Washington changes course.

U.S. Air Force to buy Echodyne radars for Italy rescue squadron
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:17:00 UTC
21:17:00 KST

- The U.S. Air Force is seeking quotes for four Echodyne EchoShield counter-drone radars for the 57th Rescue Squadron at Aviano Air Base, Italy.
- The solicitation states that funding is not yet available and no award will be made until it is, with quotes due September 11.
The U.S. Air Force is seeking to buy four Echodyne EchoShield counter-drone radars for a rescue squadron based at Aviano Air Base, Italy, according to a solicitation the service’s 31st Contracting Squadron published September 4.
The notice is a request for quotes, not a completed purchase. The Air Force explicitly states in the solicitation that funding for the buy is not yet in place: “Funds are not presently available for this effort. No award will be made under this solicitation until funds are available.” The service also reserves the right to cancel the solicitation at any point without reimbursing companies for their costs.
The requirement comes from the 57th Rescue Squadron, a combat search-and-rescue unit based at Aviano that flies HH-60W Jolly Green II helicopters. The Air Force is asking for four EchoShield radar units, one Rapid Deployment Kit that lets operators link up to four radars into a single system, and three years of software updates and technical support for each radar. Companies have until September 11 to submit quotes, and the Air Force plans to award a single fixed-price purchase order without further negotiation.
EchoShield is built by Echodyne, a Kirkland, Washington-based company that makes counter-drone radar using a technology it calls MESA, short for Metamaterials Electronically Steerable Array. The design steers the radar beam electronically rather than relying on a mechanically rotating dish, letting Echodyne pack radar performance once limited to larger, more expensive military systems into a compact unit.
According to the Air Force’s technical requirements, each EchoShield radar must detect small Group 1 drones, such as a DJI Phantom, at 2.7 to 3 kilometers (1.7 to 1.9 miles), and larger Group 2 drones, such as a DJI Matrice 600, at 4.8 to 6 kilometers (3 to 3.7 miles). The radar must also track a dismounted person at 8 kilometers (5 miles) and a vehicle at 11 kilometers (6.8 miles), while tracking more than 40 high-priority targets and over 1,000 lower-priority targets simultaneously. Each radar panel weighs no more than 17.8 kilograms (39.2 pounds) and draws under 250 watts of power at full operation.
The Rapid Deployment Kit the Air Force is requesting is designed to let a single operator assemble up to four radars into one system, without tools, in under an hour. The full kit, including its tripod and cabling, must pack down into no more than three transport cases.
Echodyne’s radar has already been fielded across multiple U.S. and allied programs. The company told The Defence Blog in July that its EchoShield radar serves as the primary sensor on Trust Automation’s SUADS counter-drone platform under a $490 million Air Force contract, and that the U.S. State Department separately awarded Echodyne $14.9 million to supply radars for use in Ukraine. Echodyne-equipped weapon stations have also been tested by soldiers at Fort Hood, where the company says they engaged drone targets in under three seconds. To meet rising demand, Echodyne is building a new $40 million, 86,350-square-foot (8,022-square-meter) manufacturing facility near its Kirkland headquarters, which it says will be capable of producing more than 30,000 radars a year.
The Air Force has not disclosed the total value of the anticipated purchase order or said when funding might become available to allow an award.

EU gas storage facilities are around 65% full, with no further action needed for the time being, a European Commission spokesperson said Friday.
Anna-Kaisa Itkonen told reporters that the bloc's Gas Coordination Group assessed the situation Thursday and determined that existing measures were sufficient to ensure gas supplies for the coming winter.
“For the time being, there is no need for further action,” Itkonen said.
She said EU member states had been informed that reaching an 80% storage level would be sufficient to meet gas needs for the coming winter, despite legislation setting a general target of 90%.
The bloc's storage legislation also provides additional flexibility, allowing the European Commission to reduce the target by 5 percentage points through a delegated act, she added.
Itkonen said the commission continues to monitor storage levels and remains in contact with member states over their progress in filling facilities.
The Gas Coordination Group is due to meet again in September, when the Commission will reassess the situation based on developments in member states.
EU gas storage levels currently stand at around 65% of total capacity.
Europe's gas storage levels remain below seasonal norms, raising concerns that a prolonged disruption to Middle Eastern supplies could leave the region exposed to sharper price volatility during the winter.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Aspeed Technology Inc. reported its 10th consecutive monthly revenue record in August, supported by higher shipments of its baseboard management controllers (BMCs), a key component in server systems.
The company posted consolidated revenue of NT$1.6 billion (US$51.3 million) in August, up 118.42% from the same month a year earlier. Revenue for the first eight months totaled NT$10.2 billion, an annual increase of 74.49%, CTEE reported Friday.
Aspeed expects its revenue performance in the second half of the year to be significantly better than in the first half. First-half growth fell short of expectations due to component shortages.
Supply constraints have since improved, with additional testing and packaging suppliers beginning production and allowing the company to gradually increase BMC shipments. These chips allow servers to be monitored and managed remotely.
A BMC operates independently of a server's CPU and operating system, allowing administrators to remotely power servers on or off, monitor temperatures, and update firmware. The growth of cloud computing and large-scale data centers has made BMCs standard components in modern servers, according to Sinotrade.
Aspeed has maintained a 70-80% share of the global server BMC market. Roughly eight out of 10 servers operated by major cloud service providers such as Amazon, Microsoft, and Google are equipped with the company's chips.
With shipments expected to return to normal, Aspeed expects its revenue to continue growing quarter by quarter in the second half. The company currently has order visibility extending into 2028.

Extreme drought now covers 44% of Puerto Rico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:12:53 UTC
21:12:53 KST

Extreme drought now covers 44% of Puerto Rico
- Date:
- September 4, 2026
- Source:
- NASA Earth Observatory
- Summary:
- Puerto Rico’s normally rainy season has instead brought a severe and fast-growing drought. By August 25, three-quarters of the territory was in at least moderate drought, with extreme drought covering 44 percent and some areas receiving less than 20 percent of their usual rainfall. Water shortages have forced rationing, while farmers are losing crops and ranchers are running low on hay. The situation has become serious enough to trigger both local and federal disaster declarations.
- Share:
Puerto Rico typically enters its wet season in May, but 2026 has unfolded very differently. By late August, rainfall had remained scarce across much of the U.S. territory, allowing drought conditions to spread rapidly. The lack of rain has contributed to water shortages and rationing in some communities, prompting Puerto Rico's governor to declare a state of emergency in late July. In late August, the U.S. government also issued a drought disaster declaration covering more than two dozen cities and towns.
The map shows the severity and geographic extent of drought across Puerto Rico on August 25, 2026. It was created by the U.S. Drought Monitor, a collaboration involving the National Drought Mitigation Center at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and NASA.
NASA has supported the project for years with Earth observations and scientific expertise. That involvement expanded in 2026 when two NASA scientists joined the small group responsible for producing the weekly drought assessments.
David Mocko, a senior research scientist in the Hydrological Sciences Laboratory at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, said the effects of the unusually hot and dry conditions were visible across multiple types of satellite and ground-based data used by the U.S. Drought Monitor.
For recent Puerto Rico updates, particularly important information included satellite estimates of soil moisture, along with weather measurements and observations of streamflow and well conditions, Mocko said.
Mocko prepared the U.S. Drought Monitor update for August 18, 2026. He and Jonathan Case of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center are the first NASA scientists to produce the weekly maps.
Extreme Drought Covers 44 Percent of the Territory
By August 25, 2026, about three-quarters of Puerto Rico was experiencing at least moderate drought, according to the assessment. Extreme drought zones (dark orange) in eastern and southwestern parts of the main island had expanded during the previous week and covered 44 percent of the territory.
The change happened quickly. Just three months earlier, none of Puerto Rico was classified as being in drought, and less than 20 percent of the territory was considered abnormally dry.
Late winter and early spring had actually been wetter than normal across the U.S. Caribbean, according to a National Integrated Drought Information System (NIDIS) report. Conditions then shifted sharply toward dryness.
Rainfall Falls Far Below Normal
From mid-May through mid-July, most of Puerto Rico received less than 60 percent of its normal precipitation, according to NIDIS. Southern and southwestern areas were even drier, receiving less than 20 percent of normal rainfall. That translated to a rainfall deficit of 3 to 6 inches (76 to 152 millimeters).
High temperatures made the drying worse. San Juan, for example, experienced one of its warmest Julys on record. River levels also fell sharply, with streamflow reaching record lows in waterways including the Rio Fajardo in northeastern Puerto Rico.
Water Shortages Hit Residents and Farmers
The strain on water supplies has affected residents, farmers, and ranchers across Puerto Rico. Water rationing has been in effect in several municipalities since early August, according to news reports. Observers have also pointed to infrastructure issues as a factor worsening the shortages.
The drought has also created serious challenges for agriculture. For farmers, dry soils have disrupted the growth of fruit and cacao trees as well as banana and coffee plants, contributing to crop losses. Ranchers, meanwhile, are seeing their hay supplies dwindle.
Drought Maps Help Guide Emergency Response
U.S. Drought Monitor maps have been published since 1999 and are used by federal, state, local, and tribal officials to help guide drought response decisions.
The USDA, for example, relies on the maps as part of a "fast track" process for issuing disaster designations. Those designations can help direct emergency assistance and other resources to affected communities.

Materials provided by NASA Earth Observatory. Original written by Lindsey Doermann. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

The nearest available date for hosting the FIFA World Cup is sometime in the 2040s, so we need to plan for this prospect right now

Supplement
In 2012, Ukraine and Poland jointly hosted the European Championship. The right to host Euro 2012 was awarded to the two countries in April 2007.
In preparing to host the 2012 European Football Championship, the host countries spent considerably more money than the hosts of previous tournaments because the infrastructure of the host cities and the countries as a whole was poorer compared with that of their Western European predecessors (stadiums, hotels, roads).
As of the end of 2011, Ukraine had spent approximately 115–140 billion hryvnias preparing for the European Championship. Poland, according to some estimates, would spend up to 80 billion zlotys (approximately 20 billion euros) on hosting the tournament.
Also, after Ukraine was approved as a host country for the final matches, it emerged that the new stadiums hastily built for the event had design flaws and did not meet modern requirements. It turned out that budget funds were allocated to construction companies for building them in exchange for substantial kickbacks to officials involved in distributing the financial resources.
Because of delays in the construction of the stadiums (especially the NSC "Olympiyskiy" in Kyiv and the stadium in Lviv), as well as infrastructure (airports, roads), UEFA threatened several times to take away the right to host the tournament or reduce the number of host cities.
The cost of reconstructing the NSC "Olympiyskiy" and building the stadium in Lviv increased several times compared with the initial plans, triggering a wave of criticism in Ukraine over the embezzlement of budget funds.
It should be recalled
Since the beginning of the war, Russian occupiers have damaged or destroyed 88 stadiums in Ukraine, 14 of which were completely destroyed. Direct losses inflicted on sports infrastructure are estimated at $4 billion.
Since the beginning of the Russian Federation’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, 930 sports infrastructure facilities have been damaged or completely destroyed. The largest number are in the Kherson, Kharkiv and Luhansk regions.

U.S. Navy demonstrates at-sea refueling for unmanned surface vessel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:09:53 UTC
21:09:53 KST

- The Navy demonstrated an at-sea refueling system off Virginia that transferred 400 gallons of fuel to an unmanned surface vessel across roughly 100 connection cycles.
- The system moved from concept to on-water testing in seven months, and the Navy's next goal is a fully autonomous refueling sequence.
The U.S. Navy demonstrated a system last month that can refuel an unmanned surface vessel at sea without any crew on board, a step toward keeping robotic boats on station indefinitely instead of returning to port when they run low on fuel.
The Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division ran the demonstration off the coast of Virginia using a towed connector that repeatedly captured, refueled and released a Navy-owned USV called the T38. A Navy-industry team went from concept to on-water testing in seven months, according to the warfare center.
The T38, also known as the Devil Ray, is built by Maritime Tactical Systems Inc. and measures 38 feet (11.1 meters) long, with a payload capacity of up to 4,000 pounds (1,814 kilograms) and burst speeds exceeding 70 knots depending on its engine configuration. The Navy operates this particular T38 through its Blue Water Instrumentation program, based at the Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division’s Point Mugu Sea Range in California. In May, the same vessel completed a record 192-hour autonomous mission 400 nautical miles (740 kilometers) off the California coast without any chase boats or escorts.
“At Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division, our immediate focus is supporting hypersonic and precision long-range fires testing, where flight profiles can extend thousands of miles beyond fixed-range boundaries and require data-collection assets to be distributed across a vast area,” said Spencer Holloway, director of the Blue Water Instrumentation program’s future capabilities office. “But the underlying challenge applies more broadly. Every time an unmanned vessel must return to port for fuel, we lose persistence, reduce coverage and redundancy, and interrupt the mission.”
During the Virginia demonstration, the training support vessel USNS Vindicator towed the refueling system and transferred a total of 400 gallons (1,514 liters) of fuel to the T38 across dozens of full-cycle exercises at sea, in addition to pier-side testing. The refueling system completed roughly 100 connection cycles over the course of a few days leading up to and including the event, which took place in the waters off Joint Expeditionary Base Little Creek-Fort Story, Virginia.
Ronald Raymer, branch head for capability, innovation, science and technology integration at U.S. Fleet Forces Command, said the capability could change how the Navy uses unmanned vessels operationally, not just for testing.
“This will allow us to have greater reliance on unmanned vessels … and we can push the USV into higher threat areas without risking manned vessels and personnel,” Raymer said. “It will also allow us to distribute greater capability into an area without having to invest in large, expensive manned vessels, and the refueling supports that.”
U.S. Fleet Forces Command, Naval Surface Warfare Center Dahlgren Division and Naval Surface Warfare Center Carderock Division sponsored the demonstration. The Littoral Combat Ship Mission Modules Program Office and the Navy’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Robotics and Autonomous Systems provided contracting support that allowed the Blue Water Instrumentation team to work directly with industry partners on the project.
“Working directly with our industry partners allowed us to bring the platform, control systems, operators and engineers together as one integrated team,” Holloway said. “We could make changes, test them on the water and iterate quickly based on what we observed.”
The program’s next milestone is a fully autonomous, end-to-end refueling demonstration that will combine vessel rendezvous, approach, capture, fuel transfer, disconnection and return to mission into a single automated sequence, according to the warfare center.

China Focus: From sightseeing to sweating: "sportcation" gains momentum among young Chinese
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
20:09:22 CST
21:09:22 KST

YINCHUAN, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- As dusk settled over the wild Helan Mountains, Ye Shuai eased off the gas and wound his way down from the off-road Hooke Trail, calling it a day.
Tearing across rugged mountain terrain in his off-road vehicle, Ye spent the day as he had throughout his weeklong summer vacation, braving the blazing sun in the rolling mountains in northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, some 1,000 km away from his home in central China.
Ye is among a growing number of young vacationers fueling the popularity of a fresh kind of travel experience that blends sports and fitness with leisure and social interaction -- summed up as "sportcation."
SWEATING OUT SUMMER VACATION
Ye had been planning his mountain adventure for some time. He teamed up with fellow enthusiasts from across the country, shipping their vehicles to the Hooke Park, long before their flights. "It's crazy, but well worth it," he said.
Their venture started each day at 8 a.m. with a drive into the mountains. Challenging rough trails, they repeatedly stopped for repair breaks. By nightfall, they descended from the mountains, exhausted, then headed back to their lodgings beneath a starry sky.
Tucked away in the Helan Mountains, the park boasts 88 off-road trails of varying difficulty, catering to outdoor adventurers seeking thrills behind the wheel, on a motorcycle, bicycle, or even on foot.
Some enthusiasts put the park on a par with renowned off-road destinations such as the Rubicon Trail and Moab in the United States.
The young people are looking for vacation experiences that bring them joy and a sense of fulfillment, instead of merely sightseeing or photo-taking, said Gao Jinsong, founder of Hooke Park.
"Off-road driving is an extreme challenge," Ye said. "It helps me blow off steam from work and just be myself. It's tiring, but it feels great!"
In recent years, marathon tours across the country have also become a popular form of micro-getaway. For Shi Nali, a young woman from Beijing, combining running with travel has opened up a new way to explore a city.
"In the past, vacations were basically about beautiful scenery and good food. Sometimes I found them boring," said Shi.
An avid traveler, Shi became addicted to urban running in 2023, and has since traveled to multiple cities across China just to hit the road -- along the historic city wall in the ancient capital of Xi'an, along the seaside trails of Xiamen, and through the winding alleyways of Chengdu.
"Compared with the cookie-cutter attractions you find everywhere, the scenery and local interactions you encounter along the way feel much more genuine," Shi said.
The growing popularity of sports-themed vacations also boosted consumption. Shi's sports gear stock, from hats, sunglasses and sportswear to knee braces, running shoes and trekking poles, costs her more than 10,000 yuan (about 1,475.2 U.S. dollars).
But she considers the money well spent. "What matters most is the joy and satisfaction it brings me."
TAPPING TOURISM OPPORTUNITIES
The growing popularity of sports-oriented vacations reflects a broader shift in how young people spend their leisure time, driven by greater health awareness, a growing appetite for immersive experiences, and more diverse forms of social interaction, according to industry insiders.
In May, online travel platform LY.com released its 2026 travel trends report on "sportcation," showing a sharp rise in searches and bookings.
Yang Wei, a professional travel planner, said that "sportcation" will go beyond a short-lived fad and become a long-term shift in urban lifestyles.
The rise of "sportcation" also comes as China moves to diversify its tourism offerings and cultivate new growth drivers for the industry.
The latest five-year tourism development plan, approved by the State Council and released in July, calls for nurturing new drivers of tourism growth and enriching the supply of high-quality tourism experiences.
Across China, localities have been quick to tap into the trend and put various "sportcation" opportunities on offer.
Wanning, a surfers' haven in China's southernmost Hainan Province, has emerged as the poster child of the growing trend, with "Traveling to Wanning for sports school" becoming a viral catchphrase on social media.
With its long, surf-friendly coastline, Wanning has become a haven for young people burned out by the grind of big-city office life. They come here not to slow down, but to embrace a different kind of packed schedule -- one filled with sports and workouts.
Some start their day with a run or a gym session, then spend the rest of the day surfing, paddleboarding or rock climbing, joking that they are attending a sports school with a strict daily schedule.
The inland city of Zhongwei, Ningxia, also tapped into its unique landscape of deserts and the Yellow River to attract "sportcationers" eager to combine outdoor workout and sightseeing.
"From dusk into the deep of night, you run on soft sand, with the meandering Yellow River by your side and a brilliant galaxy overhead," an internet user by the name "Xiaoweishi'er" from Gansu Province described her experience after taking part in the 2026 Ningxia-Zhongwei Desert Starry Sky Half Marathon in June. "There's no need to chase speed. Just embrace the wilderness," she added. ■

COLOMBO, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lankan authorities on Friday advised farmers to bring forward planting for the 2026/27 Maha paddy cultivation season to withstand heavy rains and prepare for an El Nino-driven dry spell early next year.
The advisory came as meteorological forecasts indicate above-average rainfall across the island in October and November due to prevailing El Nino conditions and a positive Indian Ocean Dipole.
The Department of Agriculture urged farmers to begin land preparation as soon as possible and complete sowing between Oct. 15 and Oct. 25, while noting that earlier sowing would ensure crops are about a month old when heavier rains are expected in November, reducing the risk of damage from flooding.
Sri Lanka is targeting about 830,000 hectares of paddy cultivation during the upcoming Maha season. The revised schedule follows forecasts for above-average rainfall in October and November.
In the meantime, water conservation is also advised as meteorological authorities forecast temperatures to rise and rainfall to decline during January, February and March 2027. Authorities said that stricter water discipline is vital to guarantee a successful Yala cultivation season in 2027.
In paddy areas facing water shortages, farmers are encouraged to cultivate other field crops, including maize, green gram, cowpea and finger millet. Those shifting to such crops on paddy land will remain eligible for fertilizer subsidies.
Sri Lankan agricultural cultivation is traditionally carried out on two monsoon cycles. The Yala cultivation season, spanning from May to September, is driven by the southwest monsoon, while the Maha cultivation season from October to January next year is driven by the northeast monsoon. ■

Kyiv region

Chernihiv region

====================================================================================================

Neuroticism intensifies the transfer of fear and negativity during associative learning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:00:38 UTC
21:00:38 KST

People who score high in neuroticism not only experience more intense emotional reactions to aversive images, but they also tend to transfer those negative feelings more strongly onto unrelated, neutral objects. This heightened capacity for emotional learning provides evidence for how specific personality traits contribute to generalized anxiety and emotional vulnerability in daily life. The findings were recently published in the Journal of Personality.
Our brains constantly scan the environment, learning which objects or situations are safe and which are dangerous. One of the primary ways we learn these associations is through a process called evaluative conditioning. This occurs when a completely neutral item, such as a random geometric shape, is repeatedly presented alongside an emotionally charged item, such as a disturbing photograph.
Over time, the neutral shape takes on the emotional flavor of the photograph. Associative learning of this kind is a fundamental building block of human emotion, as a study covered by PsyPost in 2021 indicates that repeatedly pairing specific personal attributes with negative social feedback leads individuals to develop heightened anxiety toward those attributes.
While the basic mechanism of evaluative conditioning is universal, individuals do not all experience it with the same intensity. A 2026 study suggests that personal psychological dispositions influence how strongly we form positive or negative feelings toward neutral objects through associative conditioning. One of the most prominent traits related to emotional reactivity is neuroticism.
People with high levels of neuroticism tend to experience negative emotions more frequently and intensely. A study covered by PsyPost in 2026 provides evidence that this trait is tied to heightened connectivity between the brain regions responsible for emotional processing during affective tasks.
Another psychological factor related to emotional vulnerability is the looming cognitive style. This refers to a mental bias where an individual perceives potential threats not as static, but as rapidly approaching or escalating in space and time. A person with a high looming cognitive style might view a minor, distant problem as an incoming disaster that is quickly gaining momentum, which frequently leads to heightened anxiety.
The research was led by Darian Faur, an assistant professor at the West University of Timisoara in Romania. His team aimed to understand how neuroticism and the looming cognitive style interact to shape emotional learning.
“Tracking individual differences in conditioning was a preoccupation for behavioral scientists in the ’80s (see Levey & Martin, 1981), but slowly faded away due to developments in both fields that eventually established them as separate research traditions,” Faur told PsyPost. “The lab I am currently involved in (Social Cognition and Personality Assessment from the West University of Timisoara) revived this interest.”
“I was coming from a clinical background with a desire to study transdiagnostic models, and I found in this interdisciplinary approach an excellent experimental gateway to match my own research interests,” he explained.
Traditionally, studies on evaluative conditioning only measure whether a stimulus is perceived as generally positive or negative. The authors wanted to introduce a more specific measurement by asking participants to evaluate exactly how threatening an image felt, and then testing how that specific sense of threat transferred to a neutral object.
To investigate this, the researchers conducted an online experiment with 806 adult participants, primarily from the United Kingdom. The participants first completed standardized questionnaires to measure their levels of neuroticism and their looming cognitive style. The participants then viewed a series of twenty computer-generated grayscale fractals, which are complex, abstract geometric patterns. They rated how pleasant or unpleasant they found each fractal. The computer system then selected the six fractals that each participant rated as the most perfectly neutral, ensuring the conditioning process started from a blank slate.
During the conditioning phase, the participants viewed these neutral fractals paired with different photographs. The photographs had been pre-tested in a pilot study to fall into three distinct categories: positive images, negative but non-threatening images, and negative images that were highly threatening. Each neutral fractal was presented on the screen alongside one of the photographs. To mimic the psychological experience of a looming threat, the photographs were not static. Instead, they slowly expanded on the screen over a period of four seconds, growing by at least half their original size to simulate the feeling that the image was approaching the viewer.
After viewing all the pairings multiple times, the participants were asked to rate the original photographs based on how positive, negative, and threatening they were. Finally, they were asked to rate the initially neutral fractals again to see if their feelings toward the shapes had changed.
The scientists found that the evaluative conditioning procedure worked as expected. Fractals that had been paired with negative or threatening photographs were rated much more negatively than fractals paired with positive photographs. This shift in attitude was driven by how the participants individually appraised the original photographs. When a participant rated a photograph as highly negative or highly threatening, that intense rating directly predicted how negatively they would evaluate the paired fractal.
Personality traits played a major role in shaping these reactions. Participants with high levels of neuroticism evaluated the negative and threatening photographs much more harshly than participants with low neuroticism. Beyond just seeing the original images as worse, highly neurotic individuals also demonstrated a stronger learning effect. They transferred more of that negative emotion onto the neutral fractals.
“The findings from this study suggest that general emotional vulnerability (the trait everyone shares to a certain extent in the general population that makes us respond with anxiety or depression to certain life events) impacts not only how we perceive stimuli with a valence of their own, but also how that valence is further transferred to a neutral stimulus that happens to be in the same environment as the pleasant/unpleasant stimulus,” Faur said.
“In other words, if you are a highly emotionally-reactive person, you will most likely learn to dislike neutral stimuli that were associated with negative stimuli more than a person with lower reactivity,” he noted.
The researchers observed that this effect seemed to be driven mostly by the self-consciousness and vulnerability components of neuroticism, suggesting that an inward-focused cognitive awareness might heighten the associative learning process. “Moreover, for highly neurotic individuals, the study indicates that learning might not only be explained by the conscious evaluation of the valenced stimuli (i.e., I dislike this gray box because it was paired with a bunch of insects that I found unpleasant), but also by the general exposure to negative stimuli,” Faur added.
The results regarding the looming cognitive style were more complex. Generally, participants with a higher looming cognitive style tended to rate all the fractals more negatively overall. However, when the researchers isolated the specific transfer of threat from the photograph to the fractal, the looming cognitive style appeared to have a mild buffering effect. People with this trait transferred slightly less of the threat to the neutral object than expected.
“I did not anticipate the interesting interaction between the looming cognitive style and the evaluative conditioning process,” Faur said. “While this cognitive vulnerability was associated with contingency awareness (and contingency awareness was further associated with larger evaluative conditioning effects), it buffered the valence transfer from unconditioned stimuli to neutral stimuli instead of amplifying it.”
The researchers speculate that because the looming cognitive style causes people to focus so intensely on an approaching threat, they might fixate entirely on the threatening photograph and pay less attention to the neutral fractal beside it, weakening the associative link. But Faur added a note of caution regarding this finding: “It is important to note, however, that these results were uncertain and should be interpreted cautiously, as they require replication.”
Interestingly, this buffering effect disappeared when a person possessed both high neuroticism and a high looming cognitive style. When these two traits were elevated together, the individual’s heightened emotional reactivity overrode any attentional buffering, resulting in a massively amplified transfer of negative emotion to the neutral object.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study utilized a highly controlled digital environment with an artificial zooming effect to simulate looming threats. While this allowed for precise measurements, human emotional learning in real-world scenarios is often messier and more complex.
Another important consideration is the magnitude of these influences. “As per our experience with personality and conditioning models, the moderation effects, although replicable, are very small,” Faur pointed out. “Therefore, personality can be seen as impacting distally and broadly the learning process.”
However, the context of the sample matters. “Another study of ours (which is currently under review) returns much larger effects of the association between neuroticism and evaluative conditioning in the clinical population (anxiety disorders or related), so we further need to identify which mechanisms drive or which conditions amplify the effects of personality on learning,” Faur said.
Additionally, the researchers only measured how threatening the participants found the original photographs, not how threatening they found the neutral fractals after the conditioning was complete. Because of this, the study can only confirm that general negative feelings were transferred to the fractals, rather than a specific sense of physical threat.
Future studies could build on this work by testing these personality interactions in more ecological settings or by asking participants to rate the threat level of the conditioned objects. Exploring how different relational cues alter the way threats are learned could offer deeper insights into how anxiety disorders develop and how they might be treated.
“My intention is to use conditioning paradigms (and other learning frameworks) as experimental proxies for studying how personality and cognition interact to produce psychopathology,” Faur concluded.
The study, “Beyond the Moderating Role of Neuroticism on Evaluative Conditioning: Threat Appraisal,” was authored by Darian Faur and Florin Alin Sava.

UK’s Supacat starts production on Czech special forces vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:00:15 UTC
21:00:15 KST

- Supacat began production on 18 HMT Extenda vehicles for the Czech Republic's 601st Special Forces Group, with deliveries starting in 2027.
- The contract, signed in October 2025, is valued at roughly 2.16 billion Czech koruna ($98.4 million) including vehicle chassis, weapons integration and support.
British vehicle maker Supacat has started production on 18 HMT Extenda military vehicles for the Czech Republic’s special operations forces, with deliveries scheduled to begin in 2027.
The vehicles will go to the Czech Army’s 601st Special Forces Group, the country’s premier special operations unit, replacing an aging fleet of Land Rover Defender 110 vehicles that have exceeded their 15-year design life. Supacat and its Czech partner, LPP, signed the contract in October 2025. Pre-production work began in June, and full production is now underway at Supacat’s newly opened manufacturing facility in Dunkeswell, Devon.
The deal splits the work between the UK and the Czech Republic. LPP is supplying the bare Extenda 6×6 chassis for £32.6 million ($42.6 million), while the Czech Military Technical Institute will install weapons, communications and other mission systems separately, at a cost of 810 million Czech koruna ($36.9 million). Including spare parts, training and other subsystems, the full package is valued at roughly 2.16 billion koruna ($98.4 million) with tax included, according to earlier reporting on the contract.
The HMT Extenda, known to the British Army as the Jackal 3, can be reconfigured between a 4×4 and 6×6 layout using basic workshop tools, letting operators adjust the vehicle’s size and payload capacity for different missions. It can reach speeds of up to 120 km/h (75 mph). The platform traces back to the original HMT, which the UK Ministry of Defence rushed into service in Afghanistan as an urgent operational requirement, and it has since been adopted by special forces in at least eight other countries, including Norway, New Zealand, Ukraine and the United States.
“A joint team, consisting of the LPP project team and specialists from the Czech Special Forces, visited the new production facility earlier this year,” said Miroslav Žižka, Managing Director at LPP. “This was the team’s first visit since production of the HMT Extenda began, and the main purpose of the visit was to familiarise the members of the joint team with the current status of combat vehicle production.”
“LPP and Supacat have been collaborating on this project for several years now, and communication between us is close. I would like to thank Director Phil Applegarth and his team for their dedication to the Czech project, and for meeting the vehicle delivery deadlines,” Žižka said.
“The start of the Czech production marked an important milestone for the delivery of this programme. We continue to remain on track to deliver the programme as scheduled, reflecting the maturity of the HMT Extenda platform and the dedication of the teams involved. We also look forward to other export vehicle programmes being produced in the near future,” said Phil Applegarth, Director at Supacat.

2026-09-04

21:00:00 KST

A Mars probe from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) may answer some longstanding questions about the Red Planet and its moons. The mission—dubbed MMX for “Martian Moons eXploration”—aims to collect at least 10 grams of samples from Phobos, one of two moons orbiting the planet, and if successful, these will be the first rocks from a Martian moon ever brought to Earth.
They won’t arrive quickly, however. The MMX probe will take approximately one year to reach Mars. It will then collect samples during three years of operations while orbiting the red planet before taking another year to return to Earth. If all goes well, scientists expect to receive the moon rocks in 2031.
One of the most interesting questions the probe can answer is how Mars’ moons, Phobos and Deimos, formed. There are two main possibilities. One is that the moons condensed from material ejected during a massive collision with Mars. The other hypothesis is that the moons were asteroids from the outer solar system that were captured by Mars’ gravity.
The moons are dark in color, and their light-reflecting properties closely resemble those of asteroids rich in water and carbon. Their orbits, however—which are nearly circular along Mars’ equatorial plane in the same direction as the planet’s rotation—are better explained by the giant impact hypothesis. Comparing samples from Mars’ moons to those previously collected from the Martian surface could help settle this debate.
To get the Martian moon rocks and transport them back to Earth, however, means overcoming some significant technical challenges in space flight and communication. At launch, the spacecraft will have a mass of 4,480 kilograms (9,900 pounds). More than half of this weight will be fuel, divided into three reserves: one for the outbound leg, one for exploration, and one for the return leg. Once in the vicinity of Mars, MMX will jettison the outbound module after its propellant is exhausted; following the flyby of Deimos, the exploration module will also be jettisoned.
The probe, designed by Mitsubishi Electric, will then land on the surface of Phobos, a delicate procedure given the moon’s size, with an approximate radius of just 11 kilometers. (In comparison, Earth’s moon has a radius of more than 1,700 kilometers.) Descent methods used on Earth’s moon rely on its specific gravity, which is about 300 times as strong as that of Phobos. However, Phobos’ gravity is approximately 50 times greater than that of the asteroid Ryugu, where JAXA has previously landed probes. Landing on Ryugu involved prolonged hovering, a typical method for landing on smaller celestial objects, but this is not feasible for MMX as it would consume too much fuel given Phobos’ greater pull.
To overcome this challenge, the probe is equipped with high-precision autonomous navigation, which it will need, given that there will be a delay of up to 20 minutes for radio signals to travel between Earth and MMX. The probe must therefore autonomously decide on and execute the descent, landing, and later takeoff sequences.
During the descent, the probe will compare the terrain to data on the topography of Phobos’ craters, using this information to adjust its position toward the target landing site. Once it’s reached an altitude under 300 meters, the probe will also detect whether parts of the surface have changed in elevation, labeling significant discrepancies as hazardous areas. This mechanism allows the probe, if necessary, to change the landing site or abort the landing and temporarily ascend.
Just ahead of the main spacecraft’s landing, the IDEFIX rover—jointly developed by the French and German space agencies—will be deployed onto the surface of Phobos to conduct approximately 100 days of independent exploration. This preliminary survey by the rover will serve as a scout to ensure a safer landing.
Once on the surface, a robotic arm will drill cylindrical tubes into the surface to collect samples. The probe is also equipped with a device first developed by NASA that uses a stream of nitrogen gas to collect fine particles from the very top layer of dust. Whether or not Phobos originated from an impact with the planet, experts believe Martian sand can be obtained from the lunar surface. Over time, meteorite impacts have blasted materials off Mars, coating its moons. Scientists expect about 0.1 percent of the samples collected will be debris from Mars itself.
Costing about $345 million US, this mission marks Japan’s first Mars probe launch in 28 years. Beyond the scientific insights it’s expected to provide, from an engineering perspective, the mission aims to test new technologies that could aid future sampling and round-trip travel to Mars.
MMX is scheduled to launch from the Tanegashima Space Center on October 20, 2026.
This story originally appeared on WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.
