APA Member Interview: Briana Toole
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

The APA Blog is publishing excerpts from Cliff Sosis’s long-form interviews with philosophers, which appear at his blog, What Is It Like to Be a Philosopher? The excerpts below are from an interview originally published on August 20, 2026 and are reprinted with permission from Cliff Sosis.
In this interview, Briana Toole, Associate Professor in the Department of Philosophy at Claremont McKenna College, talks about growing up in Chattahoochee, Florida, Left Behind, Crash Bandicoot, geometry, Greenpeace, beauty pageants, money anxiety, Myspace, 9/11, Florida State University and the Bright Futures scholarship, a difficult to comprehend accent, working evenings at TCBY, working with David McNaughton, a brutal but helpful epistemology TA, switching from law to philosophy, committing to grad school and going to University of Sheffield, her first snowfall, Jenny Saul, Teach for America and meeting her husband, pursuing a PhD at UT, sexism and the “golden boys,” grounding, complaining to her understanding dissertation advisor, standpoint epistemology, depression, a fellowship at MIT, Sally Haslanger, Corrupt the Youth, landing a position at Claremont McKenna College just before COVID hit, bouncing between positions before she landed in a green place, her Feminism for Men class, #metoo, Thi Ngyugen, The Poisonwood Bible, Zillow Gone Wild, and cornpone…
What was your earliest memory?
My earliest memory is of a dog we had when I was a baby, around 2 or so. A shih tzu named Biscuit, because she was the buttery color of a biscuit. Biscuit loved me, and I remember that whenever my parents would try to discipline me (at that age, a pop on the hand or behind), she’d growl at them and wouldn’t let them touch me. My earliest protector!
Where did you grow up?
My parents were in the military, and so I was born on a military base in Killeen, Texas. When I was 3, we moved to Chattahoochee, Florida, across the river from my dad’s hometown of Sneads. The twin cities, as we called them, were about an hour from the Alabama and Georgia borders (Dothan, AL on one side, Bainbridge, GA on the other). This is relevant exposition because when people meet me, they always want some explanation of my accent.
The twin cities are home to a state prison (Sneads) and state hospital (in Chattahoochee, rumored to have underground tunnels dating back to the Civil War), which is where most people would end up one way or another (either as an employee or as a resident).
All my dad’s family had stayed in the area, so I grew up surrounded by aunts and uncles and cousins. And, because I went to school where my dad did, we had many of the same teachers, and the same high school principal. There were a lot of families like that in Sneads.
The town where I lived was so small that when we didn’t have stamps, we’d just put change in a little cup with the letters we wanted mailed out. Going to the grocery store was an hours-long event, because you’d run into people you knew. I knew a kid in high school who rode his lawnmower to school.
All to say: I grew up in the country. The deep, deep south.
As a little kid, what do you think, or what did others think, made you unique? What did you want to be when you grew up?
As a kid, I always thought I’d be a lawyer. My dad used to say that I could argue with a brick wall. I don’t really think I was that argumentative, actually. My dad just wasn’t used to having people disagree with him. It’s fortunate for me that he found it cute for his baby girl to do so (though he grew to dislike it as I became older, and he especially hates it now!).
I’m not really sure, beyond that, where I got the idea that I’d grow up to be a lawyer. Though I was, even as a very young kid, concerned about issues of justice and fairness. I was very much the kid who felt the need to stand up for other kids when they were being picked on, and I was always worried about other people. Do they have enough food? Enough clothing? Love and support? As a younger person I thought lawyers were the people who fought for those things, and I was enamored with that idea.
As a teen, what were you passionate about, if anything? Any sign you’d be a philosopher?
I was most consistently passionate about the environment. As a little kid, I really worried about pollution, so I made signs and posted them to trees around my neighborhood. I vaguely remember one neighbor – not that we had many, we lived in a very quiet and out-of-the way neighborhood – coming to ask my parents if I was attacking him personally, because things would sometimes fly out of the back of his truck as he sped down our hilly road (I wasn’t.) Then, in high school I got really involved with Greenpeace. I even staged a protest at our local grocery store (the Piggly Wiggly) to discourage people from buying Kleenex products, as they were clearing areas in the Brazilian rain forest to make their products. My art teacher from high school even had her class help paint a giant sign for us on a plastic, white shower curtain, and two of my friends painted themselves brown and adorned themselves with leaves to look like trees. Of course, folks in small towns don’t take kindly to being (from their point-of-view) lectured, especially not by teenagers. And so many people scoffed at the fact that we were asking folks to sign a paper petition while also advocating against the use of certain paper products. My annoyance that they didn’t see the distinction between using recycled paper and using Kleenex products was probably an early indication that I’d be a philosopher.
Why major in philosophy? Did you ever consider doing anything else? Wait a minute, you were there when I was a grad student there! Did we cross paths?
Well, my plan, when I started college, was law school. Having little family guidance, I assumed I should major in political science, and so that was the plan going into FSU. But I was in the honors college and my freshman year they were piloting a new honors colloquium. They would have folks from across the colleges give a short session, and early on they brought a professor from the law school. She said that the three majors that perform best on the LSAT are history, English, and philosophy. Having had exposure to the former two in high school I was least attracted to those options. Plus, I had a little romantic entanglement with this guy from back home who was always ending my arguments with “Well, Plato says so-and-so”. So I figured that by taking on a philosophy major I’d kill two birds with one stone – finally beat that guy in an argument and prepare myself to excel on the LSAT.
I really didn’t have plans to take philosophy seriously, but then two things happened, both involving the same philosophy professor, David McNaughton. I enrolled in his Ethical Theory course my sophomore Fall, and I was so excited to take that class. But, hand-to-God, I’d never met a British person in real life, and the first day of class I couldn’t understand a single word David said. I thought for sure I’d have to drop the course, but I gave it another day before making a decision, and the second class I had a much easier time processing his accent. That became my favorite class, the class that made me realize that I really liked philosophy and was good at it. With regret I admit I became that annoying clinger-on of a student who followed Professor McNaughton as he walked from class each day back to his office (which was no short trek, especially in the Florida humidity). For the record, this is why I don’t complain when students trail after me – I know I’m only reaping what I’ve sown!
Then, the summer before my senior year, I was talking to David and he suggested that I consider writing a philosophy thesis and applying to graduate school. I remember being told, when I started at FSU, that to graduate with honors I’d need to write a thesis. And I remember thinking there was no way I could do that; it sounded so intimidating, so I put it out of mind entirely. But if a professor I really admired and respected was encouraging me to do it, it felt like maybe it was possible.
In the process of writing my thesis I realized how un-psyched I was about applying to law school, and how enthusiastic I was about continuing to read and write philosophy. So I abandoned my law school applications and shifted gears towards grad school in philosophy.
On whether we crossed paths – I’m not sure. I remember really well a few grad students who were TAs for classes I was in. Tracey Mahaffey was one, I think, and there was a guy who TA’d for Michael Bishop’s epistemology course who gave brutal (but very helpful) feedback on my writing. That was pretty much the extent of my interaction with the grad students, so I suspect we never met!
Tell me a little bit more about your time at Sheffield. Why’d you leave?
Well, mostly because it was only a one-year program and I had finished. I would have happily stayed, however. People are always surprised when I say this, but I love Sheffield. It was the first place I got to live that had reliable public transportation, so I felt connected to everything. It was also really the first place I lived that was a walkable city, and that I could go grocery shopping or get to the Peak district (to hike) without a car was amazing to me. I also really liked the people (who called me “duck”) and the food – yes, the food! Yorkshire pudding and Sunday roast. The cool social events the uni put on, like “silent discoes”. I even went to a roller derby match and I got to experience my first Christmas market and my first snowfall.
Tell me a little bit about your time with Teach for America.
I did Teach for America between graduating from Sheffield and beginning grad school at UT. Teaching high school was a major formative experience for me in a lot of ways. I remember feeling intense anxiety in my first week of teaching, because I realized that if I did a bad job, I could be ruining the lives and futures of a hundred kids. Also, it was hard! Trying to get a bunch of teenagers to trust you takes so much work, like months and months of relationship building. Truthfully, the kids didn’t really trust me until I came back the 2nd year. I think they were so used to people coming in-and-out, they just couldn’t afford to invest themselves in someone who might disappear.
I pretty much hated teaching that first year – it was hard and I was very bad at it. But experience is the best teacher, and when I came back the 2nd year, I knew what I was doing. I prioritized relationship-building over new content in the first few weeks of school and I felt more confident with the material I needed to teach. That year I came to love teaching and to love my kids. I’m still close with the students I taught when they were sophomores/juniors, and I even went back to Baton Rouge for their 10-year reunion last year.
What I learned from TFA is this: Many people are incompetent. Worse than incompetent, they are also often cruel. In my 2nd year, a big scandal broke out in the teaching community because it was discovered that some higher-ups in the school district had paid for degrees that they didn’t earn from a local university. At least one of the teachers at my school legitimately just did not teach – he played trashcan basketball with his students. I know this because my students would instead use that time to read The Great Gatsby (the assigned text for my English class) and he decided to ruin it for them by spoiling the ending. The next period a group of devastated kids trudges into my classroom begging me to tell them that Gatsby doesn’t die in the end. Asshole.
Before TFA, I thought most people were good, kind-hearted, and well-meaning. Maybe people disagreed about how best to pursue a certain end, sure, but I was confident we all wanted what was good, and we certainly all wanted what was best for our kids. My experience teaching disabused me of this notion.
On the upside, I met my best friend there, as well as my husband! Working with kids made me a kinder, more compassionate person. It taught me the value of thinking about the world from another person’s perspective. Truthfully, I suspect my standpoint epistemology origin story is in this experience.
Was UT what you expected?
No, it was not. Pretty immediately when I started grad school, I realized that I had been naïve and obtuse in my philosophy classes as an undergrad. In retrospect, there was obvious sexism and racism that I just didn’t notice at FSU, like the male undergrads interrupting and speaking over the only female philosophy professor (and professor of color, for that matter) I had (Maria Morales). I realized this when I started UT, because all the other women in my cohort mentioned that, before accepting the offer from UT, they had reached out to women grad students about their experience. That never
even occurred to me. The reports were apparently not good. I will not revisit those reports here – I believe they are well-known within the philosophy community.
Sexism was also very prevalent at UT. Sometimes the female grad students would be asked by male graduate students to make copies for them. We had a few male students that were considered “the golden boys” – it seemed to the rest of us that they received extra attention and resources. The department gave out a prize each year for the best paper by a graduate student (the Cogburn Prize) and usually a male student won. One year a woman graduate student, whose paper was published in a top-ranked specialist journal and won a prize in that journal (two supposed criteria), still was not selected.
The department technically did not have a bathroom for women students – our department, located in Waggener Hall takes up the 3rd and 4th floor. There is a men’s bathroom on the 3rd floor. A bathroom for women is on the 1st and 2nd floor, located in the classics department. Apparently, once upon a time the bathroom on floor three was gender neutral, but since the department was mostly men anyways, they just converted it to a men’s only restroom. The women staged a protest and hostile takeover of that bathroom. Rumor has it that a professor in the department emailed the chair, David Sosa, about his being “hen-pecked”. Needless to say, the bathroom was quickly returned to its men-only status.
I would say the biggest distinction between what I expected and what happened is this: I thought that as teachers, these professors, this department, would fully support their graduate students, mentor us, teach us how to do research and succeed in this profession. But that is not, to my mind, what they viewed their role to be. It seemed to me that they viewed their job as breaking us, thinning the herd. They literally gave us what was known around the department as a “scare talk” in our first semester, the basics of which were “a lot of you will drop out and most of you won’t get jobs”. They were just giving it to us straight, I guess.
But, as a result, the environment could be kind of cutthroat. I remember in my first or second year of grad school, there was a post that made the rounds identifying which Hogwarts house various philosophy departments would be. Ours was Slytherin.
What was the dissertation on?
My dissertation was on the relationship between knowledge and social identity and focused in particular on standpoint theory. A large part of the dissertation was really just me trying to work out for myself what that relationship was, how standpoint epistemology related to traditional epistemology, and what the value or insights of standpoint epistemology might be. The thing I’m proudest of in the dissertation is the chapter in which I argue that epistemic oppression is a consequence of some of the commitments within traditional epistemology, and that we can’t make sense of the occurrence of epistemic oppression without the resources that standpoint epistemology provides.
I think this interview series might provide some evidence for standpoint epistemology. How do you pitch standpoint epistemology to people skeptical of it?
I usually ask them if they have ever been to NYC, and if so, to reconstruct their route from one place to another (from home to the Cloisters, for example). Did they use the subway? If so, which lines? Did those lines have elevators? Usually, they can’t recall. Alternatively, I ask them to think about which buildings they access through campus, or to get to work. Do those buildings have ramps? Elevators? If so, are they easy to access or out of the way? These examples usually get people to see, rather quickly, that there are aspects of their environment they don’t think about or pay attention to at all, but that others must know about if they are to navigate effectively. They get quickly at the heart of the idea, central in standpoint theory, that there is an important relationship between embodiment, power, and knowledge.
What are you working on now? Any projects you’re especially excited about?
Yes! I’m writing a book about social and political resistance from an epistemic perspective, sort of bringing my work in standpoint epistemology to bear on questions in political philosophy. I suspect that many people can’t understand or appreciate what certain social and political acts or movements mean to accomplish, because they live in a world where the injustices these acts/movements mean to address are obscured. And I wonder what this means for the possibility of resistance to achieve its aims and how, thinking about this perspective, might empower us to rethink how we go about social and political reform.
If you could ask an omniscient being one question and be guaranteed a truthful answer, what would you ask?
What’s wrong with my dad?
This section of the APA Blog is designed to get to know our fellow philosophers a little better. We’re including profiles of APA members that spotlight what captures their interest not only inside the office but also outside of it. We’d love for you to be a part of it, so please contact us via the interview nomination form here to nominate yourself or a friend.

Repeated attacks on humanitarian warehouses put vital medical aid at risk in Ukraine: WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04

Repeated attacks on humanitarian warehouses put vital medical aid at risk in Ukraine: WHO
A new airstrike overnight damaged one of the main warehouses used by the World Health Organization (WHO) in Ukraine to store humanitarian medical supplies in the Kyiv region, the UN agency said on Friday.
This is the third attack to affect a WHO-used storage facility in the last three months.
“Yesterday, overnight, between 3 and 4 September, an air attack in Kyiv oblast affected one of WHO's main warehouses, storing humanitarian medical needs and supplies,” said WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier.
Speaking to journalists in Geneva, he explained that “the access to the site remained restricted due to heavy smoke and safety concerns, while assessments of possible damage and stock losses are ongoing.”
No WHO personnel were affected, he said.
Healthcare under fire
This incident follows two other attacks on warehouses used by WHO in different parts of the country in the last three months, with essential medical supplies intended for people living in frontline and hard-to-reach areas.
Two weeks ago, an attack destroyed a WHO humanitarian warehouse in Dnipro, resulting in the loss of half of the medical supplies and equipment intended to support an estimated 225,000 people living in the frontline and hard-to-reach areas, according to the WHO.
“Another warehouse used by WHO in Kyiv oblast was damaged during a large-scale wave of attacks on Kyiv and the region in July,” said Mr. Lindmeier.
Lifeline for civilians
Humanitarian medical supplies are a lifeline for people who need healthcare in frontline and hard-to-reach areas. The WHO spokesperson stressed that attacks on warehouses storing these supplies can delay or disrupt the delivery of essential health support to people who need it most.
The agency is increasingly concerned about the growing pattern of attacks on humanitarian storage facilities nationwide.
“The attacks are part of a broader pattern affecting humanitarian operations across the country. In 2026, at least 20 attacks have affected warehouses storing humanitarian supplies, including 15 attacks on warehouses holding health-related humanitarian supplies,” Mr. Lindmeier said.
He stressed that the locations of United Nations and WHO facilities and warehouses are known to all parties to the conflict as they are communicated through established deconfliction arrangements.
“In my understanding, all warehouses, all UN locations, all WHO locations, are de-conflicted. That means the whereabouts are communicated to all sides of the conflict, and that is well known,” Mr. Lindmeier explained.
Commitment to deliver
Despite the attacks, the WHO continues to work with health partners across Ukraine to ensure that essential medical supplies reach health facilities and communities in need. Following the latest incidents, alternative storage arrangements have already been identified, while efforts are underway to assess the damage and replace lost supplies.
In 2026, the WHO's overall humanitarian response comprised provision of equipment and supplies to over 300 health-care facilities, including primary care centres, hospitals, laboratories, and transit centers, supporting the health system to reach three million beneficiaries.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began on 24 February 2022, WHO has verified more than 3,000 attacks on healthcare including strikes on health facilities, ambulances, medical supplies and warehouses.

UN tells the world: Stop making Africa look small
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

UN tells the world: Stop making Africa look small
The UN General Assembly has voted overwhelmingly to encourage governments, schools and tech companies worldwide to stop using maps that make Africa look far smaller than it really is.
By 164 votes to one, Member States on Friday endorsed a resolution promoting map projections that more accurately reflect the true size of continents – the culmination of an African-led campaign against the 16th-century Mercator projection, still the most widely used map in the world.
The United States cast the sole vote against, dismissing the initiative as part of a “radical ideological project.”
Six countries – Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine – abstained.
The resolution does not ban the Mercator projection or impose a replacement. Instead, it encourages governments, schools, international organizations and technology companies to use the Equal Earth projection and other so-called equal-area maps when relative size matters, and to teach the limitations of any flat map in representing a spherical planet.
Behind that seemingly technical debate lies a larger argument about history and power: whether a map designed for European sailors in the 16th century has, over generations, distorted not only geography but perceptions of a whole, vast and complex continent.
“Maps shape our understanding of the world,” Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign minister, said before the vote. “They guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions.”
Made small
Gerardus Mercator, a Flemish cartographer, devised his projection in 1569 to solve a practical problem of maritime navigation. Because straight lines on his map correspond to constant compass directions, sailors could use it to plot their courses.
But preserving direction came at the expense of area. Landmasses appear increasingly enlarged the farther they are from the Equator.
Greenland, for instance, can look roughly comparable in size to Africa, even though Africa is about 14 times larger. Northern Europe and North America are similarly magnified, relative to equatorial regions.
Despite its original navigational purpose, Mercator remains common in educational, media, digital and official materials. The resolution says those distortions have contributed to the “symbolic minimization” of Africa and perpetuated an unbalanced view of the world.
‘A fair map’
Togo led negotiations on behalf of the African group, building on a campaign backed by the African Union.
The resolution describes correcting such distortions as an act of “cognitive justice and memorial reparation” and points to Equal Earth, developed in 2018, as a projection that more accurately represents relative size.
Mr. Dussey emphasized that the effort was not meant to condemn Mercator, whose usefulness for navigation he acknowledged, or to impose a single projection.
“A fair map does not change the geography of the world, it changes how we see the world,” he said.
Washington objects
The United States saw something far more political in the effort.
“This resolution mocks the work and purpose of this institution,” the American representative said, arguing that what was presented as an innocuous attempt to update cartographic proportions was part of “the much larger and more radical ideological project it belongs to.”
The representative singled out the resolution’s references to reparations and “cognitive justice,” calling initiatives like it “barnacles on our work here and the reason this institution is losing its credibility.”
France moved in the opposite direction. Hours before the vote, Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot announced Paris was planning to abandon Mercator for its maps of the world, aligning his Government with the broader effort championed by the African Union.
The shift means France itself, like the United States and Russia, will appear smaller relative to equatorial countries.
It illustrates the unusual dynamics of this decades-long debate. Equal-area maps do not make Africa larger; they remove the exaggeration Mercator gives landmasses closer to the poles.
Borderline revolt
Ukraine said it supported efforts to correct historical distortions affecting Africa and other parts of the Global South but objected to the way some maps using Equal Earth depict Ukrainian territory occupied by Russia.
Its representative warned that endorsing the projection without adequate safeguards could open a “Pandora’s box,” allowing maps to create ambiguity over disputed territories.
The European Union supported the resolution but addressed the same concern.
Speaking on behalf of the bloc, Ireland stressed that the measure applied only to the relative size of landmasses and had no bearing on sovereignty, territorial status or internationally recognized borders.
The bloc also said its support did not constitute an endorsement of the maps displayed on the Equal Earth website.
Imperfect view
The resolution itself acknowledges a fundamental problem that no vote can solve. No projection can perfectly reproduce the curved surface of the Earth on a plane. Each sacrifice something – area, shape, distance or direction – and each is suited to different purposes.
The measure is nonbinding, and Mercator is not disappearing into the library vaults, never to be seen again.
But Friday’s vote gave near unanimous international backing to an argument which many African governments have increasingly pressed: that the choices we make over maps can shape how generations understand the world.

West Bank: UN rights report warns of forcible displacement from three refugee camps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

West Bank: UN rights report warns of forcible displacement from three refugee camps
Israeli security forces forcibly displaced the entire population of three Palestine refugee camps in the occupied West Bank in January and February last year – and continue to prevent their return, in violation of international law, according to a new report by the UN human rights office, OHCHR.
The report said military, police and other forces deployed during Israel’s Operation Iron Wall offensive killed civilians, destroyed hundreds of homes, damaged roads and other infrastructure, cut off water and electricity, and blocked humanitarian access to the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem refugee camps.
Israeli forces went door to door ordering residents to leave.
Some displaced Palestinians told OHCHR that Israeli officers said there would be no more refugee camps and that they should “all go to Jordan”.
Widespread destruction
By October 2025, 52 per cent of structures in Jenin refugee camp, 48 per cent in Nur Shams and 36 per cent in Tulkarem had been destroyed or damaged.
The report said the large-scale, long-term and systematic displacement of over 33,000 Palestinians from the camps during the operation raises serious concerns of the crime against humanity of forcible transfer.
It said Israeli forces used airstrikes, armoured bulldozers and controlled detonations to render entire camps uninhabitable in the absence of imperative military necessity – actions it said also raise concerns of collective punishment and ethnic cleansing.
Some 102 Palestinians, including 21 children, were killed during the period covered by the report – 46 per cent of all killings by Israeli forces in the West Bank over that period.
Shot on the way to pray
Among them were Sondos Shalabi, who was eight months pregnant and was shot dead as she tried to drive away from Nur Shams camp, and ten-year-old Saddam Hussein Rajab, who was shot in the stomach in Tulkarem as he waited for his father to walk to the mosque with him.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the way the operation was conducted suggested its aim was to expel as many Palestinians as possible and make way for more illegal Israeli settlements.
He called on Israel to end what he described as its 59-year occupation of Palestinian territory and to comply with the International Court of Justice’s finding, more than two years ago, that it must end its unlawful presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory as rapidly as possible.
On 23 February 2025, Israel’s Defence Minister ordered the military to remain in the three camps and said displaced Palestinians would not be allowed to return.
The UN’s Palestine refugee relief agency, UNRWA, says around 33,362 people remain displaced as of July this year.

The UN and its humanitarian partners launched a $49.6 million flash appeal on Friday to deliver emergency assistance to more than 84,000 people affected by last week’s catastrophic floods in Nepal.
On 26 August, a glacier on the border between Nepal and the Tibet autonomous region of China collapsed, triggering floods that have now claimed more than 1,250 lives and left thousands missing, according to the UN’s office in Nepal.
The UN’s local humanitarian team estimate that 84,270 Nepalis – or 19,284 households – were affected by the floods.
Devastating toll
Across the Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading regions of northern Nepal, critical infrastructure such as roads, schools, power grids and water systems have been damaged or destroyed, while many survivors have lost their homes and family members.
Working with Nepali emergency operations, the UN aims to help families buy essential goods, revitalise local economies, restore power, prevent disease outbreaks and help prepare residents for the upcoming winter.
Humanitarian workers will deliver direct cash assistance, cold-weather shelter materials, portable solar power units, water purification systems and food aid, while emergency mobile clinics will provide medical treatment and nutritional support.
“Families have lost everything: their loved ones, their homes, their livelihoods, swept away in minutes,” said Lila Pieters Yahia, the UN’s Resident Coordinator in Nepal.
“Working under the Government’s leadership, this appeal will get cash, shelter, healthcare, clean water and protection to the hardest-to-reach communities before winter closes in.”
In a country where agriculture makes up 24 per cent of gross domestic product, half of which comes from livestock, according to the World Bank, aid teams will even help locals keep surviving animals alive and safe.
UNICEF aid influx
But the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) isn’t waiting, and neither are other UN agencies, as they support rescuers still racing to find survivors.
On Friday, a flight supported by UNICEF and the European Union carrying 84 metric tonnes of humanitarian supplies landed in the capital Kathmandu.
The children’s agency will distribute diarrhoea treatment kits, water tanks, hygiene kits, water treatment supplies, winter clothing and learning materials – which it says will support hundreds of thousands of people.
“This shipment will help us deliver urgently needed support and reach children and families with services that protect their health, wellbeing and future,” said Alice Akunga, UNICEF’s representative in Nepal.
Humanitarian partners have already mobilised and transported relief items to some of the hardest-hit areas, focusing largely on disease prevention and essential infrastructure repairs.
In the days since the flood, UNICEF has allocated emergency supplies and helped establish child-friendly spaces with recreational materials for children most affected by the disaster.
“Continued support is essential to help children recover, stay healthy, return to learning, and rebuild their lives in the weeks and months ahead,” Ms. Akunga said. “As the scale of the disaster is enormous, the needs remain significant and every day matters.”

UNN выяснил how to act in such situations and whether there are legislative mechanisms of influence.
Details
On January 27 of this year, the Office of the Military Ombudsman officially began operating in Ukraine. Under the law, its main tasks are to exercise democratic civilian control over ensuring respect for rights; identify violations of the rights of military personnel, reservists, conscripts, and police officers, as well as the causes and conditions leading to such violations.
In accordance with the tasks assigned to the Military Ombudsman and within the scope of his or her competence, the ombudsman has the right to consider complaints and conduct investigations into alleged violations of the rights of military personnel.
Rada adopted the law on the military ombudsman: what is foreseen17.09.25, 12:20 • 46869 views
According to the Office of the Military Ombudsman in response to a request from UNN, from the beginning of its operations through August 31, the Office received 14,427 complaints and appeals on behalf of military personnel, of which 13,922 complaints and appeals were reviewed, while another 505 are under consideration.
As a result of reviewing complaints, 2,535 inspections were ordered since the Office began operating. A total of 1,203 complaints were returned to the complainants because they were not subject to review under the law. In particular, a complaint was essentially identical to one that had already been reviewed by the Military Ombudsman; the complaint concerned the provision of a legal position or interpretation of the legislation of Ukraine; or the demands in the complaint were the subject of court proceedings. The Office also does not review complaints if a representative acting on behalf of a service member has not provided documents confirming his or her authority

-  referrals to the Military Medical Commission and treatment;  
-  discharge from military service;  
-  monthly financial support and additional remuneration; 
-  transfer to another place of service.  
It should be noted that, simultaneously with the bill on establishing the Office of the Military Ombudsman, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy submitted another draft law, No. 13267, which provides for liability for failure to comply with the lawful demands of the Military Ombudsman or obstructing the exercise of his or her powers.
Such a violation would carry a fine of between UAH 8,500 and UAH 17,000.
For a repeated violation, the fine would range from UAH 17,000 to UAH 34,000, along with disqualification from holding certain positions or engaging in certain activities for one year, or without such disqualification.
The document was adopted back in October 2025 and currently remains stalled. The Office of the Military Ombudsman noted that findings are one of the key instruments for responding to violations of the rights of military personnel.
Following consideration of a complaint, the Military Ombudsman or deputy may order an inspection. Upon its completion, the Office prepares a finding stating whether a violation occurred, who committed it, and how to restore the complainant’s rights. The finding, together with the relevant requirement, is sent to the commander (chief), a military administration body, or an official of a state authority. They are required to consider it within ten working days and inform the Military Ombudsman of what has been done to remedy the violations
At the same time, the Office said that numerous cases have been recorded in which commanders, military administration bodies, and officials fail to respond to them, consider them only formally, or delay the deadlines, while "the legislation still does not provide for appropriate liability for this".
Back in October last year, the Verkhovna Rada adopted Bill No. 13267 in the first reading, which is intended to grant the Military Ombudsman the right to draw up administrative offense reports and bring offenders to justice through the courts for failure to comply with lawful demands. This provision will apply both to commanders and to officials at all levels—from local self-government bodies and heads of Regional Military Administrations to ministers. In a comment to UNN, Member of Parliament and member of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Law Enforcement Oleksandr Danutsa said that "work on preparing the document for the second reading is proceeding in accordance with the established procedural rules."
The stage of processing and systematizing all amendments and proposals submitted by entities with the right of legislative initiative is currently underway, as is their coordination with the relevant state authorities and specialized experts, so that the result is an effective and balanced mechanism. The bill will be considered at a committee meeting immediately after all necessary preparatory procedures have been completed and the comparative table finalized. Accordingly, following the committee's decision, the issue of submitting it for consideration in the plenary chamber will be decided during the formation of the agenda for plenary meetings of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine

OpenAI said Astra is initially being rolled out to a limited set of enterprises and will become available more widely to developers and paying ChatGPT users in the coming days.
The model is designed to carry out multistep computer tasks, including working across software and browsers, completing spreadsheets and building websites.
“Astra can do anything a human can do with a computer,” OpenAI co-founder and President Greg Brockman said.

Safety concerns and oversight
The launch comes amid growing scrutiny of the risks posed by increasingly capable and autonomous AI systems.
In a report released last week, OpenAI said an experimental version of Astra obtained administrator-level control over parts of the company's infrastructure during internal testing without staff being immediately aware.
The company also said Astra is capable of discovering previously unknown security flaws and developing "new ways to exploit them across many well-protected systems without a person guiding each step."
In response, the company said it "significantly strengthened” its “protections against the model taking harmful cyber actions."
The launch follows scrutiny over a July incident in which OpenAI agents breached systems belonging to AI platform Hugging Face during testing.
Last week, an independent report raised further concerns about the OpenAI agents' hack of Hugging Face, saying roughly 700 agents participated in the attack, communicating among themselves and trying to cover their tracks.
OpenAI said Astra itself was not involved in the Hugging Face incident and that it subsequently developed an evaluation based on what happened to test whether models would act beyond their authorized scope.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Astra underwent the White House's voluntary review process and that government officials did not request changes to the company's safety measures.

MIT turns bacteria into living transistors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:52:39 UTC
20:52:39 KST

MIT turns bacteria into living transistors
MIT scientists have turned bacteria into living transistors, opening the door to plants with built-in biological computers that can sense and respond to their environment.
- Date:
- September 4, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- MIT researchers have created bacterial “transistors” that can be wired together into living circuits capable of performing calculations and directing chemical signals. One day, these biological computers could coat plant roots or leaves, detecting environmental threats and automatically triggering defenses.
- Share:
MIT researchers have engineered bacteria to work like transistors, creating living "circuit boards" that can be printed onto growth material inside a Petri dish.
In conventional electronics, transistors act as switches that control whether electrical current can pass through a circuit. In the MIT system, engineered bacterial cells perform a similar role by regulating the movement of small signaling molecules. Those molecules then carry information to other components in the biological circuit.
The researchers created two types of bacterial transistors and three additional bacterial strains that act as relays between them. Together, these five strains provide a modular set of components that can be arranged to build nearly any kind of circuit. In the new study, the team demonstrated circuits capable of adding two or three inputs and directing a single input toward a selected destination.
"We've built some initial computer architecture components that are commonly used, but any operation can be built with these five strains," says Hamid Doosthosseini PhD '25, an MIT postdoc and the lead author of the new study.
One potential use is to place these living circuits on plant leaves or roots. There, the bacteria could process information about environmental conditions, helping plants detect and respond to stresses such as drought or pest attacks.
Christopher Voigt, head of MIT's Department of Biological Engineering, is the senior author of the paper, which was recently published in Nature Chemical Biology. Former MIT postdoc Haorong Chen is also an author of the paper.
Turning Bacterial Cells Into Transistors
Synthetic biology circuits are usually built by engineering cells to produce proteins and transcription factors that interact with one another. These systems can be programmed to carry out tasks such as detecting a particular molecule and then producing a specific response.
Such circuits can perform different logic functions, but their complexity is limited. Researchers generally need distinct transcription factors for separate operations so that signals do not interfere with one another. Because only a limited number of suitable transcription factors are available, there is a practical ceiling on how complicated a circuit can become inside a single cell. Packing too many circuits into one cell can also overwhelm its protein production machinery.
The MIT team approached the problem differently. Rather than placing an entire circuit inside one cell, they engineered individual cells to serve as transistor-like components that could be connected in different arrangements.
For these components, the researchers used Pantoea agglomerans, a bacterium that commonly grows on surfaces, including plants. They engineered two versions of bacterial transistors that respond to a molecule called OC 6. One type switches on when it encounters the molecule, while the other switches off.
Each transistor also senses a second target molecule, OC 12. Depending on whether OC 12 is present and whether the transistor has been activated, the bacterial cell produces an output molecule called OHC 14.
Wiring Living Cells Together
The team then engineered three strains of Pantoea agglomerans to function as relays. These cells convert the OHC 14 signal into another output that can serve as the input for the next transistor. In this way, individual bacterial components can be "wired" together much like parts on an electronic circuit board.
For instance, the researchers built a bidirectional switch using two transistors that detect OC 12. Depending on a separate switch input, the system sends that information through different relay strains before passing it to additional transistors for further processing.
To assemble the circuits, the researchers printed bacterial colonies onto plates containing agar, which serves as a growth medium. Each colony was positioned about 5 millimeters from its nearest neighbor. This spacing helps ensure that chemical signals reach only the next colony in the sequence, allowing information to move through the circuit in a single direction.
Building More Complex Biological Circuits
The researchers showed that the same bacterial transistor could perform several logic operations depending on where it was positioned within a circuit. These included "multi-input," "or," and "imply" gates.
By connecting multiple transistors, the team also created more sophisticated systems. The circuits could add two signals, process several signals at the same time, or operate as a demultiplexer, which receives one incoming signal and routes it to one of several possible destinations based on a separate control signal.
The largest circuit demonstrated in the study contained 24 interconnected bacterial colonies and was designed to add two inputs together.
"This work shows that we can get toward more complicated functions by linking up simpler functions in individual cells," Voigt says. "Computationally, there's nothing that your iPhone can do that these circuits couldn't do."
There is, however, a major difference in speed. Each calculation performed by the bacterial circuits takes about eight hours, far longer than an electronic computer would require. For biological applications, though, the researchers say that pace can still be practical.
"We're not trying to replace computers, but rather put computational control into biology. If you have bacteria on the root of a plant, or the plant itself is doing the computing, running a simple calculation overnight is fast enough relative to a growth season," Voigt says.
Living Computers for Agriculture
One possible application is agriculture. If these circuits can eventually be placed on plant roots, they could be programmed to detect different forms of stress. When the system recognizes a particular signal, it could trigger a corresponding response, such as producing a fungicide.
The research was funded, in part, by the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and by the U.S. Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Original written by Anne Trafton. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Hamid Doosthosseini, Haorong Chen, Christopher A. Voigt. Living circuit boards built by printing bacterial transistors. Nature Chemical Biology, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41589-026-02300-3

NATO says it is shadowing Russian ships in the Mediterranean
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:50:56 UTC
20:50:56 KST

- NATO's Allied Maritime Command said Standing NATO Maritime Group 2 is tracking Russian naval vessels transiting the Mediterranean as part of routine monitoring.
- The post did not name a specific Russian ship or aircraft, but included a photo of a Russian Ka-27 helicopter near a NATO warship.
NATO’s Allied Maritime Command said this week that its ships are keeping a constant watch on Russian naval activity from the Baltic Sea to the Mediterranean, with Standing NATO Maritime Group 2 tracking Russian vessels transiting the Mediterranean as part of that effort.
The command, known as MARCOM, did not name a specific Russian ships or aircraft involved in the current monitoring in its social media post, saying only that its forces “remain alert 24/7” across NATO’s northern and southern flanks. The post included a photograph of a Russian Ka-27 naval helicopter, marked with the tail number RF-19160 and the numeral 51, flying near what appears to be a NATO warship at sea and a Russian naval group and escorted merchant vessels.
Standing NATO Maritime Group 2, known as SNMG2, is one of four permanently active multinational naval forces NATO keeps at sea, alongside a sister group in the Atlantic and two mine-countermeasures groups. SNMG2 typically draws ships from the U.S., France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Turkey and the U.K., and its main job in the Mediterranean is building a continuous picture of naval activity in the region, including the presence of Russian Navy units transiting the area.
That kind of shadowing has produced several public incidents this year. In one recent case, the Italian frigate Virginio Fasan, operating with SNMG2, tracked the Russian Kilo-class submarine Krasnodar as it moved through the Mediterranean, escorted by the Russian destroyer Severomorsk. NATO ships have also monitored Russian frigates Admiral Golovko and Admiral Grigorovich in the eastern Mediterranean over the past year, according to Spain’s Ministry of Defence.
NATO has used the phrase “We. Are. Watching.” in similar public statements before, including in December 2024, when it publicized the Portuguese Navy’s escort of Russian ships through the Mediterranean using frigates NRP Álvares Cabral and NRP Sines. The recurring messaging is part of what NATO describes as routine maritime security operations, rather than a response to a specific new provocation.

This UAE-backed Fatah dissident is allying with Hamas and pushing a proposal to change Palestinian politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:48:06 UTC
20:48:06 KST

The Palestinian legislative elections scheduled for next November are already shaking up Palestinian politics in ways not seen in years, with different actors across the Palestinian political spectrum making power moves in an attempt to secure their position within a shifting political landscape in the fallout from the Gaza genocide. The latest of these moves is the announcement of a plan by UAE-based dissident Fatah leader Muhammad Dahlan to “end Palestinian division.”
Dahlan’s plan is more than an election program, going so far as to propose a complete remaking of the Palestinian political system and a change to the decades-old way power balances have been managed in Palestinian institutions.
Dahlan’s move doesn’t come in a vacuum. It follows the earlier announcement of an electoral alliance between Hamas, the Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ), and the two main dissident currents in Fatah — one led by former Palestinian diplomat and nephew of the late Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, Nasser Al-Qudwah, and the other led by Dahlan.
The alliance brings together most of the main Palestinian political forces, with the exception of the leftist factions and the dominant Fatah leadership of Mahmoud Abbas, who runs the Palestinian Authority (PA) and serves as its President.
Dahlan’s plan hasn’t been endorsed yet by his electoral allies, but they haven’t disavowed it either. The presentation of the plan right after forming the alliance establishes Dahlan as the alliance’s leading figure and puts him at the center of the Palestinian political game, closer than ever to a comeback to Palestinian leadership and decision-making.
Long exiled to the UAE and declared persona non grata in both Gaza and the West Bank, Dahlan now seeks to claw his way back into political relevance with the financial backing of his Gulf sponsors. The reason he has a chance of succeeding is that his plan offers all sides — Hamas, Abbas, and the UAE-U.S. axis pushing Gaza’s postwar order — a way to claim national unity without settling who actually governs. That ambiguity is precisely what has kept such plans alive.
Who is Muhammad Dahlan?
Muhammad Yousef Shaker Dahlan was born in 1961 in the Khan Younis refugee camp in the southern Gaza Strip to a Palestinian refugee family from the village of Hamama near Asqalan, destroyed by Israeli forces in 1948. He joined Fatah as a teenager and spent five years in Israeli jails for his activism.
In 1987, he was released and later deported by Israel shortly before the start of the first Palestinian Intifada. He joined Fatah’s exile apparatus, moving among multiple Arab capitals for several years, during which he grew closer to Yasser Arafat and eventually returned to Palestine with him after the Oslo Accords.
Upon the establishment of the Palestinian Authority, Arafat named Dahlan head of the Palestinian Preventive Security Forces in Gaza, making him the main security officer in the Strip. As the man in charge in his own hometown, Dahlan increased his support base among Gaza’s Fatah supporters, all while strengthening his contacts with Israeli intelligence through his role in security coordination between the PA security and Israel.
This role also allowed Dahlan to cultivate contacts within regional governments, mainly the Egyptian government, and with U.S. officials. Dahlan became an outspoken critic of Hamas and was accused by the group of arresting many of its members.
Hamas and Dahlan: a complicated relationship
During the Fatah-Hamas conflict in 2007, Dahlan was seen as Hamas’s number-one nemesis in Gaza, publicly challenging the group and trading accusations of treason. Dahlan was one of the first Fatah leaders to leave the Strip after Hamas’s takeover of the PA’s institutions in Gaza in June 2007.
In 2011, tensions grew between Dahlan and the dominant current in Fatah, led by PA President Abbas, culminating in Abbas’s official expulsion of Dahlan from Fatah. Dahlan left for the UAE, where he began to reorganize his alliances.
In 2017, while Gaza was marking 10 years of strict Israeli blockade and isolation from Palestinian political life, Hamas was scrambling to find a way out of the crisis. The group released a new “political charter” that year, in which it accepted the PLO’s legitimacy to represent the Palestinian people, as well as the principle of a Palestinian state within a two-state solution framework. The same year, Hamas announced its complete organizational disconnection from the global Muslim Brotherhood and its independence as a Palestinian movement.
These moves to achieve progress in Palestinian reconciliation reached a dead-end as the PA imposed its own set of restrictions on Gaza’s bureaucracy, halting the payment of salaries to thousands of employees hired by the Hamas administration. Hamas needed a political lifeline, and it found an unlikely one in its old foe: Muhammad Dahlan.
Dahlan and Hamas announced an understanding which included a “social reconciliation,” paying reparations to families of victims of the inter-Palestinian fighting of 2007 through a special fund supported by the UAE. It also included a plan to facilitate humanitarian and social aid, and the entry of fuel through Qatar. The implementation of the plan would involve Gulf states and Egypt, in addition to U.S. approval.
While some parts of the understanding were implemented, namely the social reconciliation part, the political part of reaching a full agreement didn’t go through, as both the PA and Hamas saw that the political part of the reconciliation needs to be reached between them, and not between Hamas and Dahlan. The continuous stagnation of the political scene, the continuation of the Israeli blockade, and the deteriorating conditions of Gaza’s population led to the 2018 Great March of Return protests, which were violently repressed by Israel and ignored by the international community. Dahlan went back to the shadows, but only for a while.
What is Dahlan’s plan?
Dahlan’s plan is based on a simple idea: separating political competition between Palestinian factions from the running of Palestinian institutions, by making the Palestinian Authority a “neutral” body, where decisions on who gets to hold key positions are irrelevant to power balances between parties. Dahlan’s plan calls this a “national partnership instead of a struggle for power.”
This would mean a dramatic change from the way things have been handled in Palestinian politics for decades, where the larger and more dominant factions controlled most positions in the PLO and the PA, to the point that public institutions became practically an extension of party organizations. Political affiliation, or loyalty, has also been a criterion for holding office and even getting a job in government, which was one of the reasons why the reconciliation between Fatah and Hamas became so difficult, since thousands of Hamas-hired public servants in Gaza were payrolled on the Ramallah-based, Fatah-run PA budget. Dahlan’s proposal is to keep the competition between factions limited to elections for political office, and leave the rest of the PA body of institutions separated from politics.
To do this, Dahlan’s plan proposes a “new national social contract,” through a new Palestinian constitution that recognizes the people as the only source of legitimacy, and elections as the only way through which a Palestinian may hold office. The current Palestinian Basic Law already stipulates popular legitimacy through elections, as well as the separation of powers and the impartiality of public institutions, but political practice has been following unwritten rules inherited from the “revolutionary” era of the PLO in the 1960s and 1970s, where parties secured their share in the PLO institutions based on the size of their support base.
Even in that era, the idea of “national partnership” through collective decision-making among factions was a celebrated principle, practiced or ignored depending on the particular conditions of any given day. Dahlan’s plan doesn’t offer a practical approach to solving these inherited gaps between principles and practice. It only reaffirms the principles.
Gaza: the gateway to Palestinian politics and regional deals
For both Hamas and Dahlan, the main goal remains finding a way back into Palestinian politics and participation in the Palestinian decision-making process, which has been monopolized by the PA leadership represented by Fatah’s dominant faction under Abbas. Both Hamas and Dahlan have their main support bases in Gaza, at precisely the same moment that Gaza has now become the center of gravity of the Palestinian cause.
After the Israeli genocide in Gaza, international and regional focus shifted to how Gaza will be run in the future phase, after Hamas’s handing over of its control over the Strip. The plan of U.S. President Trump, including handing the administration of Gaza to a Palestinian technocratic committee under the so-called “Board of Peace,” remains in limbo, waiting in Egypt and unable to enter Gaza due to Israel’s insistence that the reconstruction will not move forward without Hamas’s total disarmament. Israel has also continued to reverse its partial withdrawal to the so-called “Yellow Line” during the October 2025 ceasefire by moving the Line further west, eating up more territory under Israeli control while hemming Gaza’s population into tighter spaces.
Politically, moving Trump’s plan to its second phase depends largely on the potential understandings over who would be in charge of Gaza on the Palestinian side. Hamas has agreed to give up its control of the strip, and even to disarm. But its main focus is to keep a place in Palestinian politics as a partner in national decision-making. But this internal Palestinian issue has been affected by the international dimension of the future of Gaza, which has become a regional political question in which several forces are vying for influence.
To the U.S., resolving the question of the future of Gaza is important to move on with the normalization efforts between Israel and Arab countries, which are themselves important for larger economic mega-projects in the region. The UAE is a key player in this regional normalization and in regional economic plans, and Dahlan — being the Palestinian leader enjoying the lion’s share of support from the UAE — has positioned himself as the figure to secure the missing piece of the puzzle: a Palestinian administration of Gaza with roots in internal Palestinian politics, enjoying a support base in Palestine, and capable of garnering the trust of regional players and the U.S.
What does this mean for Palestinian politics?
Dahlan’s election allies, namely Hamas, haven’t officially endorsed his plan, but they haven’t rejected it either. This places Dahlan as the leading figure in the alliance and makes his plan the de facto election platform of the alliance. The overall logic of the plan gives space for all players, including Hamas and Abbas, to maintain their status and their influence, while providing a patriotic, reconciliatory, and democratic discourse to present the Palestinian need to accept Trump’s plan in order to alleviate the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza.
The core idea of the plan is already the product of a Palestinian consensus: Palestinians need national unity to have any leverage over their own destiny. But the idea of this unity being reached through a figure who has been at odds with every party to the Palestinian division — sponsored by an Arab country leading normalization efforts with Israel, and aligned with Trump’s agenda — was not expected to have a serious chance of success under different conditions.
Today, it does have a chance, and in the background are the Palestinians’ hope to bring some relief to Gaza’s devastated population and have some chance to face Israel’s offensive in the West Bank united. Dahlan’s serious attempt to make a comeback in Palestinian politics through an alliance with Hamas speaks to how much Palestinians are ready to reconsider and politically accept under the shock of three years of genocide, destruction, and devastation.

Fury across India after Delhi Police assault two Muslim women journalists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:46:35 UTC
20:46:35 KST

A political and media storm has erupted in India after two women journalists said they were detained and brutally assaulted by Delhi Police while covering an event in south Delhi, with the assault becoming worse after officers learned that they were Muslim.
The journalists, Shaheen Khan and Nafisa Khan, work with digital news platform 4PM News Network. Videos showing their bruises and injuries have gone viral on social media, prompting condemnation from opposition parties, journalists' organisations and the Press Council of India.
Delhi Police, meanwhile, have strongly denied the allegations, saying the two women were taken to the Saket police station after allegedly obstructing a designated VVIP route during an event attended by Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta.
Rejecting the journalists' account, the police described the allegations as "factually incorrect", "misleading" and "baseless."
What happened in Saket?
The incident took place on Thursday, when Shah and Gupta were attending the inauguration of a new wing at Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital in Saket.
According to Khan and her colleague, they had gone to cover the event and were attempting to ask questions from the chief minister. They allege that police personnel stopped them, detained them and took them to Saket police station.
In videos circulated by 4PM News Network, Shaheen Khan is seen inside the police station describing the assault and showing injuries. Another video shows Nafisa Khan unable to walk and being carried away. The journalists have alleged that they were beaten with sticks and slapped.
Shaheen has said that police personnel asked her name and, after hearing "Khan", asked which community she belonged to. She alleges that the assault subsequently intensified after officers learned that she was Muslim.
According to Shaheen, an officer saw an incoming call from someone identified as “Mohammed” on her phone and said: “Muslim hai… do dande zyada maaro (She’s Muslim… hit her twice more with sticks).”
Videos fuel public outrage
The controversy escalated after 4PM News Network released videos in which the two journalists displayed visible bruising and described their treatment inside the police station.
The footage has been widely reposted, including by political leaders and news organisations.
The Press Club of India, Indian Women's Press Corps, Delhi Union of Journalists, Press Association and Kerala Union of Working Journalists jointly condemned what they described as a brutal assault on the two freelance journalists.
They called for punitive action against the police personnel involved, including the station house officer, and urged Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar to order a free and fair investigation.
The organisations also called on the Press Council of India to take suo motu cognisance of the matter and conduct an independent investigation.
Opposition parties condemn the beating
Opposition party Congress’ spokesperson Pawan Khera described the visuals as “horrifying” and questioned whether Delhi was becoming a "police state".
The Congress itself circulated the video and accused the BJP government and Delhi Police of detaining and assaulting Khan after she attempted to question the chief minister. The party demanded strict action against the police personnel involved.
The Aam Aadmi Party has also attacked the Delhi government, with leader Saurabh Bharadwaj alleging that the journalists had been brutally beaten for asking the chief minister questions, while party leader Somnath Bharti called for intervention by Delhi's Lieutenant Governor.
Indian politician leader Tejashwi Yadav from Rashtriya Janata Dal party also joined the chorus of opposition condemnation. In a post on X, Yadav called the incident a serious assault on press freedom and democratic accountability.
“In Modi ji's so-called Amrit Kaal New India, being a Muslim, being a woman, and being an impartial journalist is now the greatest sin,” he wrote, adding that the BJP has crossed every limit of twenty-four tyrannical authoritarianism across the country.
“Amrit Kaal” is the Indian government’s term for its vision of India’s development towards 2047 and “New India” is its broader slogan for a modern, transformed India.
The journalists’ own organisation, 4PM News Network, has also taken the matter to the highest constitutional office, petitioning Indian President Droupadi Murmu for intervention and seeking an impartial investigation into the alleged assault.
The organisation has also called for relevant CCTV and video evidence to be preserved and for action against any police personnel found responsible.

Russian-made spy drone washes up on Finnish shore near Porvoo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:44:43 UTC
20:44:43 KST

- Finnish authorities said a drone found near Porvoo appears to be a Russian-made Geoscan 701 surveying aircraft, though President Stubb said Finland faces no direct threat.
- The find is part of a pattern of drone incidents in Finland through 2026, most previously tied to stray Ukrainian drones rather than Russian devices.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Wednesday that Finland faces no direct threat after a drone was found on a shoreline in the Pellinki archipelago near Porvoo, even as Finnish authorities said the device now appears to be Russian-made.
A resident discovered the drone on September 1 on the shore of an island in the archipelago, roughly a two-hour drive east of Helsinki. The Finnish Border Guard identified it as a Geoscan 701, a fixed-wing aircraft built by the Russian company Geoscan for aerial surveying and mapping. The Border Guard confirmed the device carried no explosives.
“We are not worried, we need to be calm,” Stubb said, adding that authorities were still investigating the drone and would release more information once confirmed.
Finland’s Ministry of Defence said it is investigating the incident as a possible violation of Finnish territory, with the Border Guard and police working to determine the drone’s origin and how it reached the shoreline. Two officials told Finnish broadcaster Yle they now believe the drone is Russian, a shift from authorities’ initial description of it only as a surveying aircraft that posed no danger.
The Geoscan 701 is a civilian fixed-wing drone designed for aerial photography and mapping. It launches from a catapult, lands by parachute, and can fly for up to 10 hours and cover as much as 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) on a single flight, according to the manufacturer. The aircraft has a maximum takeoff weight of 22 kilograms (49 pounds) and a wingspan of about 3.3 meters (11 feet). Geoscan markets the drone for civilian survey work, including projects in Siberia, the Russian Arctic and Antarctica.
Stubb said the discovery fits into what he called a “new normal” Finland must prepare for, and warned that hybrid attacks, including sabotage, cyberattacks and information warfare, are likely to increase. He said Russia’s aim is to make Europeans afraid.
Finland has reported a string of drone incidents through 2026, most involving stray Ukrainian drones that drifted off course during Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure along the Gulf of Finland. In late March, Finnish officials confirmed drones that landed near Kouvola came from Ukraine, and an F/A-18 Hornet was scrambled to identify one aircraft as a Ukrainian AN-196 drone. A separate drone crossed into Finnish airspace near Virolahti in May. Not every incident has been tied to Ukraine, however; the Pellinki find is the latest case where Finnish authorities have pointed to a Russian origin instead.
Finland has moved to build up its counter-drone defenses over the past year. In December, the Finnish Armed Forces confirmed they had purchased hundreds of SkyWiper Omni Max jamming devices from Lithuanian manufacturer NT Service, intended to block drone control and navigation signals around critical infrastructure such as military bases.
Finnish authorities have not said when the investigation into the Pellinki drone will conclude or whether they can determine how it reached Finnish territory.

daniel arsham turns barley grains into moving sculpture for the balvenie at frieze seoul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:43:15 UTC
20:43:15 KST

daniel arsham TIME-WORNs BRONZE sculpture for the balvenie
A circular bed of grain welcomes designboom to the floor of Space S50 in Seongdong-gu, Seoul. Four performers move within the material, gathering, spreading, and reshaping the loose barley using sweeping, continuous gestures. Choreographed by Sukyung Yoo to a soundscape recorded inside The Balvenie distillery, the eight-part performance translates the manual labor of turning grain on a traditional malting floor into kinetic art. Conceptualised by artist Daniel Arsham, the live performance marks the debut of The 1931 Collection, created by the Speyside whiskey maker and unveiled during Frieze Seoul 2026.
daniel arsham’s circular bed of barley grains becomes a canvas for movement during frieze seoul 2026
the installation at space s50 references traditional techniques inside the balvenie’s historic home malting floor
The performative installation centers on a specific historical milestone for The Balvenie. In 1931, the whiskey maker opened its Home Malting Floor — a space that remains functional today. That same year, workers filled a European oak sherry butt from Jerez, Spain, labeled cask #239. The spirit matured for eighty-eight years until Malt Master Kelsey McKechnie bottled seventeen decanters in 2019. Rather than presenting the liquid within standard glasswork, Arsham developed an architectural vessel that treats the decades-long maturation process as a physical, geological transformation.
The Balvenie opened its Home Malting Floor — a space that remains functional today – in 1931
Daniel aArsham inspects malt during a research visit to the distillery in Speyside, Scotland
images courtesy of The Balvenie
eight layers of hand-patinated bronze and eighty-eight of oak
The sculpture housing the 88-year-old single malt is built as a split vessel made of contrasting industrial and natural materials. Its front fascia comprises eight flowing layers — each representing a decade of aging — cast in hand-patinated bronze. The surface treatment reproduces the verdigris textures and oxidation that naturally occur over time on copper stills.
The back half of the sculptural form consists of 88 layered sections of oak. Positioned at the core of the piece is a round copper disc salvaged directly from a decommissioned distillery still. Inside this enclosure sits a hand-blown crystal decanter detailed with 18-karat gold gilding and topped with a stopper shaped after the distillery’s copper pot stills.
‘At The Balvenie, I encountered a spirit that has been carefully shaped by generations of people who have protected and refined their craft, while remaining deeply connected to their origins,‘ artist Daniel Arsham explains. ‘Much of my work explores time, material transformation and the histories that objects carry. This collaboration has brought these themes together naturally; I wanted to create something that feels both ancient and contemporary, to make the passage of time tangible.‘
Arsham and malt master Kelsey McKechnie introduce the project alongside the immersive installation in Seoul
liquid expressions of the balvenie: the 1931 collection
The visual language of the central sculpture extends to two additional limited-edition releases within The 1931 Collection: a Twelve-Year-Old and a Fifteen-Year-Old single malt. Both expression packages feature heavily debossed exterior surfaces with green verdigris undertones fading into warm copper hues. Inside, a textured copper-colored substrate lines the box, referencing the raw metals of the production floor.
The Fifteen-Year-Old expression relies on 100 percent home-grown and home-malted barley, matured in American oak before finishing in ex-sherry European oak butts from Jerez. The Twelve-Year-Old mirrors the technical maturation process of cask #239, combining home-malted barley with the same sherry finish.
The installation at Space S50 transitions visitors, like designboom, from the live grain performance into an adjoining gallery space displaying Arsham’s bronze relic, accompanied by guided tastings led by McKechnie. Following its initial showing during Frieze Seoul, the performance and collection will travel to New York, Shanghai, and Taipei.
the eight-layered bronze fascia patinas over time, mirroring oxidation on the distillery’s copper stills | image courtesy of The Balvenie
at the sculpture’s core lies a central copper disc cut from a decommissioned distillery still

At the same time, he stressed that Ukraine expects a new dynamic in its engagement with the United States on peace efforts.
"And we expect, I repeat, a new dynamic with our American partners in the peace efforts. We are currently engaged in an active dialogue with them, and I hope this dynamic will be achieved in the short term," the minister said.
The Kyiv Independent reported, citing its own sources, that U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had planned to visit Moscow and Kyiv on September 5-6.
