A longer exhale may push your brain toward bolder decisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:33:12 UTC
20:33:12 KST

A longer exhale may push your brain toward bolder decisions
- Date:
- September 4, 2026
- Source:
- German Center for Diabetes Research (DZD)
- Summary:
- Slow breathing with a prolonged exhale made people more willing to take risks by changing heart activity and increasing the brain’s sensitivity to rewards. The findings suggest that something as simple as controlling your breath can directly influence how you evaluate choices.
- Share:
A new study suggests that deliberately changing the rhythm of your breathing can influence how you make decisions by altering activity in both the heart and brain. Researchers from the German Institute of Human Nutrition Potsdam-Rehbruecke (DIfE) and Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin found that longer exhalations increased heart rate variability and made the brain more responsive to rewards, which was associated with bolder choices. The findings were published in Neuron.
Fast breathing and an elevated heart rate are often linked with rapid decision-making. Under pressure, people may become more cautious in an effort to avoid losses, whether they are making an investment, handling a tense workplace situation, or choosing a meal quickly. Slower breathing and a calmer cardiovascular state, by contrast, may encourage a more positive assessment of potential outcomes and make people more willing to take risks.
How Breathing Connects the Body and Brain
Decision-making has traditionally been viewed as a process centered mainly in the brain. The new research examined a broader possibility: that signals from other parts of the body can change brain activity and influence the choices people make.
The study was led by Prof. Soyoung Q Park in collaboration with researchers from institutions including the Neuroscience Research Center at Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Freie Universität Berlin, and the German Naval Institute of Maritime Medicine.
"Our decisions are rarely determined solely by external information. Rather, our judgment emerges from the interplay between cognitive processes and our current bodily state. It was previously unknown how the conscious regulation of our body, for example through targeted breathing, could actively control our decision-making process. We wanted to create a physiological shift using a slow breathing pattern to change the quality of our decisions," explains Soyoung Q Park, head of the Department of Decision Neuroscience and Nutrition at DIfE, summarizing the research question.
Testing Whether Longer Exhales Change Decisions
The researchers studied 41 healthy participants while they made risky choices under carefully controlled breathing conditions. Participants followed visual breathing instructions and either breathed at their normal individual pace or slowed their breathing while extending the exhalation phase (2:8 inhale-exhale ratio).
As the participants completed a series of risk-related decisions, the research team measured several aspects of their physical and neurological responses. Functional magnetic resonance imaging was used to track brain activity, while breathing patterns, heart activity, skin conductance, and pupil responses were monitored at the same time.
This combination of measurements allowed the researchers to test whether extending the exhale did more than simply lower heart rate. They also wanted to determine whether the breathing pattern directly changed how the brain processed potential rewards.
Longer Exhalation Shifted Choices Toward Reward
The results showed that extended exhalation slowed heart rate and was associated with riskier choices. Importantly, the change appeared to come from greater attention to possible rewards rather than reduced concern about potential losses. Participants still responded to losses in a similar way.
The researchers also detected stronger activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the precuneus. These brain regions are involved in reward processing and in regulating the timing between heartbeats, a measure known as heart rate variability.
"Our study thus underscores the transformative role of breath-based interventions. The interplay between breathing and cardiac dynamics makes the brain more receptive to rewards," explains lead author Wenhao Huang, interpreting the results.
What the Findings Could Mean for Breathing Techniques
The work adds to a growing field focused on body-brain communication and supports neurovisceral models, which propose that a person's physical state can strongly shape cognitive processes.
Park explains: "Breathing techniques have accompanied humanity for millennia across various religions and cultures. With this study, we provide scientific proof that it is a reliable and targeted method capable of controlling our decisions."
Because controlled breathing is simple, inexpensive, and relatively easy to learn, the researchers say it could have value as a tool for everyday self-regulation. It may also have potential as a supportive, non-pharmacological approach in clinical settings, particularly for conditions such as anxiety disorders or depression, which can involve disrupted autonomic regulation and altered responses to reward.
Could Breathing Influence Eating Behavior?
Future studies will need to determine whether the same effects appear in broader clinical populations, including people with overweight. The researchers are particularly interested in whether breathing techniques could influence food-related decisions, since eating behavior is strongly affected by both reward processing and a person's physical state.
"Since dietary decisions are strongly influenced by reward assessment and physical state, targeted breath regulation could also play a role in consciously perceiving and more effectively managing eating behavior," Park summarizes for future research activities.
This study was supported by the Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space [Grant 01GP2210C (DecEnt-Project), Grant 01EE2301E for the conceptual development of the German Center for Mental Health; Grant 82DZD03D03 (German Center for Diabetes Research)], the Ministry for Science, Research and Culture of the State of Brandenburg (MWFK). Ignacio Rebollo was supported by the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Action (MSCA) BRAINSTOM (grant agreement no. 101028203).
Story Source:
Materials provided by German Center for Diabetes Research (DZD). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Wenhao Huang, Mine Schmidt, Ignacio Rebollo, Felix Molter, Min Pu, Beatrix Keweloh, Lok Yan Lam, Peter N.C. Mohr, Gabriele Bellucci, Stefan Röttger, Soyoung Q. Park. Slow breathing impacts inter-organ dynamics modulating brain function and risk behavior. Neuron, 2026; DOI: 10.1016/j.neuron.2026.04.044

Concrete Land: Asmahan Bkerat on Palestine, land and belonging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:32:10 UTC
20:32:10 KST

Breadcrumb
Asmahan Bkerat's Concrete Land captures a Palestinian Bedouin family's disappearing homeland
For eight years, Palestinian-Jordanian filmmaker Asmahan Bkerat followed a Palestinian Bedouin family as the land beneath their lives was gradually swallowed by concrete.
What began as a friendship eventually turned into Concrete Land, her debut feature documentary, created from more than 400 hours of footage and two years of editing.
The film, which was recently presented at the Critics' Week section of the Locarno Film Festival, follows three generations confronting displacement, contested identity and the disappearance of the landscape that has anchored their lives.
Originally Afro-Palestinian Bedouins from the Negev Desert, the family was displaced from Palestine after Israeli occupation and eventually settled in Jordan, where they continued their traditional life as shepherds and farmers.
Along the journey, their situation remains precarious, caught between Palestinian and Jordanian identities, Bedouin tradition and urban development, and memories of a homeland and an uncertain future.
For Asmahan, the story is about what happens long after displacement, when exile has passed but the question of where and how to belong remains unresolved.
"Once you lose your land and home, you lose a big part of yourself," she tells The New Arab. "And it's devastating."
Asmahan did not initially set out to become a documentary filmmaker. With a background in business information systems, and while working as a photographer and social-justice advocate, she spent years listening, observing, and returning to her family, which eventually led her to find her direction behind the camera.
Her first short documentary, Badrya (2017), won the Jury Prize for Best MiniDoc at the Sebastopol Documentary Film Festival.
She subsequently developed Concrete Land as her first feature, with support from organisations and programmes including IDFA, Sundance, and Doha Film Institute.
"I think I learned how to become a filmmaker through this film," she adds.
A minority within a minority
The family's community, once isolated from Amman, is now surrounded by the city's expansion. Yet moving further away is not a simple solution, as proximity to the city means access to education for the younger generation.
"If they remove themselves, if they get away from the city, they lose access to the school," Asmahan explains. "And they're trying to keep access to the school for the children."
Their Palestinian Bedouin identity further complicates access to land, leaving them outside the structures through which Jordanian Bedouin communities have historically accessed it.
Israel's current war in Gaza added another dimension. Part of the extended family fled there after being displaced from Palestine, while another branch ended up in Jordan.
"Unfortunately, they lost their family in Gaza; a big part of it is gone," Asmahan explains.
For the younger generation, the war sharpened their understanding of their own history.
"The war changes children's awareness," she explains. "They start to understand what it means to be Palestinian, to be a refugee, to be attached to a homeland that does not exist."
That raises a question extending beyond this family.
"Refugee stories are abundant," Asmahan continues. "There are so many refugees every single day. But we don't know what happens to them. Who asks, did you integrate into society? Were you able to get a good life?"
A friendship before a film
When Asmahan first met the family, she wasn't looking for a documentary subject. She had previously lived near the area and one day drove out of Amman with her colleague Ban Maraqa, who would later become the film’s co-producer, editor and co-writer.
"Amman is such a crowded city," Asmahan recalls. "It's like this. No space, no air, nothing."
Looking for somewhere to have tea and coffee, they saw an old woman walking with her sheep. "We were like, ‘Oh my god, what is this? How is there an old woman and the sheep walking?’ It was so unusual."
They approached her and were invited into her tent. "We were very surprised because we didn't see the tents at first. It was just the big white buildings. And as we walked, the building separated, and we saw the tents."
At the time, Asmahan had little understanding of documentary filmmaking. "I wasn't a filmmaker," she says. "I was interested in film. But I had no idea what a documentary film was. Observation, nothing, zero."
The relationship came first. "It was a friendship before it was a film," she confirms.
When the construction arrived
The project began as a nine-minute short, but its direction changed when construction started around the family’s land.
"When the construction started, we went to the guy who was building, and we said, 'Are you okay with the family here? Or are you going to ask them to leave?'" Asmahan recalls.
The answer was that they would have to go. "So my colleague Ban and I approached the family: ‘How about we just film what’s happening? Maybe it will change something. We can at least document where you were and where you’re going to end up.’"
Asmahan met the family in 2016, made the short in 2017 and began shooting Concrete Land in 2018. The filmmakers eventually accumulated more than 400 hours of footage.
"I think I can make an entire series out of the material that I have," Asmahan jokes. "Because I was there constantly. I was almost there four times a week for years. And if I wasn't there, Ban would replace me.
"We had a room full of storage just for the material of the film, much more than needed," she clarifies. "The film is purely observational, with no staged events."
Asmahan discovered that an observational documentary could use the dramatic structure of fiction.
"The idea of structuring a documentary film like a fiction one was a completely foreign idea to me," she explains. "I had no idea that it was possible. And that documentary film could follow the rules of fiction in the editing."
Ban helped organise the archive. "We had a huge Excel sheet, organising the material by date, name, character and event." From there, Ban built the film's three-act structure.
"Sometimes we would say, okay, we have something missing here. Maybe we should shoot a family conversation or have some elements that are complementary to what we have right now."
The meaning of lost land
The grandfather – the oldest family member whom we encounter yet in the melancholic opening – gradually emerged as the film's emotional centre, although Asmahan initially found him difficult to approach.
"I was scared of him at the beginning," she admits. "I was not approaching him as we were mutually avoiding each other."
Over time, the camera became a space where he could express feelings he struggled to communicate elsewhere.
"He found an escape in the camera, like a place for him to vent his feelings. Because he thought, like, nobody was listening to him. And nobody wants to be around him," Asmahan elaborates.
His attachment to his sheep became central to understanding him. They represent his livelihood, purpose and connection to a disappearing way of life.
"His purpose in life was the sheep; he cannot live without them," Asmahan says. "He wanted to get more sheep and be with them and graze them. But that was taken away from him."
When the sheep are lost, so is something larger. For Asmahan, his story became a metaphor for the loss of land and Palestine, the meaning of land and the relationship to the land: "He reflects Palestine most, in a way, for me."
The sheep also became an unlikely source of humour during editing. "How do you keep the sheep? Because in many, many cuts, we lost the sheep and spent a lot of time to bring them back."
The humour is part of the film’s refusal to reduce the family to suffering. Everyday life remains alongside displacement and loss, despite the deliberately slow pace.
Concrete against land
The title brings together the film’s opposing forces. "Land is something that's living," Asmahan says. "And concrete is dead."
Around the family, that transformation has become increasingly stark. "There's no greenery. There are no parks. Nothing. It's a very dry land."
Asmahan remains particularly critical of the destruction of agricultural areas in Jordan: "Jordan is one percent forest. And all of it is desert. And the government wants to destroy agricultural land. What are they even thinking?"
The Arabic title, Tiyaha, adds another layer: "It refers to people who are lost. Who can find no place to belong to."
A camera built on trust
The family’s openness to the camera was essential to the film. Asmahan believes it stemmed from their sense of making it together.
"All the members were amazing," she tells The New Arab. "I think it’s because it was a collaborative decision to make the film together. So they were part of the decision process."
With time, the camera has integrated into everyday life. The grandmother particularly embraced it: "She loves the camera," Asmahan shares. "She and her sheep, they're divas."
The grandfather, initially the most difficult to approach, eventually became "the most accessible" family member.
That trust allowed Asmahan and Ban to capture change without staged scenes or conventional interviews: construction, ageing, family tensions, loss and shifts in the younger generation's understanding of Palestine.
A sense of home and community
Asmahan is now producing two films and developing her next feature, which will again explore displacement, this time through the lens of an Indigenous community in southern Jordan.
"I care about what it means to have a home, identity, and displacement. It’s something I deeply care about," she tells The New Arab.
She is also working with colleagues across West Asia and North Africa to establish a regional documentary association.
"We don't have one. There's one for Europe, one for America, an international one, but not in our WANA region – West Asia and North Africa."
For Asmahan, the project is part of a wider commitment to documentary cinema and to creating space for stories that might otherwise remain unseen.
"In general, I’m trying to build a life that stays in documentary. Hopefully."
Mariana Hristova is a freelance film critic, cultural journalist, and programmer. She contributes to national and international outlets and has curated programs for Filmoteca de Catalunya, Arxiu Xènctric, and goEast Wiesbaden, among others. Her professional interests include cinema from the European peripheries and archival and amateur films

The Economic Security Bureau cannot independently establish new taxation rules - lawyer
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:31:32 EEST
20:31:32 KST

The Economic Security Bureau cannot independently establish new taxation rules - lawyer
Kyiv • UNN
The Economic Security Bureau interprets aircraft leasing as royalties and has opened cases against airlines. The lawyer emphasized: the final decision on taxation is made by the court.
The Bureau of Economic Security may formulate its own legal position on the taxation of particular transactions and use it in criminal proceedings. However, such a position does not change the legislation, create new tax obligations, or constitute a binding consideration for the court. Lawyer Rostyslav Kravets expressed this view in a comment to UNN.
The BES interprets aircraft leasing as royalties
As UNN previously reported, in 2024 the Bureau of Economic Security began interpreting transactions involving the leasing of air transport from non-residents of Ukraine as the use of equipment. According to the investigators’ version, Ukrainian air carriers were supposed to pay royalties for leasing aircraft and helicopters.
In connection with this, the BES opened criminal proceedings against at least 5 air carriers, including MAU, "Constanta Airlines," "Windrose," N3Operations, and "Skyline Express." According to UNN, another airline — "Urga" — may also figure in a similar case.
The criminal proceedings were opened despite the fact that almost all air carriers had successfully passed tax inspections, and the tax authorities’ only leasing-related objections concerned one company.
Representatives of the aviation industry insist that the problem arose because of an ambiguous interpretation of the legislation and requires the establishment of a unified state approach.
In response to a request from UNN, the Ministry of Finance reported that the taxation of aircraft leasing transactions is carried out in accordance with the Tax Code and Ukraine’s international treaties. At the same time, the Tax Code of Ukraine does not provide for the possibility of taxing aircraft leasing as royalties. Therefore, the Bureau’s approach to interpreting aircraft leasing without changing the tax legislation is described as pressure that could destroy the entire passenger and freight transportation industry. After all, according to data from the State Register of Civil Aircraft of Ukraine, 86% of the aircraft fleet of Ukrainian companies is leased.
That is why the issue of aircraft leasing was submitted for consideration by the Tax Committee of the Public Council under the Ministry of Finance. Following the first meeting, it was decided to initiate the establishment of a working group under the Ministry of Finance, which is to develop a draft generalized tax consultation on the taxation of lease payments made to non-residents.
The BES’s position is not a new provision of law
Lawyer Rostyslav Kravets explains that, as a law enforcement agency, the BES has the right to analyze the circumstances of a specific case and formulate its own legal assessment of companies’ actions. In particular, if the Bureau believes that certain transactions indicate possible tax evasion, the relevant conclusions may be used to substantiate the investigators’ position.
However, the lawyer emphasizes that it is essential to distinguish between the position of a law enforcement agency and a provision of legislation.
As a law enforcement agency, the BES cannot change the law or establish new taxation rules through its conclusions. Ultimately, it is the court that interprets the law. Therefore, the court is not obliged to agree with the legal assessment provided by the BES
He added that the Bureau’s own interpretation of the legislation may be sufficient for carrying out certain procedural actions. However, this does not mean that the law enforcement officers’ conclusions are automatically correct from a legal standpoint.
In addition, Kravets recalled that the relevant procedural documents prepared by the investigators must be approved by a prosecutor, who will subsequently represent the prosecution in court.
This issue is of particular importance in the situation involving the taxation of lease payments made by Ukrainian airlines to foreign owners of aircraft. As already mentioned, the BES interprets such payments as royalties.
According to Kravets, it is incorrect to conclude how the relevant payments should be taxed solely on the basis of the Bureau’s position. The mere fact that a law enforcement agency interprets tax legislation in a particular way does not mean that this interpretation should automatically be applied to businesses.
The final assessment is made by the court
As the lawyer explained, if the case proceeds to a substantive court hearing, the court will take into account the arguments of both parties, judicial practice, academic research, and other materials. At the same time, the conclusions of the Economic Security Bureau (ESB) do not have predetermined force for the court.
No conclusion of the ESB in itself is binding on the court and may not replace the law. It is the court that has the final say on how the relevant provision of legislation should be applied in a particular case
Thus, the ESB’s right to investigate possible tax crimes does not grant the Bureau the authority to independently create new taxation rules. If a law enforcement agency considers a particular transaction to be subject to taxation, this position must undergo review in accordance with the procedure established by law, and if the matter is considered on its merits, the court will have the final say.

Tehran plays host to Royan Intl. Twin Congress
TEHRAN – The Royan International Twin Congress, including the 27th Congress on Reproductive Biomedicine, the 22nd Congress on Stem Cell Biology and Technology, and the 21st seminar on Nursery and Midwifery, was held from Wednesday to Friday.
Bringing together Iranian and international researchers and specialists, the three-day event was held in person and online, providing a great opportunity to examine the latest scientific achievements in infertility treatment, assisted reproductive technologies, regenerative medicine, cell-based and gene-based therapies, and novel applications of artificial intelligence in biomedicine, IRNA reported.
This year, a total of 447 articles out of 589 submitted articles were accepted to be presented, including 197 posters and 7 articles in the Reproductive Biomedicine Congress, 186 posters and nine articles in the Stem Cell Biology and Technology Congress, and 45 posters and three lectures in the Nursery and Midwifery Seminar.
This degree of scientific participation has established the Royan Congress as a prominent specialized forum in the fields of reproductive medicine and stem cells—an event that, beyond showcasing research findings, fosters connections among researchers, clinicians, and professionals in the technology and therapeutic sectors.
The 27th Congress on Reproductive Biomedicine hosted 31 lecturers, including eight from England, Australia, Belgium, Russia, Italy, Germany, and Switzerland, who attended the event online. Out of 34 lecturers addressing the 22nd Congress on Stem Cell Biology and Technology, 14 were from Turkey, Russia, Malaysia, Canada, the US, and the Netherlands. Moreover, 19 Iranian scholars delivered lectures at the 21st seminar on Nursery and Midwifery.
 
 In the 21st seminar on Nursery and Midwifery, the main themes focused on:
 
 • The Latest Achievements in Infertility
 
 • Reproductive Health Screening in Patients with Poor Ovarian Response
 
 • Examining the health of patients with premature ovarian failure
 
 • Donation in Infertility
 
 • Complementary Medicine and Infertility
 
 • The Impact of Environmental, Cultural and Occupational Factors and Lifestyle on ART Results
 
 • Emotional, Psychological and Sexual Changes in Infertility Treatment and Management
 
 • The Role of Counseling and Training in the Treatment of Infertile Couples
 
 • Familiarity with the Methods of Fertility Preservation in Women and Men
 
 • Management and Treatment of Recurrent Abortion
 
 • Managing the Evaluation of Patients with Recurrent Implant Failure
 
 • Prenatal Care After ART
 
 • Managing The Process of Support and Recovery in the Occurrence of Infertility Treatment Complications
 
 • Nursing and Midwifery Interventions in New Infertility Techniques
 
 • Endometriosis and Reproductive Health  
 
 • Evaluating the Health of Children Resulting from ART Treatments
 
 • Application of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Health Technologies in Infertility Management and Treatment
 
 • Genetics and Infertility
 
 • Prevention of Influential Factors in Infertility
 
 • Evaluating the Effect of Couples' Participation in Improving the Treatment Process
In 2025, out of 600 submitted articles, 514 were accepted. The event hosted 22 lecturers from 19 foreign countries, including Germany (Prof. Janems Adjaye), Qatar (Dr. Mohammad Mostafa Arafa), France (Prof. Laurent David), Austria (Dr. Victori Deneke), Spain (Dr. Nicholas Garrido Pushalt), Italy (Dr. Local Gianiroli), Japan (Prof. Kazuhiro Kawamura), Russia (Dr. Daria Kuznetsova), New Zealand (Prof. Bjorn Oback), and China (Dr. Zhen Liu), as well as 59 national lecturers.
Eight specialized workshops and a pre-congress symposium on obesity, infertility, and Sanger Sequencing methods were held on the sidelines of the event.
Royan Institute
Royan Institute was established in 1991 by the late Dr. Saeid Kazemi Ashtiani and a group of researchers and physicians at the Iran University of Medical Sciences of the Academic Center for Education, Culture, and Research (ACECR) as an outpatient surgery center to provide medical services to infertile couples, as well as research and training in reproductive sciences.
Reproductive Biomedicine and Stem Cells Biology and Technology has been demonstrated to be one of the most successful experiences of scientific gathering in Iran and West Asia since 2000.
In 2002, the research fields at Royan Institute also extended into stem cell studies. Afterward, the research findings were adjusted for application in regenerative medicine and cell therapy approaches. After three decades, the Royan Institute focuses on increasing the success rate of infertility treatment alongside embryo health and the level of public health through cell therapy clinical services.
During these twenty years of active involvement in sharing and exchanging scientific knowledge and expertise with renowned scientific institutes and scientists, the Royan Congress has helped to form many shared scientific projects and exchanges.

Over 80 earthquakes hit Iran in a week

Unknown Publisher

Over 80 earthquakes hit Iran in a week
TEHRAN – A total of 81 earthquakes have been recorded across the country in a week from August 22 to 28, according to the seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran.
Statistically, 73 earthquakes with magnitudes smaller than 3, and eight earthquakes with a magnitude between 3 and 4 have occurred in the country, irsc reported.
Of the total quakes, one had a magnitude of 3.8 on the Richter scale, which occurred on August 25th in Lorestan province.
Among the provinces of the country, Semnan experienced the highest number of earthquakes with 14, followed by Khorasan Razavi with 11, and North Khorasan with 8 earthquakes.
During the same period, two earthquakes hit Tehran. No earthquakes were recorded in East Azarbaijan, West Azarbaijan, Alborz, Bushehr, Chaharmahal-Bakhtiari, Zanjan, Sistan-Baluchestan, Qom, Qazvin, Kordestan, Kohgiluyeh-Boyerahmad, Markazi, and Hamedan provinces.
A total of 2,380 earthquakes with a magnitude of more than 2.5 on the Richter scale were recorded across the country over the past calendar year (March 2025–March 2026), according to the Seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran, Mehr news agency reported.
Out of recorded earthquakes, 910 had a magnitude greater than 3, 130 had a magnitude greater than 4, and 15 had a magnitude greater than 5 on the Richter scale.
The Iranian plateau is located in a very seismically active region of the world and is known not only for its major catastrophic earthquakes but also for the disasters relating to natural hazards, especially earthquakes.
About 2 percent of the earthquakes in the world occur in Iran, but more than 6 percent of the victims of the world’s earthquakes during the 20th century are reported from Iranian earthquakes.

Members of an Israeli-backed militia infiltrated the home of a Palestinian in the town of Al-Qarara, north of Khan Younis, abducted him, tied him up, and executed him, local and medical sources told Anadolu.
A medical source said the body of Fadi al-Abadla, 31, arrived at Nasser Hospital with his hands tied.

Since 2025, Israel has expanded its reliance on armed militias inside Gaza, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu admitted in June that year that Israel had armed some groups based on recommendations from security agencies.
The militias are deployed in several parts of Gaza, including Beit Hanoun and Shujaiya in the north, Deir al-Balah in central Gaza, and Khan Younis and Rafah in the south, mostly inside areas occupied by the Israeli army or near its positions.

Feature: New York forum highlights people-to-people ties between China, U.S.
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:21:20 CST
20:21:20 KST

People attend the forum themed "Our Shared Expectations: Conversation on China-U.S. Relations" in New York City, the United States, Sept. 2, 2026. From social media and student exchanges to memories of the Flying Tigers, personal stories featured prominently at a local forum Wednesday, where more than 150 representatives from U.S. business, education and academia explored ways to strengthen China-U.S. ties. Hosted by the Chinese Consulate General in New York, the forum, themed "Our Shared Expectations: Conversation on China-U.S. Relations," focused on people-to-people exchanges and cooperation between the two countries. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo)
by Xinhua writer Shi Chun
NEW YORK, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- From social media and student exchanges to memories of the Flying Tigers, personal stories featured prominently at a local forum Wednesday, where more than 150 representatives from U.S. business, education and academia explored ways to strengthen China-U.S. ties.
Hosted by the Chinese Consulate General in New York, the forum, themed "Our Shared Expectations: Conversation on China-U.S. Relations," focused on people-to-people exchanges and cooperation between the two countries.
Andrew Cap, an English teacher and content creator, recounted his journey from a student who studied in China ten years ago to an online influencer sharing Chinese culture with American audiences.
"U.S. younger generations want to see real people on the ground in China, and that's an opportunity for social media where you can show them real, authentic China," he said.
For Clifford Long Jr., vice chairman of the Sino-American Aviation Heritage Foundation, his connection with China reaches back to a wartime bond forged by his father, a member of the Flying Tigers.
Formed in 1941, the U.S. air units fought alongside Chinese forces against Japanese aggression during World War II.
"The Flying Tigers wouldn't work without the Chinese people," Long said.
Today, Long is helping promote that legacy to a new generation. "We're passing this history along to kids," he said.
Kate Sullivan, executive director of the Greater Columbus Chinese Chamber of Commerce, drew on her own experiences of traveling to China to underscore the value of people-to-people connections.
"The more times I travel to China, the more impactful parts of my experience have been bonding with the Chinese," she said.
Sullivan urged concrete steps to expand exchanges and enhance mutual understanding and confidence between the two countries, viewing such ties as a foundation for mutually beneficial cooperation and new business opportunities.
Chen Li, Chinese consul general in New York, described such connections between the two peoples as a deeper force underpinning the bilateral relationship.
He opened his remarks with the story of Ronald Sakolsky, an American who once taught English in China and helped Chinese farmer Yin Yuzhen plant trees in the Maowusu Desert.
"China and the United States differ in many ways. But before nationality, political systems or other labels, we are all human beings," Chen said. "People in both countries want stable lives and fulfilling careers. They want a good education for their children and a better future for their families. They want their countries to prosper and the world to remain at peace."
"The root of China-U.S. relations is in the hearts of our people. When the root is deep, our relationship can survive any storm," he said. ■

Xi's cultural journey through museums
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:21:05 CST
20:21:05 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- On the Giza Plateau, the majestic pyramids, silent witnesses to millennia of history, now gaze across at the Grand Egyptian Museum.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, visited the museum on Wednesday during his state visit to Egypt, where they were warmly received by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and his wife.
Surrounded by ancient artifacts, the two presidential couples toured the grand galleries, posing for a photo before a towering statue of Ramses II, one of the most famous pharaohs of Egypt, as curators delivered a swift primer on pharaonic history.
"This museum is a book with endless pages," Xi said.
He, during the tour, also urged the two countries to promote the inclusive coexistence and mutual learning among different civilizations, and pool greater strength from civilizations to advance the building of a community with a shared future for humanity.
As the world's largest museum dedicated to a single civilization, the Grand Egyptian Museum houses more than 100,000 precious artifacts. Locals have newly dubbed it the "fourth pyramid of Giza."
The Grand Egyptian Museum is just one of the many museums Xi has visited over the years. Whether on domestic inspection tours or overseas trips, his visits have taken him to the Sanxingdui Museum in southwest China's Sichuan province and the Yinxu Museum in central China's Henan province, key sites of early Chinese civilization, as well as the Amir Timur Museum in Uzbekistan, and the ancient Maya ruins of Chichen Itza in Mexico. The list goes on.
Such frequent museum visits stem from Xi's longstanding emphasis on preserving and carrying forward traditional culture. For Xi, museums are important places that protect and pass on human civilizations.
In November 2019, during his visit to the Acropolis Museum in Athens, Greece, Xi paused to admire the relief of the "Pensive Athena," the Greek goddess of war and wisdom. He and then Greek President Prokopis Pavlopoulos explored how ancient Chinese and Greek civilizations expressed their reflections on war and their shared longing for peace.
Museums have also been a frequent choice for Xi to present traditional Chinese culture when hosting foreign dignitaries.
During U.S. President Donald Trump's two visits to China in 2017 and 2026, Xi hosted him at the Forbidden City, or the Palace Museum, and the Temple of Heaven, respectively, using the historic sites to illustrate the Chinese philosophy of pursuing peace and harmony.
In Xi's eyes, museums are not simply repositories of the past. They offer people a chance to discover unfamiliar histories, recognize common threads of human creativity and gain a deeper understanding of one another.
During his first state visit to Egypt in 2016, Xi toured Luxor, a city widely known as one of the world's largest open-air museums. Walking along the main avenue of Luxor Temple, Xi and Sisi discussed the distinctive features of their two ancient civilizations, recalling their long history of exchanges and mutual learning. At the temple, they also witnessed the launch of the 2016 China-Egypt Culture Year, a landmark moment in bilateral cultural exchanges.
Today, the Grand Egyptian Museum provides a new setting for that dialogue between the two ancient civilizations. In a message to Sisi on its opening last year, Xi said that the museum will leave a profound mark on Egypt's cultural history and play an important role in preserving and passing on the ancient Egyptian civilization.
It is encouraging to see the two ancient civilizations reaching out to each other, with the two peoples growing ever closer through mutual understanding and affinity, Xi said in the message.
From Beijing to Cairo, Xi's museum visits underscore how history can bridge rather than divide civilizations, enabling them to deepen mutual understanding and draw on the wisdom of the past to shape the road ahead.
As Xi has observed, "Museums bridge the past, present, and future." ■

Xinhua Headlines: Direct Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb flight opens new gateway to Central, Eastern Europe
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:21:04 CST
20:21:04 KST

* Air China now serves 27 European destinations with nearly 260 weekly flights between the two continents, with the Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb route adding another thread to this growing network.
* For Croatia, where tourism accounts for about one-fifth of GDP, the direct flight is a long-awaited gateway to the world's largest outbound tourism market. For Romania, it restores a connection that has been absent since 2003. And for Chinese travelers, it offers a new, hassle-free entry point to the wider Balkan region.
by Xinhua writers Yao Yulin, Ma Zhen and Li Xuejun
BUCHAREST/ZAGREB, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Air China launched its maiden Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb flight on Friday, restoring direct passenger links between China and Romania after more than two decades and inaugurating the first-ever scheduled passenger service between China and Croatia.
Operating three times a week, the new route comes as Central and Eastern Europe -- known for its Adriatic coastline, medieval towns and rich cultural heritage -- is attracting growing interest from Chinese travelers. Travel has become more convenient than ever following China's unilateral visa-free policy for ordinary citizens of both Romania and Croatia.
For Croatia, where tourism accounts for about one-fifth of GDP, the direct flight is a long-awaited gateway to the world's largest outbound tourism market. For Romania, it restores a connection that has been absent since 2003. And for Chinese travelers, it offers a new, hassle-free entry point to the wider Balkan region.
VISA-FREE BENEFITS
China and Romania once enjoyed direct air links, with Air China operating the route until 1994 and Romania's TAROM taking over until its suspension in 2003. For the next 23 years, travelers had to transit through third countries, turning a straightforward journey into a half-day ordeal. The new Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb route has finally restored that missing link.
The timing is no coincidence. In November 2024, China expanded its unilateral visa-free policy to include Romania and Croatia, along with seven other countries. Ordinary passport holders from both nations can now stay in China for up to 30 days without a visa for tourism, business, family visits or transit.
The results have been striking. Around 35,000 Romanian citizens traveled to China in 2024, twice the figure recorded a year earlier. In the first seven months of 2025 alone, nearly 36,000 Romanians visited China, up 78 percent year-on-year, according to the National Association of Travel Agencies in Romania.
Dan-Horia Maxim, Romania's ambassador to China, described the restored direct flights as "a major diplomatic and economic success aimed at bringing our communities closer together" in a press release.
Chen Feng, China's ambassador to Romania, told Xinhua that the resumption of regular direct passenger flights has been a shared aspiration of the Chinese and Romanian peoples and reflects sustained joint efforts on both sides.
"It is expected to help further strengthen bilateral economic and trade cooperation, deepen cultural and people-to-people exchanges, promote mutual understanding, and inject fresh momentum into the sustained and healthy development of China-Romania relations," Chen added.
For Croatia, the numbers tell a story of promise still waiting to be fulfilled. In 2024, the country welcomed over 250,475 Chinese tourist arrivals, up more than 41 percent from the previous year. Yet that figure remains barely half of the pre-pandemic peak of some 490,000. Industry insiders view the new air link as a key step toward unlocking further growth.
Qi Qianjin, China's ambassador to Croatia, called the route "the first direct flight in the history of the two countries and the latest achievement in deepening bilateral relations," adding that it would "significantly reduce travel time and costs, further unleash cooperation potential, and promote exchanges in trade, tourism, culture, sports and people-to-people ties."
For China, the route fits into a broader pattern of deepening air connectivity with Central and Eastern Europe. Air China now serves 27 European destinations with nearly 260 weekly flights between the two continents, with the Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb route adding another thread to this growing network.
BALKAN HUB
Kristjan Stanicic, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board (CNTB), described the air link as "an important step forward" that "opens up additional opportunities for Croatian tourism to position itself more strongly on the large and promising Chinese market."
He said Croatia is reaching out to Chinese visitors "through its exceptional diversity, but also through an authentic experience of our country, the local way of life, tradition and values."
The CNTB, through its Shanghai office, plans to continue working with Chinese partners to "enable Chinese guests to get to know our homeland, its heritage and people in a quality and deeper way," Stanicic added.
Dubrovnik, Split, Zadar and the capital Zagreb remain among the most popular Croatian destinations for Chinese tourists, but industry observers believe the new route could broaden that map.
Leon Jiang, president of the Balkan Chinese Tourism Association and the Croatian Chinese Tourists Guide Association, said that direct access eliminates the inconvenience of transfers, making travel easier for both Chinese tourists heading to the Adriatic and Croatians interested in visiting China.
Romania, too, stands to benefit significantly from the restored air link as the new route responds to long-standing calls from the tourism industry and provides infrastructure to meet growing two-way travel demand.
In the first half of 2025 alone, Romania welcomed 21,682 Chinese tourists, the highest number of Asian visitors on record. With direct flights now in operation, the bottleneck that once held back the market's full potential is being removed.
Romania has been actively positioning itself to capture a larger share of the Chinese outbound market. In May, Romania made its debut at ITB China in Shanghai, one of the most important B2B travel trade events dedicated to the Chinese market. The delegation promoted destinations including Bucharest, Transylvania and the monasteries of Bucovina.
Earlier in October 2025, the China Tourism Fair was held at the Chinese Cultural Center in Bucharest, bringing together over 100 representatives from the tourism, culture and education sectors of both countries.
Zagreb's strategic location also gives the route broader regional significance. Ljubo Jurcic, professor of economics and former Croatian minister of economy, pointed out that Chinese travelers arriving in Zagreb can easily continue to Italy and Austria, while the Adriatic coast is only a short journey away.
Jurcic added that the route also signals Chinese interest in expanding cooperation with Croatia beyond tourism.
"Croatian business people have long considered China an interesting market, because China is today the largest and most influential country in the world when it comes to business," he said. "Unfortunately, Croatian business people were not turned to China in time, but today that is changing." ■

China Focus: China brings lifesaving emergency care closer to home
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:20:42 CST
20:20:42 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- A 72-year-old man suffering a heart attack recently received life-saving treatment at a rural health center in central China's Hubei Province -- a procedure that, until a few years ago, was beyond the expertise of most grassroots medical institutions.
When the man was brought to Wuli Township health center in mountainous Hefeng County, Enshi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture, doctors quickly diagnosed an acute myocardial infarction and administered intravenous thrombolysis. After his vital signs stabilized, he was transferred to a higher-level hospital for further care.
"This was the fourth emergency thrombolysis procedure since our health center set up a chest pain treatment unit," said Tian Jianbing, head of the health center.
"Cardiovascular diseases can progress rapidly and require timely intervention, making it essential to bring lifesaving capabilities to the grassroots level," said Huang Kai, a senior executive at Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University.
In remote rural or mountainous areas, where residents may live far from hospitals equipped to handle emergencies, many township medical centers previously lacked the expertise and experience to perform thrombolysis. They would often refer patients to higher-level hospitals, sometimes at the cost of precious treatment time.
To address this challenge, Hubei has in recent years established standardized chest pain treatment units at grassroots medical institutions, bringing emergency expertise, treatment protocols and quality medical resources closer to patients' homes.
Over the past five years, the province has set up 1,404 such units. A total of 320 grassroots health centers have performed nearly 3,000 thrombolysis procedures for heart attack patients. The province's mortality rate from cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases fell from 240.4 per 100,000 people in 2020 to 190.7 in 2025.
Hubei's experience is part of a broader national push to strengthen primary healthcare. In 2021, the National Health Commission (NHC) launched pilot areas for improving grassroots medical services, focusing on tasks such as bolstering the primary care workforce and enhancing service capacity. To date, 12 national pilot areas have been established, and 20 provinces have launched 186 provincial-level pilot areas.
One of the national pilots, Suixi County in east China's Anhui Province, has in recent years focused on building a more coordinated grassroots emergency response network.
The county has integrated its emergency dispatch center with two sub-centers run by county-level medical consortia and 14 grassroots emergency stations, creating a three-tier emergency network covering the county, towns and villages.
In 2025, the network handled 18,000 emergency transfers, with ambulances dispatched within three minutes in 99 percent of cases. The average response time was about 12 minutes.
Suixi County People's Hospital has established five specialized emergency and critical care centers covering chest pain, stroke, trauma, critically ill pregnant women, and critically ill children and newborns. In 2025, the hospital handled 8,991 cases involving emergency and critical care patients.
The hospital has also strengthened coordination between pre-hospital and in-hospital emergency care. When a patient is transferred from a grassroots facility, medical information is transmitted in real time to the hospital's emergency center via a pre-hospital emergency platform.
Doctors at the center can provide remote video guidance to grassroots staff as they treat the patient in the ambulance, while an emergency "green channel" is activated at the hospital, ensuring the patient is admitted and treated without delay.
As grassroots emergency networks are strengthened, localities are also turning to technology to improve response efficiency. In Zhangjiajie, a mountainous tourist city in central China's Hunan Province, a unified emergency medical command and dispatch system integrates Beidou satellite positioning, electronic mapping, vehicle monitoring and real-time information on hospital emergency resources.
The system automatically identifies callers' locations and helps dispatchers assign the nearest available ambulance based on real-time traffic conditions and hospital capacity. Ambulance routes and patients' vital signs can be transmitted to receiving hospitals, allowing medical teams to prepare in advance and linking pre-hospital with in-hospital care.
"Dispatching now relies on data, making it faster and more accurate," said an official with the municipal health authority.
These efforts reflect China's broader push to strengthen primary healthcare. Official data show that primary-level medical institutions -- including township health centers and village clinics in rural areas, as well as community health centers and stations in urban areas -- grew from 882,000 in 2009 to nearly 1.06 million in 2025, accounting for more than 95 percent of all medical institutions nationwide.
By 2025, compact county-level medical consortia had been established in 2,199 counties, with more than 70,000 county-level hospital staff deployed to grassroots institutions. Remote diagnostic centers for medical imaging and electrocardiography had been set up in more than 90 percent of counties.
The push will continue under a three-year action plan (2026-2028) launched by the NHC, which calls for improving the quality of primary care services, including strengthening emergency and critical care capacity, upgrading facilities and equipment, improving early identification and initial treatment of critically ill patients, and enhancing coordination with higher-level hospitals. ■

====================================================================================================

Researchers in Australia uncover pathway controlling timing of brain development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
19:20:26 CST
20:20:26 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have uncovered a critical signaling pathway that controls the timing of brain development, shedding new light on how neurodevelopmental disorders may develop.
The research, led by Australia's Murdoch Children's Research Institute (MCRI) and published in Nature Communications, revealed genetic processes that shape brain development and what can happen when they are disrupted, according to a MCRI statement released on Thursday.
"The brain develops rapidly before birth, and cells must receive the right instructions at the right time in order to move to the correct place to develop properly. We have uncovered new clues about one of the brain's most important developmental switches," said MCRI Research Associate Ryan Leung.
Using genomic techniques, researchers tracked how thousands of genes shape the developing brain. They used mice genetically engineered to lack DLX1 and DLX2, two key genes that control how brain cells form, move, and survive.
Leung said DLX2 acts like a "traffic controller" during early brain development, ensuring young brain cells become neurons at the right time while preventing them from prematurely developing into specialized support cells.
"When these genes were removed, we saw changes in how these cells developed and where they were located in the brain," Leung said. The team also found previously unidentified subregions of the developing forebrain, revealing how the location of cells impacts their development.
MCRI Neuro-oncology Group Leader Professor David Eisenstat said the findings could inform future research into childhood brain cancers and neurodevelopmental disorders, as many of the same molecular pathways are disrupted in childhood brain tumors, including high-grade gliomas. ■

Details

At present, based on the evidence collected, investigators have notified two suspects, aged 16 and 17, who have reached the age of criminal responsibility, of suspicion under Part 2 of Article 127 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — torture committed by a group of persons by prior conspiracy against a minor.
It should be noted that this crime is punishable by imprisonment for a term of five to ten years. The pre-trial investigation is ongoing

IRCS keeps supporting Afghan children facing malnutrition
TEHRAN – A medical center affiliated with the Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) operates in Zaranj, Afghanistan, providing ongoing medical care for children suffering from malnutrition.
The IRCS health center in Zaranj offers health services, monitors children’s nutritional status, and distributes nutritional supplies among the target group. Given the current situation in Afghanistan and the number of children grappling with malnutrition, the main objective is the early identification and treatment to prevent the further development of nutritional issues among children.
The health center, in cooperation with Relief International and local medical staff, works to identify malnourished children and give them the care they need to recover, which serves as a typical example of the ongoing humanitarian and health-focused initiatives undertaken by the IRCS in Afghanistan, the IRCS website reported.
Children’s growth and nutritional status are assessed using indicators such as height, weight, and mid-upper arm circumference. Subsequently, Relief International provides the required food supplies to the IRCS branch in Zaranj to be distributed among identified malnourished children.
According to international reports, malnutrition remains a critical challenge in Afghanistan; millions of children need nutritional support.
Benefactors support IRCS to boost health services in Afghanistan
With support from benefactors, the IRCS has enhanced health services for Afghans at its branch in Nimruz province, Afghanistan.
The development of charitable partnerships serves as a symbol of empathy, social responsibility, and the expansion of humanitarian cooperation, the IRCS website quoted Hamid-Reza Dehqan, an official with the IRCS, as saying in July.
Besides offering health services, the IRCS health facility plays an important role in reinforcing human ties, developing health-oriented cooperation, and alleviating human suffering, he added.
Benefactors’ contributions will help improve the quality of medical and diagnostic services, reflecting local community trust and support for the IRCS humanitarian measures.

Referring to the historical and cultural relationships between the two countries, Dehqan said any medical services provided to the people in this center are not merely a health measure but a manifestation of solidarity, compassion, and shared responsibility of the two nations in safeguarding human dignity. The expansion of humanitarian assistance will elevate health services and deepen friendly ties between Iran and Afghanistan.
IRCS is a key humanitarian actor
In November 2025, Hossam Elsharkawi, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), highlighted the role of the IRCS as one of the key humanitarian actors in the region and the world.
Lauding the IRCS's efforts, Elsharkawi congratulated Pirhossein Kolivand’s re-election as the head of the IRCS, saying that the IRCS makes highly effective decisions at international levels, IRNA reported.
The official made the remarks in an online meeting with Kolivand. During the meeting, the two officials discussed ways to foster collaborative efforts, develop rescue systems to enhance the country’s preparedness and response capabilities, and conduct international meetings and conferences in Iran.
The IRCS proposed hosting an international Islamic youth conference and a conference of leaders of national societies from Islamic countries.
The two sides also emphasized the need to implement the previously signed memoranda of understanding between the two organizations to lay the ground for promoting educational, operational, and logistic collaborations.
The IRCS also suggested introducing an expert to follow up on managerial and technical cooperation with the Regional Office for MENA.

Lebanese lawyer and lawmaker Melhem Khalaf told Anadolu that Razi and other Lebanese detainees retain the right to seek investigations, accountability and reparations for any violations suffered during detention.
Arbitrary detentions in Lebanon
Razi, born in 2005, disappeared on October 12 2025 after leaving his home in eastern Lebanon to exercise in a mountainous area. His motorcycle was later found and residents searched for him before it emerged that Israel was holding him.
Israel did not publicly announce charges against him or bring him before a court during his detention.
Lebanon’s National Human Rights Commission has documented other cases involving Lebanese civilians detained while working, fishing, tending livestock or returning to their villages after the ceasefire deal.

Violating the international law
Khalaf said civilian detainees in international armed conflicts are protected under the Fourth Geneva Convention, while those meeting the conditions for prisoner-of-war status are covered by the Third Geneva Convention.
He said detainees are entitled to protections including humane treatment, medical care and fair-trial safeguards, and that release does not remove their right to seek accountability or reparations.

Spanish PM says no 'solid proof' Morocco planned Ceuta migrant rush
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Thursday insisted there was no "solid proof" Morocco orchestrated July's migrant rush into Ceuta, after a police report alleged failings by Moroccan security forces.
However, Sanchez slammed "unacceptable" Moroccan government comments about Ceuta since the crisis began, in rare public criticism of neighbouring Rabat which claims the north African enclave.
More than 70,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta from Morocco on 30-31 July in an unprecedented surge that left scores dead, most by drowning as they tried to swim around a breakwater.
Spain's leftist government has consistently avoided blaming Morocco and has tried for years to improve their historically delicate relations -- notably over the status of Ceuta and Spain's other north African territory, Melilla.
But a Spanish police report seen by AFP on Wednesday flagged a Moroccan police response of "total permissiveness" that it said facilitated the rush, with some officers directing migrants towards the water.
Moroccan police numbers around the border post were "clearly smaller than usual" and officers "made no serious attempt" to stem the surge, said the report, based on satellite images, open-source videos and migrant testimonies.
Addressing parliament on Thursday to offer explanations about the crisis, Sanchez said no police, legal or international institutions had submitted "solid proof to the government of Spain that Morocco planned or executed the incident".
"If this solid proof existed, we would act accordingly," said Sanchez, who maintained that the government received no prior warning of the scale of the incident.
A few days after the influx, a Moroccan source close to the case denied to AFP any "relaxation" at the land border crossing.
The Moroccan interior ministry has blamed the sudden surge on the "malicious exploitation" of social media and the "spread of misleading information".
'Unacceptable' comments
Sanchez also slammed as "unacceptable" comments about Ceuta and Melilla by two Moroccan government ministers, revealing Spain summoned Morocco's ambassador on 21 August.
Moroccan media quoted Justice Minister Abdellatif Ouahbi in August as saying Rabat had "historic" and "geographical" rights over Ceuta and Melilla, calling for a "final solution" that would allow the territories to "return to the fold of the motherland".
Ceuta and Melilla will remain Spanish "until the end of time", Sanchez told parliament on Thursday.
The conservative and far-right opposition has consistently questioned Morocco's role and accuses Sanchez of subservience to Rabat.
The leader of the main opposition right-wing Popular Party, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, rubbished Sanchez's explanations and demanded his resignation "for incompetence" or "complicity" after "a possible act of hybrid warfare".
Some analysts have suggested Morocco used the migrant rush to exert political pressure on Spain after Sanchez visited Rabat's historic enemy Algeria in July.
The disputed Western Sahara is a source of tension, with Morocco largely controlling the former Spanish colony that is claimed by the Algerian-backed pro-independence Polisario Front.
King to visit?
Sanchez revealed the government had urged King Felipe VI to travel to Ceuta and Melilla "in the coming weeks", in rare public comments about royal matters that could inflame relations with Morocco.
The last trip by a Spanish monarch to the cities in 2007 sparked a diplomatic crisis.
Although most of the migrants who streamed into Ceuta have returned to Morocco, thousands continue to roam the small city's streets and sleep rough, increasing tensions among locals who feel abandoned.
Tens of thousands of people protested across Spain on Wednesday in solidarity with Ceuta and to criticise the government's handling of the crisis.
"Ceuta needs to be supported by the state more than ever," Sanchez said in justification of his plea to the king.
But he later denied having "the slightest intention of triggering a diplomatic conflict" with Morocco.

Egyptian poet Qaradawi receives UAE presidential pardon days after 10-year prison sentence
UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on Friday issued a presidential pardon for Egyptian-Turkish poet Abdul Rahman Yusuf al-Qaradawi, days after he was sentenced to ten years in prison and fined 200,000 dirhams in a case before the Abu Dhabi Federal Court of Appeal, the Cybercrime Department.
The Emirates News Agency said that on August 27, the Abu Dhabi Federal Court of Appeal had ruled to convict al-Qaradawi "for the crimes attributed to him". Emirati authorities did not clarify in their statement the nature of the crimes of which al-Qaradawi was convicted or whether the pardon also includes a fine. The Emirati system allows the head of state to grant pardons for the execution of penalties issued by the federal judiciary.
Al-Qaradawi's case dates back to late 2024, when he was arrested by Lebanese authorities upon his return from Syria, with requests and arrest warrants issued against him by Egypt and the UAE.
During a visit to Damascus, al-Qaradawi had posted a video criticising authorities in Egypt, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia. In January 2025, Lebanese authorities decided to extradite him to the UAE.
Al-Qaradawi, who was born in 1970, is a poet with dual Egyptian and Turkish citizenship, and is the son of the late preacher Yusuf al-Qaradawi. The Egyptian judiciary also sentenced him in absentia in 2017 to five years in prison in a case that included accusations of spreading false news.
His arrest and extradition to the UAE sparked widespread criticism, with Amnesty International calling on Lebanese authorities not to extradite him to Egypt or the UAE, warning of the risk of persecution and ill-treatment. Human Rights Watch also said that during his arrest and extradition he was denied regular access to his family and lawyer.
The case has also sparked UN action, with the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights noting that in January 2025, UN special procedures experts expressed concerns that al-Qaradawi, if extradited, could be subjected to torture or ill-treatment, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearance, and violation of fair trial guarantees.
The Emirati pardon comes at the end of a judicial and security process that lasted nearly two years, beginning with al-Qaradawi's arrest in Lebanon.

Weeks after mass abduction, Nigerian families seek news from kidnappers, action from government
KANO, Nigeria, Sept 4 - Two weeks after gunmen raided the northwestern Nigerian village of Dekera, killing dozens and kidnapping hundreds, residents and family members say they have heard nothing from the kidnappers and seen little action from the government.
Mass kidnappings for ransom are relatively common across much of northern Nigeria, but the coordinated August 22 attack on communities in north-central Niger state was one of the biggest in recent years, underscoring the extent of insecurity as the country heads towards an election next year.
"We haven't heard anything from the kidnappers since the abduction," Isa Zaki, a Dekera resident with 10 members of his extended family among those seized, told Reuters by telephone.
Zaki said years of insecurity had already resulted in local schools and markets closing, but residents were increasingly desperate after the August attack, which he said had killed dozens and resulted in much of Dekera being burned.
"People have fled, soldiers have taken over the town, houses have been burnt, there is nowhere to live, and it is raining," he said. "It's been sadness over sadness since the abduction."
"NO ONE IS TELLING US ANYTHING"
Residents say about 600 people, mostly women, children and older people, were abducted in Dekera and nearby Gidan-Zana and Sabon Gida communities in the raid. At least 40 residents were also killed, they said.
Authorities have not commented on the number of hostages or deaths, but President Bola Tinubu has ordered security agencies to rescue the hostages.
"We have no update yet. When we have, we will share accordingly," said Wasiu Abiodun, Niger state police spokesperson.
Civil servant Habibu Salihu said his sister gave birth a week before she, her husband and three children, including the newborn, were kidnapped.
Salihu said seven other family members were killed and he saw his sister breastfeeding her child in a video of hostages released by the kidnappers soon after the attack, but has had no news since then.
"We have no information on what is going on. No one is telling us anything and we have no idea what action the government is taking to rescue the hostages," he said.
'OUR HOUSES ARE NOTHING BUT ASHES'
No group has claimed responsibility yet, but analysts suspect a breakaway sect in the area of the Islamist militant group Boko Haram, which usually operates in north-eastern Nigeria, was involved.
Local authorities in north-eastern Benin have confirmed a number of people fled into the country after the incident but they gave no details on numbers.
Residents say the deployment of soldiers has brought some relief, but families are still homeless and growing increasingly hungry.
"Our town has been burnt," said Aminu Inuwa, who lost two brothers in the raid. "I have only one shirt, no food to eat, nothing else and our houses are nothing but ashes." REUTERS

Cockroach Jolt Opens Up Opposition Space for Mocking Modi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:05:00 UTC
20:05:00 KST

No great movement designed to change the world (or a nation) can bear being laughed at or belittled, argued Czech-French novelist Milan Kundera in his 1967 novel, “The Joke.”
“Mockery is a rust that corrodes all it touches,” he wrote.
In the summer of 2026, a satirical protest movement calling itself the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) — a wry play on India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) — did something few observers thought possible in Narendra Modi’s India: it made mockery of the prime minister feel normal.
The movement was born out of the mockery of a remark by the chief justice of India and quickly resonated with youth anger over recruitment and examination controversies. Examination paper leaks became a rallying point. Demonstrators adopted the cockroach as their emblem — a creature that has survived fumigation, starvation, and every known odds.
During agitations in the national capital, young protestors carried posters with caricatures of Modi, performed skits mimicking Modi’s mannerisms, and chanted slogans laced with profanity directed at the prime minister. Videos of these performances spread rapidly across Instagram, X and WhatsApp.
Modi has been ruling the country with tight control since 2014. His government does not respond well to dissent and criticism. Satirists and stand-up comedians have had an increasingly tough time in Modi’s India. Cracking jokes at ruling party politicians, or anything even obliquely related to the Hindu faith and practices, can lead to court cases or mob violence.
Kundera’s larger insight was that authoritarian structures rely on total obedience, absolute gravity, and a carefully manufactured image of infallibility. Jokes, satire and parodies of state propaganda weaken the regime’s psychological control. But once the powerful become objects of collective laughter, their aura of inevitability can begin to crack.
In India, July 2026 unleashed waves of mockery. A chant that emerged from the demonstrations — “Chhappan inch ka chhota bandar” (the 56-inch little monkey) answered by the crowd’s refrain of “Baal Narendra, Baal Narendra” (little Narendra) — went viral as a direct jab at Modi.
The slogan drew on two long-running political references. During his 2014 campaign, Modi famously invoked his “56-inch chest” as a symbol of strength. Around the same time, an illustrated children’s book titled “Bal Narendra,” based on stories from his childhood, hit markets. Protesters fused the two into a mocking refrain that soon appeared in graffiti and memes depicting a “56-inch-high monkey.”
When Modi first appeared in a midnight address on social media on July 23 to break his silence on the protests, that too triggered a wave of reels and memes — some making fun of his camera angles, others mocking the content of his speech.
Modi was visibly unnerved when he appeared in another video at midnight on July 31. In the address, he said he was forgiving “misguided children” who had abused him and his late mother, while expressing concern that girls and young women were using abusive language. It was a “cultural shock,” he said. This speech, too, faced a wave of meme attacks.
The BJP ecosystem was in no way ready to take these attacks like sitting ducks. After the protests were called off, allegations of police action and harassment against participants emerged. Police cases were registered in several states. BJP social media functionaries circulated videos seeking to identify participants. Opposition parties and civil liberties groups described these actions as intimidation, while BJP leaders argued they were responding to abusive and unlawful conduct.
One such student is a 15-year-old identified in press reports by the pseudonym Ruchika Singh, whose abusive slogan against Modi went viral during the protests. She was named in a police case. A day after Modi’s speech promising forgiveness, Singh appeared in a video with folded hands apologizing “from the heart.” She said she had been swept up by the crowd and insisted she was not under pressure. She described it as her “first and last mistake.”
The apology did not end the episode. Singh’s mother told reporters that police officers, television crews and aggressive strangers showed up daily at their rented accommodation. This eventually forced the family to leave the city altogether.
But the courage of India’s youth had emboldened the political opposition by then. By mid-August, senior Congress leader and former Chhattisgarh Chief Minister Bhupesh Baghel was using the “56-inch ka chhota bandar” slogan in his rallies. The chant also entered parliament. Congress MP Pawan Khera held up a toy monkey and chanted “Chhappan inch ka chhota bandar, kabhi to aao Sadan ke andar” (56-inch little monkey, come inside the House at least sometimes), mocking Modi’s limited attendance during the recent monsoon session of parliament.
At the end of August, another video went viral. Here, Singh says she has had enough. She had apologized under pressure, but what she has endured since then has erased her fears. “Mr. Modi, you have made my life hell… you’re a coward,” she said in the latest video. Whatever she had previously is all gone, she said. She can neither go anywhere nor live freely. She has nothing more to lose. “I won’t back down this time,” Singh asserted.
Opposition parties shared this video from their social media platforms, criticizing the government’s response to dissent. Meanwhile, in a major victory for the CJP, the Supreme Court on September 2 quashed all police complaints against student protesters in different states.
Whether this will have any lasting impact remains to be seen. The cockroach movement has, nevertheless, demonstrated that satire aimed at Modi’s carefully constructed image of invincibility could travel, resonate, and survive an extensive state and party communication apparatus.
Even if briefly, it has expanded the social space in which publicly mocking India’s most powerful political leader became less exceptional.
